name: Washington State Standard
title: Democrat pulls ahead in tight Washington House race
description: Democrats could now gain 10 seats in the Washington state House as a Republican incumbent fell behind Thursday, over a week after ballot tallying began. Rep. Cyndy Jacobsen, R-Puyallup, was up by 109 votes when the first batch of ballots dropped on election night. But Democrat Jenn Marie Strickling jumped ahead of Jacobsen for the […]
text:
Rep. Cyndy Jacobsen, left, and Jenn Marie Strickling. (Photos courtesy of the Washington Legislature and the Strickling campaign)Democrats could now gain 10 seats in the Washington state House as a Republican incumbent fell behind Thursday, over a week after ballot tallying began.
Rep. Cyndy Jacobsen, R-Puyallup, was up by 109 votes when the first batch of ballots dropped on election night. But Democrat Jenn Marie Strickling jumped ahead of Jacobsen for the first time on Thursday by 82 votes. 
Strickling has 28,480 votes to Jacobsen’s 28,398. Going into Thursday’s ballot drop, Strickling had trailed by four votes.
The counting will likely continue up until the election is set to be certified Nov. 23, as the campaigns and election officials seek to reach voters with mismatched or missing signatures who need to cure their ballots so they can be counted. More votes are expected to be counted Tuesday.
“We’re going to continue being patient while every single vote is counted over the next few weeks,” Strickling wrote on Facebook after the latest vote tally.
Pierce County election officials report having 350 votes left to count, spread across several legislative districts. Generally, the 25th District, which covers Puyallup, accounts for 16% of the county’s votes, said Pierce County Elections Manager Kyle Haugh. The 350 figure doesn’t account for ballots that haven’t been received yet, like those put in drop boxes in other counties that need to be mailed to Pierce County.
“I think there’s still a statistical chance to come out on top, we’ll keep working,” Jacobsen said in an interview Thursday.
As of Thursday afternoon, 280 ballots were being challenged in the 25th District due to signature issues that could be cured, Haugh said. There have been 36 write-in votes so far.
Given the current totals, the election is likely headed for a recount.
A machine recount is required if the difference between two candidates is under 0.5% of the total ballots cast and fewer than 2,000 votes. To trigger a manual recount, candidates have to be separated by fewer than 150 votes and 0.25% of the total votes. Recounts rarely flip election outcomes.
Going into the election, Democrats held 59 of the House’s seats, compared to 39 for Republicans. Democrats will take a two-thirds supermajority in the chamber, and if Strickling wins, could get up to 69 seats. 
Jacobsen’s seatmate in the 25th is among the casualties. Republican Rep. Michael Keaton will lose to David Berg, a Democrat who serves on the Puyallup school board. Keaton currently trails by nearly 1,000 votes.
Jacobsen has been in office for three terms. She won her previous races by 5% in 2020, 15.5% in 2022 and 11.5% in 2024. 
Jacobsen is blaming her underperformance on the national politics that has turned people away from Republicans, as seen in races all across the country.

“Ultimately, we didn’t get our message out,” Jacobsen said. “I think that the national environment caused people to make decisions nationally and not think about their local elections.”
She is no stranger to a close race. She won her first campaign for Puyallup City Council by 13 votes, but that amounted to more than one-half of a percentage point in an election with fewer than 2,600 ballots counted.
Jacobsen is known for having a large family, with 20 grandchildren. If they were all old enough, their votes could’ve helped. She says some of her children’s families’ have left the Puyallup area and Washington due to state policies.

Alabama Supreme Court Justice Greg Cook listens to Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey deliver the State of the State address in the Old House Chamber at the Alabama State Capitol on Feb. 4, 2025 in Montgomery, Alabama. The U.S. Senate on Thursday confirmed Cook to be the U.S. District Court Judge for the Northern District of Alabama. (Will McClelland for Alabama Reflector)The U.S. Senate on Thursday confirmed Alabama Supreme Court Justice Greg Cook to be the U.S. District Court Judge for the Northern District of Alabama.
The upper chamber confirmed the associate justice along party lines 49-27. He was nominated by President Donald Trump in June at the recommendation of U.S. Sens. Katie Britt and Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala. 
Before the vote, Britt commended Cook’s service on the Supreme Court. He was elected in 2022 after a career at Balch & Bingham, LLP.

“Greg wrote the Alabama Civil Procedure Rules of Civil Procedure book, which is quite thick. Greg would take it out around as he talked to what he would hope to be the people he was able to serve on the Alabama Supreme Court, the citizens of the great state of Alabama,” she said. “He would always tell them the one thing that they could count on from him is not only his tireless hard work, but that he would be boring and predictable. What he meant by that was he was going to follow the law.”
Cook recused himself in now-Gov.-elect Tuberville’s Supreme Court case that challenged the then-candidate’s qualifications to be governor. 
In a social media post, Tuberville congratulated Cook.
His nomination leaves his seat vacant on the Alabama Supreme Court. Gov. Kay Ivey will nominate a replacement. Ivey also congratulated Cook in a social media post. 
“Governor Ivey is prepared to make an appointment to the Alabama Supreme Court. As we await the president’s signature on Greg Cook’s judicial commission, we anticipate being able to make an announcement soon,” said Gina Maiola, a spokesperson for Ivey, in a statement Thursday evening.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Independent Fiscal Office warns Pa.’s structural deficit could balloon if no action taken
description: Democrats in Harrisburg could face tough decisions ahead of their first budget negotiations with majorities in both chambers of the general assembly.
text:
Gov. Josh Shapiro shakes hands with House Appropriations Committee Chairman Jordan Harris after signing the 2026-27 FY budget (D-Philadelphia) after signing the 2026-2027 state budget as members of the General Assembly watch Sunday, July 12, 2026. (Photo by Ian Karbal/Capital-Star)The commonwealth’s structural deficit could exceed $7 billion by 2030 unless state lawmakers can cut spending or find new sources of reliable revenue, according to a new report from the Independent Fiscal Office. That’s up from more than $4.5 billion in the last fiscal year.
The structural deficit is a measure of how much more money the state is spending than it’s bringing in.
While lawmakers have found ways to balance recent budgets, next year, Democrats in Harrisburg could face tough decisions ahead of their first budget negotiations with majorities in both chambers of the general assembly.
“Permanent policy changes need to be enacted,” IFO Director Matthew Knittel said during a presentation of the office’s findings Thursday. “Especially if the Rainy Day Fund is to be maintained.”
Spokespeople for Gov. Josh Shapiro and Democratic leaders in the House and Senate did not respond to requests for comment. Neither did spokespeople for the Republican caucuses’ leaders.
Here are some of the topline takeaways from the IFO’s latest annual budget outlook report.
Temporary bandaids may no longer cut it
While some temporary measures have helped to balance past budgets on paper, the IFO warns that lawmakers may be running out of wiggle room.
For example, during negotiations earlier this year, lawmakers agreed to balance the most recent state budget using an accounting trick called a “cycle roll.” 
Two months of payments to managed care organizations that provide services for Medicaid patients were delayed into the next budget cycle. At least on paper, that brought down the state’s projected spending in relation to its revenue by $2.6 billion.
Lawmakers can continue making those monthly payments on that delayed schedule, but they won’t be able to claim the same savings in the future.
Residual COVID-19 funds have also helped to balance recent budgets, but Knittel warned that well has likely run dry.
“At this point, we think those are largely used up, as are most of the larger one-time measures that can be used,” he said. “For that reason we do think that permanent revenue changes or spending changes are needed to address the structural deficit.”
IFO expects booming economic growth to ease, demographic changes to rack up costs
A booming stock market, driven in large part by tech and artificial intelligence companies, has been a boon to the state’s revenues. Corporate profits have been high for the last three years, allowing the state’s corporate net income tax collections to beat estimates.
But the IFO, while it isn’t projecting a recession, is predicting that those gains will level out.
“Right now, an important question is, ‘are those revenues permanent going forward, since much of it was driven by one sector of the economy?’” Knittel said. “Currently, we are treating them as permanent, however we do have a modest slowdown built in for next calendar year.”
There was also a large boost to corporate net income tax revenues during this budget cycle due to taxable tariff refunds, netting the state around $230 million.
Demographic changes also present a challenge. Pennsylvania’s population is getting older. The IFO predicts that retirees will make up a greater portion of the population, while the school-age and working-age cohorts shrink.
That can mean increased spending on services like healthcare.
The risks of relying on cannabis and skill games to close the gap
For the last several years, Republicans have blocked Democratic efforts to tax and legalize marijuana and skill games. In his last budget, Shapiro estimated those efforts could bring in $2 billion annually.
With majorities in both chambers of the general assembly, Democrats may finally be able to make those policies reality. But the IFO is warning lawmakers not to rely on projections of how much they will earn the state to balance their budget.
”The downside of these estimates is there’s a lot of uncertainty and variability associated with them,” Knittel said. “One reason for that is that oftentimes we have little or no data.”
As an example, he pointed to how a 2013 law legalizing small games of chance or “tavern games” in some establishments was estimated to bring in around $156 million annually, but actual collections in the latest year were a mere $1 million.
In lieu of relying solely on these projections, the IFO has recommended lawmakers budget estimated revenues from more predictable sources, like 0.5% increases to the personal income tax or sales tax. Those could be quickly implemented if projected revenue from new sources falls short.
But that could be a hard pill to swallow, as lawmakers in both parties have said they’d like to lower taxes.
And Democrats have long been averse to cutting spending on services like education and healthcare.
There are other taxes Democrats have proposed increasing, which target corporations.
Earlier this year, some Democrats pushed to implement a 5% gross receipts tax on digital advertising platforms, targeting big tech companies like Meta and Google. The proposal was estimated at the time to bring in as much as $500 million.
And Shapiro has proposed a change to corporate tax policy that require what’s called “combined reporting,” meaning parent companies and their subsidiaries would have to file their taxes like a collective organization. The goal is to close what’s known as the “Delaware loophole” that allows companies to shift profits to related businesses in other states.
Shapiro’s office projected the measure could net the state up to $1.1 billion annually.
Keeping the rainy day fund for a rainy day
In the past, Shapiro has called for transferring money from the state’s rainy day fund to cover deficit spending. But the IFO says lawmakers should hold onto that money for a crisis, instead of using it to cover recurring expenditures.
Pennsylvania’s rainy day fund currently has around $8 billion.
A Pew Charitable Trusts report found that leaving rainy day funds intact can help states navigate downturns and emergencies like recessions. (As a note of disclosure, the Pennsylvania Capital-Star is part of the States Newsroom network, which has received funding from the Pew Charitable Trusts.) It’s also a finite account, meaning that the funds can only close a deficit gap for so long.
The IFO has been warning about Pennsylvania’s structural deficit for years, but so far the state has managed to stay afloat and keep its budgets balanced, even improving its credit rating, according to Moody’s, in 2024.
Knittel says he’s often asked about this, and what’s different now.
“The difference is the deficits are real, and they’re large,” he said, noting that recent boons like COVID-19 funds or tobacco settlement money have helped to stabilize past budgets. “But right now, as we discussed, the one time transfers and the delays and shifts have been largely used up … and the general fund surplus is exhausted. So this time it is different, and we do feel that permanent changes will be required.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Blue Ribbon Commission on education settles on key policy ideas
description: Recommendations include changes to CT's  Education Cost Sharing grant, special education funding and stronger accountability mechanisms.
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont’s Blue Ribbon Commission on K-12 Education Funding and Accountability has largely settled on a list of policies around which to shape its final report, due Jan. 15.
The recommendations include changes to Connecticut’s main school funding formula, the Education Cost Sharing or ECS grant; restructuring special education funding, including the SEED grant; strengthening Regional Educational Service Centers to promote greater inter-district collaboration; and stronger state accountability mechanisms for academic and fiscal performance. More details, including concrete dollar amounts, will be determined in December.
Commission members reviewed the full list Thursday. After a break for small group discussions, members appeared generally satisfied with what they had in front of them — though several noted that, without firm dollar amounts, there was still a great deal of uncertainty.
“I think, fundamentally, we’re OK with where we are,” Windsor Board of Education Vice President Leonard Lockhart said.
New Haven Mayor Justin Elicker expressed concern about the commission’s timeline vis-a-vis the governor’s budget proposal, which is due at the start of the session. 
“A concern that I’ve heard from a number of people is that we come up with the recommendations and it’s too late, because the [Lamont] administration’s already put together a package,” Elicker said.
Natalie Wagner, the chair of the commission and Lamont’s deputy chief of staff, reassured him that the budget proposal was already taking the commission’s work into account.
“That process is going on very much informed by the work of this commission,” Wagner said.
Key takeaways
The commission is considering several changes to the ECS grant in the hope of making it more effective and more resilient over time.
The current ECS grant has a number of problems. The most glaring is the foundation amount — ostensibly what it costs to educate one student. The whole formula is based on that number, but it has been stuck at $11,525 since 2013 and has not been adjusted for inflation. If it had, the number would be over $16,000 — that’s a difference of hundreds of millions of dollars annually schools could be receiving from the state.
Another problem is how the grant handles enrollment declines. Per the formula, districts with declining enrollment should get less ECS money. In practice, however, the state has held those districts harmless year over year, with the result that many are now considered overfunded. The term is potentially misleading; many “overfunded” schools get much less money than they would have if ECS had been rising with inflation this whole time and are struggling financially.
Increasing the ECS foundation amount is one of the policy ideas the commission is advancing, though it will not determine the amount until December. It is also advancing tying ECS to inflation, updating weights in the formula for certain groups of students and ensuring choice schools receive similar increases.
The commission is also advancing changes to how enrollment declines are handled. That includes basing ECS on a three-year enrollment average to limit the shock of yearly declines, as well as phasing districts out of hold-harmless as the rising foundation amount lifts them over their current funding level.
Education Committee co-Chair Rep. Jennifer Leeper, D-Fairfield, told her fellow commission members she expects that last point to be a tough sell.
“I think just realistically, politically, that will be really a nonstarter for a lot of folks. Even if we’re gonna say that likely won’t happen until year 10,” Leeper said.
Raising the foundation amount may not be easy, either. Even a relatively modest boost will quickly run up hundreds of millions of dollars in additional costs for the state budget. Lamont, who does not sit on the commission himself, has signaled he does not like the idea of raising the income tax to pay for that.
University of Connecticut education professor Casey Cobb pointed out the state still lacks an empirical basis for determining what the foundation amount should actually be — in other words, it doesn’t know how much it actually costs to educate a student. He also suggested the state should conduct a regular adequacy study to confirm the foundation amount remains accurate.
The commission is also advancing the idea of increasing the SEED grant, which legislators created in 2025 to direct state dollars into in-district special education programming. It is currently funded at $30 million; fully funded, it would distribute about $180 million annually. 
The commission also wants to expand what SEED money can be used for so that the state’s six Regional Educational Service Centers (RESCs) and other state-approved vendors can access it.
Commission members are advancing a number of ideas to expand the role RESCs play in meeting Connecticut’s education goals. Those include expanding RESC capacity and expertise to deliver on state priorities (for example, expanding special education services) and staffing RESCs with fiscal advisors or business managers to help districts manage their finances. The expansion would come with new progress reporting and other accountability mechanisms.
The commission also discussed reconfiguring Connecticut’s fiscal accountability systems. Many states require districts to submit multiyear budget projections to a state office annually, but Connecticut does not (though a recent law did require districts to share some budget information locally). Also common outside of Connecticut: a formal tiered system of support and oversight when problems pop up. 
The overall goal is to make it easier to catch problems and intervene early, before schools are in crisis — ideally preventing a repeat of what is currently happening with the Hartford and Bridgeport school districts.
Elicker flagged some potential concerns.
“That assumes adequate state funding, correct?” he asked. “Because if the state doesn’t adequately fund, and then says, ‘Ah, but we need to hold you accountable, you have financial problems,’ I think that’s, you know, a tough thing to swallow.”
He also noted that some districts can’t get adequate funding on the local side — for example, because voters turn down a referendum. 
Wagner said it would be important to ensure the new oversight system doesn’t worsen tensions between municipalities and schools. 
“Because of that specific relationship in Connecticut, that might look very different than some of these other states,” she said.
Most other states give districts themselves taxing authority, but Connecticut does not.
As commission members offered their closing thoughts, Middletown Superintendent Joseph Macary identified which items he said have his full, unequivocal support: raising the ECS foundation, indexing it to inflation, increasing the weight for poverty, fully funding and removing restrictions on SEED and maintaining hold harmless until a district’s ECS funding lifts it over.
“I think these five are … this is how we need to go forward to make a win for us, to help kids,” Macary said.
Several other commission members voiced their agreement.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Appeals court: Federal judge must reconsider whether ‘buffer law’ is in effect during media lawsuit
description: A federal judge in Nashville who decided against blocking Tennessee’s “buffer law” must reconsider while a coalition of media organizations challenge its constitutionality, an appeals court ruled Tuesday. Tennessee’s General Assembly passed the law in May 2025, allowing law enforcement to order members of the public, including media, to stay 25 feet away fro[...]
text:
The Fred D. Thompson U.S. Courthouse and Federal Building in Nashville, TN. (Photo John Partipilo)
A federal judge in Nashville who decided against blocking Tennessee’s “buffer law” must reconsider while a coalition of media organizations challenge its constitutionality, an appeals court ruled Tuesday.
Tennessee’s General Assembly passed the law in May 2025, allowing law enforcement to order members of the public, including media, to stay 25 feet away from crime scenes, traffic stops and any “ongoing and immediate threat to public safety.” Violators can be charged with a misdemeanor.
A coalition of media organizations — including the Tennessee Lookout, the Nashville Banner, Gannett, Scripps Media and TEGNA — sued later that month, arguing the law is vague and prevents newsgathering, violating the First Amendment. The plaintiffs, represented by Paul McAdoo and Grayson Clary of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, asked the court to block the law’s enforcement.
U.S. District Judge William Campbell Jr., who was appointed by President Donald Trump in 2018, ruled in February that the law would remain in effect while the lawsuit moves forward.
Memphis task force using TN ‘buffer law,’ preventing up-close recording of police activity

Campbell stated the plaintiffs had not shown a particular situation where the law “impacted a reporter or anyone” and so failed to show how the law’s continued enforcement would cause irreparable harm.
A three-judge panel in the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found Tuesday that Campbell failed to consider whether the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their claim, “the most important (factor) in First Amendment cases.”
The panel also found that the media organizations have standing to sue at this stage because “their reporters routinely face a choice between defying a direct order of a police officer — with an attendant threat of criminal punishment for the reporters and their employers alike — or ceasing activity protected by the First Amendment.”
Chief Judge Raymond M. Kethledge, a Bush appointee, Senior Judge R. Guy Cole, Jr., a Clinton appointee, and Judge Andre B. Mathis, a Biden appointee, served on the panel.
The injunction request now returns to Campbell’s court for further consideration.
The buffer law has been invoked on multiple occasions by the Memphis Safe Task Force, a group of federal and state agencies formed by Trump. Task Force officers used the law to order observers to back away from traffic stops and arrests, keeping task force activities in public spaces out of view, according to a separate lawsuit filed by the ACLU of Tennessee on behalf of four observers.
Lebanon Republican Sen. Mark Pody sponsored the legislation and said during the legislative session that it was intended to protect the work of law enforcement. 
Similar laws in Indiana and Louisiana were struck down for giving police overly broad discretion after lawsuits from the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press. 
Adam Friedman and Anita Wadhwani contributed to this report.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Governor seeks more tax cuts in budget priorities
description: Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte said Thursday the biennial budget proposal he will submit to the 2027 Legislature will include additional income tax cuts and  investments in education and the state’s fiscal stability. Holding a press conference at the state Capitol at the start of his final two-year budget in the executive office, Gianforte emphasized the […]
text:
Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte delivers the State of the State address before a joint session of the Montana Legislature on Jan. 13, 2025. (Micah Drew/ Daily Montanan)Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte said Thursday the biennial budget proposal he will submit to the 2027 Legislature will include additional income tax cuts and  investments in education and the state’s fiscal stability.
Holding a press conference at the state Capitol at the start of his final two-year budget in the executive office, Gianforte emphasized the work he’d done for Montana during his six years in office. 
He was elected twice to the governorship on a platform of getting government “off the backs of hardworking Montanans” by cutting regulatory “red tape” and taxes, stewarding tax dollars, promoting individual freedoms, and backing law enforcement. 
“The budget I’m presenting this morning is about one thing: Realizing the ‘Montana Comeback,’ and knowing that at the end of my term, we will have left Montana in better shape than when we found it,” Gianforte said. 
Outlining a budget he says underpaces inflationary growth, Gianforte began with a principle he’s held every day in office: “this money belongs to the people of Montana, not the government, and you know how to spend your hard-earned money better than the government does.”
A primary pillar of Gianforte’s budget proposal is to move Montana to a flat income tax so that every Montana would pay the same 4.7% rate, and increase the earned-income tax credit from 20% to 30% of the federal credit. 
Gianforte has sought to decrease income tax rates every biennium, and has succeeded in simplifying the state’ income tax brackets from seven to two, and cut the top tax rate from 6.9% to 5.4%. 
“Now we need to finish the job. Thanks to our strong budget reserves, Montana is able to move to a flat income tax rate,” Gianforte said. “A flat tax is a fair tax. If you make more, you pay more. If you make less, you pay less. It’s that simple.”
While Republican leadership in the state Senate have backed the governor’s proposed flat tax, it will face united opposition from Democrats, who are in the minority in both chambers. 
“The governor’s proposed flat tax does absolutely nothing for 80% of Montanans. For your average working Montanan, they will get literally not a dime,” said House Minority Leader-elect SJ Howell on Wednesday. “Instead, what the flat tax does is it says, ‘Let’s take $100 million a year and give it to the four or five thousand richest households in the state. That is not what Montana voters want.”
Under current tax law, in 2027 the move from the 4.7% and 5.4% tax rate kicks in for single filers after their first $65,000, and for joint filers after their first $130,000. 
Gianforte is also proposing to raise the business equipment tax exemption from $1 million to $3 million. When he took office, the exemption was set at $100,000. 
“Restaurants had to count every fork, knife and spoon to see if their inventory added up to be taxed,” he said, adding that the changes had saved “over 5,000 small businesses from this nuisance.”
Another major part of the budget to realize what the governor has repeatedly termed “Montana’s Comeback” is the addition of a one-time investment of $300 million to the budget stabilization fund, bringing it to a record $900 million. 
“That’s money set aside to protect taxpayers, essential services, and underscores our ability to further reduce income taxes,” he told reporters. 
Gianforte said that putting aside money for a rainy day is important  for future economic downturns when state revenues might see drastic dropoffs. 
“We don’t want to be in a position where we can’t fulfill essential services,” he said. “Fortunately, today we have a very strong economy and revenues. That’s why we can make the investments that we’re making.”
The governor outlined a series of additional one-time investments into education programs including $13 million in the school facilities trust and $1 million in incentives for schools to adopt cellphone-free policies.
“The ‘Montana Comeback’ can only last if we continue to support students, parents, and teachers. Every Montana student deserves a great education, and this budget keeps that commitment by fully funding public education, keeping that promise for the next generation,” Gianforte said, adding that his administration had heard “loud and clear” from educators and administrators that schools need maintenance investments.
He has also made it clear in previous years that he would like to see a way to keep cell phones out of classrooms to eliminate distractions to students and help with mental health problems buoyed by social media. 
The governor’s budget also proposes increasing the Big Sky Scholarship program to $24 million. The program offers tax credits for public and private education programs, allowing more lower- and middle-income families to consider school-choice options for their kids. 
Additional one-time funding proposals the governor highlighted include $125 million in the state highways trust; $100 million for county roads and bridges; and $40 million in emergency services and victims shelters; and $45 million for state employees. That includes $14 million in one-time bonuses for state employees. 
The investments in state and county roads, the governor said, are all tied to federal matching programs which would allow the state investment to leverage up to seven times as much investment, and the investment in state highways trust would stave off a need to raise the state’s gas tax. 
“We’ve come a long way, but there’s more to do,” Gianforte said. “We’ll keep cutting red tape that holds back Montana businesses and workers. We’ll act on the recommendations of our energy and licensing task forces so that Montanans have affordable, reliable energy, and so that workers can get to working without needless barriers. We’ll let hardworking Montanans keep more of what they earn, and will keep Montana the best place to live, work, and raise a family.”
The governor’s full budget will be released on Monday. The following are highlights from Gianforte’s 2029 biennium budget proposal:

Reduce the state’s top income tax rate from 5.49% to 4.9% — a flat rate
Raise the business equipment tax exemption from $1 million to $3 million
Invest $25 million in the Behavioral Health Systems for the Future Generations Fund
Invest $5 million to expand shelter capacity for victims of human trafficking and violent crime
invest $10 million in local 911 emergency systems
Allocate $30 million to the state health plan
Allocate $14 million for one-time bonuses for state employees
Raise the cap on the Big Sky Scholarship to $24 million
Allocate $1 million in cell-phone free policy incentives
Invest $13 million in school facilities trust
$100 million in one-time funding for county roads and bridges
$125 million in one-time funding for state highway trust

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana’s improves ranking with conservative Tax Foundation
description: Since Gov. Jeff Landry took office in 2024, Louisiana has jumped 17 spots on the business friendly Tax Foundation’s state competitiveness index.
text:
The Tax Foundation has improved Louisiana's ranking on its tax structure competitiveness index for 2027. (Photo by Wesley Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)Since Gov. Jeff Landry took office in 2024, Louisiana has jumped 17 spots on the business friendly Tax Foundation’s state competitiveness index. Republican elected officials say the group’s rankings are a factor in where major corporations are willing to locate their facilities and offices. 

The state ranked 40th in overall tax structure competitiveness in 2024 and will be ranked 23rd in 2027, according to the latest Tax Foundation report. The improvement is largely attributed to a tax law overhaul that Landry, a Republican, pushed three years ago. 

In 2024, Landry and legislators lowered the state’s personal and business income tax rates and permanently eliminated Louisiana’s corporate franchise tax. As a result, Louisiana’s corporate tax ranking moved from 29th to tenth, and its individual income tax ranking moved from 27th to ninth, according to the Tax Foundation. 
In order to offset the decreased business and income tax collections, Landry and lawmakers raised the state sales tax rate from 4.45% to 5%. This contributed to Louisiana having the highest average combined state and local sales tax rate of 10.13%, according to the Tax Foundation. It ranked the state’s sales tax structure almost dead last at 49th. 
The organization said Louisiana would have an easier time lowering its sales tax rate if it applied the levy to a wider range to more services. The Landry administration attempted to extend the sales tax to a new range of services — lawn care and hair services, among others — in 2024, but legislators refused and opted for a higher rate instead. 
A high sales tax rate creates more of a burden for low-income people than higher income tax or business tax rates. Progressive groups, such as Invest in Louisiana, have been critical of the elected officials shifting the tax burden from income and business taxes to sales taxes. 

When compared to adjoining states, Louisiana has a better Tax Foundation ranking than Arkansas (32nd) and Mississippi (27th), but it remains well behind Texas (fifth).SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE

text:
Colorado Gov. Jared Polis speaks in his office at the Capitol in Denver before signing the 2026 budget bill. (Photo by Sara Wilson/Colorado Newsline)Colorado Gov. Jared Polis on Friday granted 27 pardons to people convicted of various crimes in the state over the last several decades. 
One of those pardons went to Vanessa Peoples, who police charged with reckless endangerment in 2017 after her 2-year-old briefly wandered away from a family picnic. Her story has been cited in criticism of the child welfare system. 
Peoples, who also received a settlement from Aurora police over the use of excessive force during her arrest, struggled to find a job because of her conviction. She has since earned a nursing certificate from Emily Griffith Technical College, and her loved ones said her strength, work ethic, perseverance and determination have carried her “through extraordinary adversity.”  
“You have found the courage to speak out about your experiences and advocate for justice, bringing national attention to your case and support from people across the country,” Polis said in his pardon letter.

Bruce Korum, who was convicted in 1975 of crimes related to the sale of marijuana in El Paso County, has since dedicated himself to living as a good member of his community, Polis said. 
“You ran a successful environmental construction business for 30 years with up to 50 employees, raised four children, and are now considering running for public office,” Polis said in his pardon letter. “I hope this pardon will provide a clean slate for you, allowing you to contribute even more to your family and community, as well as being able to hunt recreationally.”
In 2020, Polis pardoned 2,732 people for past marijuana convictions — the most people ever pardoned by a Colorado governor at one time.
Pardons are typically granted after someone’s sentence is complete, while a commutation is granted to someone still serving their sentence. Both are forms of clemency, which only the governor has the power to grant.
Timothy Cordova, whom Polis pardoned of a 2011 conviction of possession of a controlled substance, has maintained sobriety and established a career in property management. His friends describe him as dependable, hard working, dedicated and a caring father, Polis said. 
“I hope this pardon will remove barriers to housing, allow you to obtain professional licenses, and enable you to hunt with your son,” Polis said in his pardon letter. 
Polis granted pardons to people convicted of various drug crimes, trespassing, theft and criminal impersonation. Many of the people whose convictions he pardoned have gone on to obtain degrees and establish successful careers, maintain sobriety, start families and give back to their communities. 
Others pardoned include: Victor Arellano, Richard Batdorf, Luis Day, Mitchell Downing, Scott Ellison, Daniel Emmans, George Soon Fah, Matthew Focht, Craig Gipson, Phillip Hengemuhle, Ethan Hilton, Daniel Kelly, Thomas Knowles, Christina Latimore, Michael Low, Yeu Ly, DeAnna Martinez, Justin Mills, Sabrina Montoya, Joshua Moore, Walter Spangler, Veronica Stewart, Kelly Stoval and Jordan Wood.
Earlier in 2026, Polis faced intense backlash from the Democratic Party and bipartisan election experts after he commuted the prison sentence for Tina Peters, the former Mesa County clerk convicted for her role in a breach of her office’s election system.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Commentary: Customers get higher bills while Black Hills Energy discovers data center gold
description: While Rapid City residents debate whether data centers belong in their backyard, a homegrown corporation is quietly anchoring some of the largest tech developments in the country — just across the state line. Back home, its South Dakota electricity customers face substantial rate increases. Meanwhile, Black Hills Corp. expects to earn $150 million annually b[...]
text:
Electric transmission lines near Clark, South Dakota. (Photo by Robert Zullo/States Newsroom)While Rapid City residents debate whether data centers belong in their backyard, a homegrown corporation is quietly anchoring some of the largest tech developments in the country — just across the state line.
Back home, its South Dakota electricity customers face substantial rate increases. Meanwhile, Black Hills Corp. expects to earn $150 million annually by 2030 from supplying electricity to Google. That’s more than half the $291.6 million that Black Hills Corp. earned for shareholders in 2025.
On Nov. 5, Google announced a $17 billion investment in a data center near Cheyenne, Wyoming. Rapid City-based Black Hills Corp., parent company of Black Hills Energy, has agreed to help power it.
Black Hills plans to invest $1.8 billion in natural gas generating plants and coordinate electricity from other producers through a privately managed power system.
Regulators approve $16 monthly Black Hills Energy rate hike as extra $20 surcharge looms

Altogether, the arrangement involves 2,700 megawatts of generating resources.
At the end of 2025, Black Hills owned 1,386 megawatts of generating capacity across its electric utilities in four states.
Black Hills plans to build 564 megawatts of new generation, enough capacity to match the average electricity needs of about 410,000 South Dakota households. The state had approximately 434,000 residential electric customers in 2024.
Google isn’t alone. Black Hills already supplies electricity to Microsoft’s Wyoming data centers and is preparing to supply Meta’s upcoming artificial intelligence facility. Microsoft recently purchased 3,200 acres for possible expansion.
Black Hills’ November investor presentation outlines 600 megawatts of planned demand from Microsoft and Meta alone by 2030. Including Google and other prospects, the company describes a development pipeline exceeding 3,000 megawatts, with another 2,500 megawatts or more being explored.
Wyoming has spent years attracting data centers with available energy, tax incentives and fiber-optic infrastructure. Black Hills is capitalizing by pursuing another $686 million in transmission investments. And its expansion isn’t limited to data centers.
Black Hills received Montana’s approval this week for a merger with NorthWestern Energy, following an earlier approval by South Dakota. The combined entity will be called Bright Horizon Energy and will be headquartered in Rapid City.
Residents of Rapid City have packed public meetings about a proposed data center ordinance to voice anxiety over energy and water consumption, noise and property values. Nearly 940 public survey responses were submitted, and the Planning Commission subsequently decided to postpone consideration of the ordinance until January. 
Electricity prices are another sore point in the Black Hills, and the latest compounding increases carry sticker shock.
On Nov. 4, the South Dakota Public Utilities Commission approved a rate increase expected to raise bills by 13.62% starting Dec. 1.  The commission estimates $16.34 will be added to the monthly bill for a household using 650 kilowatt-hours. In a separate proceeding, Black Hills seeks another $17.26 monthly per average household for its Lange II generating plant under construction in Rapid City, this time using 600 kilowatt-hours.
South Dakota households averaged 994 kilowatt-hours monthly in 2024. At that consumption, the combined increases will add an extra $53 a month — or $636 annually — if the separate Lange II charge takes effect as proposed.
My calculations, based on commission documents, show that a Rapid City household, at the state average, would pay $208.32 per month, well above the state’s 2024 average of $127.81. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
But on Monday, commission staff objected to Black Hills Energy’s application for the Lange II surcharge. Staff contends the interim rate hike proposed did not comply with state law and urged the commission to at least suspend the implementation of a rate hike for 180 days. It also noted the impact on consumers during the Christmas and winter heating months. 
News that the parent corporation expects to earn $150 million annually from Google may not generate quite the enthusiasm around the kitchen table that it does in the corporate boardroom.
The Wyoming tech investments aren’t driving these local rate hikes. Black Hills says its Google contracts are structured to prevent costs from being shifted to existing customers.
Still, the optics aren’t particularly flattering.
Rapid City is struggling with whether to accommodate even small data centers, while a corporation headquartered in the city is helping power some of the nation’s largest.
Black Hills Energy has found a new gold rush in Wyoming, with extraordinary earnings potentially ahead.
Back home, its electricity customers are discovering that not everyone strikes gold. Some just get the bill.

name: Source New Mexico
title: ‘Here we go again’: New Mexico conservationists decry US Interior public land selloff plan
description: The U.S. Interior Department this week released its four-year strategic plan, which includes offering states, localities and tribes the opportunity to purchase federal lands.
text:
U.S. Interior Department Secretary Doug Burgum on Nov. 10, 2026, released the department’s four-year strategic plan, which includes plans to sell federal lands to states and tribes. Above: An anti-Burgum message projected on a Santa Fe hotel on June 23, 2025, during his visit to the state for the Western Governors’ Association annual meeting. (Source NM file photo)The U.S. Interior Department this week released its four-year strategic plan, which includes offering states, localities and tribes the opportunity to purchase federal lands.
Public lands advocates in New Mexico and across the country immediately criticized the 28-page plan published Tuesday as another effort by President Donald Trump’s administration to initiate mass selloffs of public lands to private interests. Waves of protests in New Mexico and across the country early in Trump’s first term contributed to lawmakers excising a similar proposal from the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” Trump signed last July. 
“After Americans across the political spectrum rejected efforts to sell off millions of acres of our shared lands, the Trump administration is once again pushing a dangerous agenda that puts our outdoors at risk,” said Loren Blackford, the executive director of the Sierra Club, in a statement Thursday. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The strategic plan marks the first time the Trump’s administration has formally announced its intention to sell federal lands. And it demonstrates that Interior Department Secretary Doug Burgum is still set on shuffling public lands off the federal government’s balance sheet, Garrett Veneklasen, New Mexico Wild’s northern conservation director, told Source NM on Thursday. 
“Here we go again, right?” Veneklasen said. “This is their last-ditch effort. It’s like they’ve dusted this thing off and put new dressing on it.”
The department’s strategic plan does not specify which lands it might sell to states or tribes, but it outlines doing so in a section dedicated to reducing bureaucracy and improving collaboration with state, local and tribal governments. 
The same section also suggests the department intends to reduce its workforce to “advance operational efficiencies” and strengthen its focus to unspecified public lands of national importance. 
“The Department will work to decrease the size of the federal estate by offering to states, localities and Tribes the opportunity to purchase federal lands,” the plan reads. “Through these sales, the Department will be able to focus its resources on primary federal responsibilities and nationally significant federal lands.”
Jesse Deubel, executive director of the New Mexico Wildlife Federation, told Source NM on Thursday that the plan’s language aims to deceive the public from the department’s real intent. 
“It doesn’t sound as egregious as it actually is, but transferring land to the state or selling land to the state or some other entity ultimately results in privatization,” he said. “These are lands that belong to the American people.”
Keegan King, founder and executive director of the Native Lands Institute, told Source NM on Thursday that the department’s plan “confirms a lot of our fears” about Trump’s public lands agenda. 
“This strategic plan is basically letting people know that the Department of the Interior is open for business. Our children’s inheritance, public lands, are being sold out from under us,” he said. “If this goes through and DOI changes its mission from stewarding our public lands to selling them off to the highest bidder, I’m not sure what we’ll have left.”
U.S. Interior Department officials did not respond to Source NM’s emailed request for further comment Thursday. 
Public lands protesters picket Western governors’ conference

The department released the plan a week after midterm elections in which Democrats won sizable majorities in both chambers of Congress. 
Veneklasen said new majority Democrats — including all of New Mexico’s congressional delegation, whose five members have consistently opposed public lands sales — will be instrumental in preventing Trump’s administration from implementing its plan over the next four years.
U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) is expected to become the next chair of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and, in a statement his office sent Thursday to Source NM, denounced the U.S. Interior Department’s plan.
“These lands belong to the American people,” Heinrich said. “Public lands belong in public hands.” 
In addition to congressional Democrats, Veneklasen predicted members of the recreating public — including hunters, anglers, hikers and others — will rise again in opposition. 
“We’ve got to do everything we can to fight it,” he said. “And I think that there will be an even bigger uprising, especially now that the blue wave has happened.”

name: VTDigger
title: In a challenging year, Vermont’s outdoor business leaders are full of optimism
description:
While federal policy has left some businesses on shaky ground, officials and business owners agree that outdoor recreation could increase its role in the state’s economy.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  In a challenging year, Vermont’s outdoor business leaders are full of optimism.
text:
Chairlifts at Okemo Mountain Ski Resort. Photo via Adobe Stock

Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
LUDLOW — For Vermont’s outdoor economy, it’s been no ordinary year.
State officials estimate that the sector — which by their reckoning includes businesses ranging from ski resorts to bike shops and inns — generated roughly $2.2 billion for Vermont’s economy in 2024. But this year, federal policy has left some businesses on shaky ground, forced to face tariffs and strained relations with the Canadians who used to frequent the Green Mountain State.
Vermont’s outdoor commerce operates in the fading shadow of New England’s older forest economies, said Sarah Waring, who leads the Northern Border Regional Commission, a joint federal and state economic development agency.
“For this region, both wood and paper industries were our (source of) rural capital,” she told audience members at the Vermont Outdoor Economy Summit in Ludlow on Thursday. But “starting in about the 1970s, this industry began to decline.”
Though the market for wood products has been deteriorating for half a century, new changes are still causing trouble for Vermont’s forestry industry. This summer, a Glens Falls, New York, papermill announced that it would no longer accept Vermont pulpwood, a heavy blow for the state’s loggers.
All this adds up to the need, Waring said, for “a new and different forest economy,” which the outdoor recreation sector is helping to provide.
But in recent years, fast-changing federal tariff policy has shocked the finances of even the state’s healthier industries. Orvis, a 170-year-old Vermont outfitter based in Manchester, has been rocked by the new fees.
“The economic impact was huge,” said company President Simon Perkins of the tariffs in an interview between events. “But what was also really, really hard was the uncertainty that came with it.”
Orvis makes some equipment, such as fly fishing rods, in Vermont but sources other products from across the globe, Perkins said. Last year, the company announced it would close 36 locations — a large fraction of its retail footprint — after a round of layoffs that leadership attributed to tariffs.
In an environment where business owners are constantly worried about unpredictable costs, Perkins added, they’re much less likely to take risks or make substantial investments in new projects.

From left: Northern Border Regional Commission Executive Director Sarah Waring, Mark Kane and Simon Perkins speak at the Vermont Outdoor Economy Summit in Ludlow on Thursday, Nov. 12. Photo by Theo Wells-Spackman/VTDigger

Vermont’s tourism economy in 2025 showed a roughly 2% dip from 2024, according to Heather Pelham, Vermont’s commissioner of tourism and marketing. She attributes the drop largely to tensions with Canada.
Nonetheless, Perkins said he believes the state has enormous potential for growth in its outdoor economy. Vermont’s combination of vast natural resources and deep outdoor recreation traditions means that business owners have a lot to lean on when it comes to curating experiences for visitors — or locals, he said.
“Now that we’re starting to measure (the outdoor economy),” Perkins said, “I think maybe it will open our eyes up to what we actually have that we can tap into.”
That might mean investing more public money in the sector over the long term, he added, though he acknowledged that lawmakers are under pressure from all sides as they seek to assemble the state budget. 
Vermont has several grant programs designed to assist outdoor recreation businesses with funds and other assistance, including through the Vermont Outdoor Recreation Economic Collaborative. 
Pelham agreed that such growth is possible and said an increased flow of tourists could bring much-needed tax revenue into state coffers to ease costs for locals. Rural communities in particular could benefit financially from the increased visitation and commercial activity that outdoor recreation can provide, she said.
That’s a priority for Waring, too. In certain cases, she’s observed that irresponsible outdoor recreation development can raise an area’s cost of living without providing sufficient high-quality employment. But Vermont is a long way from that extreme, she said, adding that local businesses tend to provide good support to their employees.
Brian Maggiotto, who owns the Inn at Manchester, echoed the need for “responsible tourism” standards in relation to both people and lands. He compared his philosophy to the “leave no trace” ethos applied in national parks and other public areas.
“If we pass (those values) on to our visitors, our guests, they too will own that sense of stewardship,” he said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Healey takes next step in bid to get in on Canadian offshore wind
description: This article first appeared on CommonWealth Beacon and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.  President Donald Trump blocked Massachusetts from unlocking new offshore wind from its own coasts, dealing a crucial blow to the state’s energy transition. So Gov. Maura Healey is testing the waters to the [...]
text:
Massachusetts Energy and Environmental Affairs Secretary Rebecca Tepper speaks at the signing of an agreement with Nova Scotia to pursue offshore wind. (Photo by Jordan Wolman/CommonWealth Beacon)This article first appeared on CommonWealth Beacon and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License. 
President Donald Trump blocked Massachusetts from unlocking new offshore wind from its own coasts, dealing a crucial blow to the state’s energy transition. So Gov. Maura Healey is testing the waters to the north instead.
The Healey administration is spearheading an effort alongside other New England states to tap into work underway in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia to advance offshore wind projects there, as it eyes potential energy supply and economic benefits here at home.
Massachusetts is issuing a formal request for information with Nova Scotia to test market interest and feasibility among energy developers, supply chain companies, port entities, organized labor, utilities, and the fishing industry. Maine, Connecticut, Vermont, and Rhode Island are also participating.
It’s just one procedural step on what would be a long road to achieving an ambitious vision of bringing energy generated by Canadian offshore wind into New England. But the move is a concrete signal of the state’s seriousness in collaborating with Nova Scotia to boost offshore wind and find a Plan B to the now-stalled domestic wind industry on which Massachusetts had been relying.
“We need more affordable, reliable energy, and that’s going to take working with our neighbors,” Healey said in a statement. “Massachusetts and Nova Scotia have a strong partnership, and we’re building on that relationship to explore new opportunities to bring offshore wind power to New England. This work has the potential to lower energy costs, strengthen our energy supply and create good-paying jobs in our port communities.”
Nova Scotia appeared ready to launch bids this winter to lease areas off its coast for wind development, though that timeline may be delayed.
Still, Massachusetts is looking to establish itself as a player in the province’s wind development well before any projects even get off the ground.
The 12-page RFI, issued Thursday, asks stakeholders to weigh in on how big potential Canadian offshore wind projects should be, what specific type of technology should be deployed, realistic timelines for project completion, and how existing US port capacity and supply-chain infrastructure could be leveraged to bring potential projects to life.
And the document starts to tackle what will be the pressing and likely messy question of transmission, pondering whether an undersea cable or a new power line is the best mode of actually getting the wind power into New England.
Stakeholders have until the end of the year to respond to the request.
Massachusetts is fresh off the completion just last month of Vineyard Wind, the country’s largest offshore wind project, and is finally seeing Revolution Wind to its south reach full-scale operations.
Now, the movement in Canada is another welcome sign as the state navigates soaring energy costs, rising power demand, and looming clean energy targets. And it’s part of Healey’s all-of-the-above approach to energy, in which she has also championed solar, adding more nuclear power, and expanding natural gas supply.
The opportunity in Nova Scotia for the Bay State could be twofold: Massachusetts and other states in the region could serve as customers for the wind power generated in Canada, and the state could see economic and jobs benefits given the role the state’s port in New Bedford has played in offshore wind construction in the Northeast.
Still, big questions remain about how much Canadian offshore wind can do to serve Massachusetts electric customers — much less provide a way out of the energy affordability crisis any time soon.
Even before Trump canceled permits and ground domestic offshore wind to a halt, cost overruns driven by record inflation and supply chain constraints roiled the industry, spooked developers, and stalled progress.
Plus, some recent energy projects built to deliver power from Canada into New England have left room for skepticism.
A 10-year process kickstarted by Massachusetts under Gov. Charlie Baker to build a hydropower transmission line from Quebec into the region, known as the New England Clean Energy Connect, finally came to an end when power started flowing through the project this past January.
Then came the problems.
Almost immediately after NECEC turned on, the region endured a stretch of frigid temperatures during what turned out to be the coldest winter in 20 years. Electricity didn’t flow into New England on the line for 12 days, arguably when the region needed it most to meet high demand — prompting a legal brawl between Massachusetts utility companies and Hydro Quebec that’s now winding its way through court.
The NECEC then inexplicably shut down during another two-week period this past May and June. The transmission line is estimated to supply one-fifth of the state’s energy demand.
The new joint effort with Nova Scotia is filled with hurdles that could make NECEC look simple, from financing the wind projects to clearing the extra regulatory steps needed to get them sited and carry that energy across international borders to the long distance that energy would need to travel to reach New England.
The RFI follows a memorandum of understanding that Healey and Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston signed earlier this year at the State House. Rebecca Tepper, secretary of energy and environmental affairs, told CommonWealth Beacon exclusively last year that she had visited Nova Scotia to meet with Canadian officials on offshore wind.
“If you’re going to start an energy infrastructure project,” she said at the MOU signing back in February, “the best time to do that is today.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Hugley is officially nominated as Georgia House speaker as Democrats choose their leaders
description: Georgia House Democrats unveiled their picks to lead the chamber Thursday after winning a majority for the first time in two decades, officially naming Rep. Carolyn Hugley as their nominee for House speaker. Hugley, who has represented Columbus in the Legislature since 1992, will become the first Black woman to serve as House Speaker in […]
text:
Georgia House Speaker-nominee Rep. Carolyn Hugley, a Columbus Democrat, speaks at a press conference on Nov. 12, 2026, at the state Capitol, announcing the caucus' picks for leadership roles. Alander Rocha/Georgia RecorderGeorgia House Democrats unveiled their picks to lead the chamber Thursday after winning a majority for the first time in two decades, officially naming Rep. Carolyn Hugley as their nominee for House speaker.
Hugley, who has represented Columbus in the Legislature since 1992, will become the first Black woman to serve as House Speaker in Georgia if she is elected by the full House in the legislative session that starts in January. She would take the gavel from House Speaker Jon Burns, a Newington Republican who has presided over the chamber since 2023. 
The speaker is one of the most powerful elected officials in Georgia and wields influence over the entire legislative process, appointing leaders to committees and deciding which bills make it to the floor for a vote. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Rep. Billy Mitchell from Stone Mountain, who was first elected in 2002, is also poised to become the chamber’s second-in-command as the House Democrats’ nominee for speaker pro tempore. Mitchell would succeed Speaker Pro Tem Jan Jones, a Milton Republican who did not seek another term. 
House Democrats also elected new caucus leaders, selecting Rep. Stacey Evans from Atlanta to be majority leader.
Lawrenceville state Rep. Sam Park, the House Democratic whip, is pictured at the Capitol on Nov. 12, 2026 at a press conference. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
Rep. Sam Park from Lawrenceville will go from being minority whip to majority whip, and Rep. Bryce Berry from Atlanta will serve as majority chief deputy whip. Rep. Spencer Frye from Athens is the caucus chair, replacing Rep. Tanya Miller who is the incoming attorney general, and Rep. Imani Barnes from Tucker will serve as caucus vice chair.
Rep. Anissa Jones from Macon will be the new caucus secretary, and Rep. Robert Flournoy from Hampton takes over as treasurer.
House Democrats officially flipped the chamber earlier this week. They currently have a slim majority with 91 seats, which is the minimum required to control the chamber, but they could still gain more seats depending on the outcome of three still-unresolved races. 
Hugley described the new Democratic leadership as “a team that looks like Georgia.”
“We didn’t come this far to settle into new titles and new offices and get that new letterhead. We’re here because Georgia has given us the opportunity to deliver for them, and deliver is exactly what we’re going to do,” Hugley said at a press conference at the state Capitol.
Park added that “the diversity of our caucus reflects the diversity of our state, and unity is our power.”
Hugley said House Democrats would prioritize expanding Medicaid, saying that it sits “first and foremost” on the agenda. She said they are glad Democrats “have a partner in the governor’s office to help (them) get it done,” referring to Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, who put the issue at the center of her campaign for the state’s top office. Aside from expanding Medicaid, Hugley said House Democrats will focus on addressing issues surrounding affordability.
“We’re here because we listen to parents worried about the cost of raising their children. We listen to seniors struggling to make ends meet. We listen to working families trying to afford groceries, gas, housing, healthcare and childcare,” Hugley said. “Throughout these conversations across Georgia, one thing is crystal clear: affordability is the issue.”
Georgia House Speaker-nominee Rep. Carolyn Hugley, a Columbus Democrat, speaks at a press conference on Nov. 12, 2026, at the state Capitol, announcing the caucus’ picks for leadership roles. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
Democrats flipped the House and governor’s mansion, but Republicans still control the state Senate. Hugley acknowledged that the House would have to negotiate with Republicans and that House Democrats may not be able to “do all the things on our agenda in the first two (years),” but she offered Republicans some words of goodwill.
“I believe that everyone in this building has the best interests of Georgians at heart. We may want to get there differently, but I have to operate from that premise,” Hugley said.
House Republicans, who will be now in the minority for the first time in more than 20 years, are expected to elect their leaders on Monday.
Senate Republicans, who have a two-seat majority, announced their leaders earlier this week. 
Sen. Larry Walker III from Perry is the nominee for president pro tempore – a role he currently holds – and Republican state Sen. Jason Anavitarte from Dallas will keep his post as majority leader. Majority whip state Sen. Randy Robertson from Cataula and majority caucus secretary state Sen. Kay Kirkpatrick from Marietta will also continue in their roles. State Sen. Tim Bearden from Carrollton is the new majority caucus chairman, replacing state Sen. Shawn Still from Suwanee after his loss to Democrat Laura Murvartian, and state Sen. Drew Echols from Gainesville will become majority caucus vice chairman, replacing Sen. Clint Dixon from Buford, who was ousted by Democrat Scott Tippetts.
Senate Democrats, who will remain in the minority, are set to elect their leaders Monday.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Gov.-elect Donalds talks humility, higher ed, college sports in post-victory speech
description: In his first public appearance since his historic electoral victory, Gov.-elect Byron Donalds delivered a brief speech Thursday calling the results humbling. Donald’s 12-minute speech carried none of the partisan fire that has come to mark Gov. Ron DeSantis’s public appearances, and struck a more conciliatory message than his predecessor favored. ‘Elections [...]
text:
Gov.-elect Byron Donalds delivers a speech Nov. 12, 2026, during a Board of Governors retreat at Florida International University. (Screenshot from FIU)In his first public appearance since his historic electoral victory, Gov.-elect Byron Donalds delivered a brief speech Thursday calling the results humbling.
Donald’s 12-minute speech carried none of the partisan fire that has come to mark Gov. Ron DeSantis’s public appearances, and struck a more conciliatory message than his predecessor favored.
‘Elections are a mirror that are basically held up to our state, and what we saw last week is that Florida is a very passionate, diverse, and deeply engaged place. The margins were close. The reality carries with it a profound lesson in humility, and it serves as a powerful reminder: The leaders in this room do not serve a single faction or a single ideology,” Donalds said.
“We serve all 23 million Floridians, regardless of how any citizen casts their ballot.”
Donalds delivered his speech during a State University System Board of Governors summit at Florida International University. As such, his prepared comments were education-specific. The university system has for the past decade been ranked No. 1 in the nation by U. S. News & World Report — an assessment that takes into consideration the length of time it takes for students to complete two- and four-year college programs, the cost of in-state tuition and fees, and the debt burden graduates carry.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.‘Our mission now is to stay that way, and then to continue to expand our capabilities,” he said. “A decade at the summit, at the summit of higher education, is not a partisan achievement. It is a Florida achievement.”
Donalds said he’ll continue to stand behind performance-based funding for state universities, which, he said, “rightfully ties resources to tangible student outcomes.” Going forward, he said, he’d like state universities to set the “bold goal” of graduating more engineers.
‘I rely on candor’
Seemingly nervous at first, Donalds quickly found his footing as he finished his prepared remarks and interacted directly with people in the audience.
Donalds mentioned he was going to meet with other governors next week for an event and said the focus should be on policy, not sizing up “potential future rivals on a presidential debate stage.”
Without missing a beat, Donalds quickly added: “I’m not running for president. I just want to be clear on that. You got to say that stuff now, crazy.”
When asked how the universities could best work with his administration, Donalds said he likes to maintain open-door communication. “I rely on candor. Like I’m a big boy. Like you could just tell me what it is.”
‘The toddler phase of NIL’
Florida Gulf Coast University Board of Trustees member Paul V. Applegarth (Image via FGCU)
The governor-elect held nothing back when Florida Gulf Coast University trustee Paul Applegarth asked about his position on the federal Protect College Sports Act. The legislation follows legal rulings that forced the NCAA to lift its longstanding prohibition on compensating student athletes, a move Donalds supports.
The Protect College Sports Act would establish a national framework for the enforcement of name, image, and likeness deals and give an antitrust exemption to the NCAA and college athletic conferences. It has passed the U.S. Senate but not the U.S. House. While it is supported by President Donald Trump, who endorsed Donalds for governor, it is opposed by the Congressional Black Caucus.
“I hate that bill. I’m just telling you, I don’t like it. I’m not a fan of it,” Donalds said, adding he had shared his sentiments with Sens. Rick Scott and Ashley Moody before the Senate voted 77-22 to pass it (Scott opposed it but Moody supported it.)
Donalds said college sports are in the “toddler phase of NIL right now.” As he continued — only half jokingly adding that he was “really going to get in trouble now” — Donalds said the collapse of some conferences and realignment of others may reflect a faulty business model.
“I am a market-based system person. I believe in free markets, and so if somebody has the talent and ability to leverage their name, to go to make money, good.”
Dollars and “sense” 
One professor asked what lessons Republicans should take away from the elections. Donalds said the outcomes reflected kitchen-table issues like rising costs of living as well as concerns about the future and being able to “sustain a great life.”
Specific to higher education, Donalds stressed it’s about ensuring students graduate with degrees that would make graduates economically viable.
“So, that’s the way I look at the world. I try to keep things pretty simple. If it don’t make dollars, it don’t make sense. And when you talk to somebody in their life, if they cannot figure out how to pay rent-slash-mortgage, pay utility bills, put food on the table, gas in the car, pay for insurance, pay for healthcare, etc. — if they are struggling, either to do it or don’t have the confidence that they’re going to be able to do that into the future, I think you’re going to continue to see this push and pull electorally throughout the United States of America,” he said.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont to raise minimum wage by 49 cents in January
description:
Vermont has the second-lowest minimum wage in New England. Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts and Rhode Island all have minimums of $15 an hour or more.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont to raise minimum wage by 49 cents in January.
text:
Chris Winters, who is now the deputy commissioner of the Vermont Department of Labor, testifies before the House Human Services Committee at the Statehouse in Montpelier in May 2025. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This story by Sophie Levenson was first published in the Valley News on Nov. 10, 2026.
Vermont’s minimum wage will rise from $14.42 to $14.91 an hour on Jan. 1, the Vermont Department of Labor announced Monday.
Though a 49-cent hourly increase could seem marginal, it amounts to about $1,000 more a year for someone who works 40 hours a week.
The raise is automatic. Under 21 V.S.A. § 384, the state adjusts the minimum wage every year by the lesser of 5% or the increase in the Consumer Price Index. The Department of Labor uses the CPI-U, not seasonally adjusted, from August to August. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported a 3.4% increase over that period this year, which produced this year’s 49-cent bump. Last year, the minimum wage rose 41 cents, from $14.01 to $14.42.
The current version of the law took effect in 2020, when the Vermont Legislature overrode Gov. Phil Scott’s veto. It raised the minimum wage to $12.55 by 2022 and resumed annual inflation adjustments after that.
The minimum wage for tipped workers, which is set at half the regular rate, will also rise, from $7.21 to $7.46 per hour — though all tipped workers make more than or equivalent to the full minimum wage with their tips or are compensated by their employers in the rare cases when their tips do not amount to minimum wage pay.
Few workers in the Upper Valley earn the minimum wage, according to Dartmouth College economics professor Patricia Anderson.
“In the actual Upper Valley, it won’t have an impact,” Anderson told the Valley News on Tuesday.
Chris Winters, deputy commissioner of the Vermont Department of Labor, told the Valley News on Monday that the minimum wage is only one part of affordability for workers, and not one the state wants to prioritize above others.
“When it comes to wages and affordability, we really need to focus on the big picture, which is taxes, housing costs, healthcare costs,” Winters said.
Winters said a worker’s income goes farther when those costs come down and that lowering the cost of living has a bigger effect than small increases in pay.
Business groups have long raised concerns about minimum wage increases. In 2018, while lawmakers debated a bill to raise the wage to $15 an hour, Ashley Romeo-Boles, then a government affairs specialist with the Vermont Chamber of Commerce, told the Senate Economic Development, Housing and General Affairs Committee that every $1 increase in wages can raise an employer’s labor costs by $1.25 or more. She said wage increases can push businesses to cut jobs or limit benefits.
Anderson said studies on the minimum wage often point to a trade-off. A large increase over a short period can help workers who keep their jobs while costing others theirs. In rural parts of Vermont, she said, the increase could lead a few small businesses to hold off on hiring.
“But 49 cents isn’t really a lot,” Anderson said.
“The question really becomes: Are you growing slower than you would have if you hadn’t been forced to increase your compensation?” she said. Short-term studies can’t really answer that question, she said.
As of Jan. 1, 2026, Vermont had the 19th-highest minimum wage in the country and was one of 19 states that adjust for inflation every year, according to the Economic Policy Institute. Twenty states use the federal minimum of $7.25 an hour, according to the institute.
Vermont has the second-lowest minimum wage in New England. Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts and Rhode Island all have minimums of $15 an hour or more. New Hampshire is one of the 20 states that use the federal minimum. It hasn’t raised its wage floor since the federal minimum went to $7.25 in 2009.
Still, typical salaries for most jobs are higher in New Hampshire than for the same jobs across the Connecticut River, according to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Living Wage Calculator.
MIT’s calculator estimates a living wage in Vermont of $24.92 an hour for one adult with no children, based on the cost of housing, food, medical care and other basic needs. The state’s Joint Fiscal Office put Vermont’s livable wage for 2024 at $19.53 an hour in urban areas and $17.68 in rural areas, in its January 2025 report. The Public Assets Institute’s State of Working Vermont report from 2025 found that minimum wage growth has not kept pace with the cost of living.
In the Upper Valley, where the cost of living is high, companies know they can’t pay their employees under $15 an hour. Open jobs on Indeed.com indicate this, as pay for a cafe associate at King Arthur Baking Co. in Norwich starts at $18.04 per hour; at Abracadabra Coffee Co. in Woodstock, it starts at $15 plus tips. In 2025, 10% of Vermonters made $15 an hour or less.
