name: Rhode Island Current
title: Commentary: The small mind of a big man on campus
description: Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth proposed an answer that won’t work to a problem that doesn’t exist during his visit this week to the U.S. Naval War College in Newport The problem, according to Hegseth, is that professional military education — the coursework and experiences that prepare service members for their next jobs or promotions […]
text:
Faculty applaud as a procession of students passes by on graduation day at the U.S. Naval War College in Newport, Rhode Island, on June 13, 2025. The ceremony celebrated 273 in-resident and 720 distance education students who completed senior and intermediate graduate level courses, including officers from all branches of the armed forces, more than 30 federal agencies and departments, and 60 partner and allied nations. (U.S. Navy photo)Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth proposed an answer that won’t work to a problem that doesn’t exist during his visit this week to the U.S. Naval War College in Newport
The problem, according to Hegseth, is that professional military education — the coursework and experiences that prepare service members for their next jobs or promotions — has succumbed to “academic drift,” without enough emphasis on warfighting. The answer, he says, is reducing civilian faculty. 
Even scratching minimally below the surface, his Nov. 9 speech was largely political theater rather than thoughtful consideration of military and national security needs.
Hegseth attacks civilian-led education in Naval War College speech

Hegseth wants to make the fighting force more lethal and laser focused on “victory.” But the U.S. military is already the best trained, most lethal and effective military in the world, as evidenced by every other military in the world wanting to train and operate with it. The U.S. military is very good at tactical jobs when not put into impossible situations, like trying to eradicate terrorism or democratize a country largely composed of internally warring elements, or being overtasked to be everywhere all the time. Unfortunately, our nation’s leaders have failed to understand our adversaries’ motives and how to link our political objectives to military strategy. Iran, for example, doesn’t have to match U.S. military capabilities, it just has to keep surviving the beating the U.S. can inflict, thus keeping the U.S. in a military and political quagmire.
If there were any substance beyond Hegseth’s 33 new directives, the first step would be to “fix” who attends the nation’s six war colleges, a problem professional military education leaders have been trying to address for years. At the Naval War College, there are as many or more staff officers and officers on their last tour attending in person than line officers who see combat. Is Hegseth looking for more lethal logisticians, dermatologists and retirees? Most officers fulfill their education requirements online while working full time. Completion is largely a hoop to be jumped.
Professional education for intermediate and senior personnel prepares officers to transition from tactical to operational and strategic positions. That means teaching officers how to think, not what to think. How to think is education; what to think is training, or indoctrination. Senior service and war colleges began hiring civilian academics to achieve this purpose after the passage of the 1986 Goldwater-Nichols Act. The reasoning is simple: Being the best pilot or ship driver does not prepare an officer to teach subjects like policy development and implementation — critical for their inevitable Pentagon tour — or strategy development and implementation critical for higher level assignments and working with allies. 



Quotation







Even scratching minimally below the surface, his Nov. 9 speech was largely political theater rather than thoughtful consideration of military and national security needs.


There is little incentive for active-duty military line officers to teach; it does little for promotion purposes and takes them from the field. Hiring military retirees works in some cases, if they are willing to get and keep up the subject matter qualifications needed. Some of the best professional military educators I have worked with fit this category. When teaching operations, however, their value rapidly diminishes the longer they are away from active duty because operating procedures and parameters change quickly.
Last month, the Pentagon ended a 12-year joint research and teaching partnership with Brown University’s Watson Institute for International Studies. Hegseth went out of his way to disparage Brown, calling the Providence Ivy League school “the only place more stridently ideological in one direction more than Columbia or Harvard. A Princeton University graduate, Hegseth is among several other Ivy League graduates who benefited from the educational rigor those elite schools offered only to denounce them for the sake of populist appeal. 
In his speech, Hegseth, railed that professors are indoctrinating students with Frankfurt School Marxism, which apparently left many students wondering what the Frankfurt School even is. He obsessed on culture war themes and accused previous military officers, specifically Gen. Mark Milley, of not supporting an insurrection. Missing from Hegseth’s speech was any reference to a soldier’s first responsibility to defend and protect the U.S. Constitution. 
Professional military education needs to be more challenging, more broadening, and more academic. Once military officers leave their tactical jobs, they will need to hold their own in venues where they must deal with very smart civilians. Unfettered, civilian politicians rarely recognize the limits of military power and are overly willing to task the military to achieve their political goals. Military officers must be able to parry with their Ivy League educated peers. Gen. David Petraeus won academic awards from professional military institutions throughout his career. But when he was sent to earn a doctorate at Princeton, Petraeus was forced to step up his game after he got a D on his first exam and one professor called a paper he wrote “simplistic.”
Hegseth made it clear in Newport that he sees little difference between training and education. He even seemed OK with indoctrination, telling students what to think, thereby avoiding anything that could later be used as the kind of “derogatory information” that could block an officer from promotion or get them fired. As the saying goes, control the classrooms and you control the future. 
The main effect of Hegseth’s raid on professional military education will be more emphasis on training, brain drain of the best faculty, and a hollowing out of the U.S. military’s strategic thinking. Focusing on fighting future wars, another of Hegseth’s themes, requires not just thinking how to do what we’ve always done better, but to think about how to do things differently. 
The educational agenda Hegseth advocates has only one answer to all security problems — ham-fisted military force. It says the U.S. will not be ready for a fight as a last resort, it says the U.S. is itching for a fight – bring it. 
But as the midterm election showed, the American people are tired of political theater, politics by spectacle and wasting taxpayer money on unwinnable wars of choice. Rhode Island’s Democratic Sen. Jack Reed is expected to reclaim the chair the Senate Armed Forces Committee in the upcoming Congress. Professional military education falls well within that panel’s purview. Hopefully the committee will use its investigative power to consider how professional military education can serve national security.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana Republican chair steps down week after sweeping election losses
description: Indiana Republican Chair Lana Keesling resigned from the position Thursday amid the party turmoil following last week’s widespread election wins by Democrats.
text:
Indiana Republican Party Chair Lana Keesling speaks during a party rally in Indianapolis on Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana Republican Chair Lana Keesling resigned from the position Thursday amid the party turmoil following last week’s widespread election wins by Democrats.
Keesling will be replaced temporarily by party Vice Chair Jim Johnson until a permanent chair is selected, the state party office said in announcing her decision.
Gov. Mike Braun tapped Keesling in February 2025 to become the fourth state Republican chair in less than 18 months, calling her an experienced party leader who would be “a strong partner for grassroots leaders and elected Republicans in Indianapolis and Washington.”
The state GOP central committee ratified the selection of Keesling, who was then the elected Fort Wayne city clerk before stepping down this past January.
Keesling said in the statement that serving as state chair has been an “incredible honor” and thanked Braun and other party leaders for their support.
Braun: Election results a ‘wake-up call’ for GOP

“It has been a privilege to stand alongside them and witness firsthand the dedication that drives our organization,” she said. “As I step away from this role, I do so with gratitude for the relationships built and experiences gained. I wish the next chair and the entire Indiana Republican Party continued success as they move forward.” 
Keesling maintained a fairly low public profile as the state Republican leader, keeping her public appearances principally to local party events.
Her resignation comes as Indiana Republicans are recalibrating from last week’s elections that saw Democrats gain their first statewide victories since 2012 as Beau Bayh captured the secretary of state’s office and Jessica Bailey prevailed for comptroller.
Democrats also flipped a congressional seat with J.D. Ford’s victory over Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz and at least 21 state legislative seats previously held by the GOP.
Braun last week called the sweeping election gains by Democrats a “wake-up call” and an “opportunity” for Republicans to refocus their agenda on issues of affordability. 
The governor, however, did not mention the election results in remarks issued by the party about Keesling’s resignation. He thanked her for her service and said he would work with the Republican state committee on the search for a new party chair.
“We have a golden opportunity to strengthen our party and address the kitchen-table issues facing families across Indiana,” Braun said in the statement.











The party leadership change also comes as Braun is expected to announce his 2028 re-election bid during a Nov. 16 campaign event.












Johnson, who will be the interim party leader, became the state Republican vice chair when Keesling was elected while also serving as the Montgomery County GOP chair.
He has been deputy chief of staff at the Indiana Department of Transportation since August 2025 after previously working as the agency’s intergovernmental affairs director and as a state Senate staffer.
The GOP leadership change continues the frequent turnover that’s happened since Kyle Hupfer, a confidant of then-Gov. Eric Holcomb, stepped down in August 2023 after six years as state party chair.
Anne Hathaway then led the party for 10 months before Randy Head held the position for five months through the 2024 election, setting up Keesling’s tenure.

description: Democrat Lanon Baccam has been tapped by Gov.-elect Rob Sand to lead his inauguration team. Zach Nunn for Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District seat in 2024 — a race he lost to the Republican incumbent. The son of Tai […]
text:
Democrat Lanon Baccam gave a victory speech at an election watch party held at the New Northwestern in Des Moines after winning the Democratic primary for Iowa's 3rd Congressional District June 4, 2024. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Democrat Lanon Baccam has been tapped by Gov.-elect Rob Sand to lead his inauguration team.
Baccam is likely best known to many Iowans as the Democratic candidate who ran against U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn for Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District seat in 2024 — a race he lost to the Republican incumbent. The son of Tai Dam refugees, he has prior experience in politics, having served in the U.S. Department of Agriculture under former Secretary of Agriculture Tom Vilasck — a previous Democratic Iowa governor — during President Barack Obama and Joe Biden’s administrations. Baccam is also a veteran, having served as a combat engineer in Afghanistan.
Sand announced Baccam will be in charge of planning and coordination for inaugural services as Sand and Lt. Gov.-elect Dave Muhlbauer take office in January, succeeding Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds and the current administration. Inaugural events are set to be held Jan. 15 through 17, 2027, according to the news release.
“I am proud to have Lanon Baccam leading our inauguration efforts as we prepare to begin a new chapter for Iowa,” Sand said in a statement. “Lanon is a dedicated public servant who understands the importance of bringing people together. I know he will help us put together an inauguration that reflects the values of our state and celebrates all Iowans. I’m excited to have him on our team as we prepare to get to work for the people of Iowa.”
Baccam is the latest member added to Sand’s roster as he prepares to become governor. On Monday, Sand announced Abe Rakov would serve as his chief of staff. He also previously announced Elisabeth Buck and Morgan Miller will be co-directors of the Sand Transition Committee, who will work with former Iowa GOP chair Mike Mahaffey and state Rep. Brian Lohse on his transition team.
Baccam said in a statement it was “an honor to serve Governor-Elect Rob Sand and the people of Iowa as Director of the Sand-Muhlbauer inauguration.”
“Throughout my career in the Army and in public service to our state and country, I’ve learned that leadership is about bringing people together, regardless of party, to serve our communities,” Baccam said. “I’m excited to work with Governor-Elect Sand and his administration on planning a successful and historic inauguration that marks a new chapter for our state.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: In his book, SC legislator tells story of son’s death in sextortion scheme
description: Rep. Brandon Guffey wrote 'Tomorrow Needs You' in the hopes of reaching parents, lawmakers and teenagers with his story.
text:
Rep. Brandon Guffey, R-Rock Hill, pictured outside the federal courthouse in Columbia, S.C., with a picture of his son, Gavin, wrote a book in the hopes of teaching people about sextortion and preventing suicides like his son's. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)If you or someone you know needs help, call or text 988, the U.S. suicide and crisis lifeline, or access online chat at 988lifeline.org.
COLUMBIA — After Rep. Brandon Guffey’s son, Gavin, died by suicide following an online extortion scheme in 2022, Guffey didn’t know what to do next.
He turned to the internet for answers, typing in Google searches along the lines of, “My son just shot himself. What do I do?” But he found little actionable help there on how to move forward and deal with the grief he felt, he said.
Three years later, Guffey’s book, “Tomorrow Needs You,” tries to answer that question for other parents, while also trying to prevent them from ending up in that situation at all.
The book, which he started writing about a year ago, came out Oct. 21.
Along with Guffey’s personal story, his book includes practical advice about how to identify and protect children from sextortion schemes, how laws are passed to prevent similar tragedies, and coping mechanisms he found helpful in dealing with his grief.
Those were the sorts of answers Guffey was looking for in the aftermath of his son’s death, said the Rock Hill Republican.
“I hope that some of the things that I’ve learned are there for people that may not have made it there yet,” Guffey told the SC Daily Gazette. “It’s advice that they can follow. It’s something that resonates with them at a point in which it’s needed.”
Gavin’s story
When Gavin Guffey, a 17-year-old recent high school graduate, sent nude photos of himself over Instagram, he thought they were going to a college student in North Carolina.
But he’d been communicating with scammers, not a young woman. Once Guffey had sent the photos, those scammers threatened to share them widely unless Guffey paid them.
Sextortion schemes, as those scams are called, have grown in recent years with the popularity of social media and cellphones.
In 2022, the FBI was aware of more than 7,000 reports of sextortion targeting roughly 3,000 people, according to the most recent data available.
In more than a dozen of those cases, including Guffey’s, the person receiving the messages died by suicide, according to the FBI.
Nigerian man faces life in a US prison for sextortion that led to death of SC legislator’s son

Investigators arrested the man they believed scammed Guffey.
Hassanbunhussein Abolore Lawal, a 25-year-old from Nigeria, signed an agreement last week pleading guilty to producing child pornography by soliciting nude images of a minor, as well as cyberstalking resulting in death.
He is scheduled to officially plead guilty in front of a federal judge in Columbia next month. He faces up to life in prison.
Brandon Guffey would have liked to have had the end of the criminal case in the book as some sort of conclusion, he said. At the same time, though, he didn’t want to delay the release.
“Every day that I feel like we delay is a day that someone that might have needed it doesn’t have it,” he said.
Taking action
Since his son’s death, much of Guffey’s life has rested on a mantra he mentions in his book: “In order to change an emotion, you have to create motion.”
He learned that lesson at Gavin’s funeral, he said. The Guffey men have a tradition of always burying their own, heaping shovels of dirt onto their loved ones’ graves.
Guffey and his two younger sons, then-16-year-old Coen and 4-year-old Callahan, started the burial. Even after Guffey and Coen had passed off their shovels to other men in the family, Callahan kept working, tears cutting through the dirt that stuck to his face, Guffey said.
Guffey asked his son if he was alright.
“‘Yeah, Daddy,’” Guffey recalled his son replying. “‘It helped get the yucky out.’”
From then on, Guffey lived by the idea that work would help “get the yucky out.”
Guffey never struggled with his own mental health until his son died, but in the years since, he has had anxiety attacks and thoughts of suicide, he said. So, he tried to turn those feelings into actions.
His grief propelled him into action at the Statehouse and at a national level. Guffey won a seat in the House that November, having already become the Republican nominee, and immediately started fighting for Gavin’s Law to criminalize sextortion at a state level. That bill became law in 2023.
In the years since, Guffey has remained a staunch supporter of stricter laws around social media both in South Carolina and federally. He has co-sponsored bills to restrict social media use for children and gone to Washington, D.C., to call for Congress to pass similar measures.
Rep. Brandon Guffey, R-Rock Hill, testifying at a U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee meeting on Wednesday, Feb. 19, 2025. (Screenshot courtesy of C-SPAN)
Guffey also runs the nonprofit Less than 3, named after the last text message his son ever sent: “<3,” or a sideways heart. Through that nonprofit, Guffey speaks at schools and other events to raise awareness about sextortion and suicide.
The book is an extension of his advocacy, he said.
“My number one job, I feel like, is to stop the next Gavin from taking his life,” he said.
Working through the grief was difficult, Guffey said.
To keep himself moving, he thought about his next-oldest son, Coen. Guffey wondered what he would advise his son to do if he grew up and lost a child, then tried to follow that advice himself, he said.
“It’s tough to get forward and get moving, but if you want to enact change, you’ve got to get up and get moving,” Guffey said.
Telling the story
Guffey didn’t read the book in full until he started recording the audiobook version, he said.
He wrote one chapter at a time as a way of compartmentalizing, sometimes taking a week away from the page, sometimes several months. That way, he could focus on a single topic or moment, then move on when he finished, since the work was so emotional for him.
The book is a raw reflection of Guffey’s thoughts and feelings as he coped with his son’s death. Some parts use profanity because those were the only words strong enough to describe how Guffey felt at the time, he said.
“I was trying to describe every little detail, every feeling that I had, because I was so hyperaware during this entire process,” he said.
Guffey hopes parents pick up his book so they can learn more about sextortion and have difficult conversations with their children about what to do if they encounter someone trying to coerce them into sending nude photos or money. He wants lawmakers across the country to read it and push for stricter laws about social media use.
More than anything, he wants anyone struggling with their mental health to read the book and see they’re not alone, no matter the situation they’re facing, he said.
“My entire message is, tomorrow needs you,” Guffey said. “But in order to make it to tomorrow, we have to examine today, and I have to be able to look forward to tomorrow.”
Guffey won his re-election bid to the state House last week with 57% of the vote.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: In Alaska’s legislative elections, a handful of races remain undecided nail-biters
description: In the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, candidates in two different Alaska House of Representatives elections are separated by five votes, according to preliminary, partial ranked choice runoff data published by the Alaska Division of Elections on Wednesday night. The winners of those two races are not expected to change the balance of power in the Alaska House, [[...]
text:
People wait in line to vote on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at Scenic Park Elementary School in East Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)In the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, candidates in two different Alaska House of Representatives elections are separated by five votes, according to preliminary, partial ranked choice runoff data published by the Alaska Division of Elections on Wednesday night.
The winners of those two races are not expected to change the balance of power in the Alaska House, which is on course to be controlled by a multipartisan coalition, but they would be significant in determining who represents the state’s fastest-growing region in that chamber.
The Division of Elections doesn’t perform its official ranked choice runoff until Nov. 18, the deadline for the last absentee ballots to arrive internationally, but it publishes preliminary data that allows observers to conduct their own unofficial ranked choice tabulations.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

The Beacon, using data updated by the division on a regular basis since Election Day, has performed multiple tabulations using RCTab, an open-source computer program used to audit ranked choice results across the country.
On Wednesday, elections officials added more than 6,000 ballots, mostly from the Mat-Su, to the statewide total.
In House District 30, which covers the western Mat-Su and the Denali Borough, Republican candidate Doug Massie leads incumbent Republican Rep. Kevin McCabe by just five votes in a hypothetical ranked choice tabulation. An estimated 160 votes are uncounted in that race.
In neighboring House District 29, incumbent Rep. Garret Nelson leads Republican challenger Steve Menard by five votes in a different hypothetical ranked choice runoff. There are an estimated 101 ballots uncounted in that contest.
Other races, including Wasilla’s House District 27, Eagle River’s House District 24 and Homer’s House District 6 also remain too close to call. 
Under Alaska’s general election system, voters rank up to four candidates in a race. If one candidate has at least 50% of the top-rank votes, they win. If no candidate hits that threshold, the person with the fewest top rankings is eliminated.
Votes for them are redistributed to the other candidates, based on the rankings that voters chose. The eliminations continue until two candidates are left. The person with the most votes wins.
Five state House races remain too close to call
In House District 30, initial preliminary ranked choice results showed McCabe trailing by 49 votes, but that gap shrunk as absentee and early votes were counted and added to the Election Day total.
Similarly, Nelson held a substantial lead in initial ranked choice tabulations but has seen his lead shrink as more ballots have been counted.
With more than 100 ballots left to be counted in both races, the result remains undetermined.
In Wasilla, Republican incumbent Rep. Elexie Moore now trails Republican challenger Stephen Wright by 43 votes. Moore led Wright by six votes immediately after Election Day.
For House District 24, where longtime Republican Rep. Dan Saddler has retired, former state legislator and Republican candidate Ken McCarty leads fellow Republican candidate Gina Wall by 52 votes. The Division of Elections reports that more than 1,100 absentee and early votes remain uncounted there.
In Homer, where Republican Rep. Sarah Vance is being challenged by independent Brent Johnson, Vance has a substantial 210-vote lead, but elections officials have yet to count almost 2,400 votes — more than 20% of all ballots cast in that district. 
In both the Eagle River and Homer races, because there are only two candidates, ranked choice tabulations aren’t necessary.
Two Mat-Su races have near-certain winners after rankings
For Alaska Senate District M, which covers Wasilla, Republican candidate Ryan Berry has all but defeated incumbent Sen. Cathy Tilton, R-Wasilla.
In preliminary ranked choice tabulations Wednesday night, Berry had 51.9% of the final vote to Tilton’s 48.1%.
According to ballot data published by the division, voters who backed Republican Zane Vrvilo and Democrat Pat Chesbro in that race have so far preferred Berry to Tilton, pushing the challenger over the top even though Tilton led in first-choice votes.
The percentages are likely to change; rankings have not yet been published for about 270 ballots, and another 268 votes have not been counted, according to Division data.
Republican Rep. DeLena Johnson, R-Palmer, is on course to clinch re-election, according to preliminary ranked choice tabulations from Wednesday. While she has just over 35% of the first-choice votes in a three-way race within House District 25, voters who preferred independent Steve Merritt as a first choice have so far overwhelmingly preferred Johnson to Republican challenger Michael Bowles as a second choice. 
In the latest available tabulation, Johnson finishes with more than 55% of the vote. 
Only 147 votes in that district were known to be uncounted on Wednesday, not enough to change the result.
Ranking data unreliable in close rural Alaska races
The ranking data published by the Division of Elections comes from ballot scanners used by elections officials across the state. In rural Alaska, more than 130 precincts hand-count their ballots, which means ranking data is unavailable until those ballots are mailed to regional or state headquarters.
In southwest Alaska’s Senate District S, Speaker of the House Bryce Edgmon is leading the race to replace Sen. Lyman Hoffman, D-Bethel, but a lack of available data makes his lead uncertain.
Of 7,489 votes counted in that race, ranking data is available for only 4,904 votes. In addition, the Division of Elections has reported 595 early and absentee votes that haven’t been counted at all.
House District 38 is part of Senate District S and faces a similar issue. Rep. Nellie Unangiq Jimmie, D-Bethel, leads a four-person race, but the shortage of available ranking data makes her lead uncertain.

title: Asylum seeker claims he has been jailed illegally by Iowa ICE agents
description: An asylum seeker from India alleges he was in the United States legally for three years before being picked up and illegally jailed in Iowa by ICE agents. In a lawsuit filed last week in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa, Charanpreet Singh, 32, is suing the Polk County Sheriff’s Office, U.S. […]
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is holding dozens of individuals in Iowa jails. (Main photo by Caspar Benson/Getty Images; logo courtesy U.S. Department of Homeland Security)  An asylum seeker from India alleges he was in the United States legally for three years before being picked up and illegally jailed in Iowa by ICE agents.
In a lawsuit filed last week in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa, Charanpreet Singh, 32, is suing the Polk County Sheriff’s Office, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche.
Singh alleges he entered the United States without authorization in April 2018, was immediately apprehended and then was released by an immigration judge after posting a $17,000 bond.
For the past eight years, Singh alleges, he has remained in the United States, established family ties, maintained employment, complied with all conditions of his release, and obeyed all laws while seeking asylum.

On Oct. 26, 2026, Singh alleges, he was traveling in Iowa as part of his employment as a commercial truck driver when he was pulled over by police and instructed to go to a nearby vehicle weigh station. In Iowa and other states, ICE agents are partnering with state law enforcement officials to interrogate, at the weigh stations, any individuals suspected of being in the United States illegally.
Signh’s lawsuit alleges ICE officers at the weigh station questioned him and that he presented the officers with his driver’s license and his work-authorization papers. Despite that, he alleges, ICE officials detained him and then transported him to the Polk County Jail where he now remains.
The lawsuit claims ICE officers provided no explanation for his arrest and provided him with no opportunity to argue that he was free on a bond that was set by an immigration-court judge.
The lawsuit seeks Singh’s immediate release from the Polk County Jail, as well as a court declaration that ICE violated Singh’s rights and unlawfully detained him. A judge has yet to rule in the matter. The U.S. Attorney’s Office, which does not comment on pending cases, has yet to file a response to the lawsuit.



Cameroon man jailed for nine months sues ICE
A native of Cameroon is seeking his immediate release from jail where he claims to have been held by ICE for nine months.
In a lawsuit filed last week in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa, Emoh Yanik Fon, 33, is suing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. (State court records indicate Yanik Fon also goes by the name “Yanick Fon Emoh” which, spelling differences aside, would not be unusual in some West African cultures.)
Yanik Fon, who is from the Republic of Cameroon, alleges he sought refuge in the United States after being subjected to abduction and torture by radical militants in his home country. He alleges he entered the United States without authorization at the Arizona border in March 2023.
In December 2024, the lawsuit states, he was convicted of drunken driving and served two days in jail. In February 2026, he showed up for a routine immigration check-in at an eastern Iowa ICE office, was detained and then sent to the Linn County Jail. Federal court records indicate Yanik Fon now resides in the Muscatine County Jail.
In March 2026, the lawsuit claims, Yanik Fon was summarily denied bond without any individualized assessment as to whether he was a flight risk or posed a danger to the community.
In his lawsuit, Yanik Fan argues he kept all of his scheduled appointments with immigration officials over the past three years, establishing a presumption that he was not a flight risk. His lawsuit seeks a declaration that he was denied his due-process rights and has been unlawfully detained.
A judge has yet to rule in the matter. The U.S. Attorney’s Office, which does not comment on pending cases, has yet to file a response to the lawsuit.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Electricity grid watchdog warns of higher prices after delayed PJM market reforms
description: A capacity auction set for December will again clear the maximum price adding another $5 billion to $10 billion of data center costs to electricity bills across the region, the report said.
text:
The Montour Steam Electric Station rises above farmland the plant's owner wants to rezone to allow Amazon to build data centers. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)Electricity customers in the mid-Atlantic and parts of the Midwest could still be exposed to higher utility costs related to data centers, the independent agency that monitors the region’s wholesale electricity markets warned Thursday. 
That’s despite efforts in the last year by policymakers and PJM Interconnection to isolate the cost of additional generating capacity and connecting hyperscale data centers to the grid, Market Analytics, the independent market monitor for PJM, said.
The market for energy actually used by customers has been competitive in the first nine months of 2026, ensuring that they receive reliable power at the lowest possible price, Market Analytics said in its annual report on the state of the PJM electricity market. 
But the process PJM uses to ensure there’s enough future generating capacity to meet spikes in demand on the hottest and coldest days of the year has not been competitive, mainly because the demand from data centers, many of which have not been built, is still included.
That means a capacity auction set for December will again clear the maximum price adding another $5 billion to $10 billion of data center costs to electricity bills across the region, the report said. 
The capacity cost accounts for about one-fifth of the total cost of wholesale electricity. It increased more than 80% in the first nine months of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025, the report said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We are continuing to get closer and closer to a reliability crisis and an affordability crisis but the solutions are coming forth too slowly,” said Jon Gordon, senior director of Advanced Energy United, a renewable energy industry group.
PJM manages wholesale electricity markets and oversees grid operations for 13 states and Washington, D.C., including Pennsylvania. Its territory spans from New Jersey to parts of Illinois, Kentucky and Michigan and from the New York border to North Carolina. Its policies and decisions affect the electricity bills of 67 million consumers.
Since a July 2024 capacity auction resulted in a record price, state and federal elected officials and regulators have scrutinized the impact of data center development on consumer electricity costs. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro’s office sued PJM and reached a settlement under which prices in future capacity auctions would be capped, initially at $325 per megawatt-day.
Subsequent auctions have resulted in prices at the cap. And, in July, it fell 6,800 megawatts short of its goal to procure standby capacity, needed to ensure supply during times of peak demand.
While smaller data centers have been around since the dawn of the internet, hyperscale data centers for artificial intelligence, that can use as much electricity as a small city, are proposed throughout the PJM region.
In February, the Trump administration and governors of the PJM states adopted a statement of principles designed to insulate household and small business customers from costs associated with connecting and supplying electricity to data centers. 
The administration also reached an accord with major tech companies that it called the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, under which they agreed to obtain their own power supplies.
“PJM has failed to implement the broad public policy mandate reflected in the principles agreed  to by all the PJM governors and the White House, as well as the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, to  ensure that data centers pay their own costs,” Monitoring Analytics said in a news release.
A PJM spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
PJM did propose solutions in submissions to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), which oversees PJM and other system operators around the country. Those proceedings have been closely watched by energy industry leaders across the country as other regions face similar challenges.
FERC, however, rejected a plan to hold a “reliability backstop auction” to ensure reliable electricity supplies by matching data center owners with power plant owners and investors to negotiate directly for powers.
It also rejected much of PJM’s proposed framework to manage large loads like data centers that don’t have their own power supply. Under that plan, large loads would be cut off first when electricity supply on the grid reaches dangerously low levels. PJM has submitted amended proposals.
“The last thing FERC wanted to do is not approve these proposals that would protect ratepayers but they felt they wouldn’t do everything they needed to do, so they sent them back,” Gordon said.
As a result of the delayed approval of PJM’s proposals, the planned reliability backstop auction for data center owners will not take place before December. That means data center loads will remain in forecasts for demand that drive the capacity auctions, resulting in higher prices, he said.
“It’s taking longer than anyone wanted or anybody hoped,” Gordon added.
Marketing Analytics recommended postponing the December auction, which is for capacity in 2029 and 2030, until the reliability backstop auction can be held. 
“It is clear that continuing to simply accept the interconnection of large data center loads that cannot be served reliably … is not a reasonable path forward and is not an efficient or competitive market solution and is not a solution of any kind,” the report said.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Flu activity in Louisiana continues to lead the nation
description: Louisiana has the highest level of influenza activity in the country for a fourth straight week, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
text:
Flu activity in the U.S. as of Oct. 31. Louisiana continues to lead the nation in flu circulation for the fourth straight week in a row. (U.S. Centers for Disease Control)Louisiana has the highest level of influenza activity in the country for a fourth straight week, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. State health officials have recorded six deaths and 208 hospitalizations associated with flu so far this season.
The Centers for Disease Control currently lists Louisiana as one of two states with a “high” level of flu virus circulation, ahead of South Carolina based on the latest available data as of Oct. 31. Texas, Arkansas and Mississippi reported minimal to moderate rates of flu inflections, making Louisiana a stark outlier for the region.
Louisiana began the flu season this fall with a moderate level of circulation that quickly rose. Its flu positivity rate was 14% as of Oct. 31, representing the percent of flu tests that came back positive for the virus. Louisiana’s rate is a full five percentage points higher than the national rate.
Emergency room visits for the flu or flu-like illnesses are also more frequent in Louisiana, accounting for 5.5% of all patients. The rate is above the 2.8% national average and 3.8% regional baseline.
Crystal Rommen, co-director of the advocacy group Louisiana Families for Vaccines, said high rates of illness affect entire communities beyond just the numbers. 
“It’s not just death that is a concern, but missing school, missing work, missing activities in the community,” Rommen said. “It’s a serious thing.”
The surge in flu illnesses comes a year and a half after top Louisiana health officials ended state support for mass vaccination events and directed staff to stop taking part in community health fairs and media campaigns that encourage the public to get vaccinated against illnesses like the flu.   
The February 2025 directive came from former Louisiana Surgeon General Dr. Ralph Abraham, who said previous state-sponsored efforts to promote vaccination were “missteps,” and that individuals should “make their own health decisions” about whether to get vaccinated. 
The Louisiana Department of Health website still says that flu vaccines reduce the number of complications and hospitalizations attributed to the virus.
Abraham left the state surgeon general’s post in December to take a leadership post with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. 
His replacement, Dr. Evelyn Griffin, a Baton Rouge obstetrician and gynecologist, was one of U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s appointees to the CDC’s vaccine advisory panel. She voted to recommend ending requirements for newborns to be immunized for hepatitis B and limit access to COVID vaccines in her time on the advisory panel. 
Rommen said these vaccine policy changes have impacted efforts to promote vaccines and their connection to public health. 
“Right now, it’s hard for people to know where to go for accurate and updated information,” she said. “We did feel like the onus for vaccine education fell onto nonprofit organizations, the individual physicians and providers, organizations that usually trust the state-level leadership to provide robust guidance.”
“When it’s not a very strong recommendation to be up to date on your vaccines, then people don’t necessarily feel the urgency to take time out of their bust day to check their vaccination records and stay up to date,” she added. 
Louisiana also recorded one of the nation’s highest rates of flu activity in 2025, according to the CDC. Over 8,100 people were hospitalized with flu-like illness in Louisiana, behind only Colorado and New York for cases that required a hospital stay.

title: A third of US abortions were provided by non-physicians last year, Guttmacher says
description: In 2025, more than 360,000 abortions — about a third of all U.S. abortions last year — were provided by advanced practice clinicians rather than physicians, according to new data released by the Guttmacher Institute, a think tank that researches and advocates for abortion access.  Twenty-five states and the District of Columbia allow abortions to […]
text:
In 2025, more than 360,000 abortions — about a third of all U.S. abortions last year — were provided by advanced practice clinicians rather than physicians, according to new data released by the Guttmacher Institute. (Photo by Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent)In 2025, more than 360,000 abortions — about a third of all U.S. abortions last year — were provided by advanced practice clinicians rather than physicians, according to new data released by the Guttmacher Institute, a think tank that researches and advocates for abortion access. 
Twenty-five states and the District of Columbia allow abortions to be provided by health providers who are advanced practice clinicians, a category that includes physician associates, advanced practice registered nurses, nurse practitioners, certified midwives and certified nurse midwives. 
The new findings show that abortions provided by advanced practice clinicians – which included both procedures and those by pill – accounted for nearly a third of all abortions nationwide last year, not counting self-managed abortions or those obtained outside the formal medical system. The organization says these types of providers fill a crucial access need at a time of OB-GYN shortages and more than a dozen state abortion bans. 
Arizona nurses say Prop. 139 should give them the right to perform abortions

“These data help to illustrate the critical role that (advanced-practice clinicians) play in providing abortions across the country, including in many underserved communities,” said Isaac Maddow-Zimet, Guttmacher data scientist and study lead, in a written statement. He added that such providers also provide counseling and follow-up care “even in states where they are not permitted to provide direct abortion services.” 
Whether advanced practice clinicians can provide abortions varies by state laws and regulations, with many states limiting the types they can provide to aspiration procedures in the first trimester or pills. Twenty-five states and the District of Columbia allow at least some non-physician occupations to provide abortions. The states include: Alaska, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Montana, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia and Washington.
Arizona, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin could also consider allowing those providers to offer abortions after Democrats won trifectas in this month’s midterm elections and promised to expand abortion access. 
The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends allowing advanced practice clinicians to provide abortions, saying in an issue brief that restricting abortion care provision to only physicians or board-certified OB-GYNs “are not based in science; improperly regulate medical practice; and impede patients’ access to quality, evidence-based health care.” 
In 2016, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration changed the guidelines around the abortion drug mifepristone, permitting advanced practice clinicians such as midwives to prescribe mifepristone.  
In the years since Roe v. Wade was overturned, several states, including Alaska, Michigan, North Carolina and Ohio, have struck down physician-only abortion laws.
An ongoing lawsuit brought by nurses and midwives in Arizona challenges laws barring them from providing abortion, saying they violate the state’s constitutional amendment enshrining abortion rights passed in 2024. 
After striking down many of Missouri’s abortion restrictions earlier this year, a judge upheld that state’s physician-only law, noting the difference in training for different types of abortions.
Stateline reporter Sofia Resnick can be reached at sresnick@stateline.org.

title: Solar panels are an eyesore
description:
Vermont banned billboards to protect its scenery. So why are we ruining our beautiful landscape with solar panels?

text:
Dear Editor,
Have you ever ridden on a hay wagon or a tractor, or baled hay on a hot summer day? It’s hard work, but I’m fortunate to have had these experiences, and I wouldn’t change a thing. If you’ve never stepped in a pile of cow manure or had to shovel it, if you’ve never run into an electric fence — it usually only takes one time — you haven’t lived. 

READ MORE

When I see solar panels on the hillsides and fields, one question comes to mind. In a state where billboards are banned to help preserve rural aesthetic scenic views, why are solar panels allowed? The fields and hillsides, which were once beautiful, are being turned into an eyesore.
Sharon Moulton
St. Johnsbury, Vt.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota Development Fund hits pause as Legislature expected to weigh its future
description: Board members of the North Dakota Development Fund voted Thursday to pause new business while the Legislature weighs potential changes to the state-backed business financing program that drew critical audit findings, raising alarms for some lawmakers. The board also reviewed those audit findings – which included a lack of documentation for millions of dollar[...]
text:
North Dakota Commerce Commissioner Chris Schilken addresses the Legislative Audit and Fiscal Review Committee on Sept. 22, 2026. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)Board members of the North Dakota Development Fund voted Thursday to pause new business while the Legislature weighs potential changes to the state-backed business financing program that drew critical audit findings, raising alarms for some lawmakers.
The board also reviewed those audit findings – which included a lack of documentation for millions of dollars in transactions and inconsistent conflict of interest procedures – and a more recent audit that had lesser, more common findings.
The meeting was the first since the board’s leaders resigned last month. Separately, the Ethics Commission voted to begin an inquiry into the fund in late October.
Additionally, the head of the Legislature’s audit review committee is planning to introduce legislation to repeal the Development Fund and the Commerce Department, though he acknowledged the latter would be a heavy lift.
The Development Fund, created in 1991, provides loans and investments as gap financing to new businesses that might not be able to get loans elsewhere.
Pause
The board voted unanimously to temporarily pause new financing transactions and unsigned applications, effective immediately. The fund’s child care loan program isn’t affected.
Commerce Commissioner Chris Schilken made the motion. Four of the eight board members met Thursday. Two seats are vacant. Two members were absent.
Schilken said it’s prudent to pause as officials and lawmakers consider changes to economic development policies in the 2027 legislative session.
“I think it’s also recognizing that we are addressing some of the issues in the performance audit and taking it seriously,” Schilken said.
The decision allows the board to consider four applications in the review process. The board met during a 30-minute closed-door executive session to discuss companies’ financing applications and active loans and investments.
The board will continue administering its current portfolio, the Commerce Department said in a news release.
Lawmakers seek AG probe after audit finds problems with North Dakota business financing program

Audit talk
For the first time, the Development Fund’s board reviewed the findings of the 2019-2024 performance audit that drew lawmakers’ scrutiny earlier this fall.
Those included insufficient documentation for various transactions and application evaluations, inconsistent conflict of interest and “related party” processes and unverified job data reported by borrowers. The audit found nearly $4 million in funding for five organizations that had relationships with two board members.
Board Chair Joel Brown and Fund CEO Brian Opp said the Development Fund has made improvements, such as stronger documentation and a policy prohibiting “related party” transactions. The fund has no “related party” transactions” now, Opp said. Brown asked a special assistant attorney general to give guidance of what constitutes a “related party” or conflict of interest. 
Brown said it’s up to the Legislature, governor’s office and Commerce Department what the future of the Development Fund is.
“But we do have a responsibility as board and as staff to respond to this audit finding in a constructive way,” Brown said. He suggested that future board meetings include updates on improvements.
The fund provides flexible gap financing, which often puts it in a higher-risk environment, Opp said. 
“It’s really important to recognize that it’s not that anybody’s out here considering and approving or financing outrageous deals,” he said.
Also, Brady Martz representatives walked the board through a financial audit of the last fiscal year that gave the Development Fund overall good marks but for four findings an audit rep said were fairly common. An agreement with the Bank of North Dakota for next year is expected to help improvements, Opp said.
Resignations
Fund Board Chair Jim Albrecht and Vice Chair Rob Lindberg submitted their resignations on Oct. 20, effective immediately. They did not elaborate on their reasons or timing in resignation letters obtained by the Monitor.
Albrecht wrote: “I submit this resignation in support of the Commerce Department’s efforts to work with the legislative body to cast a new vision forward for the NDDF and other funding mechanisms in the State.”
Lindberg wrote: “I extend my best wishes to the Department of Commerce as it and the administration restructure the economic development efforts of the state.”
Albrecht did not respond to a voicemail for comment. Lindberg did not respond to a text message.
One of the board’s first actions Thursday was to unanimously elect Brown as chair for the meeting.
North Dakota Ethics Commission to launch inquiry into Development Fund problems

Ethics inquiry
Last month, the Ethics Commission voted unanimously to begin an inquiry into the Development Fund’s problems, based in part on the decision by Attorney General Drew Wrigley to decline an investigation requested by the Legislature’s audit review panel.
Wrigley cited a legal conflict of interest because his office represents current and former Development Fund board members in a lawsuit. He also said there was no criminal evidence to necessitate referring the matter to another entity to investigate.
Earlier this month, Commission Executive Chair Pam Sharp notified State Auditor Josh Gallion and Opp of the inquiry and requested documents relating to the performance audit and policies and operations of the fund, including conflict of interest disclosures.
Potential repeal legislation
Sen. Jeff Magrum, who chairs the Legislature’s audit review committee, welcomed the Ethics Commission’s inquiry. His committee voted in September to recommend the 2027 Legislature shut down the Development Fund.
Magrum, R-Hazelton, said he is in the early stages of planning legislation for next year to repeal the Development Fund and the Commerce Department and to dissolve or audit various other state grant and loan programs.
“I like that mentality for all of these funds – just get rid of them all and start over again because there should be a component in every one of these agencies to follow all of the money that’s being distributed through them,” Magrum said.
Repealing the Development Fund would encompass transferring its funding to the state’s general fund and handing the administration of its remaining loans to the state-owned Bank of North Dakota, he said.
The Development Fund is legally structured as a nonprofit corporation but functions as a state-administered public economic development entity within the Commerce Department, an agency spokesperson said in September.
The Commerce Department is a necessary state agency for helping the state’s business development and guiding people who want to come to North Dakota, said Rep. Mike Nathe, who helps write the Commerce budget in the Legislature. He said he is open to discussion about what’s working and not working with the Development Fund.
“That’s a legitimate discussion, but to have a bill to do away with Commerce? That’s laughable. That’s not even serious,” said Nathe, R-Bismarck.
This article was updated to correct that Ethics Commission Chair Pam Sharp notified state officials of the commission’s inquiry.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont set aside proposed cuts to disability services. Advocates concerned he’ll reconsider
description: Disability rights advocates called on the Lamont administration to ensure funding for programs serving people with disabilities.
text:
Disability rights advocates gathered Thursday to call on the Lamont administration to safeguard funding for programs serving people with disabilities, including a critical one that makes it possible for people to receive care of their choosing in their own homes, known as Community First Choice.
Advocates are concerned funding cuts Medicaid Home and Community Based Services programs could make it into in Gov. Ned Lamont’s budget next year, after a proposal during the 2026 legislative session threatened to end CFC. That proposal was ultimately abandoned, but it sent shockwaves through the disability rights community.
Walter Glomb, Executive Director of the Connecticut State Council on Developmental Disabilities, said Thursday’s gathering was organized to send a message to Lamont not to mess with disability services.
“Last year we were blindsided by the cuts to CFC which is not a small thing,” Glomb said. 
“I guess we got spooked,” he said.” But then the you know the thought was, ‘OK, what’s next?'” Amid surging Medicaid costs and dramatically shrinking federal aid, reducing spending on programs like CFC could be on the table, he said.
Community First Choice provides those who qualify with autonomy in choosing their own care. Earlier this year, Lamont proposed transitioning people who were using that program to home- and community-based “waiver” programs that are not as flexible and often have long waiting lists.
The move was met with disbelief and protest by those who had been using the program successfully and saw it as a bright spot in an often dismal landscape for those seeking needed support and autonomy. Lorra Jorden, a mother of a child who was using CFC, said at the time that “for the governor to even propose cutting this program is just unbelievably cruel.”
[RELATED: ‘Unbelievably cruel’: Advocates decry threat to home care program]
At Thursday’s event, more than a dozen disability, aging, mental health and civil rights organizations, as well as self-advocates, joined together to urge the governor to support all Medicaid Home and Community Based Services programs, not just CFC.
Several spoke movingly about the impact the programs had on their lives and their autonomy, like Debbie Shaffer, whose thoughts were shared with the assistance of Ruth Grobe, who read from a prepared statement. “Because people with severe disabilities deserve to live with dignity and freedom of choice, with more support, I enrolled in the [Connecticut Home Care Program for Elders] and started to work with an agency to find caregivers,” Shaffer’s statement read.
Shaffer, who uses a wheelchair and has a speech impairment and limited motor skills, added, “At first, I had a hard time because when they tried to match me up with a lot of caregivers, it didn’t work because of my speech. But the agency didn’t give up, and they found a perfect caregiver who has been with me for three years, and I love her.”
Ryan Loosemore, a self-advocate who spoke about CFC, said he broke his neck at age 16 and became quadriplegic. 
“I’ve now been receiving these services for 20 years, and I can tell you firsthand that they changed my life,” he said. “They didn’t just provide me with personal care, assistance. It gave me the opportunity to live independently, work, go to school, build relationships, and become part of my community again. I once felt like the world had forgotten about me. These services gave me my world back.”
Ryan Loosemore, a self-advocate for the Community First Choice program, speaks at a press conference in support of programming for those with disabilities in Connecticut on November 12, 2026 in Hartford.  Credit: Laura Tillman / CT Mirror
The Lamont administration won’t release the governor’s proposed budget until early next year. But for advocates like Loosemore, the programs are just too important to wait and see. 
He called on lawmakers to look beyond the numbers in the budget and ask what the true cost would be of taking the programs away. “Please protect Community First Choice. Protect home and community-based services to make sure future generations of people with disabilities have the same opportunities,” he said. 
“We’re not asking for special treatment. We’re asking for the opportunities to live, contribute, and belong. These services didn’t just help me survive with a disability; it gave you the opportunity to actually live my life.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Nessel launches antitrust lawsuit against Mackinac ferry operator, alleging monopoly
description: Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel has filed an antitrust lawsuit against the Hoffmann Family of Companies, a Florida-based private equity firm, which currently owns all of the passenger ferries that serve Mackinac Island. Nessel’s office alleges that the company’s acquisitions have created an illegal monopoly. “Every tourist, worker, and resident who rid[...]
text:
Shepler's Ferry (Photo by Laina G. Stebbins/Michigan Advance)Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel has filed an antitrust lawsuit against the Hoffmann Family of Companies, a Florida-based private equity firm, which currently owns all of the passenger ferries that serve Mackinac Island. Nessel’s office alleges that the company’s acquisitions have created an illegal monopoly.
“Every tourist, worker, and resident who rides a ferry to the Island must buy a ticket from Hoffmann, and most of them must also pay Hoffmann to park for the duration of their visit,” the lawsuit, which was filed Thursday in state circuit court, argues.
Historically, the island — which does not allow motorized vehicles — had been serviced by three passenger ferry companies, all separately owned. In 2016, the Star Line Mackinac Island Ferry purchased Arnold Transit Company when it went out of business, reducing the number of ferry companies to two; the Star Line and Shepler’s Mackinac Island Ferry. Hoffmann purchased Shepler’s in 2022 and the Star Line in 2024, which had rebranded as the Mackinac Island Ferry Company, eliminating all competition, and has since increased ticket prices for ferry riders. 
The lawsuit also lays out that Hoffmann owns “every dock on the Island, in St. Ignace, and in Mackinaw City that can serve passenger ferries,” as well as “the vast majority of long-term parking near those mainland docks, which most visitors need in order to reach the Island.”
“Hoffman wields enormous monopoly power over two markets essential to the island’s well-being: ferry service to the island and long-term parking for anyone traveling to the island overnight, or even for a quick day trip,” Nessel said in a press conference announcing the lawsuit. “Since they consolidated their control in these areas, eliminating any competition for ferry service or parking, we’ve seen Hoffman do exactly what you’d expect a monopolist to do. They’ve raised prices, limited services, and leveraged their massive power in alarming ways, even threatening to suspend ferry service to Mackinac Island entirely if local government didn’t give them favorable extended agreements to let them keep hiking their prices.”
In the past, when the Mackinac Island City Council has tried to rein in price increases, Hoffmann threatened to cease all ferry service, which the lawsuit describes as essentially holding residents and seasonal workers “hostage.”
“Ferry access to the island is far and away the most common way tourists, visitors, residents, and workers move between the mainland and the island,” Nessel said. “90 to 95% of all traffic to Mackinac Island, which receives more than 1 million guests every year, comes by ferry service from Mackinac City or St. Ignace. That’s also how the island gets much of its freighted goods, including food and medical supplies. In the summer months, the ferry service lines run all day and well into the evening, with large commercial docks on the island and in each mainland city.”
Patrons depart onto a Shepler’s Mackinac Island Ferry dock on Mackinac Island during the Detroit Regional Chamber’s Mackinac Policy Conference. May 26, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
The lawsuit also draws contrasts to the cost-per-minute charge of other ferries in the Great Lakes, including the Miller Ferry from Catawba Island, Ohio, to Put-in-Bay on South Bass Island in Lake Erie, the Kelleys Island Ferry from Marblehead, Ohio, to Kelleys Island in Lake Erie, and the Washington Island Ferry from Wisconsin’s Northport Pier to Washington Island in Lake Michigan — all of which charge around half the price-per-minute of the Hoffman ferries to Mackinac Island. 
Legislation put forward by state Sen. John Damoose (R-Harbor Springs) and signed by Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in June sought to increase the ability of the island’s local government to restrict fare increases and exert oversight over the ferry companies. That law was approved by voters on Mackinac Island in the November general election.
But the lawsuit notes that the oversight in the legislation will be delayed in going into effect — Hoffmann said publicly after the ballot measure passed that “it will continue to operate under its existing franchise agreements, which run through June 30, 2027, and that the new law cannot modify those agreements and will not affect the 2027 season.”
The lawsuit is seeking “divestiture and other structural remedies to reopen these markets to competition, provide consumers with meaningful choices, and ensure fair market conditions for residents, businesses, and visitors,” a press release from Nessel’s office explained. 
Asked what those remedies might entail — including whether Hoffmann could be forced to sell one of its ferry companies — Nessel said the details would be up to the courts. 
Assistant Attorney General Jonathan Comish said the court could also seek to increase competition among parking operators, adding, “There were three separate ferry lines, so we would seek the court to force the divestiture of some ferry operations. Now, that’s a delicate procedure, often involving investment banks and lots of consultants to make sure that the transaction goes through in a way that’s healthy and restores competition in the long term.”
A statement from the Hoffmann Family of Companies noted that they are aware of the lawsuit and will respond in court, and are “confident we will prevail, because we are not violating state or federal antitrust laws.”
“As a reminder, the federal court has already twice rejected the City of Mackinac Island’s antitrust claims in its federal litigation against us,” the statement continued. “Most important: In April, AG Nessel issued a statement encouraging all parties to resolve the ongoing disputes. We wholeheartedly agreed with her and are in active mediation. We believe this lawsuit threatens to derail those efforts. While we are surprised and disappointed by this development, our goal remains the same: reaching agreement on a viable contract extension that serves the public interest and ensures sustainable ferry service for years to come.”
Comish addressed questions about the previous lawsuits, which were dismissed for lack of standing.
“The city asserted antitrust damages, which is a tricky thing that you have to allege in a private antitrust lawsuit saying that the harms you suffered were linked to anti-competitive conduct,” he explained. “Since we are the sovereigns, we don’t have to meet that requirement. So we have the ability to bring a lawsuit against anyone who violates our antitrust laws just because they violated the laws, so we get to skip that step.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Mackinac Island Mayor Margaret Doud said in a statement released by Nessel’s office that the city’s goal has been to ensure the ferry system serves the public.
“This was never only an Island issue. More than 1.5 million people travel to Mackinac Island each year, and many of them are Michigan families,” Doud said. “Over 80% of the Island is designated as Mackinac Island State Historic Parks, which belongs to the people of Michigan. The State has stepped forward on their behalf, and we are grateful.”
Advocates who have supported the legislation and ballot initiative on the island also shared appreciation for Nessel’s lawsuit. 
“The Legislature and governor previously acknowledged our concerns about higher costs we all face when one company owns both ferry services. Their approval of SB 304 led to more than 90% of voters approving a city charter amendment on November 3 that protects residents, workers and visitors,” said John Sellek, a spokesperson for Fair Access to Mackinac Island Coalition, in a press release. “Our goal remains a swift and fair resolution between the City and the ferry owner that ensures affordable, reliable and uninterrupted ferry service for everyone.”
Nessel also took time in her press conference to address her hopes for antitrust enforcement under her successor, Eli Savit, as she will leave the office at the end of 2026. She noted that Michigan has among the weaker antitrust laws, meaning that the attorney general’s office must often be the one to respond.
“State law doesn’t require adequate pre-merger and pre-acquisition notices to state agencies, unlike many other states in the country that do require these notices, and that means oftentimes my office and others with an interest in maintaining competitive markets have to rely on reactively because we aren’t able to get involved proactively,” she said. “I strongly recommend that the next legislature address this issue, and I am hopeful the attorney’s office, the attorney general’s office, will remain under my successor as a strong advocate for these kinds of changes in the law.”
She compared Michigan’s antitrust operation, which only has one full-time antitrust attorney, to Washington’s, which has 15 full-time antitrust attorneys despite having a smaller population than Michigan.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Sioux Falls Democrat seeks recount in state Senate race
description: One of the five losing South Dakota legislative candidates with a race close enough for a recount has asked for one. Democrat Aaron Matson filed a recount request Thursday afternoon. The deadline to file for a recount is three days after the state canvass of election results. The canvass took place Tuesday. Matson lost the […]
text:
Minnehaha County election workers run general election ballots through a tabulator on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)One of the five losing South Dakota legislative candidates with a race close enough for a recount has asked for one.
Democrat Aaron Matson filed a recount request Thursday afternoon. The deadline to file for a recount is three days after the state canvass of election results. The canvass took place Tuesday.
Matson lost the District 11 Senate race to Republican incumbent Chris Karr, the chamber’s president pro tempore, by 35 votes out of a total of 8,385 votes cast. The district is in southwest Sioux Falls.
Democrats gain seats in South Dakota Legislature for the first time since 2008

The recount process is conducted by a board appointed by a local judge, consisting of a Republican attorney serving as recount referee and two other members, one each from the Republican and Democratic parties. The recount must be completed within 14 days of the recount petition’s filing.
The remaining four candidates whose close races on Nov. 3 met the recount threshold told Searchlight they don’t intend to ask for a recount.
Under South Dakota law, losing candidates can request a recount if the number of votes separating them from the winner does not exceed 2% of the total number of votes cast for all candidates in a Senate race, or 2% of twice the average number of votes received per candidate in House races.
District 11 Republican Rep. Keri Weems was 129 votes behind Republican Rep. Brian Mulder, who came in 43 votes behind Democrat Sonja Mentzer. The top two vote-getters in a House of Representatives race go to Pierre.
Making up for a 129-vote deficit “is not even in the realm of possibility, from my standpoint,” Weems said.
Weems’ race was the next-closest contest among the five where a recount would be possible. Democrats fell short in the remaining three.
One of them, District 3 House candidate Erin Ronayne Rudner, told Searchlight she might have considered a recount if her Aberdeen-area race were as close as Matson’s.
The 143-vote victory of Republican Timothy Hanigan for the second of two House seats, however, “is a big chasm to leap.”
“I have faith in our Brown County Auditor’s Office to do their jobs right,” said Rudner, whose race was the only one within recount margins outside the Sioux Falls metro area.
Weems sounded a similar note on her candidate Facebook page on Nov. 4.
“I believe in the integrity of our elections and respect the democratic process,” she wrote.
Pending a recount in the Karr-Matson race, the partisan split for next year’s Legislature is 92 Republicans, 12 Democrats and one independent.



Recount-eligible legislative candidates and spread

District 11 Senate: Republican Chris Karr over Democrat Aaron Matson, 35 votes
District 11 House: Republican Brian Mulder over Republican Keri Weems, 129 votes
District 12 Senate: Republican Kari Shanard-Koenders over Democrat Joe Zweifel, 134 votes
District 3 House: Republican Timothy Hanigan over Democrat Erin Ronayne Rudner, 143 votes
District 9 House: Republican Megan Tschetter over Democrat Amanda Potter, 157 votes

description: An Iowa biodiesel plant operated by Chevron U.S.A. Inc. that shuttered in 2024 is set to restart according to a news release from the company Thursday.  Operations at the Ralston facility will be supported by a feedstock agreement with Landus Cooperative, according to the release. The northern Iowa facility, which was closed in 2024 due […]
text:
An Iowa biodiesel facility is set to restart. Pictured is a truck driver in Urbandale filling up a truck with biodiesel. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)An Iowa biodiesel plant operated by Chevron U.S.A. Inc. that shuttered in 2024 is set to restart according to a news release from the company Thursday. 
Operations at the Ralston facility will be supported by a feedstock agreement with Landus Cooperative, according to the release. 
The northern Iowa facility, which was closed in 2024 due to a “market downturn” in biodiesel, has a production capacity of 42 million gallons per year, or enough to fuel more than 275,000 18-wheelers, according to the release. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The “timing and scope” of workforce additions are “still being assessed,” according to the release, and the company plans to follow a “staged process” for the restart with activities around staffing, maintenance, safety and operational-readiness initiating before production resumes. 
Andy Walz, the Chevron president of downstream, midstream & chemicals, said the restart “reflects improved market conditions” and the company’s “commitment” to meeting customer energy demands. The news release said the restart will help to increase regional biodiesel availability, support the broader diesel fuel market and “provide increased opportunities for soybeans raised by Iowa farmers.” 
“Bringing Ralston back online will enable additional biodiesel production capacity while supporting the communities and customers we serve,” Walz said in the statement. 
Iowa Renewable Fuels Association celebrated the news Thursday, with its Executive Director Monte Shaw saying the restart was the “biggest sign yet of the powerful impact of the robust” renewable fuel standard blending levels finalized by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. 
“A major facility is coming back online, creating new demand for Iowa-grown soybeans and creating good-paying jobs in rural Iowa,” Shaw said in a news release. “IRFA strongly urges the Trump Administration to maintain the RFS and to reject any actions that would reverse course. As the saying goes – if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it.”
The EPA finalized in March what the industry referred to as “historic” RFS targets, which stipulate how much biofuel must be blended into U.S. transportation fuels. 
On Monday, governors from Louisiana and Alabama wrote to Trump administration leadership asking for a partial waiver of RFS obligations for the 2027 compliance year in their states. The governors alleged the requirements to blend biofuels “imposes” additional cost at the pump when gas and diesel prices are already high.
Shaw opposed the move from the governors on Monday and argued that reducing supply would not help to lower fuel prices and that instead, Congress should “unleash” ethanol and U.S. supply by approving the year-round, nationwide sale of E15 fuels.
On Thursday Shaw said the Chevron restart shows that the RFS numbers “translate into real investments, real markets for farmers, and real jobs in rural communities.” 
Chevron decided to close the Ralston facility, and another biodiesel production site in Wisconsin in March 2024 due to poor market conditions. Stakeholders blamed the market downturn on low blending standards from the EPA that year. 
Eric Heismeyer, the president and CEO of Landus, said the coop was “proud to collaborate” with Chevron to restart the plant. Landus’ Ralston facility processes more than 28 million bushels of soybeans a year, according to the news release from Chevron. Soybeans are a primary feedstock for biodiesel fuel. 
“The combination of soy processing and biodiesel production at the Ralston site has long represented a powerful partnership among our companies, communities and stakeholders,” Heismeyer said in the release.
