title: Creighton’s $24M ‘Central Park’ fuels downtown Omaha redevelopment
description: OMAHA — Beneath a backdrop of fireworks and blue smoke, Creighton University on Thursday opened a $24 million amphitheater and gathering space expected to bring new energy to the campus and Omaha’s urban core. Dubbed “the Quad,” the roughly 250,000-square-foot quadrangular grassy area features a fountain plaza and picnic areas and also is referred to as […]
text:
A nearly 6-acre gathering space and amphitheater opened Thursday at the Creighton University campus in downtown Omaha. It is to be the epicenter of student life and fuels redevelopment in the urban core of Nebraska's most populated city. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — Beneath a backdrop of fireworks and blue smoke, Creighton University on Thursday opened a $24 million amphitheater and gathering space expected to bring new energy to the campus and Omaha’s urban core.
The Creighton University “Quad” project was designed by OJB Landscape Architecture and constructed by Kiewit Corp. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
Dubbed “the Quad,” the roughly 250,000-square-foot quadrangular grassy area features a fountain plaza and picnic areas and also is referred to as the university’s “Central Park.”
It is among the largest physical reshapes of the private Jesuit university founded in 1878 — and is part of roughly $1 billion in total Creighton-led investment in downtown Omaha between 2015 and 2030. That includes public and private partnerships.
Creighton’s president, the Rev. Daniel Hendrickson, was joined at the ribbon-cutting event by key donors and guests and said city officials have supported the university’s growth spurt.
“They know that this is an investment in the urban core and the way our city functions,” he said. 
Hendrickson said university leaders could have constructed a library or parking garage on the nearly 6-acre area at 22nd and Burt streets, which used to be baseball and softball fields that have been rebuilt in grander fashion on the east side of campus.
But he said they held off to create a “transformational” space. The Quad — surrounded by residence halls, the School of Dentistry building, Ahmanson Law Center and the Harper Center — is envisioned as the epicenter of campus activity and will host signature events such as graduations, alumni reunion weekends and freshman orientation.
$300M Creighton donor-funded plan aims to reshape part of downtown Omaha

Student surveys in recent years also have pointed to additional natural green space as a way the campus could be improved. The park project is entirely donor-funded.
Open for the public to stroll or visit, the nearly 200-tree park area comes as Creighton welcomed 8,948 students this fall, which the university said is an overall enrollment record. 
Other development continues on the downtown urban campus, including a 50,000-square-foot athletics facility for Creighton’s 300-plus student athletes. Set for completion next year, that facility is part of a nearly $300 million donor-funded initiative of 11 new or upgraded facilities and outdoor spaces across a 12-block corridor of downtown Omaha.
Aerial view of Creighton University’s newly opened green space nicknamed The Quad. (Photo courtesy of Creighton)

name: California
title: Estos profesores a tiempo parcial ganan mucho dinero impartiendo decenas de clases en línea. ¿Están aprendiendo sus alumnos?
description: No existen normas que regulen cuántas clases pueden impartir los profesores de colegios comunitarios. Algunos están sacando provecho de ello.
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
A medida que proliferan las clases en línea, los profesores de los colegios comunitarios han encontrado una solución ingeniosa: reempaquetar cursos similares para cientos de estudiantes a la vez e impartir más de una docena de clases en un solo semestre.
 La profesora Thien-Huong Ninh Villarreal tiene al menos dos puestos fijos de tiempo completo en colegios comunitarios, además de trabajos de medio tiempo recurrentes durante los últimos 12 meses en UC Berkeley, Cal State Sacramento y otros siete colegios comunitarios. Este otoño, imparte 30 clases de sociología, estudios étnicos y negocios a aproximadamente 1100 estudiantes. 

En 2024, con prácticamente la misma carga académica, ganó casi 800,000 dólares, según los registros públicos de nóminas. CalMatters intentó contactarla en tres ocasiones para obtener sus comentarios, pero nunca respondió.
 Se espera que los profesores de los colegios comunitarios evalúen el progreso de los estudiantes y les brinden apoyo directo sin la ayuda de auxiliares docentes, aunque esto es prácticamente imposible a tal escala, afirmó Sarah Thompson, presidenta de la Asociación de Profesores de Colegios Comunitarios de California. «Obviamente, nadie tiene tiempo suficiente en una semana para impartir 30 clases y hacerlo bien, así que esto es muy problemático».
 Sin embargo, Chris Ferguson, vicerrector ejecutivo de la oficina que supervisa los colegios comunitarios de California, afirmó que tener varios puestos docentes no es, por sí solo, prueba de una mala enseñanza. En un comunicado enviado por correo electrónico a CalMatters, Ferguson, quien dirige las finanzas y las iniciativas estratégicas de la oficina, indicó que tener varios puestos sería un problema si la carga de trabajo del profesor impide el nivel necesario de interacción, retroalimentación, evaluación o apoyo al alumnado. En ese caso, señaló que el distrito universitario —y no el sistema universitario estatal— debería ser el responsable.
 CalMatters analizó los registros públicos de nómina de la organización sin fines de lucro Transparent California y los cotejó con datos de cursos universitarios. El análisis reveló que al menos 70 profesores adjuntos, o a tiempo parcial, recibieron pagos de cinco o más distritos de colegios comunitarios, campus de la Universidad Estatal de California o de la Universidad de California en el mismo año, incluyendo muchos que impartieron más de 10 clases por semestre.
 Algunos de estos profesores figuraban entre los empleados mejor pagados de los 116 colegios comunitarios de California. Ninh Villarreal ganó más que cualquier otro administrador de colegios comunitarios en 2024, incluso más que Sonya Christian, la rectora del sistema de colegios comunitarios del estado, según un análisis de CalMatters.
 La mayoría de los más de 70 profesores no respondieron a las múltiples solicitudes de comentarios. Otros pidieron a CalMatters que no publicara los datos, que son de dominio público, por temor a cómo podrían afectar a su empleo.
 Estos profesores no están infringiendo ninguna norma. De hecho, no existen normas que impidan a los profesores adjuntos de los colegios comunitarios impartir clases en más de un distrito.
 Andrew Vanden Heuvel, profesor adjunto de astronomía, declaró a CalMatters que imparte aproximadamente 50 clases y prácticas de laboratorio en línea desde la oficina situada encima de su garaje en un pequeño pueblo a orillas del lago Michigan.
 Casi todas sus clases están pregrabadas y los estudiantes pueden escucharlas cuando quieran. Se llama enseñanza asíncrona. En la UC, la Universidad Estatal de California y, sobre todo, en los colegios comunitarios del estado, este tipo de clases en línea son populares y están muy extendidas , lo que representa un cambio importante desde la pandemia de COVID-19.
 Vanden Heuvel comentó que ha impartido clases a hasta 1000 estudiantes por semestre en todo el país, incluyendo Santa Mónica, Salinas, San José y Visalia, además de escuelas en Nuevo México, Michigan, Washington y Florida. Explicó que las clases utilizan diferentes versiones del mismo contenido, en su mayoría introductorio, sobre estrellas, galaxias y el sistema solar. Los estudiantes leen información en línea, interactúan con simulaciones astronómicas en línea, ven videos o entregan prácticas de laboratorio.
 “En su formato actual, no califico nada a mano”, dijo Vanden Heuvel. Todos los cuestionarios son de opción múltiple y se califican por computadora, una característica común en muchas clases en línea, no solo en la de Vanden Heuvel. Algunos estudiantes también entregan trabajos escritos, que él suele calificar mediante un algoritmo que solo verifica si el trabajo fue entregado o no.
Según comentó, alrededor del 20% de sus cursos se imparten en California. «En California, puedo ganar hasta ocho veces más que en Florida». En 2024, las universidades de California le pagaron un total de aproximadamente 320,000 dólares, según el análisis de CalMatters. A nivel nacional, ganó mucho más, afirmó. «Revisando mis registros, puedo asegurarles que 2024 fue el año con mayores ingresos». Dijo que ganó 758,485.12 dólares ese año.
 Los profesores a tiempo completo ganan dinero
 Por ley, los profesores adjuntos generalmente solo pueden impartir tres clases por semestre en un único distrito de colegios comunitarios, y cada distrito establece sus propias normas. La mayoría de los trabajos a tiempo parcial son precarios, sin cobertura médica, sin garantía de empleo y con contratos temporales. Los colegios pueden retirar a los profesores adjuntos sus clases —y su salario— con muy poca antelación.
 Para los líderes sindicales y docentes, quienes llevan tiempo denunciando que los profesores adjuntos están mal pagados y sobrecargados de trabajo , la carga laboral de profesores como Ninh Villarreal y Vanden Heuvel resulta impactante. «No sé cómo pueden ganar tanto dinero, cómo pueden tener tantas tareas. Es una locura», declaró Jim Mahler, presidente del consejo de colegios comunitarios de la Federación de Maestros de California. Añadió que sospecha que algunos profesores simplemente graban sus clases y las reproducen. 
Estudiantes trabajando en sus computadoras portátiles en el patio central del Fresno City College, el 13 de agosto de 2025. Foto de Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters/CatchLight Local.
 Según los registros, para ganar más de 400.000 dólares, muchos de los profesores adjuntos mejor pagados de California también tenían puestos de titularidad a tiempo completo o con posibilidad de titularidad. Por ejemplo:

 Bobby Seals, profesor de estudios étnicos, tiene un puesto de tiempo completo en Evergreen Valley College en San José. Además, imparte 14 cursos más en otros cuatro distritos de colegios comunitarios, además de la Universidad Estatal de San José, lo que suma un total de aproximadamente 930 estudiantes este semestre.
 Faramarz Mortezaie es el director del departamento de informática de Mission College en Santa Clara. Además, imparte a tiempo parcial 11 clases en otros campus, incluyendo la Universidad Estatal de San José.
 Nicholas Nardi, profesor de psicología a tiempo completo en el Santa Ana College, imparte además 11 clases en otras seis instituciones, entre ellas Cal State Los Angeles.
 Timothy Durfield, profesor de negocios a tiempo completo en Citrus College, imparte además otras 10 clases en cuatro distritos de colegios comunitarios.
 Walter Meyer, profesor titular de historia del arte en el Santa Monica College, imparte además 10 clases en línea a estudiantes de los condados de Los Ángeles y Kern.

 Ninguno de estos profesores respondió a las solicitudes de comentarios.
 Ninh Villarreal, la persona con mayores ingresos, ha tenido con frecuencia al menos dos empleos de tiempo completo, según funcionarios universitarios y registros públicos. Ha sido profesora titular en Cosumnes River College en Sacramento desde 2016. En 2023, obtuvo un segundo empleo de tiempo completo en Reedley College cerca de Fresno, aunque volvió a trabajar a tiempo parcial menos de un año después. En 2025, obtuvo la titularidad en San Joaquin Delta College en Stockton, y ese mismo año, documentos oficiales de la universidad muestran que fue la primera docente con posibilidad de titularidad en el departamento de estudios étnicos de West Valley College en Saratoga, cerca de San José. Cade Story-Yetto, portavoz del distrito que abarca West Valley College, dijo que Ninh Villarreal ya no trabaja allí y se negó a responder otras preguntas. 

 CalMatters contactó a casi todos los 73 distritos de colegios comunitarios del estado para recabar opiniones sobre su metodología antes de la publicación. Transparent California , un grupo de expertos independiente que aboga por un gobierno limitado, obtuvo información sobre las nóminas directamente de los distritos universitarios. Posteriormente, CalMatters utilizó esos datos para elaborar una lista de profesores que impartieron clases en cinco o más distritos de colegios comunitarios, campus de Cal State o de la UC en 2024, que es la información más reciente. Los datos se corroboraron mediante catálogos de cursos, directorios del profesorado y documentos de contratación de las universidades.
 Si bien algunos profesores impartieron algunas clases presenciales, generalmente en los campus de Cal State o UC, el análisis de CalMatters reveló que muchos de los que enseñaban en cinco o más distritos universitarios dependían en gran medida de la instrucción en línea y asíncrona. 
 Nadie lo está rastreando
 Las universidades tratan los cursos en línea de la misma manera que las clases presenciales: los estudiantes obtienen la misma cantidad de créditos y, por lo general, los profesores reciben el mismo salario. A medida que los cursos en línea se han vuelto más comunes, los sistemas de la UC, Cal State y los colegios comunitarios han invertido millones de dólares en fondos estatales para garantizar que tengan el mismo rigor que los cursos presenciales.
 Los colegios comunitarios evalúan la calidad de todos los cursos, pero no tienen forma de saber cuál es la carga de trabajo real de un profesor. Los distritos de colegios comunitarios de California se gestionan de forma independiente y nadie lleva un registro de quién imparte clases en cada distrito ni cuántas clases da.
 Los sistemas de Cal State y UC, que son más pequeños y centralizados que los colegios comunitarios, controlan el empleo y limitan el número de cursos que cada profesor puede impartir. Sin embargo, si el profesor también imparte clases en un colegio comunitario, es posible que no tenga forma de saberlo.
 Vanden Heuvel, el profesor de astronomía, afirmó que cree que sus alumnos reciben una excelente educación. «Doy clases en varias escuelas porque esa experiencia me brinda la estabilidad que necesito como profesor adjunto para sobrevivir y prosperar», dijo, refiriéndose a sus tres hijos, su esposa, que es maestra de primaria, y la necesidad de estar presente con su familia en lugar de tener que desplazarse de un campus a otro cada día. «Ahora bien, ¿me he extralimitado en mis funciones, más allá de lo que algunos consideran moralmente aceptable? No lo creo».
 Los investigadores afirman que no está claro si los cursos en línea son peores o mejores que la educación presencial tradicional. Los estudiantes, especialmente los adultos que trabajan y que predominan en el sistema de colegios comunitarios, elogian los cursos en línea por su conveniencia, pero existen desventajas conocidas. Las clases asíncronas, en particular, históricamente han ofrecido a los estudiantes menos interacción con sus profesores, lo que, según las investigaciones , perjudica el éxito estudiantil . 
Estudiantes trabajan en la biblioteca del San Bernardino Valley College, el 30 de mayo de 2023. Foto de Lauren Justice para CalMatters.
 Cómo impartir 50 clases en un semestre
 Vanden Heuvel publica gran parte del material de su curso en YouTube , donde sus canales suman casi 5 millones de visualizaciones, repartidas en más de 300 vídeos. En sus vídeos, se muestra carismático y cercano, llevando a sus alumnos en coche e incluso publicando vídeos durante sus vacaciones en Disney World. Según él, su ubicación no es ningún secreto; siempre ha sido transparente sobre dónde vive, tanto con las universidades de California como con sus estudiantes.
 De hecho, la primera lección de una de sus clases es un vídeo en el que se presenta y lleva a los alumnos a su lugar favorito, el lago Michigan, donde nació su pasión por la astronomía.
 Las leyes estatales y federales exigen que los profesores interactúen con sus estudiantes, especialmente en los cursos en línea asíncronos. Esta interacción puede incluir fomentar la participación en clase o supervisar el rendimiento académico de los estudiantes, escribió Ferguson, vicerrector de finanzas, en su comunicado enviado por correo electrónico. «Estos requisitos se aplican a todos los cursos, independientemente de la cantidad de universidades o distritos que empleen al profesor». El gobierno federal ha reforzado sus propias normas para las clases en línea en los últimos años.
 Vanden Heuvel comentó que presta su teléfono móvil personal a todos los estudiantes y que recibe hasta 30 correos electrónicos al día, la mayoría solicitando prórrogas para la entrega de trabajos. Aseguró que responde a todos los correos.
 Según él, sería muy fácil para los estudiantes hacer trampa usando IA, sobre todo porque los cuestionarios son de opción múltiple y la mayoría de las tareas escritas se califican solo al completarlas. «La lógica es equivalente a la del Scantron (una máquina de calificación de opción múltiple) en el aula magna. Es una práctica docente defendible evaluar de esa manera. Así es como se realizan muchas evaluaciones, ya sea el GRE o el LSAT. No me convence».
 La promesa de la educación en línea es llegar a un gran número de estudiantes y reducir el costo por alumno, afirmó, y eso es precisamente lo que está haciendo al impartir 50 clases y laboratorios en línea a hasta 1000 estudiantes en todo el país. En algunas escuelas, especialmente en zonas rurales, Vanden Heuvel es el único profesor de astronomía.
 Afirmó que sus prácticas docentes a gran escala representan su experimento “más exitoso”, aunque reconoció que muchos profesores no lo verán con buenos ojos. 
‘No soy una fábrica de educación de ese tipo’
 En cada uno de los 73 distritos de colegios comunitarios de California, el profesorado a tiempo parcial, cuyo costo de contratación es menor, supera en número a los profesores titulares, en algunos casos en una proporción de más de 5 a 1. Este mismo desequilibrio se observa en muchos campus de Cal State, aunque sus profesores adjuntos, conocidos como conferenciantes, pueden trabajar a tiempo completo y recibir beneficios. La UC, centrada en la investigación, cuenta con categorías de profesorado que no existen en Cal State ni en el sistema de colegios comunitarios, lo que dificulta las comparaciones.
Es bien sabido que los profesores adjuntos imparten clases en varios distritos, pero los sindicatos suelen argumentar que lo hacen por necesidad. Tina Leonard, profesora de lengua de señas americana, es un ejemplo perfecto. En 2024, ganó poco más de 84,000 dólares impartiendo clases en cinco distritos de colegios comunitarios.


“Soy sorda”, escribió en un correo electrónico, “y es muy difícil y competitivo para un educador sordo conseguir un puesto fijo a tiempo completo en Lengua de Señas Americana (ASL)”. Dijo que aceptó trabajos de enseñanza adicionales en 2024 para cubrir el costo de sus impuestos. “Cada universidad retiene como si fuera tu único trabajo, así que cuando sumas todas, puedes terminar debiendo dinero”.
 K. Frindell, presidenta de la federación de sindicatos de profesores California Community College Independents, afirmó no estar sorprendida de ver a muchos docentes impartiendo clases en varios distritos, incluso algunos que ganan cientos de miles de dólares. «Se ha creado una laguna legal», declaró, que permite a los distritos reducir costos contratando profesores adjuntos y, a su vez, permite a estos últimos impartir clases en múltiples distritos.
 De hecho, se desconoce el número total de profesores adjuntos en los colegios comunitarios de California, ya que los recuentos estatales no incluyen a los profesores que imparten clases en varios distritos, explicó Ferguson. El sistema de la Universidad Estatal de California (Cal State) tiene el mismo problema con los datos.
 Los profesores adjuntos suelen ser contratados para el año académico y luego recontratados cada otoño. Numerosas propuestas legislativas han intentado, sin éxito, brindarles oportunidades de mayor remuneración , beneficios o empleo a tiempo completo . En 2022, los legisladores intentaron aumentar los beneficios para los profesores adjuntos de colegios comunitarios, destinando 200 millones de dólares a los distritos para que estos reembolsaran el seguro médico al profesorado a tiempo parcial. En el año académico 2024-25, casi 7000 profesores adjuntos utilizaron el programa, de los cuales muy pocos impartían clases en varios distritos. Muchos distritos optaron por no participar, y la mayor parte del dinero permanece sin gastar. 
 Noah Thomas, profesor del departamento de arte del Long Beach City College, en el campus de Long Beach el 3 de agosto de 2026. Fotografía de Ariana Drehsler para CalMatters.
 Noah Thomas, profesor de arte en un colegio comunitario, comentó que investigó los nuevos beneficios de atención médica, pero los encontró insuficientes. “Es un sistema muy complicado y los subsidios son bastante bajos”, dijo. “La cobertura solo me aplica a mí y no a mis dependientes, y solo dura 10 meses al año porque mi contrato es de solo 10 meses”.
Thomas ganó poco más de 100,000 dólares en 2024 viajando diariamente entre cinco distritos de colegios comunitarios en los condados de Orange y Los Ángeles, donde impartía clases presenciales de artes plásticas. A veces, los viajes son tan largos y los días tan apretados que come en su coche, comentó. «Económicamente, me encantaría dar tantas clases como pudiera. 800.000 dólares suena increíble. Pero no soy una fábrica de educación como esa. Realmente me encanta enseñar a los estudiantes individualmente y mostrarles cómo cortar un trozo de cartón y usar una sierra de cinta».
 El dilema moral
 Frindell, representante de los sindicatos de colegios comunitarios independientes, afirmó que la solución no radica en centrarse en los profesores que imparten múltiples clases en línea y perciben salarios elevados de seis cifras. Su objetivo es acabar con los bajos salarios, la precariedad laboral y las leyes restrictivas que obligan a los profesores adjuntos a impartir clases en varios distritos.
 CalMatters preguntó a los líderes de la educación superior en la Asamblea y el Senado estatales sobre los profesores adjuntos que imparten clases en varias instituciones. El asambleísta demócrata de Alhambra , Mike Fong , el asambleísta republicano de San Diego , Carl DeMaio, y la senadora demócrata de Riverside, Sabrina Cervantes, no respondieron.
 Debido a las normas estatales y federales que exigen que los profesores interactúen con sus estudiantes, Vanden Heuvel rediseñó algunos de sus cursos, añadiendo nuevos tipos de tareas. A veces, comentó que las normas parecen haber sido «inventadas para impedir que la gente haga lo que yo hago», aunque añadió que, de ser así, suelen ser ineficaces. «En la práctica, se percibe como un mero trámite administrativo que no guarda relación con una experiencia estudiantil significativa».
 Aun así, comentó que ha buscado la aprobación de otros educadores sobre las implicaciones morales de impartir clases a tantos estudiantes en tantas asignaturas, incluso si legalmente está dentro de los límites. «Lo que me dicen, ya sea por amabilidad o no, es que la educación superior se aprovecha sistemáticamente de los profesores adjuntos, y que si uno ha creado un sistema que le permite prosperar a la vez que ofrece una educación excelente, ¡enhorabuena!».
 Al final de cada semestre, Vanden Heuvel comentó que les pide a sus alumnos que evalúen el curso y que, sistemáticamente, coinciden en que su calidad y los conocimientos adquiridos están muy por encima de la media, y que su dificultad es similar a la media. «Siempre existe la sensación de preguntarse: “¿Lo que estoy haciendo está bien o no? ¿Me estoy excediendo un poco?”»
 Publicó por su cuenta un libro de 600 páginas que recopila reflexiones de estudiantes, principalmente sobre cómo su relación con los planetas, las estrellas y las galaxias cambió gracias a su clase. Dijo que el libro está en su oficina, justo al lado de su escritorio.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Missing and Murdered Indigenous Peoples task force proposes creating state-level office
description: New Mexico state lawmakers in the upcoming legislative session may consider a proposal to create a state-level office dedicated to the crisis of Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons.
text:
The family of Melanie Marie James stand in front Berg Park in Farmington on May 5, 2022, to raise awareness for Missing and Murdered Indigenous People. A state MMIP task force told lawmakers on Nov. 12, 2026, that they’re seeking feedback on a proposal to create a state-level MMIP office in the upcoming legislative session. (Photo by Cyrus Norcross for Source NM)New Mexico state lawmakers in the upcoming legislative session may consider a proposal to create a state-level office dedicated to the crisis of Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Members of the New Mexico Department of Justice’s MMIP Task Force testified Thursday in Santa Fe before the interim Indian Affairs Committee, where they said “many members” of the task force have been advocating for a state-level office.
State lawmakers had several questions for the task force members about how such an office would coordinate with other state agencies. The task force members said they have had varying levels of success getting in touch with state agency heads and hope to make more progress in the weeks between Gov.-elect Deb Haaland’s inauguration and the beginning of the legislative session.
“While there has been really strong interest and we want to push this forward, we do recognize the need for additional expertise and guidance to determine how such an office should be structured, what its responsibilities should include,” Birga Alden, a task force member who also works as the chief communications officer of the anti-human trafficking nonprofit New Mexico Dream Center, said at Thursday’s hearing held at the Santa Fe Indian School. “We welcome your input as we continue to develop the proposal.”
Previously, New Mexico had an MMIP task force within the state Indian Affairs Department. Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham scrapped the task force in 2023, and New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez created one within his New Mexico Department of Justice in early 2024 after the Legislature passed a joint memorial directing him to do so.
Any legislative proposals will come during Haaland’s first term as governor. Haaland, a member of Laguna Pueblo, previously served as secretary of the U.S. Department of the Interior, where she established a Missing and Murdered Unit within the Bureau of Indian Affairs. At the time, she said the unit would coordinate with tribal governments, law enforcement agencies and families of missing people to help address the crisis.
Before her June primary election for the Democratic gubernatorial nomination, Haaland told Source NM that she would revisit the state Indian Affairs Department’s defunct task force and “be transparent about the issue and bring people to the table and find out what we need.”
State Sen. Shannon Pinto (D-Tohatchi), a Diné woman who chairs the interim Indian Affairs Committee, said that efforts to find missing and murdered Indigenous people often proves difficult because “jurisdiction has always been the conundrum.”
“We shouldn’t be having to do this because our current law and our justice system — it’s for everybody,” she said. “There should be no conundrum on having any kind of action taken for a loved one…but that’s not where we are with this issue.”

name: VTDigger
title: Chittenden parents file lawsuit challenging Vermont’s new public tuition rules
description:
A family is suing the state in federal court, arguing that Vermont’s 2025 education reform law is unconstitutional because it excludes religious schools from receiving public tuition dollars. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Chittenden parents file lawsuit challenging Vermont’s new public tuition rules.
text:
Champlain Valley School District school busses in Hinesburg in Jan. 2026. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Two Chittenden parents are suing the Vermont Agency of Education in federal court, alleging Vermont illegally excludes religious schools from being eligible for the state’s public tuition program for private schools. 
The lawsuit, filed by Carrie and Greg Bishop, alleges that the requirements for private schools to receive public tuition dollars under Vermont’s 2025 education reform law “create a de facto religious exclusion” that violates the First Amendment. 
“They’re not receiving equal treatment, yet they deserve equal access to public funding alongside other families in the state,” said Jacob Reed, the lawyer representing the Bishop family, in an interview. Reed works for Alliance Defending Freedom, a conservative Christian legal organization based in Arizona that is increasingly involved in state politics and has previously challenged the constitutionality of Vermont’s public tuition program.  
The Bishop family alleges they’re experiencing religious discrimination. And their lawsuit isn’t the first of its kind. 
Toren Ballard, a spokesperson for the state Agency of Education, declined to comment on the ongoing case. The Vermont Attorney General’s Office is representing the agency in the suit, he said. 
Some rural school districts in Vermont lack public schools for all grades. Through the state’s public tuition system, families can send their kids to private schools or public schools in another district on the public dime. About 3,500 kids in Vermont received public tuition as of 2024, according to the education agency. 
Private religious schools were formerly included in the program and saw an influx of public dollars in recent years. But that practice ended in 2025 when the state passed a wide ranging education reform law, Act 73, that created new qualifications for private schools to be included in the tuition program. 
To qualify under the new law, a school had to be in a district that doesn’t operate a public school for some or all grade levels and at least 25% of their student body from the 2023-24 school year had to be funded by a Vermont public school district. 
After the passage of Act 73, only 18 private schools — none of which is religious — qualified for the public tuition program.
While Act 73 eliminated all religious schools from the tuition program, it eliminated an even larger number of secular schools, according to court documents from a previous lawsuit challenging the law. Eighteen secular schools were eliminated from the program, while 15 Catholic and Christian schools were eliminated. 
“The idea is to have, frankly, as many Vermont kids under the roof of Vermont’s public schools as possible, in order to have that scale and reduce our-per pupil costs,” said Rep. Peter Conlon, D-Cornwall, who chairs the House Education Committee and helped craft Act 73. 
The tuition program exists, Conlon said, because lawmakers recognize that public schools aren’t easily accessible in some parts of the state. 
But Reed sees things differently. 
“What is happening here is people of faith are essentially being treated as second-class citizens,” said Reed, who specializes in representing Christian ministries and religious schools in First Amendment cases.

READ MORE

Courts in Vermont  and around the country have long grappled with the legality of excluding religious schools from receiving public tuition. 
The U.S. Supreme Court issued a landmark 2022 decision in Carson v. Makin, ruling that Maine’s public tuition program, which is similar to Vermont’s, couldn’t deny funds to some parents based on how they exercise their religion. The decision reverberated through Vermont and opened up more public tuition funds for religious schools — until the 2025 law went into effect. 
Alliance Defending Freedom has filed at least five lawsuits challenging Vermont’s public tuition system, although not all of them address the state’s 2025 law, according to Reed. The firm also represented the Mid Vermont Christian School, which sued the state in 2023 after it was banned from participating in state athletics because it forfeited against a team with a transgender player. 
A federal appeals court ruled in the school’s favor in September 2025 and said its teams must be allowed to participate, but returned the case to the lower court for further action. Last year the school also filed a new legal lawsuit challenging Act 73. A decision in the case is still pending, Reed said. 
The Bishops’ legal challenge explains why they allege religious discrimination. 
“Public schools teach evolution, which conflicts with the Bishops’ religious teachings that God created the universe in seven days,” the lawsuit said. The lawsuit also said that the Bishops’ older sons “faced backlash and scrutiny” for bringing their bibles to public school with them. 
The family lives in the Barstow Unified Union School District, which only has public schools through eighth grade. Rather than sending their daughters to public schools through the tuition program like they did with their sons, the couple wanted to send their daughters to a religious school. 
The couple decided to send their daughters to Mount St. Joseph Academy, a Catholic school in Rutland, according to the lawsuit. The private school doesn’t qualify for the state’s tuition program because it’s within a district that has a public high school, according to the lawsuit. 
The Bishops, in their lawsuit, are asking their school district to pay for one of their daughters, who is a senior in high school, to attend the Catholic school and to allow her participation in the state’s dual enrollment program, which offers high schoolers college courses free of cost. Students in private schools only qualify for dual enrollment if they receive public tuition. 
The complaint names Vermont Education Secretary Zoie Saunders, as well as the State Board of Education and the Barstow Unified Union School District, as defendants. 
“Religious families want to be treated equal. They sue. They get in, and then Vermont changes the law or does some sort of work around to exclude them again. And obviously, that’s unconstitutional,” Reed said. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Chittenden parents file lawsuit challenging Vermont’s new public tuition rules.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Scott Colom makes history in Mississippi. Two other Black men did the same 150 years before him
description: This photo combo shows from left, Hiram Revels and Blanche Kelso Bruce.
text:
When Scott Colom takes the oath of office for the U.S. Senate in January, he will not be the first Black senator from Mississippi to make history. But he will be the first in nearly 150 years and the first chosen by voters rather than state lawmakers.
U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during his election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Colom, a Democrat, was declared the winner Wednesday over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
Here are some things to know about the two previous Black senators from Mississippi, Hiram Rhodes Revels and Blanche Kelso Bruce.
The first Black member of the U.S. Congress
Revels became the first African American to serve in either chamber of Congress when he took his Senate seat on Feb. 25, 1870.
Born to free parents in North Carolina in September 1827, he traveled throughout the country as an adult doing religious work and educating other Black people, according to biographies on National Park Service and U.S. Senate websites. After the Civil War, he settled in Natchez, Mississippi, where he served as presiding elder of the African Methodist Episcopal Church.
Revels was elected as a Natchez alderman in 1868 and was one of 35 Black men elected to the state legislature the next year. Mississippi’s U.S. Senate seats had been vacant since the state seceded from the Union in January 1861. Revels was selected by his fellow state legislators to fill one of the seats, and a white man was chosen for the other.
“An opportunity of electing a Republican to the United States Senate, to fill an unexpired term occurred, and the colored members, after consulting together on the subject, agreed to give their influence and votes for one of their own race for that position, as it would in their judgement be a weakening blow against color line prejudice,” Revels later recalled, according to a U.S. Senate website.
Revels was seated two days after Mississippi was readmitted to the Union and served just over a year, until March 3, 1871, when his term ended.
The last Black senator from Mississippi
The Mississippi legislature chose Bruce to be the first African American to serve a full term in the U.S. Senate. He was seated in 1875 and became the first Black man to preside over the Senate in 1879. Born into slavery in 1841 — his father was a white man who owned his mother — Bruce was the only formerly enslaved person to serve in the U.S. Senate, according to the Senate and National Park Service websites.
Bruce was born in Virginia and his father moved his plantation operation to Mississippi, where Bruce began picking cotton at age 8. He escaped to Kansas early in the Civil War, established a school for Black children in Missouri in 1864 and attended Oberlin College in Ohio for two years before a lack of funds caused him to withdraw.
He returned to Mississippi, where he became a wealthy businessman and landowner and held several positions in local government before he was elected to the U.S. Senate by state lawmakers. He served in the Senate from 1875 to 1881.
Unlike Colom, Mississippi’s previous Black senators were Republicans
Reconstruction, the 12-year period after the Civil War from 1865 to 1877, was when the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments were adopted, abolishing slavery, establishing birthright citizenship and prohibiting denial of the right to vote “on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.”
The Republican Party was the party of President Abraham Lincoln during the Civil War. He issued the Emancipation Proclamation on Jan. 1, 1863, declaring all enslaved people in rebellious states “are, and henceforward shall be free.”
A total of 17 Black men served in the U.S. Congress during Reconstruction, 15 in the House of Representatives and Revels and Bruce in the Senate. The Senate wouldn’t have another Black member until 1967, when Sen. Edward Brooke of Massachusetts took office as the first Black person to be popularly elected to that body.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Recounts for 3 legislative races, Kennebec County commissioner seat set for next week
description: The Maine Secretary of State’s Office announced Thursday that it will hold four recounts next week, three for races for Maine Legislature and one for a Kennebec County commissioner seat after several close finishes in last week’s midterm election.  First up will be Maine Senate District 18, which includes parts of Oxford, Androscoggin and Cumberland […]
text:
Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026 in Maine: a voter fills out a ballot in the polling station at Scarborough High School. (Photo by Jim Neuger / Maine Morning Star)The Maine Secretary of State’s Office announced Thursday that it will hold four recounts next week, three for races for Maine Legislature and one for a Kennebec County commissioner seat after several close finishes in last week’s midterm election. 
First up will be Maine Senate District 18, which includes parts of Oxford, Androscoggin and Cumberland counties, which will begin Monday at 9 a.m. 
The seat was previously held by Sen. Rick Bennett, who left the Republican Party last year before running for governor as an independent.
Democrat Elizabeth Bosworth and Republican John Andrews are currently neck and neck. The Portland Press Herald/ Associated Press reported Andrews with a lead of less than 20 votes, but the Bangor Daily News, which works with Decision Desk HQ, called the race for  Bosworth, with her ahead by 50 votes. 
In a Facebook post Wednesday, Bosworth declared victory and said it was Andrews’ right to request a recount. 
“I’m looking forward to being sworn in this December and getting to work lowering costs and delivering for working Mainers in our district,” Bosworth said. 
On Tuesday, the secretary’s office will hold the recount for Maine House of Representatives District 96. The Lewiston district is currently represented by outgoing Democrat Michael LaJoie, but Republican Kerryl Clement appears to have a narrow lead over Democrat Luke Jensen. 
The AP/Portland Press Herald has both candidates at 50% but with Clement ahead by 38 votes.
“Given the many occurrences of voter intimidation that have happened in Lewiston throughout this election cycle, a recount is entirely appropriate and the right thing to do for voters in District 96,” Jensen wrote in a Facebook post.
The recount for House District 106 will be held on Wednesday. Republican Barbara Bagshaw currently holds the Windham seat, and is running for reelection against Democrat Bradley Youngs. Bagshaw appears to be lagging behind Youngs, The AP/Portland Press Herald reported Youngs ahead by just over 130 votes. 
Bagshaw told Maine Morning Star she received dozens of calls from constituents encouraging her to ask for a recount. 
“Nobody believes that I lost,” she said, pointing to the number of signs supporting her she saw around town. 
In a Facebook post, Youngs said he was aware of the recount and is confident in the results. 
Following a wave of Democratic victories nationally and in Maine, the party expanded its power in both chambers last week. If Bosworth retains her hold on Senate District 18, Democrats will hold a supermajority in the upper chamber. In the House, Republicans lost roughly a dozen seats and are expected to begin the next session with 61 of 151 seats if neither House Republican prevails in their recounts.
The final recount will be held Thursday, for the District 2 seat on the Kennebec County Commission. The Morning Sentinel reported last week that Republican Joseph Pietroski Jr. was reelected to the position, defeating Noel Madore by just 57 votes. 
The recounts will all take place at the Maine Public Safety Building at 45 Commerce Ave., Augusta and will be open to the public, and streamed online at the secretary’s office Youtube page. 
Eesha Pendharkar contributed reporting to this story.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: FTC, Utah and 16 states strike $63 million settlement with Family Dollar over pricing allegations
description: The Federal Trade Commission and 17 states — including Utah — have reached a $63 million settlement with Family Dollar stores over allegations that the company routinely overcharged customers at the register more than its shelf and tag prices.  “When money is tight, every dollar matters,” Utah Attorney General Derek Brown said in a prepared […]
text:
A Family Dollar store is pictured in Grantsville, Utah on Nov. 12, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)The Federal Trade Commission and 17 states — including Utah — have reached a $63 million settlement with Family Dollar stores over allegations that the company routinely overcharged customers at the register more than its shelf and tag prices. 
“When money is tight, every dollar matters,” Utah Attorney General Derek Brown said in a prepared statement issued Thursday. “Utah families shouldn’t have to worry that the price at checkout will be higher than the price they saw on the shelf. This settlement puts money back in consumers’ pockets and helps ensure shoppers get the prices they were promised.” 
Under a proposed order filed Thursday in U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia for the settlement, Family Dollar will be required to create a $40 million fund to pay restitution to eligible customers and a $20 million discount program for Family Dollar customers. 
The company will also be required to pay about $3 million to divide up to the states that filed the complaint against the company. Along with Utah, those states include Alabama, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Nebraska, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee and Wisconsin. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The settlement order also prohibits Family Dollar from misrepresenting the prices of its goods or services and requires the company to create a pricing accuracy program to regularly check prices and train employees to spot pricing errors. That program will also need to be independently reviewed and certified every year. 
The company will also be required to post notices in its stores, and on its website and app telling customers they may be eligible to receive payment as part of the settlement. 
In the settlement order, Family Dollar “neither admits nor denies any of the allegations” included in the states’ and FTC’s complaint. 
“The FTC is committed to ensuring price transparency and fairness so consumers can make informed choices,” Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a prepared statement. “Today’s order will ensure Family Dollar stops deceiving consumers about its prices and returns money to consumers harmed by these practices.” 
Family Dollar operates more than 7,000 stores across the nation, “and for many of its customers, shopping at Family Dollar is unavoidable,” the complaint against the company says. 
“Its locations are concentrated in low-income urban and rural communities, including areas Family Dollar itself describes as ‘food deserts,’ where residents have little access to full-service grocery stores,” the complaint says. “For many families in these neighborhoods, Family Dollar stands as one of the only accessible sources for basic household necessities.”
Many Family Dollar customers are “carefully stretching every dollar they have to cover basic needs,” the complaint says, “yet Family Dollar routinely charges more at checkout … including for essential household products such as milk, eggs and diapers.” 
“For consumers living paycheck-to-paycheck, even a slight price increase at checkout can lead to real, adverse consequences,” the complaint says. 
The complaint alleges Family Dollar “knows that it harms customers by persistently overcharging prices at the register that are higher than those it advertises,” and that scope of the company’s “unlawful pricing conduct is extensive.” 
“Since 2022, federal, state, and local regulators have cited Family Dollar for thousands of pricing violations, resulting in fines exceeding $3 million,” the complaint says. “And since 2024, Family Dollar has entered into multiple settlements with state Attorneys General, paying over $800,000 in penalties for inaccurate pricing.”
The settlement with Family Dollar comes after the FTC and 20 states, including Utah, filed a complaint on Oct. 26 against another dollar store chain, Dollar General, alleging similar deceptive pricing practices. 
The litigation against Dollar General is ongoing.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Amid clash with U.S. attorney, Sen. Blumenthal says he won’t be ‘bullied’
description: A U.S. attorney warned the CT senator over his inquiry into the White House ballroom. Blumenthal pushed back that he won't be 'intimidated.'
text:
U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal engaged in a written back-and-forth this week with a U.S. attorney over the role of congressional oversight, setting up an early preview of when Democrats regain the majorities next year and prioritize investigations into the Trump administration.Blumenthal, in his capacity as the leading Democrat on the Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, has already launched a number of congressional inquiries from the minority, including one looking into private donors helping to finance the construction of a ballroom at the White House and whether they got preferential treatment from the administration.
He expects to return as chairman of that panel next year in the Senate.
But this week, the White House and the U.S. Department of Justice are giving a prelude into how they plan to respond — and fight back — against investigations and inquiries conducted by congressional Democrats over the final two years of Trump’s term.
“They’re clearly trying to intimidate us and deter and discourage our uncovering the truth about corruption,” Blumenthal said in an interview on Thursday. “It would be ludicrous if it were not so serious, and they’re misusing and weaponizing the prosecutorial power of the Department of Justice.”
Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, posted a letter on social media Wednesday afternoon that was directed at the Connecticut Democrat and how he’s conducted an inquiry into the ballroom project. Reitz accused Blumenthal of threatening citizens who are donating and associating themselves with the president.
Reitz requested that Blumenthal preserve all documents, communications and “all potentially relevant evidence related to your efforts to suppress associational activities for philanthropic projects throughout the nation’s capital.”
“Failure to do so may result in sanctions, adverse-inference instructions, or other penalties, and may carry significant legal consequences,” Reitz wrote. “This demand applies to you, your staff, employees, agents, consultants, campaign personnel, and any other person acting on your behalf or in concert with you.”
Blumenthal said he sees that request as a threat of initiating an investigation, arguing it’s an attempt “to intimidate members of Congress for engaging in constitutionally protected activity.” He wrote back that Americans deserve to know who’s donating money to Trump’s projects “and whether lawsuits were dismissed, contracts were awarded, or regulations went unenforced in exchange for that money.”
In an interview with The Connecticut Mirror Thursday, Blumenthal said one of those donors, Nvidia, will be “front and center.” The tech company donated $25 million to the project, according to The Washington Post. 
Blumenthal said his subcommittee will investigate whether Nvidia “received more favorable treatment on its requests for chips” and whether Trump ignored intelligence about the company’s CEO Jensen Huang and his ties to a suspected Chinese spy, with whom he had an affair. Huang resigned on Thursday following those revelations.
The Connecticut senator sent his own letter responding to Reitz on Wednesday night with a request similar to the prosecutor’s: preserve all correspondence, documentation and “all communications with the White House or senior officials at the Department of Justice, related to the decision to draft and post your letter.”
“Not only are these appropriate subjects for congressional oversight, but such inquiries are among the constitutional duties that members of Congress must undertake to become informed about matters on which legislation may be necessary,” Blumenthal wrote.
When reached for comment about Blumenthal’s letter, Reitz referred to his response to the senator over the platform X.
“Received. Valid investigations must be conducted for a legitimate legislative purpose,” Reitz posted. “I believe that your threatenings may constitute the initiation of unconstitutional investigations conducted for reasons other than a legitimate legislative purpose. Semper Fidelis.”
The pushback to Blumenthal and his inquiries comes as the White House more broadly seeks to set the tone on how it plans to respond to investigations stemming from Congress.
White House counsel William Scharf sent a letter earlier this week to U.S. Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, warning about what they see as the  limitations of congressional oversight and implications of criminality, according to The New York Times.
“Beyond being inconsistent with the clear, well-recognized constitutional limitations on your investigative functions, threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality,” Scharf wrote in the letter. “And issuing unlawful subpoenas with the intention of depriving citizens of their constitutional rights and privileges may warrant further investigation.”
Garcia had a similar response to Blumenthal and noted in a statement that the Constitution provides the legislative branch with the authority to conduct oversight.
Blumenthal has co-led a series of public forums with Garcia, seeking to cast a light on the practices and conduct of federal immigration agencies, such as U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, under the Trump administration. Blumenthal said he expects a “very cooperative working relationship” with Garcia from the majority next year.
As Democrats gear up for majorities in both the Senate and House in early January, Blumenthal won’t likely be the only member of Connecticut’s delegation who will conduct oversight from their committee perches.
Several Connecticut lawmakers are expected to claim the gavel of committees that have varying levels of jurisdiction and issue areas. But there’s a common theme: They plan to wield their influence around oversight of the administration.
U.S. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-3rd District, appears poised to return next year as the head of the House Appropriations Committee. U.S. Rep. Jim Himes, D-4th District, will likely be appointed as the chair of the House Intelligence Committee. And U.S. Rep. Joe Courtney, D-2nd District, is expected once again chair of the Armed Services’ Seapower and Projection Forces Subcommittee.
U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes, D-5th District, is also running in a contested race to become chair of the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
The House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence has oversight over U.S. intelligence agencies as well as some issues concerning the Pentagon and other government agencies. As a potential chairman, Himes has previewed oversight as a main objective.
Himes has already issued warnings to defense companies about cooperating with congressional oversight, specifically on a potential investigation into corporate donations for the construction of the White House ballroom.
DeLauro has said she envisions handling some oversight “in my lane” by taking a look at where federal dollars are flowing and whether some money “has been transferred illegally.”
Courtney also see opportunities for oversight, whether that’s on the Air Force One plane gifted by Qatar or the White House’s battleship proposal. He believes oversight over the war in Iran and U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s tenure will be “front and center” for the full House Armed Services Committee. (House Republicans blocked an effort on Tuesday to impeach Hegseth over his handling of the war.)
Blumenthal said Thursday he and his colleagues will move forward with their investigations for the remaining weeks of the session and as they move into the majority in the 120th Congress.
“The whole purpose of this letter is simply to intimidate,” Blumenthal said. “I absolutely refuse to be bullied or threatened in this way. We’re going to continue our investigation undeterred.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Conservative group sues UNC-Chapel Hill over access to course materials
description: A conservative group is suing UNC-Chapel Hill, accusing the university of violating state public records law by failing to provide reading lists and other instructional materials for 29 courses. Defending Education filed the lawsuit this week in Orange County Superior Court. The group says the university failed to properly respond to two public records reque[...]
text:
UNC Chapel Hill. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NCNewsline) A conservative group is suing UNC-Chapel Hill, accusing the university of violating state public records law by failing to provide reading lists and other instructional materials for 29 courses.
Defending Education filed the lawsuit this week in Orange County Superior Court. The group says the university failed to properly respond to two public records requests, submitted in October, seeking materials used in courses during the fall 2026 semester.
The courses span several departments, including African American studies, history, political science, sociology and women’s and gender studies. They include “Defining Blackness,” “Black Feminism,” “Feminism and Political Theory,” “Critical Food Studies,” and “Slavery and the University.”
Defending Education’s complaint does not explain why the group selected these 29 courses. NC Newsline has reached out to the group for an explanation.
The first request, submitted Oct. 16, sought materials for 19 courses. The second, submitted Oct. 23, sought materials for 10 additional courses.
UNC-Chapel Hill closed both requests without providing additional documents, according to the lawsuit. Instead, the university directed the organization to Simple Syllabus, an online platform where faculty members post course syllabi.
Defending Education argues that the platform does not include all the materials used in courses. The requests also sought reading assignments,  course plans, materials shared with students through email and documents posted on Canvas, the university’s learning management system.
The complaint says UNC’s policy requires faculty members to use Simple Syllabus, but limits the information they must include. For example, faculty members are directed to list course materials students are required to purchase, while other instructional materials can be shared through other means, including Canvas and email.
The organization says that the university failed to conduct a reasonable search for the requested records, including materials maintained by instructors and documents stored on university systems.
UNC system faculty condemn proposed policy disclosing course materials to public

UNC-Chapel Hill did not immediately respond to NC Newsline’s request for comment. 
Sarah Parshall Perry, vice president and senior legal fellow at Defending Education, said the university’s alleged refusal to provide the materials prevents taxpayers from understanding what public universities are teaching. 
“The University of North Carolina’s sleight-of-hand over production of its course materials is no excuse for shirking its obligations under the North Carolina Public Records Act.” Perry said in a statement. “Taxpayers in the state have every right to know what their money is funding at North Carolina’s institutions of higher education, and we look forward to the university finally complying with its statutory obligations.”
Defending Education is a national conservative education advocacy group founded in 2021. It says it works to promote transparency, free speech and parental rights in K-12 and higher education. 
This is the latest chapter in a broader effort by conservative groups to scrutinize teaching at universities in the state and across the country. Last year, The Oversight Project, a conservative group affiliated with the Heritage Foundation, requested course materials from 74 UNC-CH classes, seeking content related to diversity, race, gender. 
The university denied the request, citing faculty intellectual property rights.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Advocates renew push for Minnesota Equal Rights Amendment
description: Democratic lawmakers gathered with advocates for an Equal Rights Amendment at the Minnesota Capitol Thursday to launch their latest campaign to add to the state Constitution sweeping protections that prohibit discrimination based on race, national origin, disability, gender identity, sex and pregnancy — including one’s decision to become pregnant or terminat[...]
text:
Rep. Leigh Finke, DFL-St. Paul, spoke at a press conference surrounded by Equal Rights Amendment advocates at the Minnesota Capitol on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Michelle Griffith/Minnesota Reformer)Democratic lawmakers gathered with advocates for an Equal Rights Amendment at the Minnesota Capitol Thursday to launch their latest campaign to add to the state Constitution sweeping protections that prohibit discrimination based on race, national origin, disability, gender identity, sex and pregnancy — including one’s decision to become pregnant or terminate a pregnancy.
During the last Democratic-Farmer-Labor trifecta in 2024, the Minnesota Equal Rights Amendment nearly passed but stalled at the last minute because of disagreements among Democrats about the amendment’s language. Democrats will enter the 2027 legislative session with another trifecta — this time with greater margins — and ERA advocates are confident that they will be able to pass legislation next year to put the question before voters. 
“Equality shouldn’t depend on who holds office, who’s making those laws,” said Sen. Mary Kunesh, DFL-New Brighton, who is a chief author of the legislation. “It’s clear that those words must be enshrined in our Constitution, not just for today, but again for the future generation.”
If the Minnesota ERA passes the House and Senate, Minnesotans would be asked on the 2028 ballot to support or oppose the ERA. The measure would require a majority of total votes cast — not voting on it would be akin to a “no” vote.
Democratic lawmakers on Thursday said passing the ERA legislation is among Democrats’ top priorities in 2027 and anticipate early passage; the session begins Jan. 12.
Dozens of states have passed legislation to add gender, race and class protections to their constitutions, but Minnesota’s proposed amendment will be inclusive of more classes, such as gender identity and abortion rights. Minnesota’s ERA advocates say their ballot measure will be similar to New York’s, which went into effect last year.
Ballot measures do not require the governor’s signature, but Gov.-elect Amy Klobuchar has expressed openness to supporting the latest ERA effort.
Critics of Minnesota’s ERA proposal say that including gender identity and abortion rights protections in the state Constitution infringes on their religious freedom. The current ERA language does not include religion as a protected category — though religion is already protected in the Minnesota Constitution’s Bill of Rights.
The Minnesota Human Rights Act, which is in statute and not the Constitution, currently protects Minnesotans from discrimination — in employment, housing, public services, public accommodation and education — based on race, color, creed, religion, national origin, sex, gender identity, marital status, disability, sexual orientation and status with regard to public assistance.
Some critics also say the measure gives too much authority to the judicial branch, which will be responsible for remedying alleged violations of the ERA’s protections.
Minnesota’s ERA advocates say they are finalizing the language, but note it will largely match the language lawmakers considered and nearly passed in 2024.
“It is long past time for us to recognize the values represented in the Equal Rights Amendment and to put them into the Constitution,” said Rep. Leigh Finke, DFL-St. Paul, who is also a chief author of the legislation. “No matter who you are, where you come from, or why you are here, you deserve to be treated equally under the law. That is what we are fighting for.”

name: Delaware
title: Delaware home-care providers seek $26.6 million in rate increases
description: Providers and families say higher payments would help retain nurses and aides who support people receiving care at home DOVER, Del. — Delaware home-care providers are asking the state to increase reimbursement rates in the next budget, saying higher payments would help keep nurses and aides with the families who depend on them. The Delaware Association for H[...]
text:
Delaware Association for Home and Community Care’s proposal calls for a 25.5% increase in private-duty nursing rates and a 10% increase in personal care service rates. Association Executive Director Sue Getman estimated the respective costs at $7.3 million and $19.3 million.
Providers and families say higher payments would help retain nurses and aides who support people receiving care at home
DOVER, Del. — Delaware home-care providers are asking the state to increase reimbursement rates in the next budget, saying higher payments would help keep nurses and aides with the families who depend on them.
The Delaware Association for Home and Community Care estimates the requested increases would cost the state $26.6 million, according to WMDT’s report on testimony at the Nov. 10 public budget hearing at the Delaware Public Archives in Dover.
The proposal calls for a 25.5% increase in private-duty nursing rates and a 10% increase in personal care service rates. Association Executive Director Sue Getman estimated the respective costs at $7.3 million and $19.3 million, WMDT reported.
Those amounts are the association’s estimates, rather than figures confirmed by the state. www.wmdt.com
The appeal comes as the Department of Health and Social Services develops its fiscal 2028 spending request. For providers, the issue is retaining workers. For families, it is maintaining dependable care that allows loved ones to remain at home.
Families describe the stakes
Providers, nurses, parents and disability advocates testified about the importance of consistent care and the disruption families face when a nurse leaves, according to WMDT.
Heather Holveck, the grandmother and legal guardian of a child with disabilities, described the uncertainty that comes with possible staff turnover.
“Knowing that there is a potential that even our current nurses could leave is terrifying for him because then we’re starting over,” Holveck told WMDT. www.wmdt.com
The testimony highlighted how reimbursement decisions can affect daily life for people who rely on in-home support. Retaining familiar caregivers can help families preserve established routines and relationships.
Different services, different rate histories
The providers’ appeal also raises questions about how Delaware has adjusted payments for different types of home care.
State records, however, describe more recent increases for some services.
In February 2024 testimony to the Joint Finance Committee, the Division of Medicaid and Medical Assistance said it would implement personal care service increases retroactive to July 1, 2023. dhss.delaware.gov
That testimony does not establish whether the increases applied to every service or provider covered by the current request. The scope of the 18-year statement remains unconfirmed, and it cannot be applied broadly to all home-care payments based on the available records.
The association is seeking separate increases for private-duty nursing and personal care services, making the distinction between those payment categories important to evaluating the request.
State proposes additional funding
DHSS’ Nov. 10 budget presentation includes approximately $2.6 million for a first-phase home and community-based services rate increase among its discretionary requests for fiscal 2028.
The presentation does not explain how that proposal relates to the association’s request or which portions of the providers’ proposal it might address.
DHSS also identified improving services for people with complex needs and lowering health care costs among its priorities. budget.delaware.gov
The providers’ request will compete with other spending proposals as the governor and lawmakers develop the budget.
What happens next
The November public hearings help shape the governor’s recommended budget, which is released in January.
Joint Finance Committee hearings follow, with legislative budget work continuing through the spring and final budget bills considered in June. www.budget.delaware.gov
For families who testified, the request puts a personal question before budget writers: whether the payments supporting care at home are sufficient to keep the workers they rely on.

Request: A 25.5% increase for private-duty nursing and 10% for personal care, with an estimated $26.6 million state cost, according to the association’s figures reported by WMDT.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Tentative contract averts Brigham nurses’ strike at the last minute
authors: Sam Drysdale | State House News Service
description: The tentative agreement remains subject to ratification by nurses in the bargaining unit, and the MNA said the union's committee has recommended that Brigham nurses vote to ratify the contract.
text:
MORE THAN 4,000 NURSES at Brigham and Women’s Hospital reached a tentative contract agreement late Wednesday night, avoiding what could have been the largest open-ended nurses strike in Massachusetts history.
Nurses represented by the Massachusetts Nurses Association and hospital officials left negotiations Monday without a resolution, and ended up back at the table Wednesday to avert the strike at the last minute. The walkout was scheduled to start Thursday.
The tentative agreement remains subject to ratification by nurses in the bargaining unit, and the MNA said the union’s committee has recommended that Brigham nurses vote to ratify the contract.
“I’m incredibly proud of the Brigham nurses who stood strong to protect the world-class patient care we provide,” Kelly Morgan, BWH MNA Bargaining Committee chair and a labor and delivery nurse, said. “We secured this agreement with the help of countless community members, patients, unions and elected officials who supported us for many months. By standing together, we protected patients and the future of union nursing care at the Brigham.”
The hospital says the agreement “was reached within the financial limits of the hospital’s last, best and final offer presented on October 10.”
“We deeply value our Brigham nurses and believe this agreement recognizes their important contributions while supporting the long-term sustainability of our hospital and our ability to care for our patients and communities,” the hospital said in a statement.
The tentative agreement follows months of negotiations, including a July 8 one-day strike, after which the thousands of nurses who went on strike were locked out of the hospital for four additional days. The union voted September 24 to authorize an open-ended strike. They voted late last month to reject MGB’s “last, best, and final” contract offer.
Nurses will receive wage increases and lower health insurance costs under the tentative contract.
All nurses below the top step would receive a $1,000 bonus prorated based on their full-time-equivalent hours upon ratification, while new top steps with greater pay are added to the pay structure. Nurses also defeated a proposed health insurance premium split increase, the MNA said.
Nurses agreed to a compromise on 40-hour nurses on individual plans. Current nurses working 40 hours will retain premium-free coverage while newly hired 40-hour nurses will contribute 2.5 percent of the premium.
The new agreement includes contract language that the hospital does not intend to replace permanent Brigham nurses with temporary nurses, per the MNA.
The hospital’s dependence on temporary and floating nurses has been a central flashpoint in the labor dispute. Union nurses frequently raised concerns that temporary nurses — who are also paid higher wages — undermine permanent union jobs and are unfamiliar with patients and hospital systems.
Hospitals use temporary nurses primarily to quickly fill critical staffing gaps and maintain safe patient-to-nurse ratios when local hiring falls short.
MGB agreed in the tentative contract to post 20 new 36-hour float pool nurse positions to help limit the reliance on temporary nurses. The hospital will track floating into and out of each unit and the use of temporary nurses, the MNA said. It will also provide the union with data that will be reviewed by a new joint Staffing and Resources Committee that will look for ways to reduce floating and the use of temporary staff.
There are other provisions in the contract to restrict reliance on temporary staffing, such as requiring the hospital to provide the MNA with a rationale whenever more than 15 percent of the full-time-equivalent positions in any hospital unit are covered by non-permanent nurses.
It also builds in more protection for nurses responsible for coordinating care at greater capacity, and reduces the acute patient assignment workload for nurses in charge or overseeing others. Other benefits include adding grandchildren to bereavement leave, adding paid time for workplace-related court appearances, and adding language that all nurses can attend conferences.
Gov. Maura Healey released a statement Thursday morning saying she was pleased the two sides reached a tentative agreement and avoided a strike. Healey and Boston Mayor Michelle Wu made appearances at Monday’s negotiating session.
“I appreciated the opportunity to meet with both sides and urge them to stay at the table and continue working in good faith toward a resolution,” Healey said Thursday. “I want to thank and congratulate everyone involved for their hard work, commitment and willingness to reach an agreement. Our nurses are essential to our health care system, and this is an important step toward ensuring stability at the hospital and the continuity of care that patients depend on.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Barboursville School to reopen as a residential treatment facility for children, Morrisey announces
description: The former Barboursville School will reopen next year as a residential treatment facility, Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Thursday. The state has entered a five-year lease with Youth Health Associates to operate the school. The facility plans to start accepting kids in early 2027.
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, announces that the Barboursville School, a residential treatment facility for children, will reopen next year. The school closed earlier this year. (West Virginia Office of Gov. Patrick Morrisey video screenshot)The former Barboursville School will reopen next year as a residential treatment facility, Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Thursday. The state has entered a five-year lease with Youth Health Associates to operate the school. The facility plans to start accepting children in early 2027. 
“Bringing our children home has been one of my highest priorities since taking office,” Morrisey said in a news release. “For too long, our kids were sent hundreds or even thousands of miles away to receive the care they need. Reopening Barboursville is an important step toward changing that, and our goal is to replicate this approach across West Virginia so we can bring all our children home.”
The Cabell County facility closed earlier this year, decreasing the number of beds the state has available for children experiencing severe mental health crises. 
Youth Health Associates has hired a facility director and is recruiting additional staff, the governor’s office said. When it’s fully operational, the school will accommodate up to 36 children and employ 50 to 60 people. Many of the beds are projected to be filled by the end of March.
Morrisey said the Barboursville facility will be a model for similar facilities throughout the state, part of his A Home for Every Child initiative. Additional announcements are expected in the coming weeks and months, Morrisey’s office said. 
Foster care officials have said that West Virginia doesn’t have enough in-state treatment options for children in need of specialized mental health or behavioral care, leading the state to send hundreds of children out-of-state for help. It has also led to some children living in hotel rooms while in the state’s care.
As of early November, the number of West Virginia children receiving residential treatment outside the state was down from 400 earlier this year to 372 in early November, the governor’s office said.  
Morrisey also announced Thursday the state will end its longstanding practice of applying Social Security survivor benefits belonging to children in foster care toward the state’s foster care costs beginning Jan. 1, 2027. Instead, those funds will be preserved for the children who receive them to provide them a financial foundation as they transition into adulthood, the governor’s office said.
About 42 West Virginia children in foster care receive survivor benefits totaling about $402,700 annually.
“When a child loses a parent, the benefits they receive should help provide a foundation for their future,” Morrisey said in the news release. “We’re ending a longstanding practice and making sure those funds remain available to the children who need them. It’s another important step toward giving West Virginia’s children the support and opportunities they deserve.”
