name: Maryland Matters
title: The author Wes Moore: Book on ‘healing a divided nation’ set for March release
description: For a guy who refuses to say he won't run for president in two years, Gov. Wes Moore sure seems to be checking all the right boxes. Traveling the country, making national media appearances and, now, publishing a book about how to heal a divided nation.
text:
Gov. Wes Moore (D) will release a new book in March. He joins a number of other Democrats listed as potential candidates for President in 2028 who have also released books. (File photo Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Fresh off a second thumping of Republican Dan Cox to win reelection to a second term as governor a week ago, Gov. Wes Moore (D) turned his attention this week to fixing the nation.
At least that’s the thrust of the book he touted Wednesday, “Repair: Healing A Divided Nation.” Scheduled for a March 2027 release, Moore’s book is billed “as a bold interrogation of where America falls short, what we still do right, and how we can fix our broken systems together,” he said in a statement from his publisher.
For a guy who refuses to say he won’t run for president in two years, Moore sure seems to be checking all the right boxes — just in case.
In the announcement from publisher Henry Holt & Co., Moore describes his latest book as “an invitation … into a broader conversation about what makes our country great, where we’ve fallen short, and how we build a better future, together.”
He said the book will tell the stories of “what happens when good people do hard things, even in the face of unimaginable odds.”
Gov. Wes Moore rolls to easy reelection win in rematch with Republican challenger Dan Cox

Moore, who became the first Black governor of Maryland when he was elected in 2022, said those stories will be interspersed with “memories of service from my life inside and outside of politics.” But the book, he said, is not a “personal political memoir.”
Moore has been coy about his plans and if they include a 2028 presidential run. Even so, Moore has spent a great deal of time in his first term traveling the country fundraising and building political relationships as well as being a regular on national news programs.
Moore’s latest release joins those of other Democrats mentioned as potential 2028 presidential candidates: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear’s “Go and Do Likewise: How We Heal a Broken Country”: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro’s “Where We Keep the Light: Stories from a Life of Service”: and “Young Man in a Hurry: A Memoir of Discovery,”
by California Gov. Gavin Newsom, among others. All three were published this year.
This is not Moore’s first book. He has written a number of others including the New York Times bestseller, “The Other Wes Moore,” as well as “Five Days” and “The Work.”
And Moore is not the only Maryland governor to write a book.
Larry Hogan released his book — “Still Standing” — in 2020. It was two years into his second term in office (the first for a Republican governor since Theodore McKeldin). It also came at a time when he was teasing the possibility of a run for president.
Martin O’Malley, a Democrat who also had presidential aspirations, published a book after he left office focused on governing in the information age. Robert Ehrlich, who became the first Republican since Spiro Agnew to be elected governor, has written more than a half dozen books. Most recently, “Trump 2.0: Revolution, Redemption, Revival” in 2025.
In addition to O’Malley and Hogan, another Maryland politician with presidential aspirations got briefly into the publishing business. Former Rep. John Delaney (D-6th) released “The Right Answer: How We Can Divide Our Divided Nation” in 2018, a year after he announced his 2020 presidential campaign, which subsequently fizzzled.
Moore said his new book is meant “to pose hard questions and spark honest dialogue. This book is about how we can rediscover our common humanity and relearn our common purpose. I offer my thoughts, with an invitation for readers to lend theirs. In the work of repair, every fingerprint matters.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Any details of Moore’s life that are offered in the book are likely to become fodder for reporters. Moore’s life and political branding are inextricably linked.
He has faced criticisms related to what some describe as embellishments, misstatements and failures to correct how others have introduced him.
A CNN report in 2022 noted details in “The Other Wes Moore,” a book that “lays out the basic details of his life factually, a less accurate version of his Baltimore roots has taken on a life of its own, fueled by more than a decade of assertions by other people in TV interviews that he is a Baltimore native, born and raised in the city.”
Moore also came under intense scrutiny over his service record and claims about receiving the Bronze Star. A New York Times story in 2024 reported that Moore had been recommended for the honor but had not received it. Moore called it an honest mistake.
He ultimately received the award in a private ceremony at Government House, the governor’s mansion four months after the New York Times story.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Democrat Scott Colom celebrates Senate victory: ‘In Mississippi, our prayers often change the course of history’
description: U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during his election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Jubilant supporters of Scott Colom hugged, danced and wiped away tears Wednesday night on the campus of Tougaloo College as they celebrated his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since a few years after the Civil War.
“For me, this journey started with a prayer. And in Mississippi, our prayers often change the course of history,” Colom told the crowd at the historically Black college in north Jackson hours after he defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.


The Associated Press called the race for Colom eight days after Election Day, with the vote count slowed by an unusually large number of provisional ballots that many people were forced to cast because they had been moved to inactive status based on unverified credit bureau data that Secretary of State Michael Watson’s office provided to local election officials. Hyde-Smith, who has been in the Senate since 2018, issued a video statement congratulating Colom and wishing him well.
Supporters gather for U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom’s election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The Tougaloo choir sang “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” and a recording of “A Change is Gonna Come,” a movement anthem sung by Mississippi native Sam Cooke, played over loudspeakers before Colom appeared onstage on Wednesday’s cool autumn evening, amid trees draped with Spanish moss. During the Civil Rights Movement, the college provided safety for young people who protested and chipped away at Mississippi’s white supremacist society that violently enforced segregation and suppressed voting access for Black people. 
Tougaloo Student Government Association President Aznii Welchlin is a native of west Jackson. She said she’s always been a “radical and optimistic thinker.” Growing up, people would often shut down her ideas, but she said she always had a sense that a day like this would come.
“We did it, y’all,” Welchlin said from the stage. 
Terry Rogers II, a senior studying political science at Tougaloo, spent Tuesday driving students in a college van between local government offices to check on their ballots as the election remained unresolved. A day later, the 21-year-old was scrolling CNN when he saw the network projected Colom as the winner. He and a friend took a moment to cry.
“This is what we’ve been praying for, for years, for generations,” Rogers said. “This makes me want to continue to be a Mississippian. This makes me love my state even more than I already did.”
Mississippi has been plagued by “brain drain,” with college educated residents fleeing to seek jobs and a more progressive environment in other states. Rogers said Colom’s triumph will help revamp Mississippi’s national image.
As Rogers spoke to Mississippi Today, a fellow student came by and shouted at him: “He won! You see that? You see that?”
Rep. Justis Gibbs, a Democratic state lawmaker, was at his Jackson law office when the race was called for Colom. He said everyone stopped working and screamed for joy.
“Scott Colom’s victory marks a true turning point for Mississippi,” Gibbs said. “Voters showed up and showed out. His authenticity on the campaign trail and remarkable ability to connect with Mississippians in both rural and urban communities have injected new energy and momentum into the Mississippi Democratic Party.” 
Nadia Colom, U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom’s wife, listens as she is introduced during her husband’s election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Scott Colom’s wife, Nadia, was a fixture on the campaign trail. She helped organize a taco truck that went to college campuses, with a “pick another protein” theme plucked from one of his viral campaign ads. She also moderated panels at several events. At her husband’s victory party, she said she knew from her first date with Scott Colom how much he wanted to make a contribution to his state.
“You did it, and I could not be more proud,” Nadia Colom said.
She said the stress of taking care of their two daughters and running a business while her husband was away campaigning felt like a “ton of bricks” at times.
“Come last Wednesday morning, for every brick I felt, there were counties like Noxubee, Lowndes, Oktibbeha, and my own Clay County that were filled with voters who dared to take back our voice in D.C.,” Nadia Colom said. “That removed the bricks.” 
U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson speaks during U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom’s election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson, who has been the only Black member of Mississippi’s congressional delegation since he was elected in 1993 and the only Democrat since two other House members were defeated in 2010, declared: “I now have a partner in Washington. I now have a partner who understands that health care is important in Mississippi.” 
Thompson said he met the Rev. Martin Luther King and Fannie Lou Hamer during his time as a Tougaloo student.
“It is fitting and proper that we’re here this evening to continue that legacy of getting it right,” Thompson said. “Guess what? We have picked our senator. We’re not picking another protein. We’re gonna do it the old fashioned way, we’re just going to get it done.” 
Tougaloo College’s choir sings during U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom’s election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayU.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom’s daughters lead the Pledge of Allegiance during his election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodaySupporters sing the National Anthem during U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom’s election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayAnzii Welchlin, Tougaloo Student Government Association president, speaks during U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom’s election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodaySupporters cheer during U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom’s election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodaySupporters wait for U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom during his election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodaySupporters dance during U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom’s election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodaySupporters wait for U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom’s election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayU.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during his election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayU.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during his election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayU.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during his election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayU.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom hugs and kisses his daughters during his election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Colom said “he kept the faith” even as calls to donors went unanswered and fewer than 10 people showed up to some of his town hall meetings. He said that during his travels around the state, he met people who worked multiple jobs to make ends meet.
“God didn’t want us to get this the easy way. He wanted us to get it the Mississippi way,” Colom said of his campaign.
“All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this,” Colom said. “I had the courage to believe that we could show the country that Mississippi matters.”
Colom told the crowd that he will have faith and remain in prayer.
“I make a solemn commitment to each and every Mississippian today,” he said. “In every decision I make, I will never forget the most important thing is, Mississippi matters.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Commentary: Feds consider letting destructive shrimping into protected Florida reef
description: So many of the things we depend on in Florida are hidden from us, out of sight and thus out of mind. We depend on water from the underground aquifer but seldom give any thought to how we’re draining it or polluting it. We depend on the karst geology beneath our feet to hold us […]
text:
Fish swarm over the Oculina Bank, a reef off Florida's Atlantic coast that's unlike any other in the world. Shrimpers damaged it before it became a protected area, and now want to be let back in. (Photo courtesy of John Reed of Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution)So many of the things we depend on in Florida are hidden from us, out of sight and thus out of mind.
We depend on water from the underground aquifer but seldom give any thought to how we’re draining it or polluting it. We depend on the karst geology beneath our feet to hold us up but, unless a sinkhole opens, we seldom think about it.
Which brings me to the subject of the Oculina Bank.
This is not the kind of bank that has an ATM or gives you a toaster for opening an account. It’s a remarkable coral reef about 135 miles off the Florida coast, one that stretches from Fort Pierce to Flagler Beach.
There’s not another reef like it anywhere in the world.
The 130-nautical-mile long reef is made of, and named for, “Oculina varicosa,” aka ivory tree coral. Its tall growth provides a home for thousands of marine species, including shrimp, starfish, and sea urchins, and spawning habitat for grouper and red snapper.
If you like fresh Florida seafood the way I do, then you should thank the bank.
Yet because this important reef sits in water about 200 to 300 feet deep, it’s largely unknown — a hidden gem just like our aquifer and karst.
Mark Perry via Florida Oceanographic Society
“A lot of people don’t know that it’s there and that it’s part of who we are and that we’ve got to protect it,” said Mark Perry, executive director of the Florida Oceanographic Society.
Before scientists fully explored the reef’s extent, shrimpers dragged their trawls through it. They destroyed a majority of the coral. That’s why, in 1984, the reef was placed off-limits to that kind of fishing, making it the first marine protected area in the United States. The protected area has been expanded several times since then.
But now the federal agency in charge of safeguarding the Oculina Bank is considering scaling back the protection and letting the shrimpers back in. The shrimpers say they need access because their industry is teetering on the edge of collapse.
Shari Anker via Conservation Alliance of St. Lucie
“It’s a collision of two vastly different worldviews,” said Shari Anker. president of the Conservation Alliance of St. Lucie County, one of several environmental groups that oppose opening the reef.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is seeking public comments on this proposal until Nov. 17.
This is the second time this idea of opening the reef has come up, by the way. When the agency considered this four years ago, the answer was no. But now it’s back again.
The difference this time? The Florida man in the White House, a guy who seems to eat nothing but fast food.
 Slower than a fingernail
John Reed via Florida Atlantic Univeristy
In the 1970s, scientist John Reed was fresh out of college when he joined the staff at Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution in Fort Pierce. He became part of a team that used a submersible craft in exploring the waters off the Florida east coast.
“Basically, we were just going offshore and documenting the continental shelf,” he recalled this week.
But the submersible brought into view something they hadn’t expected to find.
“We discovered and documented this extraordinary reef formation,” Reed told me. “We realized this was the only place on earth like it, where the ivory tree coral forms these mounds that go up to 100 feet tall.”
Soon after the discovery, though, he and his colleagues learned about something tearing the coral to bits.
Reed’s first published scientific paper was about that discovery. It detailed how the shrimp boats were destroying this unique coral formation by dragging their trawls through it. It talked about how areas that, in the 1970s, were “teeming with large spawning aggregations of grouper and snapper,” had been damaged and even destroyed by shrimp trawls.
“That coral doesn’t grow back once it’s crushed,” the scientist said.
Even in the places where the coral was merely broken, not crushed, recovery would be a slooooooooooooow process. How slow? As WMNF-FM noted in a September story on this situation: “The coral grows at less than an inch per year. That’s slower than a fingernail.”
With 90% of the entire bank demolished, Reed proposed the federal government make it off-limits to shrimpers to save what was left.
In 1984, the feds approved that plan, ordering the shrimpers out. Then they expanded the protected area in 1994, 2000, and 2014 to include buffer areas around the coral.
Yet some of those prohibited activities continue in the area where they shouldn’t.
A 2005 report showed pictures of an abandoned net wrapped around a section of the reef. A 2015 video by Harbor Branch shows that intruders discarded fishing line, bottles, cans, and even boots inside the protected area.
To Reed, it makes no sense to allow legal access to the shrimp boats that broke the coral before.
“I’ve been fighting to protect this area ever since I first saw it,” Reed told me. “I’ve been fighting them for 45 years.”
Shrimp boats docked in Carrabelle in the 1980s, via Florida State Archives
 On the cliff’s edge
This is a tough time to be a shrimper.
“The U.S. shrimp harvesting industry is experiencing a long-term decline in profits and economic stability, including a $268 million revenue loss since 2021,” according to a federal report released earlier this year.
It’s not due to low demand. “U.S. shrimp consumption more than quadrupled between 1984 and 2023,” the report notes.
Instead, a lot of the slump is thanks to competition from foreign sources, which tend to be farmed, not wild-caught.
Not mentioned by the report: Skyrocketing costs for diesel fuel, thanks in large part to the president’s unpopular Iran War. Diesel reached an average of $6.52 a gallon in September, up from an average of $3.69 per gallon in 2025.
Meanwhile, Elon Musk is responsible for yet another wrinkle. According to WPTV-TV, space launches — most of them by Musk’s Space X — closed the waters off Port Canaveral to fishing 50 times last year.
An added hazard: The string of hurricanes that’s battered Florida’s coastlines in recent years took out a lot of shrimp boats, too. It’s like that scene in “Forrest Gump” where all the competing shrimp boats are destroyed by a hurricane, but put on an endless loop and replayed over and over.
Given the shrinking of shrimping, a lot of shrimpers have chosen to get out of the business entirely. The industry these days is but a shadow of its once healthy self.
Capt. Bob Zales via Southeastern Fisheries Association
“We’re standing on the edge of a cliff,” said Capt. Bob Zales, executive director of the Southeastern Fisheries Association in Panama City. “If you just blow on us, we’re going to fall off.”
Rock shrimp via South Atlantic Fisheries Management Council
That’s why shrimpers want to get back into the area around the Oculina Bank, he explained. They want to catch rock shrimp, not to be confused with the rock lobster featured in a famous B-52s song.
Zales told me the section of the protected area where the shrimpers want access doesn’t have any coral in it for them to damage, “so there’s no reason to prevent us from going in there.”
But that’s not the way Anker, Reed, or Perry see it. They’re worried that dragging shrimp trawls near the Oculina Bank will stir up sediment that will smother the coral.
That’s a legitimate concern, said Sandra Brooke, a coral scientist at Florida State University. The area the shrimpers hope to access are in the buffer zones around the reef bank.
“That’s why this is a buffer zone,” Brooke explained. “It’s not there to protect the corals directly. It’s there to protect them indirectly. You don’t know what the currents are doing at that depth, and if you don’t know where the currents are going then you don’t know where the sediment’s going.”
 Common sense caution
The South Atlantic Fishery Management Council considered opening the Oculina Bank once before.
This was in 2022. The shrimping industry wasn’t quite as bad off as it is now, but it was already pushing hard to get back into the protected area.
The South Atlantic Council heard strong objections from its coral advisory panel, a group that includes Brooke. The coral counselors warned about the danger of the trawls spewing fine sediment all over the coral reef.
“The corals are very sensitive to sediment,” she told me.
She pointed out that the sensors for positioning are on the shrimp boats, not on their trawls, which can stretch for 1,000 feet behind the vessel. That means the shrimpers won’t know exactly where their trawls are dragging behind them, much less where the sediment ends up.
In the end, the council voted to recommend the government say yes, but NOAA said no.
Saying yes “would allow rock shrimp fishermen to bottom trawl for rock shrimp in a 22-square mile area where the gear has been prohibited since 2014,” a publication called National Fisherman reported. “As a result, the first marine protected area in the world to protect a deep-water coral reef would suffer from damage, the agency concluded.”
So, why bring it back up again?
Because the current occupant of the White House said so.
In an executive order he signed last year, President Donald Trump said the government “shall immediately consider suspending, revising, or rescinding regulations that overly burden America’s commercial fishing, aquaculture, and fish processing industries.”
The order specifically called for Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick to “identify the most heavily overregulated fisheries requiring action and take appropriate action to reduce the regulatory burden on them.”
This isn’t surprising, considering this administration’s hostility toward anything that protects nature. After all, it basically canceled consideration of the Endangered Species Act when approving offshore oil drilling permits in the Gulf of Mexico.
Plus, look at who’s going to be making the decision. Lutnick’s background is in finance, not fisheries. He wouldn’t know a grouper from a groyper.
Although Lutnick is now in trouble over the Nvidia “sex-while-spying” mess, he’ll probably still oversee the agency long enough to make this decision. He seems unlikely to do anything other than what his boss wants him to do.
The president’s favorite seafood dish is the Filet-O-Fish Sandwich from McDonalds. I don’t think he’s worried about whether letting shrimpers invade the Oculina Bank will prevent him from getting that menu item fresh from the dock.
Another indication that the skids have been greased: The fisheries council didn’t ask Brooke’s coral advisory panel for itsf opinion on reopening the protected area.
“We were not invited to be part of the discussion,” she told me. “The reason, they said, is because they already knew what we were going to say. Of course, they also knew what the shrimp advisory council would say and they still invited them to comment.”
Here’s what I found intriguing, though. Other fishing groups have splashed into the middle of this watery war.
After all, there’s more marine life at stake than “another shrimp on the barbie.” Remember how the reef is a key spawning area for grouper and snapper?
As a result, some anglers saw a different angle on the issue.
“To allow shrimping and associated silt plumes from the trawls within 400 yards of the protected area is virtually guaranteed to produce negative impacts,” the Coastal Conservation Association of Florida, part of the largest grassroots marine resource conservation organization of its kind in the country, wrote to the fisheries council. “Common sense would dictate a more cautious approach. … In this case, the benefits of this action do not outweigh the risks.”
I hope a lot more fisherfolk cast a line of protest toward the feds before next week, to tell them to scale back this awful idea.
If they do, maybe Secretary Lutnick will recognize that what’s good for the shrimping industry is bad for everyone else who counts on this reef.
But if Lutnick is still leaning toward the shrimpers, perhaps he should come to Florida and look for himself. I’d recommend he use one of the federal government’s own submersibles and plunge down deep to view the reef that’s currently out of sight.
Maybe that way he can understand why protecting this bank will pay all kinds of healthy dividends.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Student leaders call for CSCU reforms
authors: Amber Monzillo, Owen Ibey and Mathew Biadun
description: In the spirit of reform, we call for five actions to be taken to restore the stability and integrity of the CSCU system.
text:
“ I think one of the things that was really important to me is the stability of our public university system,” Natalie Braswell, Interim Chancellor of the Connecticut State Colleges and University (CSCU) System said in a recent interview . “…I think it’s important to be able to come in and lend my skillset where I think I can and help to put the system back in a place where people feel that they can believe in it again, feels that there’s credibility there, feels that there’s stability there. I think that’s an important thing for the students here.”
 As students ourselves, we couldn’t agree more. 
 For too long, CSCU has been stuck on damage control. Fire after fire has monopolized the attention of system leadership, policymakers, and the media, taking away from both the needs and successes of students and their institutions. Chancellor Braswell is correct in identifying the need. We need to have a system that is trusted, credible, and stable, not just now, but moving forward. 
 We have been pleased to see the Board of Regents take steps towards reform and stability, such as a recently-unveiled ‘Reforms Dashboard’ and a new Interim Chancellor chosen to be a steady hand. These are good steps for the system. The recent cases of Terrence Cheng and John Maduko have made resolutely clear that major problems must be taken seriously and tackled head-on. 
 As student leaders across the four state universities within the CSCU System, we hope that the system will learn from prior scandals, and will implement systemic, lasting reforms in order to prevent such circumstances from happening again. In the spirit of reform, we publicly call for the following actions to be taken by both system leadership, and state leadership, to improve the system going forward. 
1. Conduct an audit of Systems Office
 What is the purpose of the Systems Office? 
Since the CSCU System was consolidated in 2011, the central System Office has grown tremendously. What was once a rather small office housed on a single floor of a building at CCSU has ballooned into a large bureaucracy costing more money annually than all of Charter Oak State College. Naturally, this increased size has made the question of its role and purpose even more relevant.
 If the purpose of the System Office is to make the system more efficient through shared services, then recent audits put this into question, such as   one which found   that a centralization initiative dating back to 1998 has still not been finished, and that millions of dollars of assets have been mishandled. This does not seem like efficiency. 
 If the purpose of the System Office is to advocate as a unified front on behalf of all the institutions under its umbrella, this strategy does not appear to have worked either. Consolidation has tied the reputation of the broader system to the reputation of each individual campus, even when they have nothing to do with one another. Scandalous spending or failed audits in the System Office directly impact individual institutions when the System Office is responsible for their advocacy, particularly when it comes to requesting funds from the state legislature. 
 In light of this, we ask for two actions to be taken. The first is an in-depth audit of the System Office, conducted by the legislature, in order to find out what efficiencies the office does create compared to the funds it requires. If centralization is meant to eliminate inefficiencies, we must confirm that it does not create them. The second is for system leadership to consider what the purpose of the System Office is. If the Chancellor and the Board of Regents cannot clearly articulate what the purpose of the System Office should be, then they cannot expect anyone to look upon it positively.  
 What cannot be defined cannot be defended; so we ask for a clear definition and mission to be identified. 
2. Re-examine the chancellor contract
 The recent administration of former-Chancellor Terrence Cheng revealed concerning elements of his contract. One detail included moving expenses and a state-funding housing allowance which was not used, resulting in expensive, chauffeured rides being charged to his P-Card to fund a commute from his residence in New York. Another included even more-controversial ‘Professor Retreat Rights’, which guaranteed him a tenured position at Western which he now holds, despite leaving his role and the university mired in scandal. 
Given that the Chancellor serves at the explicit pleasure of the board, we ask that the Board of Regents take a close look at the chancellor contract, particularly given that a search process remains underway. Is the $442,187 salary warranted? Should a residency requirement be implemented? Are Professor Retreat Rights appropriate? These are all elements that should be examined before a new contract is written.
3. Continue the investigation Into Zulma Toro
In the Grand River Report written after the resignation of former-Chancellor John Maduko, one recommendation was to, quote, “ avoid the actual or perceived practice of dismissing Title IX complaints because a respondent is no longer affiliated with the System, as it prevents the institution from fully addressing its obligations under Title IX to prevent future harm resulting from the same or similar circumstances, and provide appropriate remedy to the complainant”. While the departure of former CCSU President Zulma Toro was not due to equivalent Title IX complaints, we believe the same logic holds. An investigation should not be cancelled simply due to the subject’s resignation. This is a disservice not only to the truth, but to the victims, and to the university and the system. How can one implement reforms and solutions if the problem is not thoroughly investigated?
 If a settlement agreement was reached preventing an investigation, that is an immensely poor decision, and such agreements should not happen moving forward. The Board of Regents already set a proper example for itself with the Grand River Report. It should continue the investigation into Pres. Toro, or at least an investigation into how people were treated and the effects it had on the university, and then respond to said investigation with any steps necessary.  
 4. Impeachment processes 
 The recent departures of former-Chancellors Cheng and Maduko, along with former Board of Regents Chair Martin Guay and former Board of Regents Vice Chair Juanita James have made one fact clear – good behavior is never guaranteed, and people in all positions in power can make bad decisions in their roles. 
 The only way to remove a failed official should not be to wait until enough public pressure mounts and they choose to resign. Motions of no confidence carry weight, but are unbinding and lack authority. There should be a more proactive option available. In light of this the Board of Regents, working with the state legislature as necessary, should create and outline clear impeachment protocols not only for Chancellors, but for members of the Board of Regents itself.  
5. Pausing the chancellor search process
 As has been acknowledged by system leadership, and as we have called for in this opinion-piece, there is significant work to be done within the CSCU System. Nine priority-reforms are currently underway. Seeing as the previous Chair of the Chancellor Search Committee was Juanita James, who has resigned, we take it that the search process has been   de facto   paused or hindered due to the circumstances. 
 Taking this into account, we request that the Board of Regents formally pause the Search Committee in order to prioritize implementing reforms and stabilizing the system. The Board of Regents specifically chose Interim Chancellor Braswell to steady the ship. She should continue in the role until the ship is steady enough to sail through a search process properly, rather than rushing through one amidst major reforms. 
 In an effort for public accountability, we share these statements not only with our fellow students, but with faculty, staff, and administrators across our universities, as well as with the media. The moment calls for a serious, public discussion on reform to take place, and we look forward to seeing those conversations happen and participating in them. 
Amber Monzillo is President of the Student Government Association at Central Connecticut State University. Owen Ibey is President of the Student Government Association at Western Connecticut State University. Mathew Biadun is President of the Student Government Association at Eastern Connecticut State University.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Moore talks military service, staffs up; poll is good news for city hall, in political notes
description: Gov. Wes Moore answers more questions about his military service for Chuck Todd, and he adds a legislative aide from the Maryland Municipal League, which got good news from a UMBC poll on how people feel about their governments, in political notes.
text:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) faces continued questions about his military service in a new interview with Chuck Todd that will run online Sunday. (File photo Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Gov. Wes Moore continues to face scrutiny over his service record and a Bronze Star.
The latest round comes from Chuck Todd in an interview that will air on Noosphere on Sunday.
In that interview, Todd asks Moore about a recent report by Fox 45 with Moore’s former commanding officer, retired Lt. Col. James A. “Jamie” Gottschling.
Gottschling told the station that Moore’s service in Afghanistan is service “he can be proud of.” But he also characterized some of Moore’s own descriptions of his service as an “embellishment.” Gottschling said he would not have signed off awarding Moore a Bronze Star, instead saying the Army Commendation Medal was Moore’s award for his service.

 

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore responds to claims from his former Army supervisor, retired Lt. Col. James Gottschling, that he never led soldiers in combat in Afghanistan.
@iamwesmoore: “I pray for him and his family. … I think his OER of me and what he wrote about me before that speaks for itself.”
His full conversation with @chucktodd releases this Sunday at 6PM, only on Noosphere
https://t.co/9Qgo6jFxUk
— Noosphere (@noosphereapp) November 11, 2026


Moore declined to respond to Fox 45, owned by Sinclair Broadcast Group. David Smith, owner of the Baltimore Sun and chairman of Sinclair Broadcast Group, has sued Moore for defamation.
In an interview with Todd, Moore was asked about the report and Gottschling’s comments.
“I’d say, you know, I pray for him and his family,” Moore tells Todd in the clip released on social media. “I know mental health and the challenges that people have to go through are real, and so I just will choose to remember the the good times that I had with him when he gave me a top ranking on my OER [officer evaluation report], and I’m proud of the service I did. Proud of service I did with him.”
During the interview, Moore tells Todd his service in Afghanistan is documented.
Todd asked Moore if he was implying that “somebody’s taking advantage” of Gottschling to score political points on Moore, a prospective candidate for president in 2028. Moore responds by suggesting that Gottschling may be politically motivated, calling it the “nastiness” of politics.
“He said to me directly, he said we just have different political … we just you know come from different political positions,” Moore said.
Todd follows up by asking if this is all about a potential bid for president.
“I just really, I want to always remember the times that we had when we served together in Afghanistan, and you know I think his OER of me and what he wrote about me before that speaks for itself,” Moore said.
Moore beefs up lobby shop
Shuffling in the Moore administration continues as the governor prepares to start his second term and fifth legislative session.
To that end, Moore is bringing on Angela Bailey Thupari as deputy legislative officer starting Nov. 25, the administration confirmed to Maryland Matters.
Angelica Bailey Thupari (File photo Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
Bailey Thupari has experience in the State House. She spent the last six years as the director of advocacy and public policy at the Maryland Municipal League. Prior to that, she spent three years with the Maryland Building Industry Association, including a year as its vice president of government affairs. She holds a bachelor’s degree in political science from American University and a law degree from the University of Baltimore School of Law.
Since easily winning re-election to a second term on Nov. 3, Moore has announced a new chief of staff as well as changes to his Cabinet. Additional changes are expected before the General Assembly reconvenes and Moore is sworn in for a second term in January.
Hometown heroes
Everybody wants government services; nobody’s really crazy about paying for them.
That would be our smart-aleck and decidedly nonacademic summary of the findings of a poll released Thursday by the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, Institute of Politics for the Maryland Municipal League. The survey asked 710 Maryland voters, from Nov. 5-9, for their feelings about their local communities and the services they want, their trust in different levels of government and their feelings about taxes from various governments.
(There was also a series of questions on news consumption, but since Maryland Matters was not offered as an option for respondents, we kind of lost interest.)
The good news, if you’re the Maryland Municipal League, is that people liked their hometowns and were more inclined to favor the government closest to them. The poll found that 67% of respondents rated their  community — defined as their neighborhood or the area right around their home — as excellent or good, while just 23% called it fair or poor.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
When asked what services or amenities were important to have in those communities — whether they had them, or just wanted them — the wish list was pretty meat and potatoes. The share of respondents who said these items were “very important” was:
• Services such as trash removal, law enforcement, or a water system: 86%
• Dedicated police or fire departments: 80%
• A good place to raise children: 67%
• Access to recreational parks and trails: 63%
• Sidewalks: 56%
• Events such as farmers’ markets, parades, arts and music, and a vibrant downtown: 51%
• A strong sense of community pride: 47%
Somehow, multimillion-dollar sports palaces and championship-caliber golf courses were overlooked. Going to have to check the methodology.
Majorities felt they were taxed too much, and most didn’t have a lot of faith in the decision-making of government. But chalk another one up for the municipal league — local government did best in both areas. On taxes, 61% said they pay “too much” in federal and state taxes, compared to 57% on local taxes. When asked about their level of trust in government, 57% said they trust their city, town or county government; 18% trust state government; and just 6% trust Washington.
“This poll reinforces something we see every day: Trust begins closest to home,” said Maryland Municipal League CEO Theresa Kuhns in a statement with the poll. “It is a powerful reminder of the importance of preserving local decision-making and ensuring our communities have the tools and resources to shape their own futures.”
The poll was conducted by live interviewers and text-to-web utilizing a dualframe (landline and cell phone) random sample stratified by county. The data was weighted by gender, age, race, geography, and educational attainment and has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: It’s time to grow more school options that help kids succeed
description: The unacceptable reality that so few students can read should force us to reckon with how we create real educational opportunities for CT child.
text:
Half of Connecticut’s students can’t perform at grade level in either language arts or math.
Of course, no single test score can capture the full picture of a child’s potential or a school’s impact. And I take nothing away from the educators across Connecticut working tirelessly every day on behalf of our students. As a former special education paraeducator, I know firsthand that teaching is far harder than most people or policymakers recognize.

Rebecca Greenberg-Ellis

But the unacceptable reality that so few students can read remains. It should force us to reckon with how we create real educational opportunities for every kid who calls our state home.
Connecticut’s 2026 Smarter Balanced Assessment (SBA) results illuminate a path forward. The SBA is given to students in grades 3-8 annually to measure learning in English Language Arts (ELA) and math. This year’s results indicate charter schools are a massive driver of academic improvement across the state, especially in our highest-need areas. Charter schools in Stamford, Bridgeport, New Haven, Manchester, and Waterbury aren’t just outperforming the traditional public school districts they neighbor. They’re posting some of the largest gains in the entire state in ELA and Math.
Critically, charter schools are excelling with the very students traditional public schools struggle to serve well. The results speak for themselves. In reading, 38% of Black charter students are proficient, compared to 32% of Black students statewide. For Latino students, it’s 39% versus 33%. Low-income charter students lead their statewide peers 37% to 33%. And English learners in charter schools reach reading proficiency at double the rate of English learners statewide, 26% versus 13%. Black, Latino, and English learner charter students also outperform their statewide peers in math.
Making these results more notable is that, in Connecticut, charter schools can only be located in what’s called an “Alliance District,” which is any district that receives one of the lowest scores on the state’s school performance framework. So these charters are working in communities that, by definition, otherwise lack high-quality public school options for families. And they’re still beating statewide averages across practically every student subgroup.
Connecticut charter schools serve more than 10,000 students. This year, more than 5,000 others sat on waiting lists. And in 26 of the state’s 36 Alliance Districts, families have no charter school option at all. Demand isn’t the problem. Access is.
Connecticut already knows what works. The question is whether more families will get access to it.
For more than a decade, the answer has been no. No new charter school has opened in Connecticut since 2014. A slow, political approval process kept new schools from getting off the ground, even as waitlists grew. That started to change this year. Lawmakers gave existing charter schools an $8.7 million funding boost. They also paid for early planning at three proposed schools in Waterbury, Stamford, and Ansonia. That’s real progress. But three schools won’t close a waitlist of more than 5,000 students.
Federal dollars can help close that gap. The Mind Trust Connecticut just received nearly $70 million from the U.S. Department of Education to expand strong school options over the next five years. And 90% of that money goes directly to new and growing Connecticut charter schools.
The money will do a few key things. It will help new schools open in communities that want them, and help strong schools grow. It will help existing schools get even better, in the classroom and behind the scenes. It will help the state make better decisions about which schools should open and how to hold them accountable. And it will help families learn what school options they have.
The State Department of Education has also committed to opening a new round of charter school applications later this year. That’s the chance for the next wave of leaders to step forward and start the schools families are asking for. All told, the federal funding could reach nearly 14,000 more students. That would more than double the number of kids charter schools serve today.
Right now, more than 5,000 Connecticut kids are waiting for a seat. In most of the state’s struggling districts, families have no charter option at all. Students deserve better. We know what works. It’s time to give more families the chance to choose schools that produce the best outcomes for students.
Rebecca Greenberg-Ellis is Executive Director of The Mind Trust Connecticut.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The Democrat dog caught the car
description: If you think Ned Lamont is going to let himself be one of the rich who gets taxed, you probably were gullible enough to vote for him … again.
text:
It might be a good idea to stay away from the dog for a little while. Now that it’s caught the car, there’s likely to be a lot of drooling, a lot of haughty posturing, a lot of snarling and snapping, and a lot of blithering that, like listening to Oprah, is likely to turn your brain to oatmeal.
In case you’re not sure why I’m writing this, here’s Exhibit A: “CT Dems preview agenda after blue wave swamps U.S. Congress”:

Democrats will need to take a two-pronged approach when they return to the majority. The party will have the delicate balance of pushing back on President Donald Trump through oversight efforts and tackling policies in the hopes of directly addressing voter concerns that led to their electoral success.

I’d recommend a six-pronged approach:

Stop promising the impossible.
Stop spending money.
Obey the law.
Keep the borders closed.
Spend more time in reality.
More generally, get a grip of your knickers.

Nobody asked me. So, those six things are more like a wish list. But we’ve just handed the keys to the bulldozer to a baby, kids. And the house won’t fare well.
In the brave new world of politics, these are the top ten tenets:

What I feel is much more important than what I know.
Emotions are good.
Thinking is bad
Discipline is hard.
I vote for people I like because I like them.
I don’t vote for people I don’t like even if I can’t substantiate my reasons for not liking them.
I’ll take to heart every promise that serves my interests.
My interests are more important than national unity.
I support democracy as long as things are going my way.
I wouldn’t know the difference between a democracy and a federal constitutional republic if it bit me.

Pardon me for mixing my animal metaphors. But since the dog caught the car, the chickens are already coming home to roost. I intend no pun whatsoever when I say this is rich and present Exhibit B: “Blue wave in CT legislature may test Lamont on taxing the rich”. And because Democrats and the people who vote for them have senses of neither irony nor common sense, you can be sure they don’t have the slightest awareness of the absurdity of the position they’ve put themselves in. Check this out:

State legislators have talked about taxing Connecticut’s wealthy to finance relief for the poor and middle class, but for most of the past eight years, it’s only been talk. Because doing otherwise meant crossing one of Gov. Ned Lamont’s deepest lines in the political sand … the governor repeatedly insists Connecticut needs “more taxpayers, not more taxes” … when asked Wednesday what mandate he believes voters delivered, Lamont said people like the status quo, “how we’re managing through these very complicated times.”

What might cause Uncle Ned to bust out his tap shoes at a time like this? Two things:

Garden-variety cronyism. There’s no way he can sell out his Fairfield County pals without being tarred, feathered, and likely impeached.
His own net wealth. It’s somewhere in the neighborhood of $400 million, if you don’t count his wife’s ballpark $650 million.

If you think Uncle Ned is going to let himself be one of the rich who gets taxed, you probably were gullible enough to vote for him … again.
Here’s my favorite part of the article.

It’s unclear whether Lamont will keep bending budget rules next year.

Unclear?! The dude’s been bending budget rules like a pretzel for eight years, and we wonder if he’ll keep doing it?
Over the last eight years, Uncle Ned has proven himself to be a surprisingly accomplished song and dance man. But now that the dog has caught the car, he’ll have to be a contortionist to keep getting away with his blatant duplicity.
Mark O’Brien lives in Middletown.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Judge dismisses petition by Peltola campaign seeking names of rejected absentee voters
description: The Alaska Division of Elections does not have to produce a report of rejected absentee voters in the midterm elections, a state court ruled Wednesday afternoon on a lawsuit filed by the campaign of Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola. The lawsuit was filed by the campaign group Alaskans for Mary against the division on […]
text:
A voter casts their ballot on the first day of early in person voting in Juneau on Oct. 19, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)The Alaska Division of Elections does not have to produce a report of rejected absentee voters in the midterm elections, a state court ruled Wednesday afternoon on a lawsuit filed by the campaign of Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola.
The lawsuit was filed by the campaign group Alaskans for Mary against the division on Friday, seeking to make public the names of voters whose absentee ballots have been rejected and the reasons for their rejection before the results are certified on Nov. 25.
In court filings, the group said they sought the list of voters “to safeguard an accurate ballot count and ensure that Peltola’s supporters are not unlawfully disenfranchised.”
But in court, attorneys with the Alaska Department of Law arguing on behalf of the division said ballot counting is ongoing and the requested records at this stage are preliminary, and do not qualify as public records. They argued that the division could not feasibly produce the information on short notice or maintain voter confidentiality. 
The state asked the court to reject the campaign’s request that the division make a new report of names of voters during ballot counting, and Anchorage Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews agreed. 
“Given that the DOE is currently busy processing ballots from the 2026 general election, it is understandable that the division simply lacks the capacity to generate the report,” Matthews wrote in the ruling. 
“Even if the request were otherwise considered reasonable outside the peak election time of year, it is simply not reasonable or required now,” he wrote. He said the information did not qualify as a public record and was not required to be disclosed.
Peltola’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday on the ruling or whether it planned to appeal.
The division published a new batch of preliminary election results Wednesday night — adding 5,618 ballots to the count. Peltola inched ahead in the lead with 48.73% of the vote, ahead of Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan with 47.13%. 
Absentee ballot review
Absentee ballots are processed at one of five regional elections offices where staff log them into a state database and make an initial determination about whether to accept or reject a ballot, based on verification requirements. Mailed absentee ballots must be received within 10 days of election day, or within 15 days if mailed from overseas. 
Absentee ballots are then reviewed again by absentee ballot review boards at each of the regional offices staffed by bipartisan teams of two, who verify voter eligibility and if the ballot was cast properly. Campaigns may have observers present with each of the review boards and can challenge the boards’ decision to accept or reject a ballot. After the review board process, the final determination on ballots is made by the State Review Board.
The Peltola campaign had sought a copy of the observers’ “details report,” but the state argued that information is preliminary until a final determination is made, according to court filings. The state said those reports are also bound by confidentiality requirements, and do not qualify as public records under law. The court agreed.
The state said the determination on whether a ballot is rejected may change up until election results are certified on Nov. 25, after which the division is required to notify the voter if their ballot has been rejected. 
The division also publishes a list of how many absentee ballots were rejected and the reason for rejection, but that list is typically released weeks after the results are certified.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Government Committee chair won’t seek same role in 2027-28 Nebraska Legislature
description: BELLEVUE, Neb. — The chair of the legislative Committee on Government, Military and Veterans Affairs won’t ask again for the top post in 2027, but two Air Force veterans have already tossed their names into the ring to succeed her. State Sen. Rita Sanders, a former eight-year mayor of Bellevue who previously worked for former U.S. […]
text:
State Sen. Rita Sanders of Bellevue. July 25, 2024. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)BELLEVUE, Neb. — The chair of the legislative Committee on Government, Military and Veterans Affairs won’t ask again for the top post in 2027, but two Air Force veterans have already tossed their names into the ring to succeed her.
State Sen. Rita Sanders, a former eight-year mayor of Bellevue who previously worked for former U.S. Rep. Jeff Fortenberry, has served on the Government Committee for six years, including two years as vice chair and two more as chair. 
But come 2027, she is seeking a different committee role before she is term-limited after 2028.
State Sen. Rita Sanders of Bellevue, left, joins Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen for a ceremonial bill signing of Nebraska National Guard recruitment and retention legislation. Dec. 10, 2024. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
In an Oct. 28 letter endorsing her vice chair for the top spot, Sanders said she wants to work on policy priorities “which I have not been able to give adequate attention while serving as chair.”
Those priorities, she told the Nebraska Examiner, are on the Natural Resources Committee, including water, energy and emerging attention on artificial intelligence.
She said she also believes in making room for “amazing upcoming leaders.”
“I only have two years left. I don’t have to be in any position of power; I’m not looking at running for any office at all,” Sanders said Tuesday. “So let me just step a little bit aside.”
The Government Committee will be front and center concerning election laws and rules about citizen-led petitions, especially with a new secretary of state having been elected this fall.
Leadership votes are selected by secret ballot on the first day of each legislative session.
‘Continuity from the first day’
So far, two U.S. Air Force veterans have announced their intentions to succeed Sanders — state Sens. Bob Andersen of north-central Sarpy County and Victor Rountree of Bellevue. More senators could announce their candidacies before the legislative session begins Jan. 6.
The Legislature in 2027 will consist of 30 Republicans, 18 Democrats and one registered nonpartisan. At least 25 votes are needed to elect a chair among the 49 lawmakers. Sanders and Andersen are Republicans. Rountree is a Democrat.
State Sen. Bob Andersen of north-central Sarpy County. March 26, 2025. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Andersen, Sanders’ vice chair, served in the Air Force for 21 years and, for the past 23 years, has been a defense contractor. In an Oct. 29 letter announcing his run for the chairship, he said he was continually put in positions of authority in active duty that required strong leadership. 
He said he worked alongside Sanders on the “full breadth” of the committee’s purview, from elections and operations of government to issues facing service members, families and veterans. Andersen added that Sanders served with “distinction” and that he was “grateful for her confidence and for the example of fair, steady leadership she has set.”
“I understand the committee’s procedures, its workload and the stakeholders who come before it,” Andersen wrote. “I am prepared to provide continuity from the first day of session.”
As a defense contractor, Andersen said, he was a senior adviser to leadership in the 55th Wing and 55th Operations Group at Offutt Air Force Base. He also worked on allied, joint and international military programs while working with virtually all national-level agencies.
“As a veteran, I know firsthand the programs and services available to Nebraska’s veterans, and where those programs can be strengthened,” Andersen said.
Andersen said he’s worked extensively with the Nebraska National Guard and serves as a member of the Offutt Advisory Council. He said this service has allowed him to strengthen the Legislature’s relationship with the U.S. Air Force and Nebraska Air National Guard, partnerships he said are “critically important” to Nebraska’s economy, communities and national defense.
Getting Nebraska ‘mission ready’
Rountree, meanwhile, joined the U.S. Air Force in 1980 and retired in 2010. He said in his 30 years of active duty, he served in 12 locations, including the United Kingdom; Germany; Washington, D.C.; South Korea; Bahrain; and, finally, Nebraska. He deployed to the Middle East after the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001.
“As chair I would work to protect our elections, support our veterans and ensure that Nebraska is mission ready,” Rountree wrote in his Tuesday letter.
State Sen. Victor Rountree of Bellevue, center. Jan. 21, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Rountree noted that in his first two years as a state senator, he’s led legislation to cut taxes for disabled veterans and support military families statewide, legislation he said “works for all Nebraskans.”
During his military career, Rountree was promoted to the highest enlisted rank, chief master sergeant, and served as superintendent of the 55th Comptroller Squadron at Offutt. He said he supported the functions of Air Combat Command’s largest wing with over 14,500 personnel and managed the wing’s $176 million budget, with total accounting of $1.3 billion in tenant unit funds.
Through the Air Force, Rountree said, he earned a degree in accounting, completed further training in financial management and “worked to ensure that every dollar was accounted for.”
After retiring in 2010, Rountree said, he entered the federal workforce as chief of financial management and analysis for the 55th Wing at Offutt. In 2017, he became an educator for Bellevue Public Schools, and in 2019, he joined FEMA to assist after historic state floods.
“I worked with devastated areas across the state, helping them assess damage and rebuild stronger and more resilient communities,” Rountree wrote. “I coordinated federal, state and local funds to ensure projects were able to progress while abiding by federal regulations.”
Leadership vision
If chosen as chair, Andersen said he would run a committee that is “fair, prepared, open to every member and every Nebraskan who comes before it.”
“I will give each bill a thorough and respectful hearing, collaborate with senators across the body regardless of where they stand on a given issue and work to keep Nebraska a state where those who serve, and those who have served, are proud to live,” Andersen wrote.
State Sen. Rita Sanders of Bellevue. Jan. 5, 2023. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska News Service)
Rountree said his service on the Judiciary, General Affairs and Urban Affairs committees, in addition to his “distinguished” military background, have prepared him for a chairship.
“I look forward to discussing with you how we can work as a body to support the needs of our veterans and what we can do to strengthen our election integrity,” Rountree wrote. “The government must be responsive to the people of Nebraska, and as your chair, I will make sure that our taxpayers are at the forefront of every decision made.”
Andersen and Rountree can both run for one more four-year term in 2028.
A new secretary of state
Whoever is selected as Government Committee chair — Andersen, Rountree or someone else who hasn’t come forward yet — will also be working with a new secretary of state who has called for changes to how Nebraska runs its elections.
Secretary of State-elect Scott Petersen has called for changes to mail-in ballots, for instance, to boost what he said are concerns from Nebraska voters on election integrity.
Scott Petersen of Omaha, the 2026 nominee for Nebraska secretary of state, talks with state Sen. Kathleen Kauth of Omaha, left, and others in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds ahead of a midterms rally featuring President Donald Trump. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
On election night at a watch party for Gov. Jim Pillen, Petersen told the Nebraska Examiner he’s looking forward to “doing some great things for Nebraska” but acknowledged a shifting Legislature more toward the middle as three Republican-held seats moved to the left.
“I was hoping for a better Legislature, so we lost some legislative seats,” Petersen said. “We’re gonna have to regroup there, but you know what? We’ll figure it out. Looking forward to working with the governor. He’s a good man. He loves Nebraska, and I’m looking forward to being part of the team.”
Choosing committee assignments
Whether Sanders might land a different leadership role in 2027 remains to be seen. She said some have approached her about chairing the Legislature’s Committee on Committees, an internal 13-person group that sets the new slate of committee assignments at the beginning of each two-year Legislature, or when there’s a vacancy, for all 49 lawmakers.
“Every day I’m going to just have to contemplate and take consideration of what’s going on,” Sanders said of the next two months.
The Nebraska Legislature’s select committee to investigate the feasibility of small modular nuclear reactors meets for its first hearing Friday, Oct. 27, 2023, in Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Committee assignments are made by three legislative “caucuses,” the members of which roughly comprise the legislative districts within Nebraska’s three congressional districts.
Of the three caucuses, membership is as follows:

1st Congressional District — 10 Republicans, six Democrats.
2nd Congressional District — five Republicans, 11 Democrats, one registered nonpartisan.
3rd Congressional District — 15 Republicans, one Democrat.

Sarpy County is in both the 1st and 2nd Congressional Districts, with Andersen part of the 2nd District caucus while Sanders and Rountree are part of the 1st District caucus.
The membership of the Government Committee was central to partisan disagreements on the Committee on Committees two years ago. During deliberations, the Government Committee moved from an initial 3-5 Republican-minority split to a 5-3 Republican-majority makeup. 
Sanders, who serves on the Committee on Committees, pushed for Andersen to join her. She had broken from conservatives to support a 4-4 split that got her Andersen but no majority.
In the end, the 1st Congressional District caucus representatives gave up two seats, previously held by state Sens. Danielle Conrad and Jane Raybould, who are both Democrats from Lincoln. The move allowed Andersen to join two Democrats and one nonpartisan progressive from the 2nd Congressional District on the committee. Both Conrad and Raybould were moved to the Natural Resources Committee.
Raybould, who didn’t seek reelection this year, had protested the move in song.
The next ‘industrial revolution’
While serving as mayor, Sanders said, she learned everything about the local levee and had found funding for the city near the river basin. When she first joined the Legislature in 2021, she wanted to be on Natural Resources, but her colleagues placed her on the Government Committee. Offutt Air Force Base is located within her Legislative District 45 in Sarpy County.
Sanders said Nebraska’s system of natural resources districts and levees is “near and dear” to her heart. As some view AI as an “industrial revolution,” she wants to be where the action is.
“I’m not sure we can have the serious chatter about it unless we have our infrastructure of our energy in place,” Sanders said.
In 2023, Sanders joined legislative efforts to examine the feasibility of small modular nuclear reactors, which the Nebraska Public Power District took up and has narrowed to four communities as of May: Beatrice, Brownville, Norfolk and Sutherland. Sanders was part of a trio of lawmakers who went to France to review nuclear and renewable energy capabilities, too.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, center left, hosts a ceremonial signing of Legislative Bill 1300, which in part created a state Commission on Asian American Affairs. State Sen. Rita Sanders of Bellevue, who is holding a copy of the bill, was joined by other advocates in May 2024. She is the first Filipina to serve in the Legislature. (Photo courtesy of Gov. Jim Pillen’s Office)
State Sen. Barry DeKay of Niobrara, a former board chair for NPPD, joined Sanders in the trip to France. He will seek to chair Natural Resources in 2027. The current chair, state Sen. Tom Brandt of Plymouth, is term-limited. DeKay chairs the Agriculture Committee.
Said Sanders: “That would be an exciting place to be and really try and put everything I’ve learned over these years on that committee, if I can do that.”
Sanders joked that her leaving the Government Committee would be fine and, if Andersen wins, it “gives him room to breathe without me in the shadow there.”
Sanders said her leaving the Government Committee was thought through and wasn’t because of health issues. She had scheduled open-heart surgery last week due to a failing aortic valve but returned home this week for recovery, which she said is going well.
She said her colleagues have taken into consideration multiple health challenges of lawmakers over the years and have always been “exceptional” about giving time to work when needed or when to plug back in.
“I’ve not felt like anyone’s tried to railroad me or leave me out of any side discussions or upcoming discussions,” Sanders said.
Sanders said challenges between lawmakers are often highlighted in media reports, but “there’s also some greatness in each one of the legislators down there that we will work together.”
The next legislative session begins Jan. 6.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Why AP called Mississippi’s US Senate race for Scott Colom
description: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom greets supporters at a campaign volunteer breakfast after the election at Brent's Drugs in Jackson on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
WASHINGTON — The Associated Press on Wednesday declared Democrat Scott Colom the winner in the race for U.S. Senate in Mississippi after several counties reported updated results — including those of last-to-count provisional ballots.
Colom led Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by 43 votes following the final election night update in Mississippi, which arrived at 2:03 a.m. CT from Pike County. 
Not only has Colom’s lead grown larger as counties in Mississippi have completed their vote count and reported on the outcome of their review of provisional ballots in the days since, but he’s won the vast majority of these final updates — in every region of the state and in all but the most Republican counties — by a large margin.
The AP called the race for the Colom just before 5 p.m. CT after officials in Jackson County updated its vote count with an additional 2,173 votes. The update put Colom up by 4,669 votes out of 962,237 counted, or 0.5 percentage points.
To come back and take the lead, Hyde-Smith needed to win these final vote updates in Republican-leaning counties such as Jackson. Instead, Colom won the update in Jackson by just over 1 percentage point.
The AP estimates there are fewer than 12,000 votes remaining for county election officials in Mississippi to review before the deadline Friday for counties to certify their election results. Many of those votes left to count are provisional ballots, which are called affidavit ballots in Mississippi, and a good number may not ultimately be counted once they are reviewed and assessed by election officials.
There is no recount law in Mississippi: Hyde-Smith would need to persuade a court to order a review of the election. In many states, the standard for conducting a recount is a margin of 0.5% percentage points between the top two candidates.
There have been about 40 recounts in statewide elections since 2000. Only three have resulted in a new winner and all three were decided by hundreds of votes, not thousands. There is no precedent this century for a recount overturning an election with a margin as wide as the one in Mississippi.

title: Chris Jones, who narrowly lost central Arkansas’ US House election, to run county planning office
description: Chris Jones, the Democrat who narrowly lost a bid for central Arkansas’ 2nd Congressional District last week, will run Pulaski County’s planning and development department next year, the county’s incoming chief executive announced Tuesday. Wendell Griffen, who won the election for county judge in the midterm election , wrote on Facebook that he chose Jones [[...]
text:
Chris Jones, a Democrat, answers questions at the press conference after the debate against Arkansas' 2nd Congressional District incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. French Hill on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026 at the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Chris Jones, the Democrat who narrowly lost a bid for central Arkansas’ 2nd Congressional District last week, will run Pulaski County’s planning and development department next year, the county’s incoming chief executive announced Tuesday.
Wendell Griffen, who won the election for county judge in the midterm election , wrote on Facebook that he chose Jones to “build a Planning and Development Department that listens to residents, works constructively with communities and applicants, and bases its recommendations on sound evidence, clear standards, and the public interest.”
Jones is a pastor and physicist from Pine Bluff who holds a doctorate in urban planning from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Griffen said Jones’ dissertation, focused on how race and socioeconomic status affect access to electricity, is one of his many qualifications for his new position.
“Dr. Jones brings strong academic preparation, experience in community development, and a commitment to public service,” Griffen wrote.
Jones ran to represent central Arkansas in Congress and narrowly lost last week’s election to Republican U.S. Rep. French Hill. Jones’ first foray into politics was his 2022 run for governor, which he lost to Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders.
If Jones had won either election, he would have been the first Black person to hold either office in Arkansas.
He indicated Tuesday via Facebook that he plans to run for office again.
“2028 is just around the corner! Don’t throw away your signs yet,” his post said.
Griffen, a former circuit and appeals court judge, will succeed Pulaski County Judge Barry Hyde, whom he defeated in the Democratic primary in March. Griffen is the first Black person elected to lead Arkansas’ most populous county.
Griffen has been an outspoken critic of data centers and has called for greater regulations over them, a heavily debated topic countywide this year as two technology companies have made plans to build data centers in Pulaski County.
Jones told the Advocate in October that he supported “innovation with accountability” regarding data centers and their use of electricity and water. He also said he believed Congress should play a role in regulating data centers.
Jones will leave his job at BCT Partners, a New Jersey-based consulting firm, to work for Griffen’s administration starting in January.

Details of service:
A memorial service will take place on June 19, 2027, at 11 a.m. at St. Catherine of Siena Church in Shelburne, VT, followed by a reception.

Holly A. Freeman Jones passed away on August 18, 2026, at the age of 71. She was born Jan. 7, 1955, in Potsdam, New York, to Mary and Philip Pepper and was later adopted by Richard Freeman.
She was predeceased by her brother Mark and her beloved husband, Dr. Dennis Jones, whom she married in 1995. Coming of age in the late 1960s, she brought a strong female force to the roles of daughter, mother, grandmother, sister, aunt and friend. She added generous doses of empathy and humor to each relationship.
Before moving to Vermont in 1992, Holly worked as a labor and delivery nurse in Rhode Island and was especially proud of her work with Women & Infants Hospital in Providence. Later, her family and friends came to know her as a doting “Mimi” to her three adored grandchildren. She also worked as a grief counselor, striving to make a positive difference in the lives of those who shared their losses.
She will be remembered for her talents as a gourmet chef (most notably, “all-day” spaghetti and hot turkey sandwiches) and “hostess with the mostest.” She loved Christmas, books, good television — including the news (MS NOW), which played in the background all day — shopping, crafting and playing Mexican Train with friends. She adored the many cats and dogs who shared her life and had a knack for enjoying the finer things. Most of all, we’ll remember her boundless generosity toward those she loved.
She spent many years living in Shelburne, raising her children, and Shelburne remained a beloved place for her. She also cherished the many winters she spent in Naples, Florida.
Holly was also a passionate Democrat who spent many years supporting and fundraising for local Democratic elections and causes close to her heart, including women’s rights. Her commitment to democracy and the causes she believed in was unwavering. We know she will do whatever she can from above to support democracy, especially in the 2028 election.
Across all aspects of her life, Holly’s sense of humor was a constant. Whether reacting to a particularly funny moment on film or TV, a joke made by her grandchildren or a comical comment made by a friend, her laughter was uninhibited and infectious. She had a particular knack for finding bits of comedy in the course of daily life, regularly bringing a smile when it was needed most.
Holly is survived by her loving daughters, Megan Daly and her husband, Dan, and Morgan Rocissono and her husband, Andrew Rome. She will be missed by her precious grandchildren, Nicky, Harper and Warren; her mother, Mary Freeman; her siblings, Crista, Jeff (Eleanor) and Mary Kaye; numerous nieces and nephews; and those who were part of her “family of friends.”
A memorial service will take place on June 19, 2027, at 11 a.m. at St. Catherine of Siena Church in Shelburne, followed by a reception.
