title: TN’s 4th district U.S. House race could be called after Nashville counts provisional ballots Monday
description: The Davidson County Election Commission will count the remaining provisional ballots in Tennessee’s 4th U.S. Congressional race at a Nov. 16 meeting, potentially allowing the outcome to be called in favor of a Democratic upstart.  After election night last week, Democrat Victoria Broderick led veteran Republican U.S. Rep. Scott DeJarlais by 285 votes in the [...]
text:
Tennessee’s 4th U.S. Congressional District likely can’t be officially called until after Nashville finishes counting its provisional ballots on Monday. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)The Davidson County Election Commission will count the remaining provisional ballots in Tennessee’s 4th U.S. Congressional race at a Nov. 16 meeting, potentially allowing the outcome to be called in favor of a Democratic upstart. 
After election night last week, Democrat Victoria Broderick led veteran Republican U.S. Rep. Scott DeJarlais by 285 votes in the 4th District.
Broderick has not officially been declared the winner because the multi-county congressional district still has about 700 provisional ballots to count. The district includes the eastern third of Nashville-Davidson County, Rutherford County and nine more rural counties in middle and east Tennessee. 
John Richardson, administrator of elections with the Davidson County Election Commission, said about 600 of those remaining provisional ballots are in the part of the district that includes Nashville-Davidson County. 
“We have a process, and it takes time,” Richardson said. 
The commission will determine this week which ballots are valid, and those will be put into voting machines to be counted at an 8 a.m. meeting on Monday, Nov. 16, Richardson said. Voters are allowed to cast provisional ballots when questions are raised about their eligibility to cast a regular ballot. Davidson County plans to certify its election results Nov. 19. 
DeJarlais has not conceded the race because the remaining votes exceed Broderick’s current lead. 
Democrats won heavily in Nashville during this election cycle, and Broderick has won 75% of the vote in the part of the district in Nashville where provisional votes remain to be counted.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Survey shows broad agreement on school screen time limits, value of devices
description: A survey of over 3,400 Alabama parents and school employees found broad agreement about time limits on screen use by students, though several instructors also noted that the devices could be useful in classrooms. The Commission on Screen-Based Instruction, formed by Gov. Kay Ivey, reviewed preliminary results of the survey on Tuesday, ahead of sending […]
text:
A child with a finger on a tablet. The Commission on Screen-Based Instruction, formed by Gov. Kay Ivey, reviewed preliminary results of a survey on attitudes about screen usage in classroom, ahead of filing a final report to the governor next month. (Oscar Lopez Rogado via Getty Images)A survey of over 3,400 Alabama parents and school employees found broad agreement about time limits on screen use by students, though several instructors also noted that the devices could be useful in classrooms.
The Commission on Screen-Based Instruction, formed by Gov. Kay Ivey, reviewed preliminary results of the survey on Tuesday, ahead of sending a final report to the governor next month.
Over 3,000 teachers and parents; nearly 400 school leaders and roughly 30 IT directors and staff participated in the survey. The survey was self-selecting, meaning people volunteered to take the survey.
Teachers who responded said they used screens in classrooms for assessment or progress monitoring, independent work, review skills, research and core instruction, among other tasks.
“What was interesting to the research team is that all of these activities are used (at least) sometimes or more (frequently in the classroom). So everything from passive practice review types of things to student creation work,” said Stefani Wind, a professor at The University of Alabama who worked on the survey.
Of the respondents, 50% of parents, teachers and school leaders strongly agreed that students are distracted by non-instructional content, or content that doesn’t directly involve teaching or coursework, and at least 30% of teachers, school leaders and parents agreed or strongly agreed that it’s difficult to bring attention back to instructional material after using devices.
Over 80% of teachers, parents and school leaders agreed that regular screen-free periods would benefit students.
The survey also took open-ended responses from teachers, parents and school leaders.
“Screen use interferes with the way the brain works and prevent(s) retention and transfer of information,” one school leader said. “Learning apps ‘gamify’ education to promote ‘engagement,’ but engagement does not mean learning.”
One parent said that while devices can be useful in classrooms, they shouldn’t be used across all grade levels.
“We need to be cognizant of how much time students are spending on screens. In my opinion, my five-year-old kindergartener should not know how to use a Chromebook and sign into Google Classroom,” the parent wrote.
One teacher wrote that they liked the access to information devices in the classroom provided and said there should be guidance.
“Sometimes, a kid might have 30 minutes on a screen, but during a research project,” the teacher said. “It might be more like an hour just because that’s the most efficient (and relevant) research tool.”
Brandy White, superintendent of Houston County Schools and a member of the commission, said in an interview after the meeting that the survey results were encouraging. 
“There were times where they may have their Chromebook open, but it’s actually guided instruction where the teacher is up at the board, and she’s going over certain questions,” White said. “So that looks like screen time, if you just calculate the amount of time that they were on it, but it’s actually guided instruction where they’re communicating back and forth.”
Rep. Jeana Ross, R-Guntersville, said after the meeting that filing legislation is a “possibility.”
“I think first you got to look at the recommendations and see exactly what’s in there, and also I want to talk some more to teachers and local school districts because that teacher autonomy I think is very important. But sometimes it helps, you know, to have some kind of guidance for them to be able to fall back on,” she said.
The committee will deliver its final report to Ivey on Dec. 1.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Power says it will not charge customers for most advertising costs
description: Alabama Power said this week it would stop charging customers for advertising costs except those related to public safety, following a request from the Alabama Public Service Commission, the state utility regulator. A state law passed in the spring will require the utility to stop using customer money for advertising by 2029. But PSC President […]
text:
Alabama Public Service Commission President Cynthia Almond (center) speaks during a meeting of the commission on Oct. 6, 2026 in Montgomery, Alabama. Commissioners Jeremy Oden (left) and Chip Beeker (right) listen. Alabama Power said Monday it would follow a request from the PSC to not pass on most advertising costs to its customers, though it was not immediately clear what effect if any that would have on power rates. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector)Alabama Power said this week it would stop charging customers for advertising costs except those related to public safety, following a request from the Alabama Public Service Commission, the state utility regulator.
A state law passed in the spring will require the utility to stop using customer money for advertising by 2029. But PSC President Cynthia Almond moved to ask the utility to implement it on an interim basis at the commission’s meeting on Nov. 3.
“I don’t see any reason that we shouldn’t take steps now to begin that process rather than waiting Jan. 1, 2029,” she said during the meeting.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The move passed unanimously. Alabama Power said in a statement Monday it planned to comply with the request.
“While the commission’s written order has not yet been issued, based on the motion approved at the November meeting, Alabama Power plans to comply by removing advertising expenses from customer rates in 2027 and 2028,” the company said in a statement Monday. “We will evaluate the order once it is released.”
The agenda did not list advertising cost as one of the items on the agenda of the Nov. 3 meeting. Almond did not say how much rates would decrease because of the decision or if it was in response to any advertising from Alabama Power.
Alabama residents pay higher than average utility rates compared to other states in the Southeast. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration website, Alabama residents paid an average of 16.33 cents per kilowatt-hour. By comparison, Tennessee residents paid an average of 13.42 cents per kilowatt-hour; Mississippi residents paid 14.43 cents; Florida residents paid 14.99 cents and Georgia residents paid 15.90 cents.
Messages were sent to Alabama Power and the Public Service Commission Tuesday seeking clarification on potential rate impacts.
The company also said in its statement it has followed Alabama law and previous orders from the PSC that “half of advertising costs are excluded from customer rates.” The statement also said that advertising costs that are part of its rates deal with “electrical safety, energy efficiency, storm preparedness and scam prevention.”
Gov. Kay Ivey in April signed HB 475, sponsored by Rep. Mack Butler, R-Rainbow City, that made several changes to the PSC, including expanding the number of members; creating a secretary of energy to oversee the commission and placing limits on when a commission can call a rate hearing.
The law also prevents utilities from charging customers for advertising, lobbying and expenses that pertain to grants offered by a company.
In October, the PSC required Alabama Power to make summaries of agreements it makes with the data center publicly available, as well as information about the project and expected power consumption.
Daniel Tait, executive director of Energy Alabama, a nonprofit that advocates for renewable energy in Alabama, praised the decision at its November meeting.
“It is great news,” he said in an interview Monday. “We were really excited by the commission President Almond’s leadership to get these costs out of rates immediately. There is no reason why customers should be paying for any advertising that Alabama Power is doing.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: ‘I don’t know if we’ve seen the worst of what’s coming.’ Medicaid changes loom for Kentuckians.
description: Cara Ellis was 27 when she got health insurance — which she’d gone without most of her life — through an expansion of Medicaid that allowed more, low-income adults to enroll in the government plan. Now Ellis, 39, a Pikeville native and senior at Morehead State University, said she’s worried she could lose coverage under […]
text:
Cara Ellis says Medicaid has been a lifeline for her. (Photo provided)Cara Ellis was 27 when she got health insurance — which she’d gone without most of her life — through an expansion of Medicaid that allowed more, low-income adults to enroll in the government plan.
Now Ellis, 39, a Pikeville native and senior at Morehead State University, said she’s worried she could lose coverage under pending, major changes in Medicaid required by federal and state law.
She credits Medicaid with saving her life after she was diagnosed in 2019 with thyroid cancer—four years after she qualified for health coverage.
“I have a lifetime of care ahead of me,” Ellis said. “This is something I worry about every single day.”
Significant changes enacted by Congress and the Kentucky General Assembly are coming to Kentucky’s $22 billion-a-year Medicaid program that provides health coverage for 1.3 million people including more than 600,000 children – making it the state’s single largest health plan. The federal government provides about 75% of the funding.
Kentucky officials worry that many beneficiaries don’t understand the changes or don’t realize they may have to follow new rules in an already complex program.
“I think the unfortunate reality is that it will catch people off guard,” said Dr. Steven Stack, secretary of the Cabinet for Health and Family Services, which oversees Medicaid in Kentucky. “No matter how hard you try to communicate, it’s hard to reach everybody.”
Key changes require most adults 19-64 to show they are working, in school or volunteering to keep coverage. And they will have to prove every six months they are eligible.
The changes take effect Jan. 1, and will be phased in with people allowed to “attest,” or self-report compliance with new rules over the first year. But that changes in 2028.
“Come Jan. 1, 2028, we are going to have to have all these systems operational and if people can’t demonstrate compliance, they unfortunately and very sadly are going to lose Medicaid benefits,” Stack said.
At the national level, 5 to 10 million people could lose Medicaid coverage in 2028 because of the changes, according to a study by the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. Many will be people who qualify because they already are working or in school but don’t provide adequate documentation or who don’t realize they are exempt for health or other reasons.
In Kentucky, “tens of thousands” could lose coverage for similar reasons, Stack said.
Still, Stack said the administration of Gov. Andy Beshear, a Democrat,  is working to notify as many people as possible to try to ensure they retain coverage.
“It is a fact that people without health insurance live sicker and die younger,” Stack said.
The ‘Big, Beautiful Bill’
Most changes were included in federal HR 1 of 2025, dubbed by the Trump Administration as the One Big Beautiful Bill. It’s estimated to cut Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion over 10 years.
The Republican-controlled Kentucky General Assembly enacted further changes to Medicaid through House Bill 2, including adding small-copays for some health services and tightening requirements for reporting work, school or volunteering.
Most changes begin Jan. 1, 2027. Newly elected Democrats, part of the recent blue wave, have vowed to make changes to the cuts, but it’s not clear if those could happen before the new rules go into effect in Kentucky.
Largely unaffected are the nearly 900,000 Kentuckians enrolled in “traditional” Medicaid—including low-income pregnant women, individuals below 100% of the federal poverty level, those with disabilities, and poor, elderly people in nursing homes.
Rather, most changes apply to those who gained Medicaid coverage through the 2014 expansion under the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare, that allowed adults earning up to 138% of the federal poverty level—about $22,000 a year—to enroll.
In Kentucky, that’s about 450,000 people ages 19-64—though some will be exempt for medical or other reasons.
Growth ‘unsustainable’
That includes Ellis, who said she already meets requirements through working and attending college full-time. But she worries that one missed deadline or piece of misplaced paperwork could cost her health coverage—and says she’s not alone.
“I think a lot of people are going to lose coverage,” Ellis said. “I think we’re going to see a lot of people across the state like me – who got health coverage for the first time – are going to lose coverage.”
Ellis is among people who spoke at a series of recent “listening sessions” House and Senate Democrats held in Louisville, Lexington, Morehead and Prestonsburg to hear people’s questions and comments about upcoming changes to Medicaid.
“It’s something I’m very passionate about,” she said. “I speak out frequently.
Rep. Lindsey Burke, D-Lexington and House minority caucus chair, attended the sessions and said she was impressed by the scope and importance of Medicaid in Kentucky.
“I would say by and large what we heard is Medicaid is a stabilizing force in the lives of Kentuckians,” Burke said. “Whether it’s the birth of a new child, helping new parents get on their feet, issues at the end of life or all the issues in between, Medicaid does a lot for the lives of Kentuckians.”
But Republicans have criticized the rapid growth and cost of Medicaid even as they express support for the health services it provides.
“What we have is a Medicaid budget (that) has nearly doubled, in fact, over doubled, over the past five years to an unsustainable level that we’ve got to do something (about) in terms of addressing the cost of this,” Rep. Ken Fleming, R-Louisville, said in February, speaking in support of HB2, which he sponsored. Fleming lost his election on Nov. 3 to Democrat Suhas Kulkarni.
What are the changes?
Changes include a requirement that individuals work, attend school or volunteer at least 80 hours a month and provide proof to the state. They also must “recertify,” or prove that they are eligible for Medicaid every six months instead of once a year.
During the first year, starting January 2027, individuals will be allowed to “attest” or report to the state they meet requirements.
But it gets more complicated in 2028 when individuals will be required to submit documents to verify employment, hours worked, income or other activities.
Stack, the cabinet secretary, said the state will use available sources, such as tax filings or public university enrollment records, to try to collect as much information as possible.
But state officials anticipate many will begin to lose Medicaid at that point.
“It will cause people to lose their coverage,” Stack said. “Not because they are ineligible . . . but because it’s a lot to keep up with.”
Who’s exempt?
The federal law cites a number of reasons individuals are exempt from the new rules including parents or caregivers of children under 14, pregnant women, foster youth or former foster youth up to age 26, those undergoing substance use treatment and disabled veterans.
It also exempts people considered “medically frail” with health conditions that prevent them from working.
For the first year, 2027, individuals will be able to attest that they can’t work, attend school or volunteer for health reasons.
But starting in 2028, they must provide proof of a health condition that counts as “medically frail.”
Stack said the state is working to come up with guidelines that define “medically frail” and how to verify it before 2028.


For more information:
The Kentucky Health Benefit Exchange, a state site that provides online information about changes coming to Medicaid as well as how to enroll or obtain other health coverage.
Also, the state is offering a site dedicated to the new, Medicaid work requirements.
Information is available through the local Department of Community Based Services office, with one in each of Kentucky’s 120 counties.
And Kentuckians whose Medicaid coverage is through one of five managed care insurance companies—Aetna, Humana, Passport, United and WellCare—can seek information through those providers. They are listed on the cabinet website.


Waivers not affected, mostly
“Waivers,” a handful of Medicaid programs that provide services to specific individuals with physical or intellectual disabilities, are not affected by reporting or work requirements, Stack said.
Cheri Kulik (right) with her daughter, Charlotte, at a T-shirt business they operate from their home in Oldham County. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Deborah Yetter)
But Cheri Kulik, an Oldham County mother whose daughter, Charlotte, 18, has autism and gets services through a program known as the Michelle P. Waiver, said even small changes can catch families unaware.
For example, the Michelle P.  program serves more than 10,000 individuals but has nearly that many on a waiting list – a wait that can last months or years because the state limits the number of slots it funds.
Previously, individuals could remain on the waiting list indefinitely.
Under a change in HB 2, families or guardians must prove they are still eligible once a year to remain on the waiting list, Kulik said.
“If you’re on that list and you miss this form you have to send back, they can take you off,” said Kulik, who attended the listening session in Louisville.
Kulik, who works with a support group for parents in Oldham County, said she’s trying to alert them to the change the state has begun notifying people about by mail.
“I said, ‘Watch for this letter. It’s coming,” she said.
Kulik, who said getting and keeping Medicaid coverage already is difficult enough, worries families may miss the waiting list renewal notice or other possible changes ahead.
“For a parent with a child with a disability, it is already ridiculously hard,” she said. “I cannot emphasize that enough.”
She added: “I don’t know if we’ve seen the worst of what’s going to happen.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Spanberger, Va. Democrats pitch medical debt relief, data center limits for 2027
description: Gov. Abigail Spanberger and Virginia’s top Democrats unveiled their 2027 legislative agenda Tuesday, proposing medical debt relief, limits on classroom screen time and tougher oversight of data centers and artificial intelligence as they seek to address rising costs for Virginia families.  Announced on the South Portico of the state Capitol in Richmond, the [...]
text:
Gov. Abigail Spanberger on Tuesday unveiled Virginia Democrats' slate of legislative priorities ahead of the General Assembly session that starts in January 2027. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)Gov. Abigail Spanberger and Virginia’s top Democrats unveiled their 2027 legislative agenda Tuesday, proposing medical debt relief, limits on classroom screen time and tougher oversight of data centers and artificial intelligence as they seek to address rising costs for Virginia families. 
Announced on the South Portico of the state Capitol in Richmond, the Moving Virginia Forward Agenda builds on Spanberger’s first-year affordability initiatives while adding proposals to address workers, help small businesses and crack down on AI-generated child sexual abuse material. 
Spanberger said healthcare, housing and energy costs remain priorities for her administration, warning that high living expenses could make Virginia less attractive to workers and businesses. 
“If the cost of living is too high, it impacts where talented people choose to live and work, where they choose to build their lives and their businesses,” she said. 
The lawmakers presented several data center proposals, including requirements for local approval of facilities using more than 25 megawatts, a ban on nondisclosure agreements with local officials and stronger oversight of cooling water use. 
Democrats also want to encourage solar development on previously developed land and working farms and create a new disaster preparedness declaration. 
The leaders repeatedly criticized President Donald Trump’s administration, blaming federal policies for adding to families’ financial uncertainty. 
Tuesday’s announcement comes ahead of another legislative election year. Democrats won 64 of the House of Delegates’ 100 seats in November 2025, a net gain of 13 that gave them a 64-36 majority. All 40 seats of the state Senate will be on the ballot in November 2027, along with the House. 
Sen. Louise Lucas, D-Portsmouth, the Senate’s president pro tempore, did not attend Tuesday’s event. She was indicted on federal corruption charges last month, a situation the governor declined to comment on Tuesday. 
Spanberger said the Democratic agenda is not yet complete, with more proposals to be announced around Virginia in the coming weeks. 
House Speaker Don Scott, D-Portsmouth, invited Republicans to work with Democrats on the legislation, saying affordability concerns extend across party lines. Senate Majority Leader Scott Surovell, D-Fairfax, said lawmakers could take steps to help Virginia families even when federal policies are beyond their control. 
 Healthcare: Debt relief and upfront prices

State Democrats want to create a medical debt forgiveness program that would work with a national nonprofit to buy outstanding debt from Virginia healthcare providers at steep discounts and cancel it. 
North Carolina, Michigan, Illinois and Arizona have established similar programs. Spanberger said the goal is to eliminate millions of dollars in medical debt. 
The package would also require healthcare providers and insurers to give patients good-faith cost estimates before non-emergency treatment. Hospitals would face new financial assistance requirements, including offering payment plans. 
“No one should walk into a doctor’s office with no idea what they’ll owe when they walk out,” Spanberger said. 
Scott said medical bills should not push families into financial hardship. Sen. Lashrecse Aird, D-Henrico, described hearing from a Virginian who was left with debt after an ambulance ride and treatment following an accident. 
The proposals follow legislation Spanberger signed earlier this year to address prescription costs, including restrictions on pharmacy benefit managers, which negotiate prices among insurers, drug manufacturers and pharmacies. 
The 2027 agenda, however, does not specify how the medical debt forgiveness program would be funded or who would qualify.
 Data centers and energy: Greater oversight, expanded solar

Spanberger highlighted some of her previously announced Data Center Accountability Framework, which outlines potential legislation that would tighten regulations on the data facilities growth and oversight as public pressure to rein in their growth intensifies.
Among those proposals is a move to ban nondisclosure agreements between data center companies and local governments. Del. Kathy Tran, D-Fairfax, said at Tuesday’s event that the controversial documents have left local residents in the dark as their elected officials make these development decisions.
“Communities deserve transparency, and a meaningful opportunity to weigh in on projects that will have lasting consequences for their neighborhoods,” Tran said. 
The governor’s priority list also includes a proposal to eliminate by-right approval for data centers using more than 25 megawatts of power and require local approval regardless of prior project approvals. 
By-right permitting is often allowed in specific zones deemed “technology overlay districts” or growth zones of counties. Projects can proceed under existing zoning without a project-specific rezoning or special-use vote in view of the public. 
Also in the governor’s plan are ways to protect “water scarcity” areas from evaporative cooling methods for the centers, putting more costs of transmission infrastructure onto those companies, and several other ideas. Official bills have not yet been filed.
Legislators also promised an increased investment in solar power on brownfields and in agrivoltaics — the method of putting solar panels on active farms that can maintain their crops concurrently. 
“That means expanding solar without paving over Virginia’s working families, working farms, and forests,” Scott said. “Through agrivoltaics, the former keeps forming, and the land produces food, and power at the same.”
 Housing: Building near transit 

Spanberger wants to increase housing near public transportation and give priority to affordable housing and transit-related infrastructure when the state sells or leases land.
She said building homes near transit could help residents save on both housing and transportation. Scott called for more walkable neighborhoods where people can reach jobs and businesses without relying as heavily on cars.
Surovell said additional housing near transit stations and above retail spaces could make it easier for younger workers to live near growing employment centers. 
The proposals follow this year’s debate over “housing near jobs” legislation, which would allow apartments, townhomes and mixed-use developments in certain commercial corridors. Republicans raised concerns about the state overriding local zoning decisions. 
Spanberger also signed legislation this year using Virginia’s bonding authority to support affordable housing and expanding efforts to reduce evictions. 
 Education: Less screen time, more career pathways 

Under a Democratic proposal lawmakers previewed Tuesday, Virginia school divisions would have to limit unnecessary student screen time, prioritize teacher-led instruction and regularly evaluate the technology used in classrooms.
Districts would also be required to develop plans to reduce excessive or ineffective use of digital learning tools.
The proposal goes beyond restrictions on students’ personal cellphones to address technology used during instruction.
Parents and former educators urged state officials in August to strengthen classroom technology guidelines, calling for greater use of physical books, handwriting and face-to-face learning. 
Senate Democratic Caucus Chair Mamie Locke, D-Hampton, said Tuesday technology can help students learn but should also not distract them or interfere with instruction. 
Locke also called for additional investments in early childhood education, teachers, literacy, mathematics and school facilities. 
Meanwhile, lawmakers are also considering changes to how Virginia funds public education. A legislative subcommittee approved hiring an expert last month to examine alternatives to the state’s decades-old K-12 funding formula. 
Democrats also want to expand pre-apprenticeship and youth apprenticeship programs, improve access to career training for underserved populations and establish quality standards. 
Transportation and childcare assistance would help more Virginians participate. 
 AI regulation: Child protection and worker pay 

Democrats proposed banning the creation, possession and distribution of AI-generated child sexual abuse material and holding AI companies accountable when their platforms or models produce such content for users.
House Majority Leader Charniele Herring, D-Alexandria, said the legislation would establish civil penalties for companies whose technology allows the material to be created.
She warned that advances in artificial intelligence could give predators new ways to exploit children while making it harder to identify victims and prevent abuse.
“The risks to our children and our communities are real, and they are growing,” Herring said. 
Another proposal would restrict employers from using AI and machine learning to determine the lowest wage or salary a job applicant might accept based on surveillance data and assumptions about their personal finances. 
Spanberger said employers should not be allowed to use the technology to take advantage of applicants’ financial circumstances. 
 Small businesses: A central source of help

The administration wants to expand the Department of Small Business and Supplier Diversity’s role in helping entrepreneurs find financing, technical assistance and other resources. 
Spanberger said small business owners often struggle to navigate the various programs offering capital, counseling and government contracting assistance. 
Under the proposal, the department would serve as a central point of contact, directing businesses to programs that fit their needs. 
Aird said workforce development is another challenge, particularly for businesses looking to expand and hire local workers who have the necessary skills. 
 Republican lawmakers respond, as legislature stares down January return 

In a statement Tuesday afternoon, House Minority Leader Terry Kilgore, R-Scott, dismissed the Democrats’ affordability message. 
“If there was anything ‘affordable’ in that press event, I didn’t hear it. There was nothing that will bring down power bills, nothing that will end the car tax, nothing that will end the grocery tax, nothing that will help young people get started in life.”
Kilgore said House Republicans would put forward their own proposals to cut taxes for working families, lower electricity bills and expand economic opportunities. 
The bills lawmakers described Tuesday don’t yet appear in Virginia’s Legislative Informative System. Drafts of all bills must be available for public review by Dec. 31, according to state law. The 2027 General Assembly session is slated to convene on Jan. 13.

title: Gun violence prevention programs saved Virginia hospitals more than $100 million
description: By Sandra Jones/WHRO Hospital-based violence intervention programs across Virginia have served nearly 10,000 patients since 2019 and helped avoid an estimated $101.8 million in health care costs, according to the Virginia Hospital & Healthcare Association. Four of those programs in Hampton Roads have served 5,290 patients since March 2020. Fitzroy Smith, hos[...]
text:
Sentara Norfolk General Hospital offers one of four hospital-based gun violence prevention programs in Hampton Roads. (Photo by Katherine Hafner/WHRO)By Sandra Jones/WHRO
Hospital-based violence intervention programs across Virginia have served nearly 10,000 patients since 2019 and helped avoid an estimated $101.8 million in health care costs, according to the Virginia Hospital & Healthcare Association.
Four of those programs in Hampton Roads have served 5,290 patients since March 2020.
Fitzroy Smith, hospital violence intervention program supervisor at Sentara Norfolk General, said the programs serve public health and financial interests.
“It really demonstrates that hospital intervention programs are not just mission-driven. We’re also financially responsible. When you stabilize patients, you also stabilize hospital systems,” Smith told WHRO News.
Sentara offers its Foresight Violence Intervention Program at Norfolk General Hospital.
VHHA reports a 3% re-injury rate among patients receiving HVIP services, compared with an estimated 40% among victims who do not receive intervention services. The reduction in repeat injuries has helped avoid more than $49 million in health care costs, according to the association.
Specifics of gun violence intervention programs differ but generally connect patients with trauma-informed care and support services during and after hospitalization. Programs can also provide assistance such as safety planning, counseling, transportation, housing resources and connections to community organizations.
A gunshot injury can cost between $30,000 and $50,000 per person, Smith said. Many patients who sustain those injuries are uninsured, underinsured or covered by Medicaid, leaving hospitals to absorb significant portions of the cost.
“So the hospital has to bear the burden,” Smith said. “Now, for a homicide, it’s anywhere from $1.6 million to $3 million per individual.”
Smith said the programs can reduce those costs by preventing further violence and keeping people from becoming hospital patients in the first place.
“When you interrupt violence, that’s an added responsibility that’s taken off of the hospitals because they have to treat the individual that comes into that hospital room. Our job is to make sure they don’t come there in the first place,” he said.
January Serda is the grant coordinator for Riverside Hospital’s Hand-In-Hand Violence Intervention Program. She said savings for hospitals come from addressing patients’ immediate medical needs and the factors that contribute to violence.
Serda said the programs also help patients maintain care by connecting them with outpatient services and behavioral health support.
“None of us are saviors over here,” Serda said. “What we’re really doing is empowering that individual to tap into their own strength and power and resiliency to save themselves.”
Research also plays a role in understanding which violence prevention strategies are effective and how programs can measure their impact.
Nicholas Thomson is the associate dean for research in Virginia Commonwealth University’s School of Public Health and director of the university’s new Center for Gun Violence Research.
He said VCU works with community organizations involved in gun violence prevention efforts to understand their goals and develop evaluations based on the populations they serve and the types of violence they seek to prevent.
“We see ourselves as a key partner in these community organizations in the gun violence prevention initiatives,” Thomson said.
For hospital-based intervention programs, that could include collecting data on firearm injuries and other firearm-related measures. Youth violence prevention programs may examine victimization, firearm involvement and changes in violent behavior, he said.
Thomson said an important part of gun violence prevention research is identifying risk factors before someone becomes involved in violence.
“Much of our research really does need to focus on a prevention standpoint,” he said. “So, that’s identifying what risk factors lead to gun violence. And that’s really the mechanism that we’re trying to target before these youth or people engage in gun violence.”
Virginia has 12 hospital-based violence intervention programs across 10 health systems, following the addition of programs in 2026 at Ballad Health’s Johnston Memorial Hospital in Abingdon in June and UVA Health in Charlottesville in April.
Other participating health systems include Bon Secours in Richmond, Carilion Clinic in Roanoke, Children’s Hospital of The King’s Daughters in Norfolk, INOVA in Fairfax and Chesapeake Regional Medical Center.
A spokesperson for Chesapeake Regional Medical Center said its Healing Opportunities Providing Empowerment (HOPE) program is on pause following personnel changes.

title: Commentary: This Veterans Day, give veterans more than thanks
description: I’m a retired Marine pilot with two Combat Action Ribbons. Today, I live in Northern Virginia and fly a Boeing 777 between New York and Europe as a commercial airline captain. My passengers trust that the training and procedures I rely on have been tested.  Veterans deserve the same rigor when they ask their primary […]
text:
Two men salute while participating in New York City’s Veterans Day parade Nov. 11, 2024. (Photo by Spencer Platt/Getty Images)I’m a retired Marine pilot with two Combat Action Ribbons. Today, I live in Northern Virginia and fly a Boeing 777 between New York and Europe as a commercial airline captain. My passengers trust that the training and procedures I rely on have been tested. 
Veterans deserve the same rigor when they ask their primary care providers at the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) whether a treatment option they seek can help them. They also deserve a government willing to listen when they describe what has helped them live with the consequences of their service.
That matters here. Virginia is home to more than 600,000 veterans, one of the highest shares of any state.
This Veterans Day, Congress faces a choice. Legislators could support research and responsible access to hemp-derived CBD and other hemp-derived products that are federally legal under the 2018 Farm Bill. 
Or they could allow a sweeping restriction to take effect on December 11 that will remove nonintoxicating hemp products that thousands of veterans already use as alternatives to highly addictive VA-prescribed opioids.
As of July 2026, the VA has dispensed more than 2.18 million naloxone (Narcan) prescriptions to more than 820,000 veterans, according to its own website. The VA points to this as evidence that it is saving lives, while failing to adequately confront the role prescription opioids have played in creating the very addiction crisis that makes this lifesaving medication necessary.
I joined the military in 1981, and later, in college, I relied on VA health care because it was the only care I could afford. VA health care is remarkable in many ways. Still, many of the Vietnam veterans I met told me it had gaps.
Steve Danyluk as a young Marine in Grenada. Photo courtesy Spartan Sword)
Some lived with persistent pain and found the side effects of prescribed medications unbearable. Some turned to marijuana bought on the street while trying to cut back on opioids. Those conversations challenged my assumptions.
In 2018, the late veterans advocate Boone Cutler, one of my closest friends, and I pressed Congress to support VA cannabis research. That same year, the 2018 Farm Bill created a federal distinction between hemp and marijuana, opening a path for hemp-derived CBD products.
Veterans’ accounts of relief deserve attention, and they do not replace clinical evidence. But that evidence continues to grow, and the VA has already shown a willingness to investigate new approaches, including a recently announced psilocybin trial for veterans with treatment-resistant depression. 
Instead of supporting that same openness on cannabis, the December 11 restriction threatens hemp products containing even trace amounts of THC far below an intoxicating level.
Virginia shows there is a better way. This year the commonwealth tightened its own rules, capping hemp products at 2 milligrams of THC per package on top of existing requirements for lab testing, labeling and child-resistant packaging. Reasonable people can debate where Virginia drew that line. But the federal restriction would override it with a limit five times stricter.
Congress should address unsafe products, misleading labels, and sales to children. But it should do so through enforceable standards that distinguish products by their contents and effects. 
Independent testing, accurate labeling, appropriate age restrictions, and sensible limits per serving and package would serve consumers better than a threshold that sweeps nonintoxicating CBD and other hemp products into the same prohibition.
Through my work with Spartan Sword on suicide prevention, I have heard veterans describe what it feels like to run out of options. I am not claiming that CBD prevents suicide. I am saying that people living with pain and trauma deserve to be heard, deserve credible research, and deserve a voice in decisions that could take away something they believe helps them.
Congress can act before December 11. Virginia’s U.S. Sens. Mark Warner and Tim Kaine and Virginia’s House delegation could lead the way in protecting responsible access while funding the research veterans and their clinicians need. 
Pew Research Center’s 2024 survey found that 88% of Americans supported marijuana legalization for medical use. That is not a verdict on every hemp product, but it is a clear rejection of blanket prohibition.
If we really want to do more for our veterans than give them a free cup of coffee and a banal “Thank you for your service” this Veterans Day, let’s give them the opportunity, and the right, to heal however they wish after returning home. I believe they have earned that right.
Will Virginia’s members of Congress agree?

title: Honolulu Affordable Housing Program Creating Far Fewer Units Than Planned
description:
A Honolulu program meant to boost the development of affordable rental housing is falling short of its goals, according to a new report from University of Hawaiʻi economists. Bill 7, enacted in 2019, offered Honolulu developers incentives to keep units affordable to moderate-income households. The law was intended to ease housing costs in a city that is […]
[...]
text:
A Honolulu program meant to boost the development of affordable rental housing is falling short of its goals, according to a new report from University of Hawaiʻi economists.
Bill 7, enacted in 2019, offered Honolulu developers incentives to keep units affordable to moderate-income households. The law was intended to ease housing costs in a city that is increasingly unaffordable.  
A report by the UH Economic Research Organization, or UHERO, found that as of September, only seven out of 85 projects have been completed since the program began — amounting to only 224 out of 2,280 units that applied for a permit since 2019. The original goal of the program was to complete 500 units per year.
The UHERO report notes development has been made harder since 2019 because of persistently high interest rates and construction costs, the latter of which increased by 30% since the program began.
Permitting has also been slow. Of the 19 city building permits issued before July 2025, none were ready within the 90 days the law calls for, with the median waiting time being 531 days. 
More: Honolulu’s Effort to Fast-Track Affordable Housing Projects Hasn’t Worked
Davis Pitner, spokesperson at the Department of Planning and Permitting, has made progress on Bill 7 projects in recent months. The most up to date totals show 412 units across 11 projects have been completed, he said.
“While annual production is below the program’s goal of 500 units,” Pitner wrote in a statement, “a complete assessment should consider both completed housing and projects moving toward construction and occupancy.”
The Department of Planning and Permitting’s processing times seem to be improving, said Trey Gordner, lead policy researcher of the UHERO report. But challenges remain. Researchers estimated every month of permit delays add roughly $74,000 to the cost of the project, which is not as significant as construction or financing costs, but it quickly adds up. 
Gordner said that the Bill 7 program works on paper, but it may not be enough under current building conditions.
“It’s directionally right,” Gordner said, “But it’s much more expensive today to build under this program.” 
The original goal of the program was to complete 500 units per year. Only 224 have been completed since 2019. (Credit: UHERO Report 2026 – Assessing Honolulu’s “Bill 7” Housing Program.) Gordner, T., Takahashi, S., & Prager, E. (2026). Introducing the Housing Policy Simulator. UHERO. https://uhero.hawaii.edu/introducing-the-housing-policy-simulator/
Bill 7 was designed to encourage small-scale apartment projects on lots of 20,000 square feet or less in areas already zoned for apartments or mixed-use development. 
In exchange for the benefits, developers must rent at least 80% of the units to households earning 100% or less of area median income, which Honolulu considers to be $107,800 for an individual and $154,000 for a family of four. Pricing restrictions last at least 15 years.
Some of the incentives include an exemption from off-street parking requirements and relaxed density and height limits. 



Data Dive
Data Dives are Civil Beat's quick takes on numbers and data sets with a Hawai‘i angle.





Read More

Hono­lulu City Council Chair Tommy Waters told the Star Advertiser that increasing the supply of affordable housing remained a “top priority” for the city. The bill falling short of its goal is concerning, he said, but that UHERO’s report “provides valuable insight into where improvements are needed, particularly in reducing permitting delays.”
UHERO put together a housing policy simulator based on pro forma, a spreadsheet model that real estate developers use to evaluate whether a project makes financial sense. 
The simulator is an interactive tool meant to estimate how much Bill 7 improves project feasibility and what sort of policy changes can improve it further. According to the simulator, the program raised estimated return on cost from 5% to 6.2%, although this still falls short of the 6.6% investors look for. 
Gorder encourages those interested to test other potential policy changes for themselves using the tool.
While Bill 7 isn’t producing the number of units policymakers had hoped for, it is still providing community benefits, according to Gordner.
The program “is ostensibly an affordable housing program,” he said, but “it also furthers many of the city’s other goals with respect to sustainability, use of transit, creating walkable communities and making the best use of existing infrastructure.”

title: ‘Free Palestine’ Stickers Get Librarian Criminally Convicted On Kauaʻi

text:
Eden Peart stood to accept her sentence in a Līhuʻe District Court on Tuesday morning, facing the possibility of up to four months in jail for misdemeanor property damage charges. The gallery was packed, standing room only. 
Such low-level charges would not normally garner so much community interest, but Peart’s crimes had touched a nerve on Kauaʻi. 
The 64-year-old librarian was found guilty in August of placing stickers on a Kapaʻa falafel truck menu sign owned by a local Israeli man. The rectangular stickers show a black fist raised in the air with the words: “This company’s funds support the Palestinian genocide. Free Palestine.”
The case on Kauaʻi is a microcosm of the tensions playing out around the world amid the conflict between Israel and Palestine that erupted three years ago. 
On Oct. 7 , 2023, the Palestinian terrorist group Hamas attacked villages and a music festival in southern Israel, killing more than 1,200 people and abducting at least 250 more. The Israeli government’s response and ensuing war has led to the deaths of more than 74,000 Palestinians, losses scholars and international authorities consider a genocide.
The conflict has sparked pro-Palestinian protests across the globe, including on Kauaʻi where demonstrators have gathered on a near weekly basis at the Kapaʻa Public Library to protest Israel’s military campaign and American involvement. Meanwhile, Jewish leaders have reported a rise in antisemitism, both locally and internationally. 

Peart was charged with placing the stickers on the falafel truck’s menu board on two separate occasions in December 2025. (Court exhibit)

Battle lines have been drawn in communities across the globe, extending into people’s everyday lives far from the Middle East, and tensions have flared in ways big and small. In this case, the battle is over stickers placed on a sign some 9,000 miles from the conflict. 
To Jewish community members on the island, Peart’s targeting of the food truck, Shakalafel, owned by Uriel Churgin, was an act of antisemitic vandalism, something that historically has been a precursor to violence against Jews. 
To Peart and her supporters, placing the stickers was a relatively minor act, intended to spark conversation about the Palestinian cause and the treatment of pro-Palestinian demonstrators on Kauaʻi. 
Lauren Miller, a Jewish community organizer on the island, said she respects anyone’s right to protest or express their opinion on the conflict, as long as they respect the humanity of the people on both sides. What Peart did, though, was not freedom of expression, she said, but rather a hateful attempt to hurt a Jewish business. 
“A line was crossed here,” she said. 
Peart, for her part, said she is not antisemitic and didn’t intend to cause harm by placing the stickers. 
A review of fourth-degree criminal property damage cases dating back to 2021 showed the count is often charged alongside a more serious felony, such as terroristic threatening or robbery. 
Judge Michael Scarbo sentenced Peart to 100 hours of community service. He told the court that the right to freedom of speech allows you to express your beliefs on your property, not plaster them on the property of someone else.
“This was not a sticker that was a butterfly or that said “Live, Laugh, Aloha,” he said. “This was a sticker intended to draw attention to someone because of their racial, ethnic, religious beliefs and a series of assumptions based on those beliefs. It was done with intent.”
He called freedom of speech “a fundamental tenet of life in the United States,” that allows us to put signs expressing our ideology in our own yards.  
“It does not allow us the right to put a political sign on our neighbor’s yard,” he said. 
Property Damage By Sticker
Shortly after 9 p.m. on Dec. 18, 2025, surveillance cameras at Churgin’s food truck captured Peart placing two 5×3-inch stickers on his menu board out front, court documents show. 
It was not the first time Peart had vandalized his business, Churgin said. Another time, a worker had seen her place a similar sticker on the board during the day and called Churgin, who rushed over to the business. He said he found Peart a few blocks away charging her electric car and pulled over to take a photo of her license plate. 
Between October and December, Churgin said he peeled the stickers from his business’s signage dozens of times only to have them reappear the next day. The constant peeling not only damaged his signage, he said, but also caused fear among his staff. 
Churgin said the stickers were placed on his business’s sign repeatedly between October and December 2025. Peart said she only placed the stickers a couple of times. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
Peart said she only placed stickers on the signs a couple of times. Court records don’t specify a number.
Miller, the Jewish community leader, remembers talking to Churgin at the time. 
“He called me, and he was like, ‘I’ve got to talk to you, this is happening on a daily basis,’” she said. “There’s lots of other food trucks in the area, nobody else’s food truck was getting stickers on it.” 
Churgin told her he’d put up surveillance cameras outside his truck. Miller encouraged him to report the vandal to the police and the FBI, which he did. 

Surveillance footage from Churgin’s business showed Peart walking toward the truck with her dog. (Court exhibit)

Churgin said it was important to him to report Peart and hold her accountable for her actions. It wasn’t just about the stickering, which he saw as a targeted antisemitic attack. Throughout history, vandalism of Jewish businesses has preceded episodes of violence. He said he recalled reading an article about the 2025 shooting at a Hanukkah celebration at Bondi Beach in Sydney, Australia.  Jewish businesses and synagogues in Sydney had reported increased rates of vandalism leading up to the shooting. 
“That’s what gave me the motivation to feel like I’m responsible to catch this individual and press charges,” he said. 
Police arrested Peart on Jan. 8 on two counts of fourth-degree property destruction, according to court records. The petty misdemeanor charge is used for cases in which a person “intentionally or knowingly damages the property of another without the other’s consent.” 
Peart said that at the time, she didn’t even know placing a sticker on someone’s property was a crime, though she now admits that ignorance of the law isn’t a defense. 
At her sentencing Tuesday, Scarbo, the judge, said that given her position as a librarian, he would have expected her to have a better understanding of the law. 
“To say you were ignorant of the law to that extent, as a librarian, also flies in the face of reason,” he said. 
‘Plain Old Racism’
Peart said she put up the stickers in hopes of sparking a broader conversation about the plight of Palestinians. She said she became especially moved watching the news and and seeing the suffering of children in Gaza. But she also described it as a kind of revenge for the way pro-Palestinian protesters, including herself, had been treated by pro-Israel demonstrators locally. 
When she decided to place the stickers on Churgin’s business in late 2025, she said she was still reeling from the trauma of something that happened to her at a demonstration nearly a year and a half prior outside the Līhuʻe airport in February 2024. 
Judge Michael Scarbo sentenced Peart to 100 hours of community service. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
That day, as she and a friend stood at the northeast corner of Ahukini Road and Kapule Highway, a man draped in an Israeli flag approached them, shoved Peart in the chest and told her he hoped her daughter and granddaughter got raped and killed, Peart said. Her friend, artist and activist Isa Maria, who’d organized the demonstration, said the threatening phrase has stuck in her mind to this day. 
“Those are the words I remember, word for word,” Maria  said. 
Neither woman pressed charges or filed a police report about the incident. Maria said she called 911 after the confrontation, but by the time an officer arrived, the man had gone back to the other side of the road. She remembers the officer went over to talk to the man and told him to stay away from her and Peart. The two women didn’t take any further action. 
“I wish I’d thought to defend myself and press charges,” Peart said. “But I didn’t think of it.” 
Peart said she doesn’t know who the man was who confronted her and Maria that day. But a photo from the event shows him standing near a group of four other men who are leaning on a blue pickup truck. One of those men was Churgin. 
“That she had an encounter with someone else that may share the same ethnicity as me as an excuse to vandalize my business is kind of crazy.”Uriel Churgin, business owner
Churgin said he remembers attending the demonstration that day to show his support for Israel. But he said he doesn’t remember seeing Peart or noticing any confrontation between the Israeli and pro-Palestinian protesters. He also said he doesn’t know the man Peart says assaulted her. 
For Peart to draw a connection between the man from the protest and Churgin’s business is “plain old racism,” Churgin said. 
“That she had an encounter with someone else that may share the same ethnicity as me as an excuse to vandalize my business is kind of crazy,” he said 
Peart said she now acknowledges that taking her frustration out on Churgin’s business was “not the best approach.”  
“I think it was like a therapeutic gesture I came up with to feel like I defended my daughter and granddaughter,” said Peart, whose 40-year-old daughter and 15-year-old granddaughter live in Sardinia. “I realize it’s illogical.” 
Concerns About Antisemitism 
Shortly after Peart’s arrest in January, the Jewish community on Kauaʻi suffered another blow. Multiple swastikas were found spray painted on the Sleeping Giant Trail on Nounou Mountain. 
A Hawai’i News Now article about the vandalism quoted Churgin, who talked about the stickers at his falafel truck. The surveillance footage from his business played on the news, and even though Peart’s face was blurred, she said people in the small community recognized her. 
Peart embraced supporters outside the courtroom after her sentencing on Tuesday. Even though she avoided jail time, some still saw her sentence as too harsh. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
After the article came out, she recalled a supervisor at the library suggested she “lay low” and remove a “Read Palestine” pin she often wore at work. 
The Hawai’i Public Library System did not respond to a request for comment. 
Churgin said he has no evidence that Peart was involved in the swastika painting, but he thinks she contributed to emboldening other vandals. 
“She’s definitely to blame with trying to normalize this very clear Jew hatred,” he said. 
Peart was horrified at the suggestion that she might be involved in painting swastikas on the trail, something she called “abhorrent.” 
Andrew Laurence, a spokesman for the state Department of Land and Natural Resources, said the investigation in the trail vandalism is ongoing. 
On Feb. 8, Peart was arraigned on two counts of fourth-degree criminal property damage and two counts of second-degree criminal tampering for placing the stickers on Churgin’s signs. She pleaded no contest to the first count and not guilty to the second. Members of Kauai’s Jewish community, including Churgin, came to the courtroom to observe. 
Shortly after her arraignment, Peart filed for a temporary restraining order against Churgin. She wrote in her petition about the Hawaiʻi News Now story and said he appeared at her court hearing with a woman who stared at Peart in a “very threatening manner.”  
Judge Robert Goldberg denied her petition the same day stating that Peart failed to show Churgin had been harassing her. 
‘Not Rainbows And Unicorns’
In June, Peart’s public defender, Samantha Mead, filed a motion to dismiss the charges. 
She said prosecutors hadn’t shown that Peart intended to damage Churgin’s sign and harm his business. 
“Churgin continued to operate his business under normal circumstances and was not substantially inconvenienced simply by having to remove some stickers,” she wrote. 
Lauren Miller, a Jewish community organizer on Kauaʻi, hugs a friend outside the courtroom. Miller said the Jewish community was shaken by recent acts of antisemitism on the island. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
She also wrote that the potential consequences, up to 30 days in jail and a $1,000 fine for each count, far outweigh the severity of the crime. 
But deputy prosecuting attorney M. Cherice Siebert wrote in a counter motion that the “hateful and racist stickers” Peart placed on Churgin’s business were intended to drive away customers. 
The business owner was “not substantially inconvenienced simply by having to remove some stickers.”Public defender Samantha Mead
“Defendant’s stickers were not rainbows and unicorns but a hateful message intended to cause not only a substantial inconvenience but harm to Mr. Churgin’s business,” Siebert wrote. 
Judge Matthew Bracken denied the motion to dismiss, and Judge Michael Scarbo found Peart guilty in August of both counts at a bench trial. 
Churn said he felt the Peart’s sentence was too lenient and feared it would not do enough to deter future bad actors. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
Churgin said he hoped Peart would do jail time to set an example for others who may want to harm people because of their identity. He was disappointed Tuesday by what he saw as a too-lenient sentence and feared bad actors would be emboldened to commit future vandalism against his business and others. 
“I don’t think the sentencing was meaningful enough to show an example,” he said. 
He and others in the Jewish community were also disappointed that Peart’s crimes were not treated as hate crimes. 
There is no separate charge in state law for hate crimes. Rather, a judge can dole out a harsher penalty at sentencing if the defendant is found to have acted against their victim on the basis of protected characteristics, including religion.
In Peart’s case, the sentencing enhancement could not be applied to such low-level charges, according to Kauaʻi prosecutor Rebecca Like. 
But Miller said it was crucial for the Jewish community that the police and prosecutors took the case seriously. 
“If this were to go unnoticed or not have consequences, then our fear as the Jewish community is it would then signal to others that it’s okay to do that,” she said. “That’s one reason why we’ve watched this case so closely.” 
Jews are an extreme minority in Hawaiʻi, making up less than 1% of the islands’ population, according to the Pew Research Center. 
There have been 12 anti-Jewish hate crimes reported since 2021, according to a dashboard run by the Hawaiʻi Attorney General’s office, which tracks hate crimes. The majority of hate crimes recorded in Hawaiʻi are anti-white, with 128 reported since 2021, according to the dashboard. 
Some high-profile cases of antisemitism have rocked the community in recent years, including a series of bomb threats emailed to synagogues around the state in 2023 and Montana man who recently pled guilty to sending antisemitic death threats to Gov. Josh Green. 
For the Jewish community on Kauaʻi, Peart’s stickers were another example, and even though the case is now closed, the harm continues, Miller said. Because Peart still works at the Princeville Public Library, some Jewish families no longer feel comfortable going in with their children.
“There are many ways to advocate for Palestinian rights and sovereignty that don’t infringe on the rights and sovereignty of Jews or Israelis.” Lauren Miller, Jewish community organizer on Kauaʻi
Peart said she was saddened to hear that and said everyone is welcome in the library. 
Pro-Palestinian activists said they planned to continue their regular demonstrations and hoped to do so peacefully and without confrontations from counterprotesters. 
Rachel Lawrence, a local activist, said she hopes Peart’s case will serve to keep people talking about the genocide and human rights violations happening in Gaza. 
“I think that that could be some of the good that comes out of this,” she said, “because the more people have conversations about this, the better.” 
Miller said moving forward, she would remain focused on uplifting positive voices for the community. She recently helped host a series of talks by Holocaust survivor Gabriella Karin. She also hopes to one day soon host Ahmed Fouad Alkhatib, a Palestinian-American activist who founded the organization Realign For Palestine and has spoken out against Hamas. 
“There are many ways to advocate for Palestinian rights and sovereignty that don’t infringe on the rights and sovereignty of Jews or Israelis,” she said. “There’s so much nuance there, and our culture and tradition invites debate and argument for the sake of learning. Jewish tradition cherishes this.”

text:
Imagine a young person growing up on Hawaiʻi island who dreams of becoming a nurse, physician, electrician or entrepreneur. Through education, mentoring and hard work, that person develops the skills to pursue a meaningful career.
We celebrate that achievement. But then comes a more difficult question: Can that person afford to remain here?
That is the uncomfortable reality we face: We can help prepare people for better-paying careers without ensuring they can afford to build a life here.
The housing numbers tell the story
Hawaiʻi island has dramatically different housing markets.
In September 2026, the median single-family home sold for approximately $399,000 in Puna and $502,000 in South Hilo. On the West Side, prices reached $1.14 million in South Kohala and $1.3 million in North Kona.
At recent mortgage rates, purchasing a $1.3 million home with a 20% down payment can mean housing costs approaching $8,700 monthly, including estimated taxes, insurance and maintenance.
To keep those costs near 30% of household income requires annual earnings approaching $350,000, along with $260,000 for a down payment.




Ideas showcases stories, opinion and analysis about Hawaiʻi, from the state’s sharpest thinkers, to stretch our collective thinking about a problem or an issue. Email  news@civilbeat.org to submit an idea or an essay.


Read More

Renting offers limited relief. Our review of recent three-bedroom rental listings found asking rents averaging approximately $2,300 to $2,750 monthly in Hilo, compared with $4,250 to $4,470 in Kailua-Kona.
A family needs approximately $100,000 annually to comfortably afford many of those Hilo rentals, compared with $170,000 or more in Kona.
For perspective, Hawaiʻi County’s official 2026 median-income benchmark for a family of four is $98,300.
This is no longer simply a challenge for low-income households. Even families earning $100,000 to $150,000 annually can struggle to secure suitable housing near their workplaces.
Even well-paid professionals face difficult choices
Consider the healthcare professionals our island desperately needs.
The University of Hawaiʻi’s 2025 physician workforce assessment identified a shortage of approximately 224 full-time-equivalent physicians in Hawaiʻi County. Although preliminary statewide figures suggest some improvement, access to healthcare remains a serious challenge.
Over the past year, the healthcare committee of my organization has met with executives of major Hawaiʻi island hospitals, practitioners in smaller medical practices, and educational leaders at the University of Hawaiʻi and our community colleges.
These conversations have reinforced the challenges of recruiting, training and retaining healthcare professionals.
A physician considering a position in Kona may earn a substantial salary, but also carry significant educational debt and face extraordinary housing costs. A comparable mainland opportunity may offer a larger home, lower living expenses and greater financial security.
Specialists establishing independent practices face additional expenses for facilities, staffing, equipment and insurance.
Even when professional salaries are competitive, purchasing power may not be. The same dilemma, often with far less income, confronts nurses, teachers, skilled tradespeople and other essential workers.
We cannot expect to attract and retain the workforce our island needs if qualified professionals conclude they can build better futures elsewhere.
A remarkable opportunity – and a missing connection
Hawaiʻi has received approximately $189 million in first-year federal funding through the Rural Health Transformation Program, creating an extraordinary opportunity to strengthen healthcare, expand professional training and support recruitment and retention.
Programs such as HOME RUN — Hawaiʻi Outreach For Medical Education In Rural Underserved Neighborhoods — can help develop pathways for future healthcare professionals and support those choosing to serve our rural communities.
These investments are encouraging and urgently needed.
But training additional nurses, physician assistants and doctors is only part of the equation.
If graduates cannot afford to establish households where their skills are needed, and experienced practitioners find the financial sacrifices of relocating here too great, we risk diminishing the long-term value of these investments.
The same challenge confronts our efforts to develop skilled tradespeople, educators, entrepreneurs and other essential members of our workforce.
Housing is an economic development responsibility
At the Kohala Coast Community Fund (KCCF), we support more than 20 organizations helping Hawaiʻi island residents acquire the skills, confidence and opportunities to pursue meaningful careers. Our mission is to create pathways for our residents to remain and thrive in their home communities.
Yet addressing Hawaiʻi island’s housing shortage requires substantial capital, land, infrastructure, regulatory coordination and long-term commitment.
These are challenges that workforce development organizations such as KCCF are not equipped to solve. Our resources and expertise are appropriately focused on education, training, mentoring and creating career opportunities.
But our experience gives us a clear perspective on what is at stake.
A 16-unit, low-income housing project previously under construction in Hilo. (Jason Armstrong/Civil Beat) Jason Armstrong/Civil Beat
Affordable workforce housing must become an explicit priority in the economic development strategies of county and state government, major employers, the business community and organizations dedicated to housing.
The responsibility must be shared by those with the resources and authority to act.
There are promising models elsewhere in the country: community land trusts that preserve affordability, partnerships that develop housing on public or privately contributed land, revolving housing funds, and employer-assisted housing initiatives.
We have a local example in Nā Hale Makoa, the 140-unit affordable rental community in Waikoloa Village, developed on county-owned land through public-private collaboration.
These approaches deserve broader consideration, adaptation and investment.
Three priorities stand out:

First, make workforce housing part of economic development planning. When government, hospitals, major employers and educational institutions assess future workforce needs, they must also consider where those workers can realistically afford to live.
Second, mobilize public and private resources to expand housing opportunities. Governments, developers, major landowners, employers and housing nonprofits should pursue partnerships that make more appropriately priced homes and rentals available near employment centers.
Third, remove unnecessary obstacles to building housing. More efficient permitting, coordinated infrastructure investments and innovative, cost-effective construction methods could help increase supply while preserving appropriate environmental and community safeguards.

None of these measures offers a simple or immediate solution. But the economic and social costs of inaction will continue to grow.
Training alone is not enough
Across Hawaiʻi island, educators, nonprofit organizations and community leaders are helping residents develop the knowledge, skills and confidence to pursue meaningful careers.
These efforts are making a difference, and they deserve continued support.
But their promise is diminished when the people who benefit cannot afford to remain in their communities.
KCCF will continue doing what we do best: supporting organizations that equip our residents with the skills and opportunities to succeed.
We are counting on our partners in government, business and the housing sector to do their part.
Affordable housing is not simply a social service. It is essential economic infrastructure, as fundamental to our future as education, healthcare, transportation and reliable utilities.
Our island needs nurses, physicians, teachers, construction workers, entrepreneurs and skilled professionals. We must also create communities where these individuals and their families can afford to live.
We can help prepare Hawaiʻi island residents for meaningful careers. But ensuring they can build their futures here requires a broader community commitment.

title: States are counting on battery farms. Some towns don’t want them.
description: SNOQUALMIE, Wash. — In the race to meet the nation’s growing power demands, states and utilities are rapidly building new “battery farms” that can store energy for when customers need it most.
