text:
A battery storage facility sits in front of wind turbines near Palm Springs, California. States and utilities are building battery farms but many communities oppose them. 
(Photo by Mario Tama/Getty Images)SNOQUALMIE, Wash. — In the race to meet the nation’s growing power demands, states and utilities are rapidly building new “battery farms” that can store energy for when customers need it most. But as the facilities grow, so too does community opposition.
The systems store banks of batteries in buildings or shipping containers. While they can take many forms, developers are increasingly building large, multi-acre projects designed to meet the needs of local utilities. 
The electricity stored by such systems nationwide has grown tenfold since 2022, and it’s projected to double again by the end of 2028. State lawmakers and renewable energy advocates say battery storage is urgently needed to stabilize the grid and support the transition to clean power. 
But in some communities, residents are wary of proposals to build industrial battery systems in their neighborhoods, noting that battery fires can produce toxic smoke and are difficult to extinguish. As the backlash has grown, nearly 200 communities have passed or proposed moratoriums to block battery farms from being built near them.
Backers say modern systems are designed to be much safer than previous versions, with data showing that fire risk has dropped significantly. But some industry leaders fear the perception of danger — along with a rising tide of community activism stirred by the buildout of data centers — could threaten an industry that’s becoming integral to the nation’s energy future.
‘Meteoric growth’
Most energy storage on the U.S. grid takes the form of battery energy storage systems, commonly known as BESS. Such facilities host banks of batteries, typically lithium-ion — a technology that has become more capable and cost-effective with the development of electric vehicles. 
At present, battery storage capacity nationwide exceeds 50 gigawatts, up from just 5 gigawatts at the beginning of 2022. Another 54 gigawatts is slated to come online in the next two and a half years. That projected total of more than 100 gigawatts would be enough to power roughly 75 million homes, although battery farms are designed to provide electricity for one to four hours, as opposed to the more continuous supply of conventional power plants. 
“The meteoric growth is continuing,” said Noah Roberts, executive director of the U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, an industry group. “For state policymakers who are focused on the energy transition and decarbonizing the grid, (battery) storage is essential.”
Data center backlash set to sway midterm elections

Policymakers and energy planners have increasingly pushed for battery farms as more renewable energy sources have come online. Solar farms, for instance, can produce massive amounts of cheap electricity during the afternoon hours — but peak demand is in the evening, when people get home from work and turn on household appliances. 
With batteries on the grid, that surplus solar energy can be stored and saved for when it’s needed, instead of firing up more costly “peaker” gas plants to meet evening demand. 
Industry leaders say battery systems can also improve reliability and affordability, even in states without clean energy goals. They note that Texas and California are home to a majority of the battery projects on the grid so far. While typically on opposite ends of the political spectrum, both states produce large amounts of wind and solar energy, while facing heavy power demands that have at times required energy conservation measures and put the grid at risk of blackouts. Battery systems, backers say, have already stabilized their grids considerably. 
Adding to the appeal of battery farms is the fact that they can be put in place quickly, in a matter of months, compared with much longer timelines for other energy projects. 
“As we’re dealing with a power supply crisis, energy storage is the obvious solution for adding capacity and getting more out of the grid that we’ve already paid for,” Roberts said. 
State policies have been a driver of the industry’s growth. Thirteen states have enacted targets requiring their utilities to deploy certain amounts of energy storage by specific dates. 
In Maryland, Democratic Del. Lorig Charkoudian authored a law in 2025 directing state regulators to issue bids for projects totaling 1,600 megawatts of energy storage. 
“It’s basically a no-regret path,” Charkoudian said in an interview earlier this year. “Over time once we bring more renewables on, they will be that much more valuable because there’s battery storage.”
Charkoudian noted that the Trump administration has stalled permitting for offshore wind and other renewable projects, while phasing out clean energy tax credits. The federal push against those forms of energy has made battery farms a more attractive option, as they’ve met with less resistance and still qualify for a 30% tax credit. 
Community concerns
For all of the potential that battery farms offer the grid, some communities are not eager to host them. Much of the opposition centers around the risk for out-of-control fires and toxic smoke. 
Most prominently, the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County, California, caught fire in early 2025, burned for several days and released 55,000 pounds of toxic metals into nearby wetlands. 
Lithium-ion batteries, when ignited, can trigger a reaction known as thermal runaway that is nearly impossible to extinguish. Across the country, community activists have been alarmed to see battery farms proposed near schools, playgrounds and senior care facilities. 
States OK solar panels for balconies. Safety guidelines haven’t caught up.

“They’re making us collateral damage,” said Phoenix Artemisia, an activist in Watsonville, California, who has helped lead efforts to oppose a proposed battery storage facility there. “We have 12 schools within two miles of us here, but these out-of-state developers are telling us what we’re going to do in our backyard.” 
The Watsonville project has stirred up significant community opposition, Artemisia said, prompting the developer to seek approval from state regulators in order to bypass local officials. 
Industry leaders say the Moss Landing facility was built using an older design, prior to the issuance of safety standards from the National Fire Protection Association that cover most systems on the grid today. Newer projects use an updated battery chemistry that burns at lower temperatures, and store the batteries in isolated, modular containers so that fires don’t spread to nearby units. 
As a result, battery fires have become much more rare and far less devastating. Earlier this month, the Electric Power Research Institute, an independent nonprofit, published an analysis of battery system failures dating back to 2011. 
The report found that failures (defined as large thermal events such as arc flashes, fires or explosions) have declined 97% in the U.S. since 2018, when adjusted for the amount of battery power on the grid. The incidents that have happened in new systems have largely remained small and contained, said Lakshmi Srinivasan, who authored the analysis. 
“Specific design choices have really reduced not only the likelihood of a failure, but the impact of a failure if it happens,” she told Stateline. 
Srinivasan said the risk profile of battery farms is similar to that of electrical transformers, components of the electrical grid that already exist in many communities. 
But some communities feel a slim chance of disaster is still too high. Residents in Snoqualmie, Washington, have voiced opposition to a proposed battery project just outside city limits, prompting the city and several neighboring communities to enact moratoriums on such facilities. 
“We need to think more carefully about what the worst-case scenario is, not just what’s typical,” said Dan Murphy, a council member in the city of Snoqualmie. “The science says (battery farms) are getting safer, but we’re still early.” 
Amid the local backlash, the developer, Jupiter Power, has indicated that it will pursue approval from state-level energy siting regulators, removing the project from King County jurisdiction. 
Murphy said his community supports clean energy, but objected to the site location near homes, a playground, a waterway and a critical evacuation route. He said Jupiter Power kept locals in the dark until they thought the project was a done deal. 
A sign in Snoqualmie, Washington, opposes a proposed battery energy storage system, known as BESS. (Photo by Alex Brown/Stateline)
“We are a very reserved and polite community,” he said. “To see the outcry and the animation and the mobilization, it’s really struck a nerve with our residents.” 
In a document responding to community concerns, Jupiter Power noted that battery farms must be built near substations, which are located in close proximity to the communities they serve. That reality, the company said, makes it unrealistic for local officials to demand that battery systems keep their distance from populated areas. In King County, the company found, all 157 substations that are suitable for a battery project are located within a quarter-mile of schools, daycares, hospitals, natural areas or other sensitive sites.
Jupiter Power did not grant an interview request, but referred questions to Clean and Prosperous, a Washington-based nonprofit focused on reducing emissions.  
“For any battery storage project there will inherently already be energy infrastructure nearby,” said Kelsey Nyland, communications director with Clean and Prosperous. “It often feels like we expect clean energy projects to be perfect in a way that we don’t expect from fossil fuel projects.”
Nyland noted that Washington state ranks dead last in the nation for clean energy growth, despite its ambitious climate goals. Battery storage, she said, can help population centers in western Washington harness surplus wind and solar power from rural eastern Washington. 
She added that Washington has only one operational battery storage facility, making it difficult to alleviate local’s concerns by touring a nearby site. 
Similar disputes have played out in dozens of communities across the country, and many have passed temporary measures banning the construction of battery storage facilities. 
Earlier this month, a pair of former economic officials from the Biden administration wrote in The Washington Post that battery farms had been caught in a case of “mistaken identity” amid the nationwide backlash to data centers, which have stirred up similar feelings about industrial siting and environmental risks. But while data centers increase pressure on the grid, battery farms reduce it, they wrote, making the “conflation” an expensive mistake. 
Some local activists have asked for battery farms to be sited in remote areas, where they would pose fewer risks. But industry leaders say they’re simply following the incentives set forth by utilities, which prioritize projects that can connect to the grid near population centers. 
“If you have a source of power right where the power’s being consumed, the more efficient your system’s going to be,” Malaquias Encarnacion, managing director with Carina Energy, a development services firm that works on battery storage projects. 
Carina Energy has tracked 175 battery farm moratoriums enacted or proposed by communities across the country. In some cases, Encarnacion said, those actions have been temporary measures enacted by local governments to give themselves time to learn about the issue. 
“If I didn’t know anything about it, I would be nervous as well,” he said, encouraging developers to engage with communities early to alleviate those concerns. 
Stateline reporter Alex Brown can be reached at abrown@stateline.org.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana child welfare agency to need $300M state infusion
description: New Director Jennifer Dorfmeyer acknowledged continued challenges for the agency but shared progress and goals with lawmakers.
text:
State agency leaders give budget presentations to Indiana's State Budget Committee on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The state agency responsible for protecting vulnerable children expects to need a cash infusion of $300 million in the coming months.
That’s according to the operating account summary submitted by the Department of Child Services for a hearing before the Indiana State Budget Committee Tuesday.
The document shows an estimated $300 million is expected to be transferred into the department’s main account for the 2027 fiscal year, which started in July.
Over the year prior, the agency spent nearly $1.3 billion in state dollars and almost $400 million in federal funding — 72% of which was spent on services for children and families.
Director Jennifer Dorfmeyer, who has led the department since April, acknowledged continued challenges for the agency, which has reported such shortfalls in recent years.
New Indiana Department of Child Services Director Jennifer Dorfmeyer. (Photo courtesy of DCS)
While the child welfare caseload has flattened, she said, the cost per case is still going up.
“To address the increased utilization we are seeing, DCS created a service utilization review team to provide the right services at the right time,” Dorfmeyer told the Budget Committee.
In mid-September, the team launched a pilot in two Marion County offices with higher spending, with a third office on track to join next week.
“All referrals are being reviewed prior to approval,” said Dorfmeyer, with an emphasis on individualized service planning over standardized service packages. About 30% of referrals are returned for changes, according to an agency slide deck.
Partial September results show a 19% drop in the average referral cost per case when compared to the average from the three months prior. There’s full data for October showing a decrease of 34% compared to the same three-month average.
The department is also reviewing services with a consulting firm, Milliman, with plans to create a smaller pool of resources for family case managers and clients.
“Many of our existing services are very broad and not addressing the underlying needs to move our families and children into permanency. We also lack services that address high acuity,” Dorfmeyer said. “By evaluating and breaking apart some of our existing services, we feel we can provide more targeted and appropriate services. This would also provide an opportunity to ensure additional funding sources such as Medicaid are identified more easily.”
Another consultant, Myers & Stauffer, is helping the department model proposed changes to the rates paid to providers.
Dorfmeyer also pointed to progress in a performance improvement plan with the feds.
The Department of Child Services presented to the State Budget Committee on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (Screenshot of slide deck)
“Every state participates in performance improvement plans in child welfare, so it’s not unusual, and we were actually one of the only states to successfully complete our PIP,” she said.
That included outperforming the federal target on timely initiation, risk assessment, caseworker visits with families and more.
The department still reported high turnover in key positions, like family case managers and attorneys. Training replacements can delay child welfare cases and costs money.
And 16 children in Indiana have not been placed with relatives, foster families or other care.
The Indianapolis Star reported in 2024 that at least 168 children removed from their families spent at least a day living in department offices — with the average being three days and the longest stay lasting more than a month.
Dorfmeyer said she aims to end that practice.
“We utilize Cooper and Isaiah (117) Houses when we can, so they’re not always in the office,” she said. And we also provide bedrooms, beds, things like that in the offices when we have to, but the welcome center is direct, targeted, to keep kids out of the office.”
“My goal in my tenure here is to close the offices to children,” Dorfmeyer said.
Her department was one of the numerous verticals and agencies that presented to the State Budget Committee this week. Budget-writers are busy preparing for the legislative session’s start January.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Commentary: A thank‑you on Veterans Day won’t close the growing military‑civilian gap
description: When the voice came over the plane’s PA system, it seemed familiar yet surprising: “Hello, everybody.” “What?!” a passenger shouted, shocked. Others laughed and rose from their seats as former President Barack Obama appeared in person and welcomed the airplane of veterans to Washington before Veterans Day in 2025. They had flown from Wisconsin to […]
text:
Veterans Day in the United States honors those who have served in the nation's military and also coincides with the anniversary of the conclusion of hostilities on the western front in World War I. (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images)When the voice came over the plane’s PA system, it seemed familiar yet surprising: “Hello, everybody.”

“What?!” a passenger shouted, shocked. Others laughed and rose from their seats as former President Barack Obama appeared in person and welcomed the airplane of veterans to Washington before Veterans Day in 2025. They had flown from Wisconsin to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport aboard an Honor Flight to see the capital’s monuments to military service.
“I wanted to stop by and just say thank you for your extraordinary service – to you, your family,” Obama said in brief remarks later posted to social media. “The sacrifices that all of you made to protect our country is something that will always be honored.”
Obama’s post was one of 399,000 references to veterans on the social media platform X on Veterans Day last year, Nov. 11, 2025. The annual holiday was established to “solemnly remember the sacrifices of all those who fought so valiantly on the seas, in the air and on foreign shores, to preserve our heritage of freedom,” as President Dwight D. Eisenhower proclaimed.
The hundreds of thousands of posts are compelling to me as a social scientist who studies how veterans are represented in the media. The volume of commentary illustrates Americans’ desire to recognize veterans, but it also captures the transience of public attention.
By the following Tuesday, Nov. 18, 2025, the number of references to veterans plummeted by 374,000, or nearly 94%. The news cycle had moved on.

This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

The shift was not particularly surprising. My research shows that social media mentions of veterans peak in positive sentiment at two points each year: Veterans Day and Memorial Day. The rest of the time, the conversations on social media are largely driven by news outlets releasing stories and politicians announcing programs and events.
Indeed, social and other mass media play a role in what experts describe as a military-civilian gap. Put simply, while U.S. adults hold the military in high regard, they do not understand the institution or the experiences of its personnel despite its importance in domestic and international affairs and its $900 billion in taxpayer funding.
This military-civilian gap can create problems when it comes to military recruitment, civilians’ ability to identify with neighbors who serve and veterans reintegrating into civilian society.
The military-civilian gap
The military-civilian gap exists in part because, since the draft ended in 1973, the share of Americans who have served in the armed forces has declined. Only about 6% of adults were veterans in 2022, a decline from 18% in 1980. Compounding the issue, a decreasing proportion of U.S. adults personally know someone who has served. That means much of the population is learning about military life through mass media representation.
Journalists gravitate toward stories in which the subject matter is timely, emotional or full of conflict, because these qualities engage audiences. They operate on tight deadlines with limited resources. They also face restricted access to the Pentagon.
That means news outlets may be more inclined to cover a holiday, charity event or violent crime involving veterans than to take deep dives into the military budget or examine the role of veteran-owned businesses in the local economy.
Because of this, veterans end up typecast as heroes or victims of their service.
Politicians also influence which issues people in the U.S. see in the news or discuss on social media, but the share of members of Congress with military experience has plummeted since the 1970s.
Veterans in the media
In a 2018 study, our research team examined how news organizations in all 50 states represented veterans in news stories shared on X. In analyzing 1,460 stories, we identified three themes, which together described a majority of stories: veterans as heroes, as recipients of charity, or as victims of mental or physical harm.
Some military veterans may be heroes, and some may face challenges related to trauma, reintegrating into civilian society or navigating government bureaucracy. Such coverage may certainly be newsworthy.
The problem, according to critics of veterans’ representation in news media, is that not much else appears in the media. As one veteran told a researcher, “It doesn’t sell newspapers that Joe Smith from Davenport went to Afghanistan three times, got out of the military, went to college, and now works as an account manager for American Eagle.”
But media representations of social groups shape our perceptions of the world. A 2021 experiment found that exposure to stereotypical news stories about veterans led readers to associate veterans with post-traumatic stress disorder, a misunderstood and stigmatized condition. This, in turn, led readers to feel less desire to be socially close with veterans. The outcome illustrated how stories can have unintended downstream consequences even when journalists are covering newsworthy topics – in this case, PTSD and homelessness.
We also tested whether reading a second story – one in which veterans talked about media stereotypes – would dampen those negative effects. It worked, illustrating the importance of a news feed that provides nuance.
In another study, we asked 1,047 U.S. adults to picture a veteran, describe the veteran and then explain where the image originated. When people depended on media for their image, rather than personal experience, they called to mind stereotypical images such as homelessness, PTSD and heroism.
Given these stereotypes, a number of veterans organizations are advocating for broader, more insightful media representation. Military Veterans in Journalism and Veterans in Media & Entertainment are nonprofits that help veterans pursue professional careers in news and entertainment media, motivated in part by the potential for veterans to produce nuanced stories about military life. There are also nonprofit news organizations, such as The War Horse, seeking to bridge the military-civilian gap through storytelling and investigative reporting.
Beyond ‘thank you’
Media can draw attention to veterans. Obama’s airport surprise racked up 10.8 million views, 136,000 likes and 18,000 shares on X. But it will take more than made-for-media moments to bridge the military-civilian gap. That includes taking conversations with veterans offline.
In a 2019 study, U.S. Air Force Maj. Nicholas J. Mercurio conducted focus groups with veterans and active-duty service members and asked how they felt about “reflexive and formulaic expressions of gratitude” from the public such as “thank you for your service.”
Responses were mixed, in part because veterans assumed civilians did not understand what that service entailed. Nonetheless, there was general agreement that civilians could go beyond thank you by showing interest in the personal experiences of veterans and having sincere conversations about their jobs.
In doing so, civilians can demonstrate “interest in the individual,” Mercurio wrote, “not what they represent.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Wisconsin Democratic lawmakers step into new era with election of two women leaders
description: The transition to a new era of Democratic leadership in Wisconsin was set in motion on Tuesday as Democrats elected Rep. Greta Neubauer (D-Racine) to serve as the next Assembly speaker and Sen. Dianne Hesselbein (D-Middleton) to serve as the next Senate majority leader.  Both lawmakers were expected to be chosen to lead by their […]
text:
Rep. Greta Neubauer, who was first elected to the Assembly in a January 2018 special election, will be the first woman to serve as speaker. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner) The transition to a new era of Democratic leadership in Wisconsin was set in motion on Tuesday as Democrats elected Rep. Greta Neubauer (D-Racine) to serve as the next Assembly speaker and Sen. Dianne Hesselbein (D-Middleton) to serve as the next Senate majority leader. 
Both lawmakers were expected to be chosen to lead by their respective caucuses as they led in the minority and helped shepherd in the Democrats’ midterm election wins for the first time in 16 years. 
Neubauer, who was first elected to the Assembly in a January 2018 special election, will be the first woman to serve as speaker. She has led Assembly Democrats since 2021 and in the upcoming session will lead a Democratic caucus of 53 members. She succeeds Republican Assembly Speaker Robin Vos (R-Rochester), who had held the position for 13 years.
Hesselbein, who was first elected to the Senate in 2022, took charge of the Senate Democrats in December 2023. At the time, the caucus only had 11 members. She will now  lead a majority caucus of 18-members.
Their elections mean the Wisconsin State Legislature will be led by two women for the first time in state history.
“It, of course, is a historic moment, and we hope to use our positions to make life better for women, for families, and for people across the state,” Neubauer said. 
Senate lawmakers were giddy as they gathered for their caucus meeting on Tuesday morning, giving hugs and congratulations to their colleagues. 
“15 years since I’ve been in the majority,” Sen. Bob Wirch (D-Pleasant Prairie) said a few times as he greeted his colleagues. He is the longest serving member in the Senate, having been elected to the position in 1996.
Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley and state lawmakers will be sworn in on Jan. 4, 2027. 
“We are united, and we are ready to govern. I cannot be more excited to work with this thoughtful and hardworking group of people from all across our state,” Neubauer said at a press conference. “I do not take this responsibility lightly. At this moment, I am thinking about my own 5-month-old daughter and every child here in Wisconsin, and what the future holds for them. Our responsibility is to do right for them. That will take a tremendous amount of work, but we are up for it.”
“What a day this is,” Hesselbein said ahead of the Senate Democrats’ caucus elections. “We know the assignment. We’ve been working towards this for years, and we are going to get it done.” 
Neubauer told reporters Democrats plan to meet over the next few months to speak about their priorities. She said there are many bills they are considering, including free school meals for students, investing in our public schools and regulating prescription drug costs, but she said they still need to discuss what comes first.
“We have a lot that’s ready to go,” Neubauer said.
Sen. Dianne Hesselbein will now lead a majority caucus of 18-members. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
Hesselbein was asked about a number of issues including marijuana legalization, opting Wisconsin into the National Popular Vote Compact and artificial intelligence. Her answer was similar for each question, saying that her caucus needs to have open discussions first. She said Senate Democrats plan to meet through November and December. 
“I understand everyone has a sense of urgency, but just for the first time today, we welcomed three new senators-elect to our caucus,” Hesselbein said. “Whereas I have knocked on thousands of doors for the past year and a half listening to voters, they have done tens of thousands of doors, and so we really want to bring those voices from those districts that really didn’t have any good representation in this building until this moment.” 
Sen. Mark Spreitzer (D-Beloit) was elected by Senate Democrats to serve as the Senate president. Some of the priorities he mentioned include placing guardrails on data centers, lowering the cost of everyday essentials, making healthcare and medications more affordable, fully funding schools, restoring the Knowles-Nelson Stewardship Program and reigning in artificial intelligence.
“After years of Republican inaction, there is so much that we must get done for the people of Wisconsin,” Spreitzer said in a statement. 
Crowley and Lt. Gov.-elect Sarah Godlewski spoke to lawmakers in their closed caucus meetings on Tuesday. Crowley dodged questions from reporters afterwards. 
Crowley has said he would be interested in a blue ribbon commission that looks at the state’s taxation system, including school funding and Act 10. 
Neubauer said Democrats need to be thoughtful, but also need to work quickly. 
“We need to be thoughtful about how we approach these pretty challenging issues. We have a lot of priorities that we hope to fund. We want to invest in schools in a serious way that sets them on a different trajectory and stops the endless cycle of referendum,” Neubauer said. “We’re always open to participating in those more comprehensive looks at deeper, challenging issues. We do want to move quickly to make sure that we are restoring collective bargaining rights and investing in our skills in the way that our kids.”
Neubauer said Democrats are discussing changes to the school funding formula and said her caucus will be “pushing very hard to restore the rights of working people in Wisconsin.” 
“I think it’s possible that we will propose some changes in the school funding formula, but our No. 1 priority is to get kids and families the resources that they need,” she said.
Hesselbein said during the press conference that she would need to speak with Crowley about his comments on a blue ribbon commission. 
Republicans prepare to be in the minority
Republican lawmakers are preparing for their own transition to minority status in the Legislature. Assembly Republicans elected Rep. Tyler August (R-Walworth) to serve as the next Assembly minority leader. 
Sen. Howard Marklein (R-Spring Green), who lost his bid for reeelection to Sen.-elect Jenna Jacobson (D-Oregon), said it was an honor to serve as the chair of the powerful budget committee.
Marklein was in the building as the Joint Finance Committee met for likely the final time under his leadership with co-chair Rep. Mark Born. The committee approved a $124,000 transition budget for Crowley. It will provide support, including staff, equipment, travel and legal support, for his transition into the governor’s office. 
Marklein told reporters that he wished the next co-chairs the best, and declined to offer  his thoughts on what the biggest challenge could be. He also said it was up to Democrats to decide what to do with the state’s $3 billion budget surplus. 
“It’s a big responsibility,” Marklein said. “You have to ask the leadership. It’s always a challenge, I think, in a caucus to unify over what their priorities are and stuff. It’s great to have the majority. Now, you have to have the government. That’s not always easy.” 
Newly-elected Senate Minority Leader Julian Bradley (R-New Berlin) told reporters that Republicans are in “uncharted territory,” but he is prepared for life in the minority. Bradley is the first Black person to hold the leadership position and only the second Black Republican in the Senate.
“I was born in the minority, so it’s a little bit easier for me,” Bradley said. “At the end of the day, we’re prepared to do everything we can. While being in the minority is new, representing the people that hired us to do this job is not, and we’re going to come here to Madison. We’re going to fight tooth and nail every day when there’s areas to work together like on tax cuts and affordability, putting money back in people’s pockets.” 
Bradley said he didn’t think the new Democratic leadership would be “punitive or vindictive.” He said he had also recently spoken to Crowley in a brief phone call. 
“He knows we’re going to be a thorn,” Bradley said. “It’s going to be really difficult to take him at his word when he’s already flip-flopped on something as big as mid-cycle redistricting.”
Bradley said he would be interested in doing anything apart from affordability legislation, including a tax cut.
“They’re talking about the national voter compact and the giving away of the votes of Wisconsin,” Bradley said. “That’s absolutely absurd and ridiculous. We’re going to fight that tooth and nail all these other things.”
Hesselbein said that Democrats didn’t plan on locking Republicans out of the legislative process. She said she had a conversation with Bradley after he was elected. 
“I assured him that we will hear Republican bills. My door has always been open for the best ideas going forward. I think it was the last session. We had five Democratic bills that had hearings and only two became law. That shouldn’t be what we do in the state of Wisconsin,” Hesselbein said. “I think people are really sick of the terrible stuff… and they just want some sense of normalcy in our state of Wisconsin.”
The other members of the Senate majority leadership are: 

Sen. Kristin Dassler-Alfheim (D-Appleton), who will serve as the Senate assistant majority leader
Sen. Dora Drake (D-Milwaukee), who will serve as the Senate president pro tempore
Sen. Melissa Ratcliff (D-Cottage Grove), who will serve as the caucus chair 
Sen. Jeff Smith (D-Brunswick), who will serve as the vice caucus chair 

The other members of the Assembly majority leadership are: 

Representative Lisa Subeck (D-Madison), who will serve as speaker pro tempore
Representative Kalan Haywood (D-Milwaukee), who will serve as majority leader
Representative Mike Bare (D-Verona), who will serve as assistant majority leader
Representative Clinton Anderson (D-Beloit), who will serve as caucus chair
Representative Karen DeSanto (D-Baraboo), who will serve as caucus vice-chair
Representative Ann Roe (D-Janesville), who will serve as caucus secretary
Representative Margaret Arney (D-Wauwatosa), who will serve as caucus sergeant-at-arms

The other members of the Assembly minority leadership are: 

Rep. Nate Gustafson (R-Ormo), who will serve as assistant minority leader
Rep. Mark Born (R-Beaver Dam), who will serve as caucus chair
Rep. Joy Goeben (R-Hobart), who will serve as caucus vice-chair
Rep. Barbara Dittrich (R-Oconomowoc), who will serve as caucus secretary
Rep. Will Penterman (R-Hustisford), who will serve as caucus sergeant-at-arms

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: When bombarded by an uncaring corporate world, focus on making a difference with your dollars
description: Like everyone else these days, I am exhausted by the news cycle. I did vote, though. And I hope you did, too. As the votes are tallied and certified, pay attention and keep steady. A recent Washington Post poll found that seven out of 10 Americans don’t believe Trump will accept Republican losses in the […]
text:
Spending money on local goods and services can send a message to big corporations and their owners, writes our columnist. (Getty Images)
Like everyone else these days, I am exhausted by the news cycle. I did vote, though. And I hope you did, too.

As the votes are tallied and certified, pay attention and keep steady. A recent Washington Post poll found that seven out of 10 Americans don’t believe Trump will accept Republican losses in the midterms.
The fact that we have to worry about whether the president will uphold free and fair elections is not normal. The fact that we have to worry whether Congress will hold the president in check if he tries to disrupt free and fair elections is not normal. We do not have to accept any of it.
I know I’m tired of living in interesting times. I know a lot of you are, too. But the difficult truth is, we cannot sit any of it out.
We can make a difference with our dollars. Where we spend our money, or choose not to spend our money, can shift the balance of power. And we can use this power to stop supporting corporations and billionaires with our hard-earned dimes.
The rich need fewer of our dimes anyway. Especially when the rich use their wealth to buy politicians and policies. Many of the problems we face today are the result of wealth concentrating at the top. It can feel like there is nothing we can do about that. But it is important to remember that there are more normal people like us than there are billionaires or corporations. The corporations need our purchases and our dollars to survive. Throughout history, time and time again, we have seen small, deliberate actions add up to big change.
Breaking the cycle of consumption doesn’t just starve the rich of profits. It is freeing. It helps us focus on what we actually care about. As Robin Wall Kimmerer writes in “The Serviceberry,” “Recognizing ‘enoughness’ is a radical act in an economy that is always urging us to consume more.”
We can live just fine without new clothes or gadgets. We need enough. But we don’t need the more, more, more that corporate marketing tells us to buy. What we really want is to be afford the basics and support our communities.
If we wait past the initial impulse to buy whatever item, maybe we can save the money we would have spent. Or maybe we can find it in a locally owned shop instead. Money we spend locally can then be part of what our neighbor spends — to buy school supplies for his kids or to donate to the school or to pay her employees and so on down the line.
We get what we need. The money stays out of corporate hands. More importantly, the money supports our community.
Knowing that is true and making lifestyle changes are very different. Our family has been slowly peeling off companies we no longer want to support since 2020. We had to learn how to shop again. It hasn’t been an easy or straightforward process. Sometimes, we stumble and click things into a cart. Sometimes there is no other choice than to buy from a place we would rather not spend our money. All any of us can do is do our best each day. Then we wake up and try again the next day.
In case you are wondering about making changes of your own, here is what we have learned about keeping our money out of the hands of big corporations:

Waiting a few days before making a purchase is smart. In a lot of cases, we decide we do not actually need the thing we would have clicked into a shopping cart for delivery.
When we do want or need an item, we check if we can repurpose something we already own. If not, we look for it in a local “buy nothing” group or at a thrift store. If that doesn’t work, we look for locally owned businesses where we can buy it. If no local choice exists, we order directly from the company website when possible.
Internet searches are an excellent resource. Researching alternate places to buy basically anything on our list is easy. A simple search of “where to shop instead of big corporations” returns a lot of good advice.

The bottom line is this: Not spending our hard-earned wages or only spending to support local businesses is a power move. If money is the only message the rich and corporations will hear, we should make sure they hear it loud and clear. The less we give to corporations and billionaires, the stronger we are. The more we support local, the stronger our community is.
This may be the only lever that the rich and the corporations truly understand. If money is all that they love, money is what they will not get.
Tamara Moots lives and works in Manhattan. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Mandela Barnes files defamation lawsuit against Milwaukee Journal Sentinel
description: Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, who ran in the 2026 Democratic primary for governor,  has filed a lawsuit against the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel, claiming that the newspaper defamed him  when it ran an anonymously sourced story about Barnes’ relationships with women. The Sentinel published two stories on the same day in July, one focused on […]
text:
Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes joins other Democratic Party officials in Milwaukee in 2023. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, who ran in the 2026 Democratic primary for governor,  has filed a lawsuit against the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel, claiming that the newspaper defamed him  when it ran an anonymously sourced story about Barnes’ relationships with women. The Sentinel published two stories on the same day in July, one focused on accusations that Barnes used his high profile political status to gain intimate access to women and another covering Barnes dropping out of the race for governor. 
“I understand that seeking public office brings scrutiny, and I respect the essential role of a free press,” Barnes said in a press release. “Accuracy and fairness matter deeply when reporting affects a person’s reputation, family, and future. I dispute the reporting identified in this complaint and believe it created a materially false picture of me and my conduct. I asked the Journal Sentinel to correct it, and the newspaper declined. I am bringing this case so the disputed facts can be examined through the legal process.”
In a story headlined “Sources detail concerns about Mandela Barnes’ behavior toward women,” journalists Mary Spicuzza and Molly Beck reported that an outside law firm had been hired by the Democratic Party of Wisconsin to review allegations of inappropriate behavior involving Barnes and young adult women. Described as a “probe,” the alleged inquiry was launched after then-party chairman Ben Wikler received an anonymous letter in 2024 accusing Barnes of using his position in the party to gain access to women. The story reported that the review found nothing actionable, and that the original letter lacked details.
The lawsuit disputes the Sentinel’s reporting that an outside law firm had been hired to investigate Barnes. Rather, the complaint states, the party’s regularly retained counsel “may have reviewed the anonymous letter in its ordinary advisory capacity, but neither counsel nor the party conducted a factual investigation or ‘outside probe.’” It added that “the anonymous letter referenced in the Articles contained no names, no specific incidents, and no concrete allegations capable of being investigated.”
The lawsuit also disputes reporting from the Journal Sentinel — using three anonymous sources — that Barnes used his position in the party to seek sexual relationships with young adult women. One of the sources claimed to have had a sexual relationship with Barnes, while the other two said they had knowledge of his behavior, though no one has said they were abused by Barnes, the defamation complaint states. 
The Journal Sentinel’s use of AI-generated summaries for the story also came under fire in the defamation suit. The AI-generated overview mentions the hiring of an outside law firm to investigate allegations and that Barnes used his position to pursue intimate relations with young women, and linked his dropping out of the race with allegations of inappropriate sexual conduct that have not led to any criminal charges. 
A subsequent story headlined “Mandela Barnes ends Democratic campaign for Wisconsin governor,” also authored by Spicuzza and Beck, mentioned that Barnes’ decision to withdraw from the race came on the heels of  the Sentinel’s report on the reputed allegations against Barnes. The defamation complaint states that Barnes’ decision was based on internal polling, support for another candidate, “the absence of a viable political path,” and financial concerns. 
The lawsuit also mentions that a Journal Sentinel reporter originally assigned the story had been removed from the effort because she  previously had an intimate relationship with Barnes. Spicuzza and Beck were brought on to re-report that journalist’s work and carry the stories forward. The lawsuit states that the Journal Sentinel’s reporting did not disclose the original conflict of interest or the reporter’s removal from the story. 
When Barnes exited the race he was polling second behind Rep. Francesca Hong at 16% to Hong’s 38% according to Marquette University Law School polling data. Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley eventually won the primary and was elected governor last week. Shortly after the stories on Barnes appeared,  Bruce Murphy, editor-in-chief of Urban Milwaukee, published a column calling the Journal Sentinel’s reporting on the Barnes accusations “irresponsible”. He began the column by asking, “What in the world were the Journal Sentinel editors thinking?”
Barnes requested retractions and corrections to the stories, and filed  the lawsuit after the Journal Sentinel refused and stood by its reporting. The lawsuit seeks damages for alleged reputational and “other injuries resulting from the publication,” but does not claim  that the stories caused Barnes to withdraw from the race. 
“The Journal Sentinel stands by our reporting,” said Greg Borowski, executive editor of the newspaper, Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported. “The story went through our standard editing and legal review, and Mr. Barnes was given the opportunity to respond before publication.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Gov. Josh Shapiro, long rumored to have presidential ambitions, claims midterm victory
description: While the victories were part of a national wave for the party, Democrats across Pennsylvania have highlighted Shapiro’s role in their success in the state. And Shapiro hasn’t been shy about touting those victories.
text:
Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro declares victory in his reelection bid alongside wife Lori Shapiro at an election-night event at the Penn Harris Hotel Harrisburg on November 3, 2026 in Camp Hill. (Photo by Joe Lamberti/Getty Images)Speaking outside the Governor’s Residence a day after the election, state Sen. Vince Hughes (D-Philadelphia), a self-described “elder statesman” in Pennsylvania Democratic politics, singled out one man in particular for his role in their party’s decisive wins.
“He took every ounce of his own personal political cachet and he put it on the line to make sure that this mission was accomplished so that we can get real stuff done for the people of the commonwealth of Pennsylvania,” Hughes said. “Gov. Josh Shapiro, my friend from a long time ago, thank you.”
Along with Shapiro’s overwhelming victory in the gubernatorial race, Pennsylvania Democrats won a majority in the state Senate for the first time in more than 30 years. They also expanded their majority in the state House and won the largest majority of Pennsylvania’s Congressional seats since the 2008 election that sent former President Barack Obama to the White House.
While the victories were part of a national wave for the party, Democrats across Pennsylvania have praised Shapiro for his role in their success in the state. And Shapiro hasn’t been shy about touting those victories.
Along with being a popular figurehead, Shapiro recruited candidates in competitive districts, helped shape the state party’s political infrastructure, donated over $10 million to help candidates down the ballot and criss-crossed the state to campaign with embattled Democrats.
Leading his party to victory in a major swing state, along with his decisive win over Republican challenger Stacy Garrity, could be a boon to his long-rumored presidential ambitions if he were to enter the 2028 race. But how the results reflect on him may depend on how his coalition governs.
“He’s got some claims now that he could make about his ability to win that I think do put him near the top tier of candidates,” said Berwood Yost, director of the Center for Opinion Research at Franklin & Marshall College. “Whether that gets him over the top, I don’t know, but I certainly think when you look at how he’s performed in an important state like Pennsylvania, some people will have to look at that and think that’s a valuable set of credentials.”
But Yost, who’s been observing Pennsylvania politics for decades, also had a warning.
“It’s all gonna come down to the policies they’re able to enact,” he said. “Could they get distracted by other things and people feel like they’re not doing what they’re elected to do? Yeah. That’s a real risk because that seems to happen a lot. Maybe Democrats will be more disciplined and be able to really advance some policies that change people’s thinking. If they don’t we’ll be right back here.”
By “back here,” Yost meant facing another election that serves as a referendum on the party in power.
 ‘He put us through our paces’

Shapiro declined a request for an interview with the Pennsylvania Capital-Star, but his campaign’s communications director, Manuel Bonder, discussed his victory and the strategies that led to it.
Bonder was part of Shapiro’s 2022 campaign, then worked in the governor’s office until leaving in September 2025 to return to the campaign side.
When Shapiro officially announced his reelection bid in January, he set some ambitious goals. He said he wanted to help Democrats flip four competitive U.S. House seats in Pennsylvania and win a majority in the state Senate for the first time in decades.
“That was something that has been a priority for us in the entire process of this election cycle,” Bonder said.
While Shapiro was always favored to win the governor’s race, Hughes, who’s represented parts of Montgomery and Philadelphia Counties since 1994, said flipping the state Senate wasn’t initially seen as a sure bet.
“In general, the districts we competed in were essentially 50-50 districts,” he said. “The best analysis would be that they were more slanted Republican.”
But Hughes said the party’s hopes grew around two months after Shapiro officially launched his campaign, when Democrat James Malone won a special election in Lancaster County, flipping a Senate seat that had been represented by Republicans since 1889.
Shapiro, he said, was very involved in early strategy meetings about the senate districts Democrats were trying to flip, discussing subjects like candidate recruitment, polling and fundraising.
“These are very long, intensive, well-researched meetings,” Hughes said. “He put us through our paces.”
Shapiro also invested heavily in the state Democratic party that he helped to reshape. In 2025, party insiders elected Eugene DePasquale, who had Shapiro’s backing, to be the Pennsylvania Democrats’ new chairman. DePasquale then appointed longtime Shapiro advisor Larry Hailsham to be the state party’s executive director.
According to DePasquale, the party was not in great shape when he arrived.
“We didn’t even have the money to make payroll for the first two weeks,” he said. “We had to do a lot of things, and we had to do it right away. We had to build up our staff infrastructure … We [had] to build up our communications team. And one of the big reasons why that was possible was that the party, myself included, had a tremendous partner in Gov. Josh Shapiro.”
Over the course of the 2026 election cycle, Shapiro donated over $7 million in campaign funds to the state party. That funding was used in part to launch what’s called a coordinated campaign, where state party organizers campaign for candidates across the state.
“I think we ended up knocking on 1.4 million doors, [made] 500,000 phone calls, give or take,” DePasquale said about the coordinated campaign. “That meant that took that off the plate of our individual other campaigns. We were shouldering that load so they could focus on getting their message out.”
Shapiro also donated $1 million to the Pennsylvania House Democratic Campaign Committee and $2 million to the Pennsylvania Senate Democratic Campaign Committee. His ability to do so was helped by the substantial fundraising advantage he held over Garrity.
It’s common for a governor or party figurehead to spend money helping their state party and other candidates on the ballot. But according to Chris Borick, a longtime pollster currently at Lehigh University, the level of involvement Shapiro had in party politics, and the amount of financial support he offered candidates, was unique in recent Pennsylvania history.
“Ed Rendell would be the closest thing,” he said, referring to the former Democratic governor and Philadelphia mayor. “But Shapiro seems to be in a different class.”
Shapiro also made his pitch for voters to give his party a trifecta in Harrisburg a centerpiece of his own campaign, in a sense tying his success to that of his party more broadly.
“You’d be hard pressed to find an event where the governor was not going out of his way to elevate multiple candidates on the ballot,” Bonder said. That included dozens of campaign stops with candidates for the state House and Senate and U.S. House.
Eli Cousin, the Mid-Atlantic press secretary for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said Shapiro also played a large role in helping Democrats flip four U.S. House seats in Pennsylvania, including through candidate recruitment.
“He was heavily involved,” Cousin said.
In Pennsylvania, national figures like Barack Obama and former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigeieg played a smaller role in Democratic candidates’ campaigns than they did in other states.
Cousin says that’s in part because they already had a strong messenger in Shapiro.
“Governor Shapiro has achieved, you know, god-tier status in the state of Pennsylvania,” he said. “There’s no better surrogate for our candidates.”
Cousin was referring, in part, to Shapiro’s high approval rating. Throughout his race, he also maintained a significant polling advantage over Garrity.
Shapiro ultimately ended up featuring in numerous campaign ads for Pennsylvania Democratic candidates. Even some Republicans tried to tie themselves to him.
While Democrats seemed poised to make big gains, with disapproval of President Donald Trump weighing on Republicans, Borick, the pollster, said Shapiro’s decision to get so involved with other races carried risks.
“In some ways his position was on the ballot in those other races. He had put himself in the game,” Borick said. “Because he’s going to be looked at as a potential candidate in the 2028 [presidential] race, the expectations were high. So if those races didn’t come through, it would be looked at less positively.”
Success in Pennsylvania could raise Shapiro’s national profile
While he was in the middle of a post-election national media blitz to discuss his party’s success in the midterms, his campaign released a seven-page memo Saturday highlighting the scope of Democrats’ victories in Pennsylvania and the governor’s role in ensuring them. It said Shapiro won more than twice as many counties as former Vice President Kamala Harris did in 2024 and flipped 11 won by Trump that year.
“These [down-ballot] candidates won by embracing both Shapiro and his agenda,” it said.
The memo also compared Shapiro’s own victory to those of other national figures in his party. It including a graphic showing Shapiro outperformed Democrats like Texas’ James Talarico, Georgia’s Jon Ossoff and North Carolina’s Roy Cooper when it came to earning support from “non-MAGA Republicans,” independents and voters who view the Democratic Party unfavorably.
According to Shapiro, the victories have earned him praise from leaders in Washington, D.C. He said he spoke with U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) on election night. Bonder also confirmed reporting from HuffPost that Shapiro received a call from former President Joe Biden.
“I thanked [Jeffries] for following my lead here in Pennsylvania,” Shapiro said at a press conference, describing his call. “I recruited those four candidates to run. He supported that, he invested in that, and ultimately those four candidates got through.”
But Borick warned that 2028 is still a long way away and, historically, midterm victories do not always translate to success in the next presidential election. He pointed to Republicans’ gains in the U.S. House and Senate in 2010, which was followed by Obama’s reelection in 2012.
This could be especially true in determining the success of a candidate in a party primary, where voters many voters come in with concerns beyond electability.
“I don’t put a lot of stake in what happened here as determinative two years from now,” Borick said.
Yost, however, said Democrats’ victories in Pennsylvania present an opportunity. 
“Somebody’s got to figure out some policy sets that appeal to voters and really kind of split up what is sort of a back-and-forth struggle,” he said. “It’s all going to come down to policies.”
Asked by liberal commentator Harry Sisson after the midterms what Democrats should do on day one in power, Shapiro said, “It needs to be a sobering moment for Democrats. We got the keys to the car and now we have to drive it responsibly.”
He also told reporters last Wednesday he’s talked to Jeffries and Schumer about the need to pass an agenda that will keep Democrats from districts that supported Trump in 2024 in office.
Despite his involvement in national politics, Shapiro has neither confirmed nor denied that he plans to run for president in 2028, stating when asked that he’s focused on Pennsylvania.
Bonder, asked whether he would join Shapiro’s campaign in 2028 if he announced, told the Capital-Star, “the governor’s been very clear what he’s focused on in getting through this past election and looking towards the horizon of what he wants to keep getting done as governor.”
Asked if he’ll now be returning to work in the governor’s office, as opposed to for his campaign, Bonder said, “we’ll see.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Commentary: ‘Red state’ Ohio may have lost some of its rouge after midterms
authors: Dominic D. Wells, Ph.D., David J. Jackson, Ph.D.
description: Victories in Ohio for President Donald Trump since 2016 have led many analysts to declare Ohio a red state. Victories for Republicans at all levels have made experts question why Ohio is no longer a battleground state. After a decade of declarations that Ohio is now a red state, this midterm cycle has made some […]
text:
Dr. Amy Acton speaks at a campaign rally in Cleveland ahead of her successful campaign for Ohio governor. Acton will become the first Democrat elected to lead Ohio in 20 years during a midterm election cycle that saw huge Democratic gains in states.
(Photo by Nick Evans, Ohio Capital Journal)Victories in Ohio for President Donald Trump since 2016 have led many analysts to declare Ohio a red state. Victories for Republicans at all levels have made experts question why Ohio is no longer a battleground state. 
After a decade of declarations that Ohio is now a red state, this midterm cycle has made some realize that Ohio may not be so reliably red. 
This year Time Magazine published an article stating, “When no one was looking, Ohio became a swing state again,” but we can assure you, we were looking. We have published work showing that Ohio voters are really not that different from Michigan voters and that the outcomes in the states can be explained by factors like redistricting and voter registration laws. We encouraged people to not write off Ohio.
The results of the election on Nov. 3 showed how Ohio should regain its swing state status. Democrats swept every statewide election except for one, winning the U.S. Senate seat as well as the governor, secretary of state, attorney general, and treasurer races. 
Democrats appear to have won eight of the state’s 15 U.S. House seats, which it should be pointed out were gerrymandered to garner 12 Republican seats and three Democratic. Democrats also broke the Republican supermajority in the Ohio House of Representatives, and won both Ohio Supreme Court races.  
The conditions were right for Ohio to elect their first Democratic governor in 20 years, and to send Sherrod Brown back to the U.S. Senate. This election cycle in Ohio felt a lot like 2006, when voters elected Democrat Ted Strickland governor and Brown to his first term as a senator.
Leading up to the 2006 midterms, there was an unpopular Republican president in his second term, falling consumer sentiment, concern over gas prices, and an unpopular war in the Middle East. All of those things should sound familiar because we are living them now.
Momentum remained with Democrats in the state through 2008, when Barack Obama won by four points. Although Obama also won the state in 2012, by 2010, state-level offices had swung back to Republicans, with John Kasich defeating Ted Strickland for governor. 
In fact, if there ever has been a “reliably red” Ohio, it has been at the state-level where Republicans have controlled the state legislature and governor’s office for most of the last 30 years.
The results from Nov. 3 certainly do not mean that Ohio is now a blue state, but they do indicate that the Democratic Party can compete in the state if they choose to make it competitive. There will not be an incumbent running for president in 2028, and newly elected Sherrod Brown will have to defend his seat after finishing out what was (now-Vice President) J.D. Vance’s term. 
The Democratic Party has a strong reason to believe Ohio is in play in 2028 and is important for keeping the Senate majority.  The days of massive ground games and high-profile campaign stops could return to Ohio. The state could be the center of politics once again.  
Nonetheless, there are some things that work against Ohio becoming the high-profile battleground state it was not that long ago. Thirty years ago, winning Ohio meant winning 21 electoral votes in the Electoral College, but now the state is worth just 17. 
While Ohio has lost electoral votes, states like Georgia have gained. The population in Ohio is dispersed across multiple major cities, while in Georgia roughly half of the state population lives in the Atlanta metropolitan area. This makes competing in Ohio more costly for parties than competing in Georgia, a state with only one fewer electoral vote.
Also, now that massive Texas appears to be competitive, the parties may divert significant resources there and away from other potential swing states.    
The Democratic Party has an opportunity to take advantage of the momentum from the most recent general election. They can invest in races in the state and keep it competitive. They can potentially win elections down the ballot and grow their bench of candidates at the state and local levels. Their wins this year statewide produce a bench for other more high-profile statewide offices.
A lot of work will need to be done to compete consistently against a strong Ohio Republican Party with no shortage of qualified candidates. The question will be if the party believes Ohio is worth the investment, and if they spend the resources to organize lower-propensity voters between elections. It also wouldn’t hurt if they are able to deliver on some of their promises concerning the cost of living, regulating data centers, and making it easier to vote.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio likely won’t pass AI regulations before year ends
description: Ohio has no substantial artificial intelligence regulations, but lawmakers from both sides of the aisle are trying to change that before their December deadline. One Republican leader is blocking them, saying none are ready for a vote. As AI chatbots become more mainstream, wrongful death lawsuits have started popping up across the country. The victims […]
text:
(Photo illustration by Getty Images)Ohio has no substantial artificial intelligence regulations, but lawmakers from both sides of the aisle are trying to change that before their December deadline. One Republican leader is blocking them, saying none are ready for a vote.
As AI chatbots become more mainstream, wrongful death lawsuits have started popping up across the country. The victims come from all walks of life, but court documents say they all have one thing in common: they received help from a bot.
“We aren’t preventing deaths right now,” state Rep. Christine Cockley, D-Columbus, said.
The latest was a 13-year-old whose parents are suing after Google’s AI Gemini allegedly helped the child make a suicide plot over a matter of weeks. She survived, but the parents and Cockley say it shouldn’t have gotten to this point.
“The current supermajority, their priority isn’t helping people who are dying by suicide, who are creating these plans using chatbots and AI,” the lawmaker said.
She, Republican state Rep. Ty Mathews of Findlay, and a bipartisan group of legislators introduced a bill that would establish penalties for developers whose AI models generate content encouraging self-harm or violence.
Under House Bill 524, the state would be able to investigate and impose civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation. The money collected would go to the state’s 988 crisis hotline and consumer protection enforcement.
“It’s not the developers; that’s the problem because it’s generations down the line from the developers and it’s a bot acting through its SI systems,” House Technology and Innovation Committee Chair Thad Claggett, R-Licking County, said after hearing bills Monday, referencing the president’s use of “Super Intelligence.”
Lawmakers have been trying to tackle AI policy for years, but it continues to stall.
There are eight bills about the topic in Claggett’s committee, including measures that would require watermarks on AI-altered images, make it a crime to generate AI child sexual abuse material and prevent AI marriage.
“I want to create really good law, not just some law that’s got to be immediately amended,” he said.
None of the bills are ready for a vote, he added.
“There are not any bills that I’m aware of in our committee that do not have downside problematic issues to liberty issues or just unnecessary burdensome issues,” he continued.
While Claggett blames the intricacy of the topic, Cockley believes that tech companies are spending money in order to delay legislation.
“There’s also the problem of a large amount of money being in politics, and unfortunately money speaks, and I think that kind of instills more fear in legislators to not do anything,” said Cockley. “So, a little bit of the money in politics, the fear of big tech, the fear of going against the status quo, in addition to the fear of the unknown of technology and of AI.”
Cockley believes that new leadership will allow regulations to be put in place.
“If it doesn’t get done this year, next year with Governor-elect Amy Acton and getting out of the superminority, there is hope for this bill either way,” she said.
The lawmakers have until mid-December to pass guardrails. Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine has repeatedly pushed for safety regulations.
Follow WEWS Statehouse reporter Morgan Trau on X and Facebook.
This article was originally published on News5Cleveland.com and is published in the Ohio Capital Journal under a content-sharing agreement. Unlike other OCJ articles, it is not available for free republication by other news outlets as it is owned by WEWS in Cleveland.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Gambling problems in Pa. used to be near casinos. Now they’re everywhere.
description: Prior to the first online casinos opening, the people banning themselves largely lived in and around counties where in-person casinos operated. But that’s no longer the case.
text:
(Photo Illustration by Natasha Khan/Pittsburgh's Public Source)The number of people banning themselves from gambling activities in Pennsylvania has been surging, according to the Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board.
This has been particularly true since the first online casino opened in 2019. It’s not just changing how many people are banning themselves – it’s changing who is banning themselves and where, according to a Public Source analysis of the board’s publicly available data.
Prior to the first online casinos opening, the people banning themselves largely lived in and around counties where in-person casinos operated.
But that’s no longer the case. Some of the counties with the highest problem gambling rates are a long drive from a casino.
For example, there was no casino located in Blair County or in any bordering county before this year. Prior to 2019, it had one of the commonwealth’s lowest rates of people banning themselves from gambling, with only six residents of Blair County having banned themselves from gambling across the previous decade.
That changed with online gambling. Last year Blair County had the state’s third-highest concentration of people banning themselves from a gambling activity, with 115 people, or just below one in every thousand residents, self-excluding in a single year.
“A lot of those people just didn’t gamble on a regular basis until the online gambling came and now they have access to it 24/7,” said Elizabeth Lanza, director of the Office of Compulsive and Problem Gambling at the Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board.
She also said the rising numbers reflect that the Gaming Control Board made it easier to sign up for self-exclusions when online gambling was introduced, by allowing everyone to sign up online, rather than having to sign up at a casino.
Matthew Mullis, a graduate student at West Virginia University’s Center for Gaming Research and Development, said Pennsylvania and West Virginia are two of only eight states in the country that have legalized online casino games – what are often referred to collectively as “iGaming.” The losses from these games, Mullis said, are greater on average than online sports gambling. That’s in part, he said, because people play more rapidly and the odds of winning are worse.
“You can spend hours just in your bed doing the slots,” Mullis said. “And it’s pretty anti-social.”
 What is gambling self-exclusion and how does it work?

Pennsylvania gamblers used to have to go to a casino and ask directly to ban themselves from gambling for one year, five years or life. If they wanted to start gambling at the end of that period, they had to go back to the casino and request to be removed. But with the legalization of online gambling, Pennsylvanians can now enroll in the program online.
The program only applies to the commonwealth’s licensed gambling platforms. Prediction markets, like Kalshi, are regulated at the federal level, because they are considered financial derivatives, rather than gambling, even though many people use them similarly. 
If a person who has self-excluded is caught trying to gamble in-person, casino operators will call the police and the person can be cited for trespassing and have any winnings confiscated. People are most commonly reported by staff who know them well, Lanza said.
When people ban themselves online, the technology effectively prevents them from gambling again using their own information. Some try to gamble using other people’s identities and get caught, Lanza said, so typically the people who violate their self-exclusion online are reported to the authorities for fraud. Online gamblers don’t need to ask for permission to start gambling again at the end of their exclusion period, when they are automatically removed from the exclusion list.
Self-exclusion programs have helped more than 30,000 people suffering from a gambling problem, Lanza said in a June podcast. “It is not a cure-all. It is not treatment,” she said. “We always do recommend that individuals seek some type of either self-help or more formal treatment when they enroll in self-exclusion. But it has been a very successful tool.”
Academic research conducted in other states and countries has shown that problem gamblers are less likely to gamble during their exclusion period if they are receiving formal help as well. But regardless of whether they get help, the people who use self-exclusion tools report fewer financial problems and improved quality of life. And some surveys suggest gamblers find bans more useful than therapy or group counseling.
Illegal gambling websites may limit their effectiveness: One study in Sweden found that between 38% and 49% of people who banned themselves from gambling continued to gamble.
The number of people who ban themselves is much smaller than the number of people suffering from a gambling problem, according to several studies. Research finds that anywhere from 1-in-200 to 1-in-6 people with a gambling problem enroll.
 Gambling ban list gets whiter, younger, more male

The people banning themselves from gambling have come from increasingly rural places, and perhaps unsurprisingly they have also increasingly identified as caucasian. 
Young adults have taken up an even larger share of the people banning themselves from gambling since online wagering was legalized. People 55 and over began to make up a much smaller share since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, though their share has started to rebound.  
That doesn’t necessarily mean young people are losing the most money. In West Virginia, Mullis said that younger players bet less often than older players. The 21-to-30-year olds made up about one-third of the people with accounts at the casino he analyzed, but they placed only about 1 in 7 of the bets.
In the course of reporting this article, Public Source discovered a mistake in how the Gaming Control Board was reporting people’s ages, which, for some early years, made it look like there were no young people banning themselves and more older people doing so. The problem has since been fixed.
In the first five years casinos were legalized, men and women were banning themselves from casinos at similar rates. But by 2020 there were about five men banning themselves for every two women who did, and that ratio held even as the total number of self-exclusions spiked.  
It’s not just Pennsylvanians who are banning themselves from commonwealth casinos and online platforms. Hundreds of residents in places like New Jersey, New York and Delaware have also opted into Pennsylvania’s self-exclusion system. It’s not clear how many of these are people who enter Pennsylvania to gamble on their phone or at a casino. 
These out-of-state gamblers aren’t clearly identified on the Gaming Control Board’s website but Public Source discovered their existence after noticing a discrepancy between the total number of people who had banned themselves (about 53,000) and the total number of Pennsylvania residents who had (about 46,000).
Lanza said the Gaming Control Board regularly finds gamblers who are banning themselves, not just in Pennsylvania, but in all the states that they live in or near. And during big gambling days, like the Super Bowl, the board can see a live online map of gamblers from out-of-state who are stopping at one truck stop after the next, until they can access Pennsylvania’s online gaming.
 How to stop the problem gambling

Lanza said self-limits, such as self-exclusions, are important because they put the responsibility in the hands of individuals. “I’m very big on giving individuals choices, not too many choices, but I think individuals need to take responsibility for their choices as well.”
Lanza said that she is paying attention to experts who are trying to grapple with the problem. One of the most promising ideas, she thinks, is to give the gambling data from casinos and online casinos to researchers who study addiction at Penn State University. “I think that that would be very helpful, to see those numbers broken down,” she said.
That’s exactly what is happening in West Virginia, which passed a law in 2024, requiring casino operators to provide data to WVU researchers, including Mullis.
Mullis has begun studying the roughly 43 million monthly bets made at one of West Virginia’s largest online casinos and his initial findings suggest a small number of gamblers, which he referred to as “whales,” are the source of the majority of the revenue. Just 5% of the roughly 16,500 people who were gambling, during the period he looked at, were the source of 70% of the bets and 90% of the revenue.
The top 1% of gamblers – about 165 gamblers at that casino – were the source of about 50% of the casino’s total revenue. This suggests problem gamblers are a large source of revenue for casinos, Mullins said, though more study will be needed.
“That’s the whole conundrum of my position,” Lanza said. “I want our operators to do the most responsible thing possible, but I also have to realize they’re still operating a business.”
Editor’s note: All self-exclusion data in this story was pulled from the Pennsylvania Gaming Commission website in October and then fact-checked on November 4, 2026. Artificial intelligence tools were used to generate code to scrape data and design the map in this story. The map was fact-checked by a human.
Oliver Morrison is the health and environment reporter at Pittsburgh’s Public Source and can be reached at oliver@publicsource.org.
