name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Scanlon, Blumenthal speak with Murphy as he recovers from stroke
description: They described Sen. Chris Murphy as sounding strong, upbeat and positive. Murphy is at a rehabilitation center recovering from a stroke.
text:
Nine days after U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy suffered a stroke, state Comptroller Sean Scanlon got a call from his old boss and friend. Scanlon picked up from a location he described as “ironic.”
“I said, ‘You’re never going to be believe where I’m at,'” Scanlon said, recounting his conversation with Murphy.
“Where, a hockey rink?” Murphy asked Scanlon, who was indeed watching his son play hockey at the time of the call. Murphy laughed when he confirmed.
Murphy noticed arm numbness while attending his son’s hockey game on Oct. 31 and was subsequently hospitalized for a stroke. Scanlon said Murphy’s humor from the outset of the call gave him reassurance about the senator’s recovery and mindset.
“That was a great sign. That’s his personality,” Scanlon said in an interview. “To hear him making jokes about something that was scary and serious, I think, shows a really healthy place that he’s in.”
Both Scanlon and U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal spoke with Murphy by phone on Monday night, some of the first people to speak at length with the senator outside of his family since the stroke.
Blumenthal and Murphy have served together as U.S. senators representing Connecticut since 2013, when Murphy was first elected (Blumenthal was elected two years earlier). Scanlon is a former staffer of Murphy’s, and the two have remained close friends since.
Murphy was hospitalized at Johns Hopkins Hospital after experiencing symptoms and was discharged last Friday. He’s now recovering at a rehabilitation center for several weeks and will miss Senate votes during that time.
“I was diagnosed with a small bleed in the thalamus region of my brain,” Murphy said in a statement released by his office last Friday. “The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far.”
His doctor wrote in a statement that he experienced “a small hemorrhagic stroke.” His physician, Dr. Jose Suarez, the chief of neurosciences critical care at The Johns Hopkins Hospital, said she expects him to make a full recovery following rehabilitation.
Murphy’s office referred back to the statement sent following his release from the hospital when asked about additional updates on his health and recovery.
Since the news broke, Scanlon said people have been reaching out to him daily for updates, given his close relationship to the senator. Scanlon said he didn’t know what to expect on the call but that he was reassured by Murphy’s positive demeanor and his voice.
“I speak for myself and a lot of people that we were really worried about him,” Scanlon said.
“It was really great to be able to talk to him and hear how well he was doing, to hear his voice sound strong and clear, hear him be upbeat and positive,” he added.
Blumenthal separately had a call with his colleague on Monday night, similarly describing Murphy in a positive mood. Blumenthal called it a “heartfelt and meaningful conversation to me.”
“The conversation was very upbeat, and I’m looking forward to his return. We need him in the fight,” Blumenthal said in an interview on Tuesday from the Senate. “There was no discussion about how long it would take, but I urged him to do whatever rest and rehabilitation was required.”
When asked about specifics on his condition and recovery, Scanlon said the call was focused on lighter topics and not about his recovery routine.
But he noted that Murphy’s “got a road ahead” in terms of his recovery. Scanlon said he’s heartened by the progress he’s made so quickly.
“He’s putting the work in every day at the facility down there,” Scanlon said. “He’s got work left to do — the people of Connecticut should know that, but he is doing that work, and he’s getting better and making really serious progress every day.”
Before his stroke, Murphy was a visible presence on the campaign trail. Murphy, who was not on the ballot last week, had been campaigning the past several weeks in Connecticut and a handful of swing states for Democratic candidates. And in early October, Murphy made a trip to the Middle East amid the ongoing war with Iran.
Scanlon said their conversation eventually shifted to politics and the midterm elections.
He said Murphy was aware of the results and Democrats’ overwhelming wins across the country. One of the first things Murphy mentioned, Scanlon said, was his shock that Republicans are down to three seats in Connecticut’s state Senate.
“I wasn’t sure if he was going to be at that level,” Scanlon said. “He was very well-versed on what had happened.”
Murphy won’t be back at the U.S. Capitol for at least several weeks and will miss votes. Scanlon didn’t have a sense of when he might return. Like Murphy’s office noted when he was discharged from the hospital, Scanlon said the senator is getting daily updates from staff on constituent work and other matters.
Scanlon, however, said he and others close to Murphy are urging him to take his time with the recovery.
“He’s got to take the time to do this work,” Scanlon said. “His doctor and family will make the decision of when the right time is to do that and transition again.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT to offer homeownership assistance to first responders
description: Recent reports have identified recruitment and retention problems among first responders nationwide. Connecticut is trying a new solution.
text:
Against the backdrop of a red and white North Haven fire truck, Gov. Ned Lamont announced the upcoming rollout of a homeownership assistance program for first responders Tuesday morning. 
The program, First Responders’ Time to Own, will provide eligible and certified firefighters, police officers and emergency medical services workers with up to $25,000 in assistance for down payments and closing costs. In order to be eligible for the program, first responders must have at least two years of work experience in Connecticut and buy a home in the community they serve.
Lamont lauded the program for giving first responders a “stake” in the town where they work.
“Being part of the community is a big part of community policing,” he said. “Being able to be nearby the firehouse just makes an enormous difference.”
The homeownership assistance program falls under Public Act 26-12, which Lamont signed into law in June. The broader law aims to increase first responder recruitment and retention through pay increases, state school tuition waivers and bolstered benefits for family members of first responders who died in the line of duty.
[RELATED: To recruit first responders, CT weighs tuition, mortgage assistance]
At Tuesday’s press conference, held at the North Haven fire department, three state police officers stood alongside Lamont and roughly a dozen state and local officials. More first responders peppered the audience, including North Haven police officers and firefighters from the Middlefield and Westfield departments.
“Take a look at who’s here today,” Ronnell Higgins, commissioner for the state Department of Emergency Services and Public Protection, said at the conference. “That tells you how important this law is.”
Several of the officials, including Higgins and Comptroller Sean Scanlon, remarked on Connecticut’s struggles to recruit and retain first responders. 
According to Higgins, Connecticut currently faces a shortage of hundreds of police officers and troopers and struggles to fill its police and fire academies. A May 2025 report by Scanlon’s office found that the number of volunteer firefighters statewide had dropped by more than 62% since 2017.
“We’re losing that fabric of volunteerism,” Scanlon said, “not because people don’t want to serve — because they can’t afford to live in the places that they want to serve.”
[RELATED: Volunteer fire departments are shrinking. For some, it’s a call to action]
Scanlon stressed that the homeownership assistance program and the broader legislation presented “Connecticut solutions to a national problem.” Recent reports have identified recruitment and retention issues among law enforcement, firefighters and emergency medical services workers nationwide. 
According to Connecticut Housing Commissioner Seila Mosquera-Bruno, the homeownership assistance program is modeled after the state’s Time to Own program, which was established in 2022 and has helped over 10,000 Connecticut families become first-time homeowners. 
Mosquera-Bruno and Nandini Natarajan, the chief executive officer and executive director of the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority, described the first responders program as a more “flexible” version of the original program. 
The Time to Own program requires participants to have lived in Connecticut for at least three years and earn no more than their area’s median household income. 
The first responders’ program requires just two years of Connecticut residency and does not restrict assistance eligibility by income. Participants will also pay a slightly reduced interest rate on their first Connecticut Housing Finance Authority mortgages, according to Natarajan.
The program will launch on Nov. 16, a month and a half prior to the Jan. 1, 2027, deadline laid out in the legislation. It will be funded through the Time to Own program and it will operate on a first-come, first-served basis, Mosquera-Bruno said.
“We’re sending a message to the people that have these jobs, and the people that want these jobs, that we’re going to be there for you if you’re there for us,” Scanlon said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Mount Vernon Republican elected as next majority whip in Kentucky House
description: After Republican House Whip Jason Nemes lost his reelection bid last week, GOP members in the Kentucky House have named his leadership successor.  Rep. Josh Bray, of Mount Vernon, will be the next House Republican Whip. In that role, he will gauge support for caucus priorities, a Tuesday afternoon House Republicans press release said.  In […]
text:
The Kentucky House of Representatives in Frankfort, Feb. 27, 2024. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Arden Barnes)After Republican House Whip Jason Nemes lost his reelection bid last week, GOP members in the Kentucky House have named his leadership successor. 
Rep. Josh Bray, of Mount Vernon, will be the next House Republican Whip. In that role, he will gauge support for caucus priorities, a Tuesday afternoon House Republicans press release said. 
In a statement, Bray said he was “honored by the confidence my colleagues have placed in me.” 
“Kentuckians made it clear this election that affordability, accountability, and trust in government matter. Those priorities have guided the work we do in Frankfort for almost a decade and will continue to do so,” Bray said. 
Nemes, of Middletown, was one of nine Republican incumbents in the General Assembly to lose reelection last week. Most of the districts flipped are in suburban areas of Louisville. 
Republicans in Frankfort still hold supermajorities in the House and Senate as the 2027 legislative session is set to begin in less than two months. 
Both caucuses have announced their remaining leadership are unchanged. In the House, Republicans elected House Speaker David Osborne, of Prospect, and Speaker Pro Tempore David Meade, of Stanford, to fifth terms in their roles. House Majority Floor Leader Steven Rudy and House Majority Caucus Chair Suzanne Miles will continue in their roles. 
Senate President Robert Stivers, R-Manchester, will continue as the top Republican in that chamber. Senate President Pro Tempore David Givens, R-Greensburg; Senate Majority Floor Leader Max Wise, R-Campbellsville; Senate Majority Whip Mike Wilson, R-Bowling Green; and Senate Majority Caucus Chair Robby Mills, R-Henderson will also continue in their roles.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission pushes back on testing timeline, offers no new estimate
description: LINCOLN — The Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission pushed back Tuesday on assumptions that cultivators could wait up to two years for testing guidelines, but commissioners offered no new estimate for when such guidance will come. In a news release, the commission said it had not established a timeline for when lab testing for harvested marijuana or […]
text:
The Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission listens to a representative of one of the commission's four licensed cultivators during a meeting on Oct. 19, 2026, at the State Office Building in Lincoln. Commissioners seated, from left: Bud Synhorst of Lincoln, Jim Elworth of Nebraska City, Lorelle Mueting of Gretna (interim chair) and former District Judge J. Michael Coffey of Omaha. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission pushed back Tuesday on assumptions that cultivators could wait up to two years for testing guidelines, but commissioners offered no new estimate for when such guidance will come.
In a news release, the commission said it had not established a timeline for when lab testing for harvested marijuana or medical cannabis products will be available. During a discussion in October, interim Commission Chair Lorelle Mueting had said one cultivator assured her that cannabis could be safely stored for up to two years.
Commissioners on the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission during an April 13, 2026, meeting. From left, Commissioners Bud Synhorst of Lincoln, Jim Elworth of Nebraska City, Lorelle Mueting of Gretna (interim chair) and J. Michael Coffey of Omaha. All but Mueting also serve on the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The commission said Tuesday that it is “committed to transparency, accuracy and public communication,” but that the commission has never given a timeline for available testing.
“The commission recognizes that uncertainty about testing and product distribution creates planning and financial challenges for licensees. It also recognizes that inaccurate information about the program’s progress or anticipated timelines can have significant consequences,” the news release states. 
The release continued: “For that reason, the commission takes a cautious, deliberate approach to communicating timelines and program milestones, ensuring that information released to the public is accurate and supported by facts.”
Updated regulations?
Commissioners are waiting for Attorney General Mike Hilgers to sign off on the legality of amended rules and regulations the commission approved in October. If approved, Gov. Jim Pillen will have the final say. Both Hilgers and Pillen were reelected to four-year terms last week.
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers, left, and Gov. Jim Pillen. Sept. 14, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
But as for when legally harvested marijuana can be tested, the commission has not said. The commission has licensed its four cultivators, the maximum number allowed under self-imposed regulations.
Should Hilgers and Pillen approve the amendments, the commission could begin collecting application fees. But licensees, too, have worried the proposed fees are too high and could damage the supply chain. The cultivators are also urging the commission to support legislation to protect physicians from legal consequences solely for recommending medical cannabis.
The licensed cultivators in October also collectively urged the commission to amend its regulations to clarify the testing process, outline who could transport samples to labs under what requirements and explain whether out-of-state labs could be used.
The Nebraska Legislature
Under the voter-approved laws in 2024, regulatory power over “registered cannabis establishments” for the possession, manufacture, distribution, delivery and dispensing of medical cannabis is “vested exclusively” in the voter-created commission.
A registered cannabis establishment is defined as a private entity licensed to possess, manufacture, distribute, deliver or dispense cannabis for medical purposes. 
State Sens. Rick Holdcroft of Bellevue, left, and John Cavanaugh of Omaha before a meeting of the General Affairs Committee regarding medical cannabis legislation led by both senators. Holdcroft is committee chair. Cavanaugh is committee vice chair. Feb. 2, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Unless the Legislature changes that definition to include testing, the commission has no authority to grant in-state private facilities legal possession of marijuana. The commission also can’t guarantee legal safety for recommending physicians.
Changing the law would require at least 33 of 49 state senators, because voters approved it.
The two legislative committees that have recently considered medical cannabis bills are General Affairs and Health and Human Services. The chairs of those committees, state Sens. Rick Holdcroft of Bellevue and Brian Hardin of Gering, respectively, will again seek those spots in 2027 after winning reelection last week.
‘Long-term success’
The commission said Tuesday that its responsibility is not to “simply move quickly” but to “establish a regulatory framework that serves patients, supports medical providers and responsible licensees, protects public health and safety and complies with Nebraska law.”
Some of that requires external approval, coordination with other agencies, legislative action or local government decisions, the commission said, which affect regulatory timing. The commission said that means definitive timelines can’t always be provided as early as some would prefer, but commissioners want to “avoid creating expectations that may not be met.”
The Nebraska Examiner has asked the commission whether it is pushing for legislation in the 2027 legislative session, which begins Jan. 6. The Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services, as of Oct. 19, had still not issued any guidance to in-state physicians.
“The commission remains focused on advancing this work in a deliberate and responsible manner,” the commission said, “with the goal of establishing a functional, compliant medical cannabis program for Nebraska patients that provides a clear regulatory framework for licensees, avoids preventable mistakes and makes informed decisions that support long-term success.”
The next commission meeting is set for 1 p.m. Monday at the State Office Building in Lincoln.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas governor embraces Trump, calls for AI guardrails in new book
description: Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders praises President Donald Trump’s leadership in a book released a week after Republicans suffered heavy losses in a midterm widely seen as a rebuke of Trump by voters. But Sanders, who won reelection last week and is considered a potential 2028 presidential hopeful, distanced herself from the president by calling […]
text:
Copies of Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders' book on sale at a Barnes & Noble in Little Rock, Arkansas on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026 (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders praises President Donald Trump’s leadership in a book released a week after Republicans suffered heavy losses in a midterm widely seen as a rebuke of Trump by voters.
But Sanders, who won reelection last week and is considered a potential 2028 presidential hopeful, distanced herself from the president by calling for “commonsense” guardrails on artificial intelligence.
Sanders’ latest book, “Unapologetic: Clarity and Conviction in a World Gone Crazy,” was released Tuesday and comes out as Republicans are grappling with the aftermath of an election where they lost control of the U.S. House, Senate and a majority of governorships.
Sanders, who was first elected in 2022, won a second term by double digits though Republicans lost control of the supermajority in the state House needed to pass most budget bills without Democratic support.
The book covers Sanders’ election and first term as Arkansas governor. She also writes about her family and Christian faith, regularly quoting the Bible and authors such as C.S. Lewis. 
Here’s a look at what’s inside the new book:
 
Arkansas Governor and former Trump Administration Press Secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders and audience members asked former President Donald Trump about the auto industry, inflation, taxes and border security at a Sept. 17, 2024 town hall in Flint, Mich. (Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
 
Governor praises Trump’s ‘bold, new leadership’
It’s no surprise that Trump plays a prominent role in Sanders’ book. The governor served as White House press secretary during his first term and touted his endorsement when she first ran for governor.
Sanders praises Trump’s actions on policies like immigration and indicates she decided to run for governor with his leadership style in mind.
“I love Arkansas, but I wasn’t blind to the problems our state faced, and I thought that the best way to fix those issues would be through bold, new leadership, like what President Trump had brought to America,” she writes.
 
Sanders urges caution, skepticism on AI
There’s some daylight between Sanders and Trump on the issue of artificial intelligence.
Though Trump has dismissed the calls for more guardrails around AI, Sanders highlights her opposition to a provision of the One Big Beautiful Bill tax and spending cut law signed last year that would have prevented states from regulating artificial intelligence. The measure was stripped from the legislation following Sanders’ and other Republicans’ objections.
Sanders, who has signed into law measures limiting youths’ access to social media, wrote that conservatives should be skeptical of Big Tech on AI.
“President Trump is right that the United States must win the AI race against China to survive — we have no choice,” she writes. “But a race against China cannot be a race to the bottom that enriches billionaires in Silicon Valley and leaves the rest of America behind.”
 
Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders along with her husband, Bryan Sanders, speak to press outside the Dunbar Recreation Center where she cast her ballot on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in Little Rock, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
 
Opponents of prison plan ‘coalition of the unwilling’
The governor devotes several pages of the book to her fight with members of the Board of Corrections and some lawmakers over her efforts to build a new prison in Franklin County.
Sanders put the 3,000-bed prison project on hold after facing resistance from locals along with members of the Legislature from both parties.
Sanders expresses frustration that she faced opposition from members of her own party on the prison plan, labeling them and Democratic opponents the “coalition of the unwilling.”
“I expected I’d be fighting the left and the ‘defund the police’ crazies to make our communities safer, but I had no idea that some of the fiercest opposition would come from within my own party,” she writes.
 
Fears about impact from cancer diagnosis
Sanders opens the book with a revealing look at the thyroid cancer she was diagnosed with in 2022, just a couple months before she was elected governor. Sanders underwent surgery and soon returned to the campaign trail after being declared cancer-free.
But, in the book, she reveals that doctors warned her before her surgery that some patients experience damage to their vocal chords or changes to their voice. The damage didn’t occur, but Sanders writes about her reaction to that possibility.
“After all the reassurances from my doctors about my good prognosis, I was now finding out that even if I beat cancer, I might experience long-term damage that could derail my career,” she writes. 
 
Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders participates in the debate against 2026 gubernatorial candidates Fred Love (D), and Colt Shelby (L) on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026 at the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
 
Her State of the Union rebuttal could have been darker
Shortly after taking office in 2023, Sanders was asked to deliver Republicans’ response to President Joe Biden’s State of the Union address.
Sanders accepted, but after some hesitation.
“Few Republicans who’d given the State of the Union response had risen to the task, and a not insignificant number had failed miserably,” she writes.
Sanders’ speech painted a bleak picture of life under Biden, saying his administration was hijacked “by the radical left.”
But Sanders says that only came after she and First Gentleman Bryan Sanders revised a first draft she wasn’t happy with. 
“The first draft was heavy on policy. It was too dark and depressing and didn’t sound like me at all,” she writes. “The speechwriter I’d contracted with reminded me, ‘Sarah, you only have one job: Eviscerate Joe Biden.’”
Sanders writes that she and the unnamed speechwriter agreed to part ways after she revised her speech into the one she ultimately delivered.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Democrats are gunning for NH secretary of state post under new majority
description: David Scanlan, a Republican who has served as New Hampshire’s secretary of state since 2022, will face at least three challengers — and possibly more — for his position this year. Carleigh Beriont, a Hampton Select Board member who ran unsuccessfully for the Democratic nomination in the 1st Congressional District this year, sent an email […]
text:
Secretary of State David Scanlan (right) huddles over a stack of ballots with his No. 2, Deputy Secretary of State Brendan O’Donnell, during an official election recount on Nov. 9, 2026, at the State Archives building in Concord. There were 16 recounts called for state House races after the 2026 midterm elections earlier that month. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)David Scanlan, a Republican who has served as New Hampshire’s secretary of state since 2022, will face at least three challengers — and possibly more — for his position this year.
Carleigh Beriont, a Hampton Select Board member who ran unsuccessfully for the Democratic nomination in the 1st Congressional District this year, sent an email to all 424 state House and Senate members Tuesday morning asking for their support to become New Hampshire’s next secretary of state.
James Butler, a policy adviser to former Gov. Maggie Hassan currently working for Eversource, similarly sent a letter to lawmakers last week asking for their support.
And state Rep. Patrick Long, of Manchester, has also been courting lawmakers in an effort to secure the position.
Under state law, the New Hampshire Legislature selects the secretary of state in December following each state election. That’s unlike many states, where citizens directly vote for the secretary of state. The position’s biggest duty is running elections, but it also regulates insurance risk pools, registers businesses and manages state archives. After Democrats took whopping majorities — almost 300 of the 400 House seats went to Democrats as well as 15 of 24 Senate seats — in this month’s election, some Democrats want change in the office, which has experienced an unusual amount of stability in recent history compared to the rest of state government.
A pitch for change
Beriont said her experience assisting Hampton’s election monitors (all Hampton Select Board members assist in running the town’s elections) inspired her to run, as did her campaign for Congress. 
“I do think there is something really special about the day and the ritual,” she said of Election Day. “And the coming together and collectively deciding what we’re going to do, whether it’s at town meetings or in a state election or federal election. It’s definitely something that I would love to celebrate and inject some new energy into in the years ahead.”
Carleigh Beriont, shown here surrounded by supporters for her congressional run on June 9, 2026, is now seeking the post of secretary of state. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
If elected, Beriont wants to encourage more young people to register to vote as just 7% of New Hampshire’s 18-year-olds are registered, according to The Civics Center. She said she would also advocate for nonpartisan redistricting committees, though only the Legislature has that authority, and encourage the Legislature to make voting easier.
Butler said he was inspired to run after hearing from “some local elections officials who basically just want to see better collaboration, more professionalism out of the office and better preparedness.”
“I’ve been in and around elections for the better part of two decades,” Butler said, pointing to his work on campaigns and as a liaison between the governor’s office and municipalities. “It’s something that I care deeply about.”
He contended that while last week’s general election went well, Scanlan left local officials unprepared in September’s primary for a large Democratic turnout he failed to predict.
Long, on the other hand, is pointing to his experience as a poll watcher during President Barack Obama’s campaign, a fundraiser for Democratic Party voter outreach and a ballot clerk.
“In terms of elections, I’ve been involved in protecting the right to vote … for 18 years in various capacities,” he said, adding that he also has experience working in the Massachusetts State Auditor’s Office and on the House Municipal Finance Committee.
Long criticized Scanlan for his interpretation of a law banning the use of student IDs to prove identity at the polls. Long argued the law, as written, didn’t outlaw student IDs being used if the voters had no other acceptable ID, due to a so-called “safety valve” provision. However, Republicans behind the law made clear that they intended for it to do so. A federal judge blocked Scanlan’s directive on the same grounds in October, but the U.S. Supreme Court overruled after determining it was too close to an election and left Scanlan’s directive in place.
“I don’t want to attribute that to malice,” he said. “It could just be that he doesn’t understand the law, but people’s voting rights are affected by that.”
Long said he would rescind that interpretation on day one.
Long also argued that Scanlan is pushing municipalities and school districts to keep funding levels in their insurance risk pool reserves too low. He called it “not fiscally responsible” and “not actuarially sound.”
Others are also considering a run.
Sarah Chadzynski, who was one of Beriont’s opponents in the 1st Congressional District earlier this year, told the Bulletin: “I am seriously considering it, but I have not yet made a decision because I think it is a position that deserves a lot of thought and consideration.”
NHPR reported last week that former Senate President Donna Soucy is also considering a run. Soucy, who served in the state Senate from 2018 to 2024, did not respond to the Bulletin’s phone calls or text messages. State Rep. James Newsom, who represents Contoocook and serves on the House Election Law Committee, was also talked about for the role, but he told the Bulletin Tuesday he decided against running.
A sign demarcating the New Hampshire Secretary of State’s Office in the State House in Concord, photographed on Feb. 11, 2026. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
A pitch for experience
For his part, Scanlan offered a straightforward pitch for reelection: “There is no candidate that has anywhere near the experience that I have in this job.”
He called Beriont’s experience helping run one town’s local elections “not even close” to the challenge of running the entire state’s elections.
Before becoming secretary of state, Scanlan served as deputy to his predecessor, Bill Gardner, for 20 years. Gardner, a Democrat, served as secretary of state for 46 years. Between the two, the Secretary of State’s Office has been isolated from the political headwinds that have caused so many positions in this purple state to flip back and forth. Scanlan warned that if Democrats decide to boot him out of office, the position will lose that consistency and will likely turn over to a Republican in a few years.
“We will lose something very, very special in the state if that happens,” Scanlan said.
Gov. Kelly Ayotte, speaking to reporters Tuesday, echoed the concern: “I just think that it would be the wrong thing to do to politicize the Secretary of State’s Office.” Ayotte supports keeping Scanlan, particularly because she thinks it will help New Hampshire keep its first-in-the-nation primary status.
Asked if she’s concerned about the position becoming a political football, Beriont said: “What’s the appropriate amount of time for one person or one group of people to serve in this role? I think that if the people of New Hampshire have told us anything over the last week, it’s that we need a new generation of people in power.”
Butler contended that if he were elected, his tenure wouldn’t kick off the back-and-forth partisan nature of the office some fear because he’s “committed to this role for the long term” — though Scanlan says he is too — and he said he’s able to work in a bipartisan manner, pointing to the work he did in Hassan’s office while Republicans controlled the state Senate.
Scanlan said he knows he has Democrats behind him.
“I have a base of Democratic support,” he said. “No question about that. I will have bipartisan support going into this election. The question is, a lot of new Democrats in the House that don’t know me, and I have to make an impact on them if I’m going to survive the numbers that I’m facing at the moment.”
He points to this most recent election as evidence for his stewardship of the office, which had record turnout and no reported issues.
Scanlan has avoided any overt partisan actions in running the office, but he has implemented a series of Republican laws, including requiring proof of citizenship and the ban on student IDs, which Democrats have argued unfairly suppressed votes. Butler accused Scanlan of “caving to the extremists in his party.”
“I have to follow the laws,” Scanlan said. “The Republicans have been in power. They’ve created the laws. I follow them. The Democrats are going to be in power. If they pass new laws, I have to follow them.”
He also pointed to his recent stand against President Donald Trump.
In 2025, the Trump administration demanded New Hampshire and other states hand over confidential voter information. Scanlan refused, citing state law that prohibits him from releasing information such as Social Security and driver’s license numbers. The fight went to federal court, where Scanlan and election officials from other states prevailed.
“I’ve exhibited backbone,” he said.
The Legislature is set to vote on the position Dec. 2.  Per state statute, the secretary of state earns between $102,599 and $143,061 annually depending on experience.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri Supreme Court rejects challenge to stadium subsidy law on technical grounds
description: The Missouri Supreme Court on Tuesday rejected a challenge to the state’s stadium subsidy law, ruling that two Republican lawmakers and a conservative activist lacked the legal standing to contest its constitutionality. In a 5-2 decision, the court upheld a Cole County judge’s dismissal of a lawsuit filed by state Sen. Mike Moon, an Ash […]
text:
GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium, home of the Kansas City Chiefs (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).The Missouri Supreme Court on Tuesday rejected a challenge to the state’s stadium subsidy law, ruling that two Republican lawmakers and a conservative activist lacked the legal standing to contest its constitutionality.
In a 5-2 decision, the court upheld a Cole County judge’s dismissal of a lawsuit filed by state Sen. Mike Moon, an Ash Grove Republican, state Rep. Bryant Wolfin, a Ste. Genevieve Republican, and conservative activist Ron Calzone.
The ruling leaves the law intact without addressing the plaintiffs’ allegations that it violates several provisions of the Missouri Constitution.
Gov. Mike Kehoe signed the legislation in June 2025 after calling lawmakers into special session amid a bidding war with Kansas over the Kansas City Chiefs and Royals.
The law authorized state aid worth up to half the cost of qualifying stadium projects, along with tax incentives and property tax relief. The Chiefs have since announced plans to move to Kansas, while the Royals are pursuing a new ballpark near downtown Kansas City that could receive substantial state subsidies.
The lawsuit alleged the legislation violated constitutional restrictions requiring bills to contain a single subject, have a clear title and not stray from their original purpose. It also challenged the use of public money to benefit private businesses.
But the Supreme Court never reached those questions.
Writing for the majority, Judge Robin Ransom concluded the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate the direct expenditure of taxpayer money necessary to establish standing.
The challengers pointed to a fiscal analysis estimating the Missouri Department of Revenue would spend $10,000 creating a tax form and potentially $175,000 on computer programming to implement portions of the law.
Ransom rejected that argument, finding the estimates were speculative rather than evidence of actual spending.
“Projections are not equivalent to the requirement that a sum be paid out,” she wrote.
The majority also rejected the argument that the stadium subsidies themselves established standing. Any state expenditure, Ransom wrote, would require several additional steps, including an application, government approval and legislative appropriation.
The court likewise reaffirmed a 2011 precedent holding that tax credits generally do not constitute direct government expenditures for purposes of taxpayer standing.
Moon and Wolfin also argued that the legislation’s allegedly unconstitutional passage diminished the effectiveness of their votes as lawmakers. But the court declined to consider that claim because it was not properly presented in their appellate briefing.
Judge Paul Wilson, joined by Judge Mary Russell, dissented.
Wilson argued the lower court’s dismissal was not a final, appealable judgment. Even if the Supreme Court could hear the appeal, he wrote, the plaintiffs had alleged enough potential government spending to survive a motion to dismiss.
He noted that the lawsuit was filed before the law took effect, making it unreasonable to demand proof that money had already been spent.
At a minimum, Wilson argued, the plaintiffs should have been allowed to amend their lawsuit to include evidence of expenditures occurring after it was filed.
He also questioned the distinction between ordinary tax credits and refundable credits, which can result in direct payments from the state treasury.
“A refundable tax credit operates just like a check or warrant drawn on the state treasury,” Wilson wrote, “no more and no less.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Uthmeier subpoenas Democratic Socialists regarding alleged foreign contributions
description: A week after the first Democratic Socialist of America (DSA)-backed candidate won a seat in the Florida Legislature, Attorney General James Uthmeier is subpoenaing the organization, alleging possible violation of state laws against solicitation of funds from Cuba and China. “We are examining whether DSA accepted contributions or support from foreign sources [...]
text:
Florida Republican Attorney General James Uthmeier in Lakeland on Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)A week after the first Democratic Socialist of America (DSA)-backed candidate won a seat in the Florida Legislature, Attorney General James Uthmeier is subpoenaing the organization, alleging possible violation of state laws against solicitation of funds from Cuba and China.
“We are examining whether DSA accepted contributions or support from foreign sources of concern, including the regimes in Cuba and China,” Uthmeier said in a short video posted on his social media channels. “And whether its fundraising from Florida donors has been fully transparent and lawful.”
A delegation of DSA members — including members from Florida — joined a coalition of activist groups such as Code Pink and Progressive International on the “Nuestra America” convoy to Cuba in March. They reportedly brought medical and school supplies and solar panels and met with Cuban government officials.
The Florida Legislature has passed laws in recent years targeting foreign influence. That includes legislation passed in 2025 (SB 700) prohibiting nonprofits from accepting donations from entities or individuals associated with “foreign countries of concern” — which include China, Cuba, North Korea, Russia, Iran, Syria, and the Venezuelan government of Nicholas Maduro (removed by U.S. armed forces in January and awaiting trial on allegations of conspiring with drug cartels).
The DSA movement has burgeoned in the past couple of years, ignited by Zohran Mamdani’s election as New York mayor in the fall of 2025. Last week, six DSA candidates won election to Congress and, in Florida, Democrat Ashley Herrmann, backed by the DSA, ousted Republican incumbent Danny Alvarez in state House District 69 in Hillsborough County.
Uthmeier was on the ballot for the first time as a political candidate last week. He narrowly defeated Democrat José Javier Rodríguez  in the race for attorney general by less than 2 percentage points.
A spokesperson for the national DSA told the Phoenix that they “are aware of the situation and have no comment at this time.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Likely Speaker-elect Reives signals bipartisan approach as Democrats flip NC House
description: Republicans have controlled both legislative chambers since 2011, often with a veto-proof supermajority.
text:
North Carolina House Democratic Leader Robert Reives speaks to reporters on Nov. 10, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)With Democrats winning a near-supermajority in the North Carolina House, likely House Speaker-elect Rep. Robert Reives said Tuesday he’s open to bipartisan efforts to lower costs across the state.
“Compromise is not capitulation. Compromise is the job,” Reives, a Democrat from Chatham County, told reporters during a press conference Tuesday. 
Democrats flipped control of the North Carolina House during last week’s elections, gaining a majority for the first time in 15 years. They’ll hold a 71-48 advantage with one independent in the 2027 term. In the state Senate, in unofficial results, it appears Republicans will hold onto a narrow 26-24 majority, with one race possibly subject to a recount.
Reives said the House Democratic Caucus will meet early next week for an organizational meeting as lawmakers return to Raleigh for a lame duck session. Members will announce key legislative leadership roles after that. However, Reives announced last week he has secured majority support in his caucus for the speakership. 
Republicans have controlled both legislative chambers in North Carolina since 2011, often with a veto-proof supermajority. That’s allowed the party to sideline Democratic governors. Lawmakers passed measures to redraw congressional and legislative districts, limit reproductive freedom, boost private schools, and expand firearm access.
NC Senate Democratic leader sees a path to bipartisanship next year

When lawmakers return next week, Republicans will still hold veto-proof or near-veto-proof majorities in both chambers. Their terms don’t end until Dec. 31.
During past lame duck sessions, Republicans have stripped power from incoming Democratic elected officials and cut their agency staffing, as well as making changes to election law and proposing constitutional amendments, all along strict party lines. In 2024, lawmakers passed a 131-page bill branded as Hurricane Helene relief, but it also made drastic changes to state government. 
Reives is hoping this year will be different. 
“This is the first opportunity to show what kind of atmosphere we’re going to have next year,” Reives said. “If we come in here with the lame duck sessions that we’ve had every cycle since I’ve been here, then that will be a signal to the caucus that there is no interest in working with us and there’s no interest in any bipartisanism or camaraderie.”
Reives applauded his GOP counterpart, Speaker Destin Hall, for bipartisanship during the 2025-2026 legislative biennium. Republicans elected Hall, a representative from Caldwell County, to the position two years ago. Hall succeeded recently ousted Republican Congressman Tim Moore, who was state House Speaker for ten years.
“Speaker Hall did an amazing job of working with us, and we passed the budget,” Reives said. “First time that we passed a bipartisan budget in this building since Republicans took over, so I know the House Republicans are ready to get to work.”
Looking ahead to next year, Reives said he wants to tackle affordability issues when it comes to housing, groceries, energy and healthcare. 
“We’re going to work as hard as we can to make life more affordable,” he said. 
More than 3 million North Carolina voters are registered as unaffiliated with a party. An independent candidate, April Montgomery, won election to serve Lee and Moore counties in the House. She’s the first unaffiliated legislator elected in North Carolina since 2010.
Reives said Montgomery ran a great campaign.
“I want her in a position that she can operate in the way that is most comfortable and aligns with her philosophies,” he said. “I want her to know that she has got 70 people who are cheering for wherever she goes. If she decides she wants to caucus with Republicans, caucus with Democrats, if she wants to caucus with nobody, I want her to be supported because she’s been elected by our people.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Commentary: Dwindling margins: Can Tennessee Democrats build on an encouraging election?
description: The blue paint that Jackson Pollacked the canvas of American politics last week didn’t miss Tennessee, but there’s a case to be made that it landed with more of a sprinkle than a splash.  Gazing longingly at the midterm miracles that stunningly remade the political landscapes of Texas, Kansas, Iowa, South Carolina, and perhaps Mississippi, […]
text:
Also-rans who almost won: In Tennessee's 6th Congressional District, Democrat Mike Cooley, left, raised $117,000 but almost beat state Rep. Johnny Garrett, who raised more than $3 million. Marquita Bradshaw, right, came within 12 percentage points of beating incumbent U.S. Sen. Bill Hagerty, to whom she lost by 27 percentage points in 2020. (Photos by John Partipilo of Mike Cooley and Karen Pulfer Focht of Marquita Bradshaw/Tennessee Lookout)The blue paint that Jackson Pollacked the canvas of American politics last week didn’t miss Tennessee, but there’s a case to be made that it landed with more of a sprinkle than a splash. 
Gazing longingly at the midterm miracles that stunningly remade the political landscapes of Texas, Kansas, Iowa, South Carolina, and perhaps Mississippi, Volunteer State Democrats are left to ponder: is Tennessee on the same path, or is it just too stubbornly red to join the fun? 
If you glance at a national map showing Republican-to-Democrat voting shifts by county comparing 2026 to 2024, it sure looks like Tennessee with its dense cluster of blue arrows was right there in the middle of the wave last week. But the actual results for Dems here were more about dwindling margins than electoral wins. 
There were, of course, some blue successes. At the legislative level a surprising six state House seats flipped red to blue . In the race for governor Democrats won a half dozen counties they lost in 2022, including Hamilton, Knox, Montgomery and Rutherford. And the capper no one saw coming was Victoria Broderick’s astonishing win over 8-term GOP U.S.  Rep. Scott DesJarlais in the 4th Congressional District. 
The collapse of GOP voters for Blackburn in TN. Two years later, and 1M fewer votes.

But the math on the ground remains grim. With those legislative flips the Republican edge in the state House drops from 75% to 69%, and the state Senate didn’t change.  And Broderick’s signature win notwithstanding, the split in Tennessee’s nine-member congressional delegation remains the same it was before last Tuesday.
Republicans survived a close call at the top of the ticket. Gov. Bill Lee won his first term in 2018 by 21 points and his second term in 2022 by 32 points. Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn’s feeble 2.5% win last week over the energetic but underfunded Democrat Jerri Green speaks not just to Blackburn’s singular unpopularity even in her own party but also tells us this was a winnable contest for Dems given more resources and a better campaign. In other words, a missed opportunity. 
Congressional races beyond just the astounding 4th District outcome also showcased blue incursions into the minds and hearts of Tennessee voters. Amply funded Democrats Chaz Molder in the 5th District, Darden Copeland in the 7th District) and Rep. Justin J. Pearson in the (9th District all ran aggressive races, losing only by low single digits — much closer than Republicans thought possible when they drew the lines to make them safe red seats. 
A fascinating thing in the U.S. House races was that these well-financed, well-staffed Democrats fared no better than a couple of barely funded candidates who ran minimalist campaigns. The $90K that Broderick raised is peanuts for a congressional race, and she had only about $40K to work with in the general election, yet she won. 
Less noticed but just as stupefying is the 6th District, where unknown Democrat Mike Croley lost this supposedly safe GOP seat to Republican Rep. Johnny Garrett by just three points. Garrett spent over half a million dollars on the general election (after blowing through more than two million to win his primary), while Croley came out of his primary with less than $5,000 in his campaign account and rustled up only about $70K to spend on the general election. I’m a voter in the 6th and never once heard a peep from Croley’s campaign. 
What should we make of the fact that unknown Democrats with little money drawing zero outside attention running muted campaigns in districts nobody regarded as remotely competitive did just as well or better than the higher-profile Democratic contenders who enjoyed money, attention, and optimistic vibes?
Victoria Broderick claims victory over U.S. Rep. Scott DesJarlais in 4th Congressional District

The simple explanation is that big political waves powered by broad dissatisfaction with the party in power will naturally pull some small fish from the other party into the incoming tide. Last week saw a number of so-called accidental wins in several states that likely surprised the victors themselves as much as anyone else. It’s also the case that unsung, underfunded Democrats like Broderick and Croley were largely ignored by GOP campaigns. With no flurry of media defining the turf, voters would see them merely as the “D” option on a ballot, free of the woke-radical-lefty-commie-socialist labels that Republicans in competitive races spent every last dime this cycle slapping on their opponents. 
The wave dynamic also explains how the Democrat running for U.S. Senate, Marquita Bradshaw, managed to come within 12 points of the GOP incumbent Sen. Bill Hagerty, despite the fact that she raised virtually no money, ran virtually no campaign, and lost to Hagerty by 27 points when he first won the seat in 2020.
For years the working assumption has been that Democrats are structurally uncompetitive in much of the South, including Tennessee. Last Tuesday makes it clear that the footprint of Republican dominance has lost a few shoe sizes. So can Tennessee Democrats turn this new jolt of optimism into something more than just a mostly close-but-no-cigar outlier election that entices but doesn’t fulfill? Is there a path to membership in the newly growing club of Southern and Midwestern red states moving past the tyranny of one-party control?
One thing that would help Tennessee look like other red states turning purple is loosening the stranglehold Republicans have had on voters in growing suburban counties. Last week’s election teased us big time here. Two years ago in her U.S. Senate reelection,Blackburn waxed state Rep. Gloria Johnson by 20 points in each of the key high-growth suburban and exurban counties of Rutherford and Montgomery. In last Tuesday’s contest for governor Blackburn lost to Green in Rutherford by almost 9,000 votes and in Montgomery by over 3,500 votes. Even Bradshaw  won the U.S. Senate race in both counties. 
Going forward, turning this into something lasting for Democrats means throwing significant money and serious talent at every crucial race and doing so early. One of Blackburn’s first acts as governor in January will be to appoint someone to fill her Senate seat until it’s on the ballot in 2028. A serious Democrat who has the chops and wants that seat should be in the fray raising money and running hard by Valentine’s Day. Others who want to give congressional seats a go should also get started without delay, publicly and aggressively watchdogging these House Republicans from the minute they take the oath at the start of the new Congress in January.
Perhaps 2028 will be another big blue election year, but even if it is it probably won’t have coattails like this one. Tsunamis just don’t happen that often. To build on 2026 Tennessee Democrats need to find candidates, write checks, and open the throttle, but quick.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Democratic Gov.-elect Weiser names Republican Cleave Simpson Colorado ag commissioner
description: Democratic Gov.-elect Phil Weiser announced his first round of cabinet appointments Tuesday, led by his pick of a top-ranking Republican at the Capitol to head the Colorado Department of Agriculture. GOP state Sen. Cleave Simpson, who represents the San Luis Valley and has served as the Republican Senate Minority Leader since June 2025, was named […]
text:
Gov.-elect Phil Weiser, Colorado's Democratic attorney general, spoke to reporters at a press conference on Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Democratic Gov.-elect Phil Weiser announced his first round of cabinet appointments Tuesday, led by his pick of a top-ranking Republican at the Capitol to head the Colorado Department of Agriculture.
GOP state Sen. Cleave Simpson, who represents the San Luis Valley and has served as the Republican Senate Minority Leader since June 2025, was named Weiser’s incoming Agriculture Commissioner.
Simpson, a fourth-generation farmer and rancher and general manager of the Rio Grande Water Conservation District, will succeed outgoing Agriculture Commissioner Kate Greenberg, who has served in the role since 2019, when she was named by Gov. Jared Polis and became the first woman to lead the department.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Weiser also named Jeni Arndt, a former Fort Collins mayor and state legislator, as his director of rural advancement, fulfilling a campaign promise to give “rural Colorado a cabinet-level go-to resource.” Scott Steinbrecher, currently deputy attorney general for natural resources and environment, will become Weiser’s senior director of water policy, another new cabinet-level position.
Weiser said in a press release that the appointments “demonstrate my commitment to building a collaborative administration that’s inclusive of voices from across Colorado and the political spectrum.”
Senate Minority Leader Cleave Simpson is seen at the Colorado Capitol in March. (Photo by Sara Wilson/Colorado Newsline)
“As governor, I will ensure that Coloradans from all walks of life have a seat at the table — because that’s the only way we will be ready on day one to make state government work better and build a brighter future for all Coloradans,” Weiser said.
Weiser’s transition team, led by a handful of veteran Colorado Democratic operatives including Alan Salazar and Pat Meyers, is inviting Coloradans to submit their ideas for his administration and to apply for key roles in the executive branch, at his website, WeiserTogether.org.
Ferrandino to become deputy treasurer
Weiser also announced that Dominick Moreno, a former state Senate majority leader and deputy chief of staff to Denver Mayor Mike Johnston, will serve as director of the Office of State Planning and Budgeting.
The office’s current director, former state House Speaker Mark Ferrandino, was named deputy treasurer of Colorado on Tuesday by Democratic Treasurer-elect Jeff Bridges, who will succeed two-term Treasurer Dave Young in January.
“I’ve spent the last three years leading the state’s budget through tough decisions without cutting what Coloradans count on most,” Ferrandino said in a press release. “The Treasury is where the state’s money can start working harder, not just stretching further. I’m grateful to Treasurer-elect Bridges for the chance to help do that, and to Gov. Polis for his trust in me to help lead our state’s budget.”

name: WyoFile
title: Barlow announces first leadership picks as Wyoming’s incoming governor
description:
Eric Barlow, so far, has selected Erin Taylor as chief of staff, Walter Eggers as nominee for attorney general and Eydie Trautwein as chief operating officer.
The post Barlow announces first leadership picks as Wyoming’s incoming governor appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming Gov.-elect Eric Barlow announced the first members of his incoming administration Tuesday, tapping three leaders with experience in public policy, law and state government. 
The Republican selected Erin Taylor as chief of staff, Walter Eggers as nominee for attorney general and Eydie Trautwein as chief operating officer, according to a press release. 

Wyoming Gov.-elect Eric Barlow has selected Erin Taylor as chief of staff of his incoming administration. (Courtesy Office of Gov.-elect Eric Barlow) 

“Wyoming deserves a government that listens, spends responsibly and delivers dependable service,” Barlow said in the release. “Erin, Walter and Eydie understand our state and bring the experience and judgment needed to help lead this work. I will count on them to build strong relationships, address problems directly and keep our administration focused on serving the people of Wyoming.”
While Taylor and Trautwein’s positions are ultimately decided by the governor, Eggers is a nominee and will be subject to Wyoming Senate confirmation. 
As chief of staff, Taylor will lead the governor’s office with more than 25 years of public policy experience at the federal, state and local levels, and will help coordinate the administration’s priorities with legislators, state agencies and communities. 
In 2014, Taylor founded a consulting firm after serving eight years as executive director of the Wyoming Taxpayers Association. She also led U.S. Sen. Mike Enzi’s 2014 campaign and previously directed the Wyoming Association of Community College Trustees. Taylor holds two degrees from the University of Wyoming. 

Wyoming Gov.-elect Eric Barlow has selected Walter Eggers as nominee for attorney general. Eggers will be subject to the Wyoming Senate’s confirmation. (Courtesy Office of Gov.-elect Eric Barlow) 

Eggers began his legal career in Cheyenne after graduating from the UW College of Law in 1997, working as both a prosecutor and defense attorney. In 2000, he joined powerhouse Mountain West law firm Holland and Hart where he served as partner for about 16 years and led the firm’s Cheyenne office. 
He later led the firm’s Energy, Environment and Natural Resources Practice Group, which included overseeing more than 100 lawyers and legal professionals. Eggers’ practice has focused on administrative law, state and local taxation, litigation and appeals. 

Wyoming Gov.-elect Eric Barlow has selected Eydie Trautwein as chief operating officer of his incoming administration. (Courtesy Office of Gov.-elect Eric Barlow) 

At UW, Eggers has taught professional responsibility, evidence, and oil and gas law. He’s also worked to expand access to civil legal assistance with the Wyoming Access to Justice Commission and Equal Justice Wyoming. 
Trautwein, also a graduate of UW’s College of Law, will bring her experience in state administration, legal services and coordination across government to the position of chief operating officer. Her responsibilities will include overseeing the governor’s office operations and supporting implementation of the administration’s priorities. 
She previously served as Wyoming’s deputy state auditor, where her work included coordinating a major upgrade of the state’s financial, human resources and payroll systems. 
Trautwein also served as director of legal resources and judicial education for the Wyoming Supreme Court. 
Barlow, a veterinarian and longtime state lawmaker, is set to be inaugurated on Jan. 4.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Commentary: Possibly coming to a classroom near you: ‘Teacher, what does “adultery” mean?’
description: Imagine this coming to a South Carolina classroom near you. It could happen if the General Assembly follows Texas and Louisiana with a law requiring public school classrooms to display the Ten Commandments: (Scene: A lively second-grade classroom. Students settle into their desks. A hand is raised.) Student: Teacher, what is “adultery”? Teacher: What?! Where[...]
text:
The U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in February 2026 that a Louisiana law requiring displays of the Ten Commandments in classrooms can be enforced. The ruling removed an injunction that had blocked enforcement in a handful of parishes where plaintiff parents had challenged the law. (Photo by Michael Smith/Getty Images)Imagine this coming to a South Carolina classroom near you. It could happen if the General Assembly follows Texas and Louisiana with a law requiring public school classrooms to display the Ten Commandments:
(Scene: A lively second-grade classroom. Students settle into their desks. A hand is raised.)
Student: Teacher, what is “adultery”?
Teacher: What?! Where did you see a word like that?
5th Circuit upholds Louisiana law requiring Ten Commandments displays in classrooms

Student: It’s on the wall.
Teacher: Someone wrote that on the bathroom wall?
Student: No, it’s in the classroom. (Points to the Ten Commandments recently placed on the classroom wall.)
Teacher: Oh, you’re talking about the Ten Commandments. The Legislature required every classroom to post them on the wall.
Student: Why?
Teacher: Well, the Legislature says they’re important.
Second Student: Is the Legislature a church?
Teacher: No. It’s not a church.
First Student: OK, but I still don’t know what “adultery” means.
Teacher: I think the Legislature wanted you to read the commandments but not ask questions about them.
Third Student: But why can’t we ask questions? Didn’t you say we can’t learn if we don’t ask questions?
Teacher: Well, yes, but some of these commandments are not what we call “age appropriate.”
Third Student: But why would they put them on the wall then?
Teacher: (Sighs) I don’t know. No one asked me. State lawmakers don’t talk to teachers.
First Student: So, what is adultery?
Teacher: Heavens. That’s when a married person cheats on their husband or wife.
Fourth Student: Is that what they call “sex”?
Teacher: You know, you really need to ask your parents. It’s time for math.
Fifth Student: What’s a graven image? It says you can’t make a graven image.
Teacher: That’s an idol.
Sixth Student: Like “American Idol”? We can’t watch “American Idol”? My parents like “American Idol.”
Teacher: No, “American Idol” is an OK kind of idol. I mean, it’s different…
Seventh Student: Is an idol like a statue?
Teacher: Yes, sometimes.
Seventh Student: We have statues at school.
Teacher: Yes.
Seventh Student: Are those idols?
Teacher: No.
Seventh Student: How do you know?
Teacher: Let’s talk about fractions.
Eighth Student: What does “covet” mean? And what’s a “manservant”? Is that like a slave?
Teacher: Oh, my. Well, sometimes it was, but…
Ninth Student: What about “Thou shalt not kill”? My dad says we’re fighting a war. Are soldiers allowed to kill people?
Teacher: Is that the lunch bell? I feel like I heard the lunch bell.
Ninth Student: Are soldiers allowed to kill people?
Teacher: That’s … a very complicated question.
Ninth Student: But it’s right there on the wall.
Teacher: Yes, but…
Ninth Student: So, is the wall wrong?
Teacher: No, I mean, yes, I mean. … It should say “murder,” not “kill.”
Ninth Student: Who decided it should say, “kill,” not “murder”?
Teacher: That’s a very good question.
Principal Smith (Energetically pops his head into the classroom). Hello! How’s everything going today?
Teacher: Oh, Principal Smith, I have a question about the Ten Commandments.
Principal Smith: Oh, what’s your question?
Teacher: What am I supposed to tell the children when they ask what they mean?
Principal Smith: We’re waiting for guidance from the district.
Teacher: What does the district say?
Principal Smith: We’re waiting for guidance from the state.
Teacher: What does the state say?
Principal Smith: The Legislature says the commandments speak for themselves.
Teacher: Not to 7-year-olds.
Tenth Student: Teacher, who is the Lord?
Principal Smith: Laterz! (Principal Smith disappears.)
Teacher: The Lord?
Tenth Student: It says, “I am the Lord thy God.”
Teacher: That’s referring to God.
Tenth Student: Which god? My family is Hindu.
SC House approves bill requiring classrooms to post Ten Commandments

Teacher: Well … The Ten Commandments are part of Jewish and Christian religions.
Tenth Student: But we’re not all Jewish or Christian.
Teacher: No, we’re not.
Tenth Student: But they’re on our wall.
Teacher: Yes.
Tenth Student: So, are they everyone’s rules — no matter what my parents believe?
Teacher: OK, everybody, recess! (Students run out.)
Teacher: I have a question, too. (Looks at the Ten Commandments.) Am I a teacher? Or a preacher?
Editor’s note: The House passed legislation 84-31 in February that would require an 11-by-13-inch poster or framed copy in every classroom, alongside a “context statement.” The Senate never took up that bill, which officially died when the regular legislative session ended in May. Supporters could reintroduce the proposal for the session that starts in January.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico could soon require co-pays for high-earning families using universal childcare program
description: High-earning New Mexico families could soon pay monthly fees to keep their kids in the state’s first-in-the-nation universal childcare program. A state Early Childhood Education and Care Department spokesperson said co-pays would only apply to 10% of participating families.
text:
The New Mexico Early Childhood Education and Care Department will hold a public hearing on Dec. 3, 2026, regarding a proposal to require co-pays for high-earning families who participate in the state’s universal childcare program. Above, Olga Grays reads to children in her class at Mrs. Olga's Daycare in Las Cruces in September of 2026. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)High-earning New Mexico families could soon pay monthly fees to keep their kids in the state’s first-in-the-nation universal childcare program.
The New Mexico Early Childhood Education and Care Department will hold a hybrid public hearing from 9 to 11 a.m. on Dec. 3 in Santa Fe and online, regarding a proposal to require co-pays for high-earning families. The department is also accepting public feedback on the proposal by email.
The law establishing New Mexico’s universal childcare program specified that co-pays would take effect only in times of economic downturn, and that they would apply to families who make at least six times the federal poverty level — $163,920 for a family of three and $198,000 for a family of four.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Under the current proposal, those families could see monthly co-pays of $15 to $99 for one child, depending on their income level, and $22.50 to $148.50 for two or more children.
In a statement provided to Source NM, ECECD spokesperson Julia Sclafani said national inflation levels are responsible for the proposed co-pays, which would affect about 10% of families who participate in universal childcare.
“Under the Child Care Assistance Program Act, copay for families at the highest income levels take effect when certain national economic conditions are met. Those conditions have nothing to do with the health of the Early Childhood Trust Fund or the state budget,” she said.
During this year’s legislative session, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham criticized proposals to require co-pays — including one from the state House of Representatives that would have set a lower income threshold for the payments — as being, by definition, not universal. Sclafani said Lujan Grisham still opposes the co-pays.
“If anything, inflation makes it harder for households to take on additional bills,” she said. “ECECD is doing everything within its authority to limit the impact on them. Universal childcare is working, it is sustainable, and this administration will keep fighting to protect it.”
The rulemaking hearing is scheduled just weeks before Democratic Gov.-elect Deb Haaland is set to take office. On the campaign trail, she frequently cited her experience as a single working mother when expressing her support for the program.
When asked at a news conference last week whether she would support co-pays, she told reporters that she hoped to spare families from the payments “to the extent that we can.”
“It’s an economic driver for our state,” she said. “To the extent that we can keep anyone from having to make co-pays for early childhood education, I think we want to see if we can do that. This benefits our children.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Whitmer asks Trump administration to end food tariffs, reimburse Michiganders for increased costs
description: Gov. Gretchen Whitmer is using her final months in office to attack food tariffs imposed by the administration of President Donald Trump. On Tuesday, Whitmer called for the U.S. Department of Treasury to end its tariffs imposed on food products, while also requesting that the federal government reimburse Michigan residents for the increased costs they’ve […]
text:
U.S. Customs station at the Blue Water Bridge in Port Huron, Michigan. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)Gov. Gretchen Whitmer is using her final months in office to attack food tariffs imposed by the administration of President Donald Trump.
On Tuesday, Whitmer called for the U.S. Department of Treasury to end its tariffs imposed on food products, while also requesting that the federal government reimburse Michigan residents for the increased costs they’ve incurred from the tariff regime.
Whitmer, in a letter to U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, noted that Trump’s federal tariff policies have had a disproportionate effect on Michigan families. She also pointed out that, according to the National Taxpayers Union Foundation, Michigan households have faced an average tariff burden of $6,485 per household since January 2025. Whitmer’s office said that burden was the highest in the country. Meanwhile, food prices have continued to rise, Whitmer wrote, and grocery prices have increased by 2.4% in 2025.
“Right now, Michigan families are paying the highest tariff burden in the nation because of DC Republicans’ agenda, and those costs are showing up every time they check out at the grocery store,” Whitmer wrote. “In Michigan, we’ve worked hard to put money back in people’s pockets, but we need a federal trade policy that works with our allies, brings supply chains home, and makes life more affordable. Families deserve relief from rising prices on the essentials they depend on every day.” 
Whitmer signs executive order to examine impact of Trump tariffs on Michigan’s economy

The letter also emphasized how the tariff regime has heavily damaged the U.S. relationship with Canada.
“Specifically, exports to Canada fell 12.3% last year, signaling severe strain with our strongest trading partner — these tariffs and sudden policy reversals have weakened Michigan’s competitiveness and disrupted long‑standing trade relationships,” Whitmer wrote. “Federal leaders can step up and make real change. I ask that you end the new food tariffs this administration has levied in 2025 and 2026, and reimburse Michiganders for the increased cost of food.” 
A request for comment was sent by Michigan Advance to the U.S. Treasury Department. This story will be updated when a response is received.

The money will target “diabetes and chronic-disease care, expand access to technology-enabled healthcare, improve care coordination, and b[...]
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey speaks to an audience in Bluefield, West Virginia, about the Rural Health Transformation Program in November 2025. On Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026, Morrisey announced that $17 million will be dispersed from the Rural Health Transformation Fund to organizations mostly in Huntington, West Virginia. (Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Office of Gov. Patrick Morrisey)In a whirlwind day of back-to-back press conferences, Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced nearly $17 million will be dispersed from the Rural Health Transformation Program to organizations mostly in Huntington, West Virginia.
The money will target “diabetes and chronic-disease care, expand access to technology-enabled healthcare, improve care coordination, and build the rural healthcare workforce,” according to a news release. 
The Marshall Research Corporation, a nonprofit that finds grants for Marshall University, will receive $11.4 million for three separate programs for remote patient monitoring on patients with diabetes and hypertension, implement lifestyle and nutrition programs for managing diabetes and training for emergency medical care in rural areas. 
Another $1.5 million will go to Cabell-Huntington Hospital for helping rural patients with follow-ups and connecting with specialists. 
The West Virginia Primary Care Association will receive nearly $2.8 million to expand diabetes management at community health centers. 
Rural Outreach and Access to Medicine West Virginia, an organization that does diabetes and other medical monitoring in central West Virginia, will receive $1.2 million. The money will be used to recruit nurses and serve patients with high-risk for neuropathy or diabetes.
