title: As ‘child predator hunters’ go viral, states grapple with the risks of civilian stings
description: Across the country, dozens of civilian groups, or vigilantes, are posing as children online, arranging meetings with adults they suspect of seeking sex with minors and livestreaming the confrontations to thousands of viewers. The groups say they are helping protect children and bring suspected predators to justice. But some law enforcement officials and lega[...]
text:
Harford County, Md., Sheriff Jeff Gahler speaks with Chris Hansen, the host of “Takedown with Chris Hansen” on the TruBlu streaming network. The sheriff’s office conducted several operations featured on the show to highlight how local investigators identify and apprehend suspected child predators. (Photo courtesy of Harford County Sheriff’s Office)Across the country, dozens of civilian groups, or vigilantes, are posing as children online, arranging meetings with adults they suspect of seeking sex with minors and livestreaming the confrontations to thousands of viewers.
The groups say they are helping protect children and bring suspected predators to justice. But some law enforcement officials and legal experts warn that their tactics can jeopardize criminal investigations, complicate prosecutions and put public safety at risk. Public accusations can also have lasting consequences for people who are never charged with a crime, while some groups encourage their followers to pressure police to make arrests.
There is no definitive count of civilian predator-hunting groups, but dozens of groups operate across different parts of the country, including major cities. Stateline identified nearly 50 individuals or groups nationwide that have posted online content exposing suspected child predators.
When foster care kids are sex trafficked, some states fail to figure it out

For state lawmakers and law enforcement officials, the growing presence of these groups adds another layer of complexity to efforts to combat online child sexual exploitation while protecting children and preserving the integrity of criminal investigations.
“What is beyond dispute is we have a massive problem of child exploitation in this country that takes various forms,” said Mary Graw Leary, a law professor at the Catholic University of America whose work focuses on the exploitation of women and children. Graw Leary is a former state and federal prosecutor. “We cannot criminalize our way out of it only because there’s just too much of it.”
Catching and prosecuting people who sexually exploit children is important, experts say, but it addresses only part of the problem. Preventing abuse also requires teaching adults and children to recognize warning signs, creating environments where children feel safe speaking up and are heard, and holding institutions and online platforms accountable.
“The criminal justice response, I think, is appropriate, warranted, and important, but it’s not the only thing that we should be doing as a society or as communities,” said Stacy Vaughan, the vice president of growth and prevention at Childhelp, a nonprofit dedicated to preventing and responding to child abuse.
When a viral video isn’t enough
The scale of online child sexual exploitation is immense. 
The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children received 21.3 million reports through its CyberTipline in 2025, including about 1.4 million reports of online enticement of children for sexual acts — a 158% increase from 2024 –– and more than 19.5 million reports involving child sexual abuse material. 
Popularized by NBC’s Dateline series “To Catch a Predator,” which aired in the early 2000s, civilian predator-hunting groups use adult decoys posing as children or teenagers online to contact people they suspect of seeking sex with minors, then confront them on camera.
The accusations can make for compelling viral content. People accused of targeting children often have little public sympathy, and videos promising to expose and humiliate them can attract viewers with little interest in what happens after the camera shuts off.



Quotation







The best way for these groups to be helpful would be for them to involve law enforcement when they get the first nibble on their line.


– Matt Irvine, a retired detective who investigated sex crimes in California and Oregon


Some vigilante groups involve law enforcement only after a sting is complete, or if a confrontation turns violent. That can leave responding officers with an incomplete picture of what happened, how the encounter unfolded and whether the evidence supports criminal charges.
Digital evidence — the online conversations and promises — must be authenticated and preserved to establish its origin, integrity and handling. Recordings can also raise legal questions, experts say, including whether groups violated state wiretapping laws when capturing private conversations.
“The best way for these groups to be helpful would be for them to involve law enforcement when they get the first nibble on their line,” said Matt Irvine, a retired detective with 29 years of law enforcement experience who investigated sex crimes and cold-case sexual assaults in California and Oregon. 
When police are involved from the start, he said, detectives  can conduct a more thorough investigation, check a suspect’s criminal history and obtain search warrants.
The financial arrangements behind the videos can raise additional concerns if group members are called as witnesses in criminal cases. Some groups can earn advertising revenue from videos posted online, while others offer paid memberships through platforms such as YouTube, Rumble, Kick and Locals, where subscribers can get earlier or exclusive access than nonmembers to videos, updates, unedited footage and chat logs.
Those financial incentives could become relevant in court, particularly if prosecutors or defense attorneys question whether a witness had a financial interest in producing a confrontation or attracting viewers.
“If they are selling the confrontation videos and profiting from that, that would be an ethical issue in a criminal case,” said Kelly Callihan, the executive director of the Pennsylvania District Attorneys Association. “If we’re going to call them as a witness, that would have to be something that we would disclose to the defense.” 
Some predator-catching groups also criticize police or prosecutors when a person is not arrested or charged, encouraging viewers to contact and complain to officials about their decisions. 
“These predator groups now, I feel like, are escalating from shaming the alleged perpetrators of these acts to crossing a line where they’re shaming district attorneys who aren’t bringing these charges, even though they have valid reasons not to do so,” Callihan said.
Public confrontations
Videos of civilian predator-catching operations sometimes show violent confrontations. In one viral video from 2024, members of Dads Against Predators surround a man at an H-E-B grocery store in Austin, Texas, and strike him in the back of the head with a pumpkin.
The man, James Schellhase, filed a federal racketeering lawsuit against the Ohio-based group in September, alleging that its members assaulted him, tried to extort him and cost him his job as a chief executive. 
Schellhase had been communicating online with people who later claimed to be minors, according to the lawsuit. He said he believed the interaction was a prank or scam and wanted to confront them. The group accused him of trying to meet a child for sex.
Their childhoods are on display for millions. States want to protect them.

Schellhase alleges that Dads Against Predators demanded $400,000 to keep the confrontation video from being released and that the footage was sent to his employer, according to the lawsuit. He says the encounter damaged his career. One of the group’s co-founders, Joshua Alvin Mundy, has denied wrongdoing.
Dads Against Predators has been linked to multiple suicides involving people the group filmed. The group has also faced scrutiny from law enforcement in California, Florida, North Carolina and Texas, where members have been arrested or authorities have urged them to stop their activities. In 2020, the Sandusky County Sheriff’s Office in Ohio warned the group that it could face prosecution if it continued its “vigilante efforts.”
But the concerns extend beyond physical safety. Public accusations may also target people who have committed no crime and jeopardize investigations by alerting suspects before police can gather evidence, identify additional victims or pursue other leads. 
In April of this year, livestreamer Vitaly Zdorovetskiy and his crew falsely accused a 25-year-old man of trying to meet a 16-year-old girl for sex during a confrontation at a Southern California park, prompting online harassment of the man and his family. Police detained the man, but released him after questioning, and Zdorovetskiy later apologized for the mistaken accusation, but clips of the confrontation continued circulating online.
Public confrontations can also expose civilian predator hunters themselves to potential criminal charges, especially if encounters turn violent or involve threats.
For some groups, that tension has changed how they operate. 
Brian Knepp founded 814 Pred Hunters in Pennsylvania in 2022 after learning that a man he had considered a friend had raped a child. The group initially focused on publicly confronting suspected predators and exposing them online, but frustration over local prosecutors’ inability to bring charges prompted Knepp to change course and seek closer cooperation with police and prosecutors.
“We wanted these guys to be held accountable, and just us exposing them, in my mind, wasn’t acceptable anymore,” Knepp said in an interview.
More states are tracking rape kits. But key support for survivors may be slipping away.

Josh Moody, chief operating officer of Alabama-based Covenant Rescue Group, a nonprofit that trains police, said effective undercover operations require preparation and coordination. The group’s training covers evidence handling, communication, intelligence gathering and surveillance, as well as avoiding conduct that could undermine a prosecution, including actions that could support an entrapment defense. The group generally does not post any content online.
“If we come in and do a one-off operation and arrest a few guys on the operation –– that’s great, but really, we want (law enforcement) to be able to continue the work,” Moody said. 
Some law enforcement agencies have adopted a different approach to publicizing undercover operations, partnering with television programs while maintaining control over investigations and evidence.
Sheriffs Chris Swanson of Genesee County, Michigan, and Jeff Gahler of Harford County, Maryland, whose investigations have been featured on the TruBlu series “Takedown with Chris Hansen,” described how their agencies conduct these operations. 
Swanson said G.H.O.S.T., the office’s specialized sex crimes unit, conducts investigations that can span months, involving background checks, surveillance, recorded online conversations and interviews. Investigators do not pursue people who chat online but never show up at a planned meeting location.
Since 2018, which is when the unit was founded, more than 270 people have been prosecuted in connection with these investigations, Swanson said.
He said the Chris Hansen segments take place in a controlled environment, and footage is not used in investigations. His office provides exculpatory video to both prosecutors and defense attorneys. He sees media partnerships such as the Chris Hansen show as a way to raise awareness and encourage victims to seek help. By contrast, he warned that civilian groups seeking viral content without coordinating with law enforcement can jeopardize investigations.
“We’re going to keep doing it, and we’re going to do it the right way,” Swanson said.
Gahler said his office has arrested at least 21 people in three separate operations in partnership with the show, adding that the public attention they generate serves as a strong deterrent.
“That’s part of why we do this job — to deter crime and prevent crime,” Gahler  said. 
Beyond the confrontation
Others disagree. Former detective Matt Irvine said public exposure can work against another important goal of an investigation: getting suspects to talk. In his experience investigating sex crimes and cold-case sexual assaults, interviews are more effective when investigators build rapport in a calm, controlled setting. 
Public confrontations designed to humiliate suspects can undermine those efforts, he said, making it harder to learn what happened or whether others may have been harmed.
High-profile sex abuse case brings test for new Ohio anti-grooming law

“Blowing somebody up and blasting them across the internet is the exact opposite of the sort of psychological environment you need to create if you want to get this person to talk to you,” Irvine said.
Texas-based former prosecutor and criminal defense attorney Veronica Chittister echoed concerns about the consequences of confronting suspects and collecting evidence without law enforcement oversight. 
Online confrontations can also create the impression of guilt before someone has been charged with a crime or had an opportunity to defend themselves in court.
Some people targeted by civilian predator hunter groups have pursued defamation lawsuits over the accusations made against them, though some cases have been dismissed or settled out of court.
But publicly accusing someone of a crime does not automatically amount to defamation. Generally, a person bringing a defamation claim must establish that a false statement of fact was communicated to others and caused reputational harm. Truth is a defense, and accurately documenting someone’s online conversations or appearance at an arranged meeting with a decoy may help groups defend against such claims. 
Chittister said the consequences extend beyond individual cases, warning of “the erosion of the criminal justice system.”
“Even if you catch somebody in this way, you may not have the elements or the evidence necessary to secure a conviction in a courtroom,” she said. She also warned that intense public hostility can make it harder to seat an impartial jury.
Laws lag behind
States generally rely on existing criminal laws to address civilian predator-hunting groups, rather than statutes specifically governing their activities. 
Some states, including Illinois, Maryland, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Tennessee, have laws declaring that only law enforcement officers can pose as a minor.  An interaction with a civilian posing as a minor may not qualify as a prosecutable offense under those specific statutes.
“Our unlawful contact of a minor statute is very clear. That’s why a lot of DAs are having difficulty with charging here,” said Callihan of the Pennsylvania District Attorneys Association. Instead, local prosecutors might only be able to charge suspects with lesser offenses, or none at all. 
Other states, including Delaware, Florida, Kansas, Michigan and Texas, do not explicitly specify who can pose as a minor in online undercover operations, potentially making it easier for civilian groups to assist law enforcement and prosecutors in bringing charges.
In 2023, Pennsylvania lawmakers considered legislation that would have allowed anyone to pose as a minor online for the purpose of identifying suspected predators. The bill stalled in committee and never reached a vote in either legislative chamber. Since then, no other states appear to have considered similar legislation, according to Stateline research.
Meanwhile, state lawmakers still face the challenge of addressing online exploitation as technology and offenders’ tactics evolve. 
“It’s almost impossible to keep up,” said Graw Leary, the law professor at the Catholic University of America.
Stateline reporter Amanda Watford can be reached at awatford@stateline.org.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: New Greater Boston housing data show recent progress but troubling signs for the future
description: Statewide housing policy moves to juice new construction are colliding with “huge macroeconomic and federal policy headwinds pushing in the other direction,” said Luc Schuster, executive director of Boston Indicators, the research arm of the Boston Foundation. “It’s really hard to know where we’re headed in the next year.”
text:
AN ANNUAL REPORT on the state of housing in Massachusetts’s most populous region offers a grim assessment of the housing crisis, just days after voters narrowly shot down a ballot question seeking to make it easier to build single-family homes on smaller lots. 
Greater Boston’s infamously high rental prices and home prices are leveling off, according to the Greater Boston Housing Report Card from the Boston Foundation and the Joint Center for Housing Studies at Harvard. But permits for new units have hit their lowest level in a decade, population growth is slowing, and new units are down, setting the stage for a period of sluggish housing growth as the state struggles to get a handle on its cost-of-living crisis.  
“There’s a bigger question on what’s the health of the region’s economy in the next few years,” said Luc Schuster, executive director of Boston Indicators, the research arm of the Boston Foundation. “We could see a stagnation or recession,” he said, and while that may bring prices down, “that’s just not the way we want to address the housing cost problem.” 
The report found 32 Greater Boston municipalities had median single-family sale prices above $1 million in fall 2026. Cambridge, Wellesley, Weston, and Brookline all had median single-family prices above $2 million, and just six of the 147 municipalities in Greater Boston had median prices below $500,000. Despite the high costs, the speed of house and rent prices slowed over the year so far. 
A decade ago, 42 towns had median single-family sale prices below that amount, adjusted for inflation. 
To afford a home in one of the lower-priced towns today, a Greater Boston household would need to earn about $180,000. Almost half of renters in the region are cost-burdened, meaning they spend 30 percent of more of their income on housing. 
Chart from the Greater Boston Housing Report Card
Macroeconomic factors are also squeezing Massachusetts. Immigration restrictions are throttling the state’s growth and interest rates remain high. Having fewer immigrants and international students in Massachusetts may have reduced competition for some rental properties, researchers note, but it bodes poorly for the overall economic stability of the state. 
The state’s aging population, with over 1.8 millon residents aged 60 or older, is creating compounding housing problems. Older adults wield significant power over the housing market, as most of them own their homes, but the large and aging baby boomer population also means a rising number of households with fixed incomes and in need of more medical and social supports, according to the state. 
The report card lands after an unsuccessful swing at housing policy change via ballot. 
Question 7 on last Tuesday’s ballot would have taken aim at the state’s inconsistent lot size requirements by barring cities and towns from requiring more than 5,000 square feet of land to build a single-family house if the lot is served by public water and sewer systems.  
It drew significant support from cities in the Greater Boston region — though Boston itself would have been excluded from the new zoning rules — and opposition from many of the smaller towns that also would have been exempt because they lack sewer systems. 
The Massachusetts Municipal Association, which opposed the measure, disputed proponents’ contention that reducing the lot size for single-family homes would bring down prices.  
In a high-demand market, the group argued after the ballot question was defeated, reducing lot size “does not compel developers to build ‘starter’ homes, as evidenced by the abundance of homes on small lots selling for $1 million or more.” 
Supporters argued the ballot measure’s defeat by a mere 1.2 percentage points did not signal a rejection of more housing supply. 
Abundant Housing Massachusetts, the state’s main “Yes In My Back Yard” organization and one of the groups supporting Question 7, noted that “yes” narrowly prevailed in towns including Winthrop and Milton, which fiercely opposed the MBTA Communities multi-family housing law.  
“The close margins on Question 7 show that despite the crowded ballot and technical nature of the question, many Massachusetts voters want more homes in their communities,” said Jesse Kanson-Benanav, the group’s executive director, in a statement. 
Gov. Maura Healey and Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll — who served as the mayor of Salem — endorsed the ballot measure.  
Healey’s administration estimates that between 2025 and 2035, the state would need to build 222,000 units to address current housing needs and future population growth projections. The first year, her housing office touted, far exceeded the 22,000 units it would need to start the decade on target. 
Massachusetts in 2025 added 34,561 units, according to a state housing tracker released in March. State housing officials said this surge included a major backlog of units stuck in the pipeline during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic and do not expect such prolific future construction. 
“It’s clear that we need to build more homes to bring down costs,” Healey said in a statement. “This report recognizes the progress we’re making through new policies to accelerate housing production – from making [accessory dwelling units] available by right and reforming zoning to speeding up permitting and converting unused state land, office space and commercial buildings into housing. As a result, we already have 100,000 new homes in the pipeline.” 
The report card authors expect 2026’s unit production will be near the 22,000 mark. 
Chart from the Greater Boston Housing Report Card
“The challenge, though, is permits for future construction appear to be down,” Schuster said. “Everyone is kind of expecting 2027 and 2028 to not meet that pace.” 
Housing permits are an imperfect estimate of future contribution, but they often offer a best-case picture of new units. 
From 2015 through 2021, annual permits in the five counties that make up Greater Boston hovered between 12,000 and 15,000. In 2025, Greater Boston permitted just 7,746 units, according to the report. 
The Greater Boston metropolitan area is responsible for the bulk of housing construction in the state. The Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities, which has been tracking units produced in MBTA Communities districts and accessory dwelling units since 2024, counts about 10,000 units in the pipeline because of MBTA Communities and about 2,000 new ADUs. The vast majority of each housing type is located in Greater Boston. 
“While this apparent uptick in 2026 is good news, it’s far from certain that this rebound will hold,” the report’s authors wrote. “The lowest-hanging fruit in MBTA Communities districts and for ADU construction may already have been permitted.” 
Chart from the Greater Boston Housing Report Card
Question 7, if passed, had been projected to create around 780 units a year, based on an analysis from the Tufts Center for State Policy Analysis. The water and sewer restrictions would have effectively excluded 78 percent of Massachusetts’s land area, according to the Greater Boston Real Estate Board, the major real estate trade organization for the region, which said in a statement that it was “disappointed” by the defeat at the ballot box. 
Starter homes have become a particularly potent political quandary for the state, which for decades has seen early-career residents flee for cheaper pastures around New England. 
Two decades ago, the Housing Report Card recounted, Greater Boston’s expensive housing stock was already “a long-term problem that has caused middle class and young workers between the ages of 25 and 34 to leave the state in increasing numbers in recent years.” Housing, researchers wrote then, “continues to be the No. 1 economic development challenge for the Commonwealth.” 
The ballot question loss raises the stakes for the handful of housing reforms currently in limbo at the State House.  
No sequel has emerged to the nearly $5.1 billion housing bond bill — the Affordable Homes Act — passed in 2024. But the House and Senate are reconciling their versions of a sprawling economic development bill, which respectively include a move to incentivize multi-family housing on land owned by religious organizations and up-zone the state to allow duplexes anywhere a single-family home can currently be built. 
A final version could emerge at any time before the two-year legislative session ends in January. When it comes to Beacon Hill and the housing crisis, Schuster said, “how productive this session will end up being depends on how the economic development bill ends up being written.”

name: VTDigger
title: A different kind of return: Investing in Vermont’s future
description:
A new short film from the Vermont Community Foundation explores how mission investing is helping build housing, support local businesses, and create opportunities across Vermont. Through stories from around the state, the film shows how charitable dollars can be put to work locally while seeking financial returns that support future giving.
Read the story on[...]
text:
What if charitable dollars could go beyond grants to help build homes, grow businesses, and strengthen Vermont communities?
That’s the idea behind mission investing at the Vermont Community Foundation. By investing 5% of nearly every charitable fund it manages in Vermont businesses and community projects, the Foundation helps create local opportunities while seeking financial returns that support future charitable giving.
A new short film from the Vermont Community Foundation takes viewers across the state to see what happens when local ideas meet the resources to bring them to life.
From Glavel, a Burlington- and Essex-based company transforming recycled glass into innovative building materials, to Barre-based Up End This, which is finding new ways to build much-needed housing, the film shows how Vermont ingenuity and investment can help address some of the state’s most pressing challenges. In downtown St. Johnsbury, the Northern Forest Center is putting that same spirit to work, revitalizing historic buildings and creating new opportunities for the community.
The value of these investments can be seen across Vermont, in homes being built, businesses growing, jobs being created, and communities becoming stronger.
Watch the film and learn more about mission investing in Vermont.
This work is made possible by the generosity of our fundholders and the dedication of our nonprofit and community partners.
Special thanks to those who helped bring this film to life:

Rob Conboy, Glavel
Stacie Fagan, Vermont Community Foundation
Tabitha Howling, Northern Forest Center
Casey Johnson, Flexible Capital Fund
Lawrence Miller, Vermont Community Foundation
Heather Henyon, Mindshift Capital
Rob Riley, Northern Forest Center
Dan Smith, Vermont Community Foundation
Janice St. Onge, Flexible Capital Fund
Michael Zebrowski, Up End This

The Vermont Community Foundation invested in the Flexible Capital Fund, which backs growing Vermont companies. Glavel and Up End This are two businesses in its portfolio.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Republican takes aim at supposed foreign donors, plans to prosecute as secretary of state
description: TOPEKA — Republican Pat Proctor suggested without evidence that foreign donors contributed to the tens of millions of dollars in cash that helped Democrats win last week, and promised to embrace his power to prosecute if he becomes the state’s top elections official. Proctor is about 8,000 votes ahead of his opponent, Democrat Jennifer Day, […]
text:
Pat Proctor, shown here on the campaign trail speaking at a forum on Sept. 24, 2026, in Salina, told the radio program Woodward and Whit that he believes dark money contributed to the Democrat's win in the general election. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Republican Pat Proctor suggested without evidence that foreign donors contributed to the tens of millions of dollars in cash that helped Democrats win last week, and promised to embrace his power to prosecute if he becomes the state’s top elections official.
Proctor is about 8,000 votes ahead of his opponent, Democrat Jennifer Day, in the race for secretary of state. Under state law, the race requires an audit of 10% of precincts in every county, which means those ballots are being hand-counted by election workers and volunteers.
Democrat Adam Hamilton defeated Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, Democrat Chris Mann defeated Republican Attorney General Kris Kobach and Democrat Cindy Holscher leads Republican Ty Masterson by about 7,600 votes in the governor’s race. Republicans won other statewide races: Treasurer Steve Johnson cruised to reelection while Dan Hawkins won the insurance commissioner’s race by about 17,000 votes.
“My race, Dan Hawkins’ race should not even have been close,” Proctor said on the Woodward and Whit radio show on KNSS. “This governor’s race should not even have been close. But when you dump $100 million into a state of 3 million people, you know it’s going to have an impact.”
He said TV advertisements were “wall to wall ‘Roger Marshall was a bad man.’ ”
“It was all these dark money nonprofits, a lot of them foreign funded,” Proctor said. “After we had a foreign funding ban, they still figured out a way to launder the money and get it into this election. So we’ve got a real money problem here in the state of Kansas and in the nation.”
He didn’t provide examples of nonprofits receiving foreign funds and donating to a candidate.
Nonprofit money poured into both Hamilton and Marshall’s campaigns for the U.S. Senate. The Senate Leadership Fund spent at least $11 million for Marshall in Kansas. The Kansas-based super PAC People over Politics Action Fund spent about the same for Hamilton.
In all, outside spending against Marshall was about $46.4 million, while outside spending against Hamilton was about $32.7 million, according to Paid for Politics, which examines campaign finance reports.
Federal election law prohibits foreign nationals from donating to or interfering in elections and defines what actions aren’t allowed.
The Federal Election Commission defines a foreign national as an individual who isn’t a U.S. citizen and who isn’t lawfully admitted for permanent residence. Immigrants who hold a green card, though, can donate.
The FEC also stipulates that a foreign principal, which includes larger organizations such as foreign governments, corporations or “other combination of persons organized under the laws of a foreign country or whose principal place of business is in a foreign country,” can’t donate.
Proctor also told radio hosts Ted Woodward and John Whitmer that he plans to take back some of the authority that hasn’t been used recently in the Secretary of State’s Office, including the ability to investigate and prosecute election crimes. Kobach handled those duties as attorney general, but Proctor said he would “rebuild that capability” in his office.
Proctor also said he intends to “shift the burden” of the business owner being aware of regulations they have to follow, so that the government will share information and help the business owner comply.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri among 3 states declining hardship exceptions to Medicaid work requirements
description: After a Tyson Foods meatpacking plant closed in Nebraska in January, eliminating about 3,000 jobs, the state secured a temporary reprieve from new Medicaid work requirements for residents of the surrounding county. Nebraska began enforcing work requirements in May, requiring most adults ages 19 to 64 covered through Medicaid expansion to work, attend school [...]
text:
While the Missouri Department of Social Services initially signaled it would adopt optional hardship exceptions for hospitalizations, medical travel and residence in disaster areas, it indicated last month that it believes it can accommodate many people in those categories through other provisions in federal law (Thomas Barwick/Getty Images).After a Tyson Foods meatpacking plant closed in Nebraska in January, eliminating about 3,000 jobs, the state secured a temporary reprieve from new Medicaid work requirements for residents of the surrounding county.
Nebraska began enforcing work requirements in May, requiring most adults ages 19 to 64 covered through Medicaid expansion to work, attend school or volunteer 80 hours a month to get or maintain health coverage. A month later, the state sought federal approval to exempt residents of Dawson County, where unemployment had surged following the plant’s closure.
Missouri is one of just three states that have decided not to offer similar protections when the federal requirements take effect nationwide Jan. 1.
The Missouri Department of Social Services said last month that it will not adopt optional short-term hardship exceptions allowed in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act — including one that temporarily suspends work requirements in counties with unemployment rates at or above 8%, or 1.5 times the national average.
Six of the eight states bordering Missouri — Nebraska, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Tennessee, Kentucky and Illinois — plan to offer short-term hardship exceptions. 
Kansas is not subject to the new requirements because it has not expanded Medicaid or adopted comparable coverage through a federal waiver. 
Iowa and Indiana are the other two states declining all four exceptions.
In addition to areas with high unemployment, the short-term hardship exceptions cover extended travel for medical treatment for oneself or a dependent, areas with a federally declared emergency or disaster an inpatient or acute outpatient care in a hospital, nursing facility or intermediate care facility for people with intellectual disabilities.
States can adopt either all or none of the short-term exceptions, but the county-level exceptions for unemployment or disasters only go into effect after additional state action.
In an email to The Independent in October, Baylee Watts, media director for the department, said Missouri plans to accommodate “situations such as acute medical events and travel for specialized medical care” through mandatory exemptions for “medical frailty” and caregivers.
Federal law requires states to exempt people who are medically frail, including those who are blind or disabled, have substance use disorders, disabling mental disorders, serious or complex medical conditions, or physical, intellectual or developmental disabilities that significantly impair daily activities.
Missouri’s caregiver exemption will apply to parents or people caring for a child age 13 or younger and people who “regularly care for” someone with a disability and live with that person, are related to them or provide 80 hours of care in a month.
Watts said the department’s approach is intended to “limit the number of separate processes participants must navigate” and avoid “an additional, burdensome bureaucratic layer for participants.”
But national experts said that while the state can likely use the mandatory exemptions to accommodate medical travel and some people who experience medical crises, the medical frailty exemption may not cover everyone hospitalized for short-term conditions.
The mandatory exemptions also provide no comparable protection based solely on where someone lives, even when a natural disaster or major employer closure disrupts the local economy.
Watts reiterated to The Independent that “unemployment rates will not be a consideration for the requirement to participate in community engagement activities.” 
Watts said the department believes its plan to verify compliance with work requirements based on one month within each six-month eligibility period “appropriately addresses employment interruptions that are caused by a natural disaster.”
 Overlapping exemptions

Whether the mandatory exemptions in the federal law can be used to cover optional exceptions for hospitalization and medical travel is “definitely worth a conversation,” said Jennifer Wagner, director of Medicaid eligibility and enrollment at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities.
Wagner said many states have interpreted guidance released in June by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to mean an individual must be medically frail in order to be eligible for the medical travel exception because the rule cross-references the section of federal law on “serious or complex medical conditions” — one of the ways someone can qualify as medically frail.
Each exception requires changes to state computer systems and procedures for determining eligibility.
“So there are a number of states that are not investing heavily in (questions of), ‘How long do you have to travel?’” Wagner said. “‘By minutes? By hours? Staying overnight?’ Because it is largely overlapping with the medically frail and caregivers (exemptions).”
But that’s “not necessarily” the case with the temporary exception for people who have received inpatient treatment, Wagner said.
“You could imagine a very acute but short-term condition that would lead you to be hospitalized, but certainly would not leave you medically frail,” Wagner said, like a broken ankle or a serious bout of the flu.
Watts said that in 2027, when states can accept self-attestation of medical frailty, the department will allow people to check a box and provide details on the medical condition or travel that prevents them from meeting work requirements.
Jeremy Bowman, deputy director of the department’s Family Support Division, said during a public webinar Oct. 28 that the self-attestation period will give the department time to develop a list of diagnostic codes that will help automate medical frailty determinations starting in 2028, when states must verify people’s eligibility for the exemption.
Watts said the department plans to “analyze data from individuals self-attesting to medical frailty in 2027” to prepare to verify exemptions on an ex parte basis — without asking individuals for additional information — when possible.
While there’s no formal duration requirement for a condition to qualify someone as medically frail, Wagner said, the medical frailty exemption “is not built to capture a sprained ankle.”
“I have not heard of any state going in that direction to make their medical frailty that broad,” Wagner said. “And it would be simpler to just go with hospitalization because you wouldn’t need to know the condition.”
Bowman said the department’s definition of medical frailty is “a physical, mental or behavioral health condition that significantly impairs ability to comply with the community engagement requirement.”
Even for people who qualify, verifying their eligibility could present another obstacle.
States’ ability to verify exemptions without asking for additional documentation depends on their access to outside sources of information such as medical records and insurance claims.
Jennifer Tolbert, deputy director of KFF’s Program on Medicaid and the Uninsured, told The Independent that’s especially true for people applying for Medicaid for the first time.
While hospitalizations or care in a nursing or rehabilitation facility would show up in current enrollees’ claims data, Tolbert said, states wouldn’t necessarily have access to private insurance claims or hospital records if the person was uninsured.
“That claim will not be anywhere for the state to check unless the state is accessing a broader set of electronic medical records or a health information exchange,” Tolbert said.
Watts said the department “is actively working to obtain additional electronic sources of information to determine eligibility.”
 Disasters and unemployment

Unlike the exceptions for inpatient treatment and medical travel, which require individuals to submit a request, the county-based exceptions for disasters and high unemployment are automatically applied to eligible Medicaid applicants and enrollees once the necessary state and federal approvals are in place..
While states have to program these exceptions into their eligibility systems, Wagner said, “it’s not over the top compared to all the other very complicated provisions of this law.”
There have been three federally declared disasters in Missouri in 2026: severe storms, tornadoes and flooding in 10 counties in April; severe storms, straight-line winds, tornadoes and flooding in 34 counties in June; and severe storms, straight-line winds and flooding in 9 counties in July. 
No Missouri counties would qualify for the unemployment exemption based on their average unemployment rates over the past 12 months or the most recent rates reported by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Tolbert said.
But the Nebraska example illustrates how quickly that can change when a major employer closes.
While the department can decide to adopt short-term hardship exceptions in the future, that would require amending the state’s Medicaid plan through the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services — which Tolbert said could prevent the state from quickly responding to an emergency.
Wagner described the state’s rejection of the short-term exceptions as a missed opportunity.
“I’m curious what the pressure will be when there is a disaster, when there is a major plant closure in a rural area,” Wagner said, “where the state clearly had an opportunity to protect those individuals and chose not to.”

name: California
title: CA pension funds were hedging Nvidia even before the affair
description: Does the global economy hinge on one leather-clad CEO’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy? You might find it reassuring that your pension fund has been preparing for some kind of AI downturn, if not that specific scenario.  We have some breaking news today. California voters officially rejected Prop. 40, the measure that would have […]
text:
Dreamforce attendees at the conference in San Francisco on Sept. 15, 2026. Photo by Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters




Does the global economy hinge on one leather-clad CEO’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy? You might find it reassuring that your pension fund has been preparing for some kind of AI downturn, if not that specific scenario. 
We have some breaking news today. California voters officially rejected Prop. 40, the measure that would have levied a wealth tax on billionaires. 
In other news, the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals scaled back a California climate law and we have a new survey for you from our friends at Your Local Epidemiologist. 
California’s biggest public pension funds were already shaving their holdings in high-flying tech companies before news about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy sent the AI giant’s stock plunging.
After last week’s Democratic blue wave, stocks — particularly for artificial intelligence companies — tumbled largely due to investors’ fears over regulation. In a single day, the S&P 500 lost $2.8 trillion. 
But even in the months before Election Day, worries about an overheated market triggered selling: In the first half of 2026, the California Public Employees’ Retirement System sold off 26% of its holdings in the top-performing tech companies, known as the Magnificent 7, according to an analysis by the Financial Times.
CalPERS’ deputy chief investment officer, Anton Orlich, reportedly told the Times it was to diversify equity risk. That analysis followed a September meeting where CalPERS board members talked openly about the tradeoffs they saw in the fund’s AI investments.
Another behemoth fund — the California State Teachers’ Retirement System — has been eying the inflated stock market and trying to assess when to shift its holdings.
In September, CalSTRS heard from advisers who pointed out that seven public companies accounted for one-third of the total value of the U.S. markets. Only the 1999-2000 tech boom — which was followed by a bust — had a greater gap between companies’ earnings and their valuations.
CalSTRS Chief Investment Officer Scott Chan at that meeting warned against putting more money into that sector.

Chan: “I believe now in a bull market that it is even more important for us to diversify the portfolio rather than move more in a bull market that has been running for some time.” 

Stocks for the Magnificent 7 haven’t been doing too hot recently. While Apple, Microsoft and Amazon have risen between 2% to 4%, artificial intelligence chip-maker Nvidia dipped this month by 22% and continued to decline as Huang confirmed his affair. Tesla, Alphabet and Meta stock also slumped this month, with the latter two falling by double-digit percentages.
But the stock market is a major reason why CalPERS and CalSTRS have been beating their earning targets as of late. CalPERS portfolio is currently valued at more than $650 billion, and in July it announced it gained an investment return of 14.8% for the 2025-26 financial year, more than doubling its target of 6.8%. 
CalSTRS’ assets total more than $415 billion as of September, with a 13.9% investment return for the same period.

Other Stories You Should Know


Billionaire tax fails


Campaign signs in support of Proposition 40 and opposing Prop. 41 and 42 at a rally in Los Angeles on Oct. 5, 2026. Photo by Jae C. Hong, AP Photo




The latest election results show that Proposition 40, which would have levied a one-time wealth tax on the 200-or so wealthiest Californians, failed. 
It was the biggest fight on the ballot with billionaires spending hundreds of millions of dollars against it and Democratic groups splintering over its potential to drive away some of the highest-earning taxpayers. Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed it, as did Democratic mainstays the California Teachers Association and Planned Parenthood.

Evan Westrop, a No on Prop. 40 campaign strategist: “Proposition 40 was a reckless experiment conducted on our state’s economy with little regard for the harms it would cause.”

Read more.
We’re still waiting for final results in one of the five tax measures that went to voters on last week’s ballot. Prop. 42, which would prohibit new taxes on assets, is leading in returns so far. 
We know that one additional measure passed and will become law. That’s Prop.38, which would issue $8.4 billion in bonds to fund medical research.



Split ruling on new CA climate laws


An aerial view of the Marathon Petroleum refinery in Carson on April 1, 2026. Photo by Jae C. Hong, AP Photo




From CalMatters’ Molly Peterson: 
California can make large companies report the greenhouse gases they produce, a federal appeals court ruled Monday. But the state can’t force them to count emissions from their suppliers and customers or predict how climate change could hurt their business. 
The divided 9th Circuit Court of Appeals panel, ruling in a lawsuit brought by business groups led by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, said the state can require companies to share basic facts about their own pollution, but the other requirements likely violate their free-speech rights. The decision lets California enforce the nation’s first broad emissions-reporting mandate for about 2,000 large public and private companies.
A dissenting judge would have blocked both laws entirely, and either side could still ask the full 9th Circuit or the Supreme Court to step in. The decision centered on a pair of 2023 climate laws, which were known as Senate bills 253 and 261.

Online gambling apps displayed on a phone in San Francisco on Sept. 26, 2022. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo




Have an opinion on what health issues should be prioritized in California? CalMatters is partnering with Your Local Epidemiologist to make the real concerns and questions from Californians heard by public health officials and journalists.
Every week, we’ll ask about health topics affecting Californians, and it’ll only take two minutes to answer.
This week, we’re asking about the health impacts of rising online gambling trends and perimenopause. Take the survey.

For California Muslims, the diversity of elected candidates from the midterm elections does not mean Islamophobia or discrimination has disappeared — but it does signal that fear did not silence participation, writes Tahra Goraya, a member of the California Commission on Asian and Pacific Islander American Affairs.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Rep. Joe Wilson heads to recount against 25-year-old first-time candidate
description: COLUMBIA — South Carolina’s longest-serving Republican in Congress is heading to a recount against a Democrat barely old enough to run for the job. U.S. Rep. Joe Wilson leads challenger Zyon Khalifa by 0.99 percentage points, according to unofficial election results. That’s just within the 1-point margin that triggers an automatic recount under state law. […[...]
text:
Roxanne Wilson and U.S. Rep. Joe Wilson look on as their son, governor-elect Alan Wilson, addresses supporters at the GOP election night party Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — South Carolina’s longest-serving Republican in Congress is heading to a recount against a Democrat barely old enough to run for the job.
U.S. Rep. Joe Wilson leads challenger Zyon Khalifa by 0.99 percentage points, according to unofficial election results. That’s just within the 1-point margin that triggers an automatic recount under state law.

Democrat Zyon Khalifa debates U.S. Rep. Joe Wilson at River Bluff High School on Monday, October. 19, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)

State election officials are expected Tuesday to order a retallying. In an era of electronic vote-counting, the outcome is unlikely to change.
But it’s a photo finish no political prognosticator saw coming. South Carolina’s 2nd Congressional District wasn’t expected to be close, much less a possible flip.
Yet less than 2,950 votes separate Wilson from Khalifa out of almost 297,000 ballots cast. It’s not only South Carolina’s tightest contest of any statewide or federal race this election, but also the closest Wilson’s ever come to losing the seat he’s held since 2001 — against far better-funded challengers.
Wilson attributed this year’s slim margin to Democratic enthusiasm. It wasn’t that Republicans stayed home, he said, noting his vote tally was roughly the same as it’s been in the past.
“I have to give credit: The turnout by the Democratic Party was remarkable,” Wilson told the SC Daily Gazette on Monday. Democrats’ “voters were motivated for whatever reason. I can’t wait to find out why. But anyway, they came. I don’t begrudge it at all. But indeed, their vote turnout was very good.”
Wilson received about 148,000 votes, or about 100 votes more than four years ago, the last midterm, when he won re-election by more than 20 percentage points.
Wilson, 79, has represented the 2nd District almost as long as Khalifa has been alive. He was 7 months old when voters first sent Wilson to Congress from the state Senate in a December 2001 special election following the death of his mentor, U.S. Rep. Floyd Spence.
Who is Khalifa?
At 25, Khalifa is just old enough to meet the Constitution’s age requirement for a U.S. House member.
The Aiken County native said his youth helped him win over voters.
“We draw the greatest contrast in every way, shape, and form,” Khalifa said. “People see that contrast. They see the excitement, the energy, and the willingness to serve.”
Adding to his remarkable finish is that he didn’t live full-time in the state until May, when he graduated with a law degree from Southern University Law Center, a historically Black college in Baton Rouge, Louisiana.
He decided in February to seek the job representing his home district. Over the next few months, he flew home most weekends to campaign, he said.
No one recruited him, he said. The opposite happened, he said, with people discouraging him from running. He didn’t say who.
But he said he wanted to bring change. His campaign mantra was “why not us.”
Khalifa, who ran track while earning his bachelor’s degree at the University of South Carolina, said his campaign momentum came from grassroots campaigning: knocking on doors, walking in community festivals and even attending local GOP meetings.
His first hurdle was winning the Democratic nomination. After placing second in a four-way June primary, he defeated David Robinson II in the runoff with 54% of the vote, according to election results. (Robinson lost to Wilson two years ago by more than 19 percentage points.)
Khalifa came close to ousting Wilson with a fraction of the congressman’s campaign cash.
According to the latest campaign filings, Khalifa raised less than $30,000 total and spent about $18,000, as of Oct. 14.
That compares to about $845,000 spent by Wilson this campaign cycle, which included sending out color, two-sided mailers so big, they had to be folded in half to fit into mailboxes. Voters received his giant mailers ahead of both the primary, when he walloped two GOP challengers, and general election.
High schoolers host only debate for this SC congressional seat

With his limited cash, Khalifa put ads on digital billboards and Roku, a streaming service, in the campaign’s final weeks, he said.
Compare that to 2020, when Democrat Adair Ford Boroughs spent more than 15 months campaigning against Wilson and outraised him every quarter in a race that was considered the most serious challenge of his congressional career. Yet, he still won with 56% of the vote.
Khalifa insists he always knew the race would be tight, adding it was “aggravating” that pollsters and reporters ignored the 2nd District. After the results came in, he said, Democratic donors called him to apologize.
Wilson’s perspective
Wilson told the SC Daily Gazette he wasn’t shocked by the results.
However, he said, “I did not anticipate the voter turnout by the Democratic Party,” Wilson said.
“I had faith in the voters,” he said, noting he was in the state Senate for 17 years before Congress. “I’ve always had faith in the voters.”
Wilson’s tight race came in an election that saw Democrat Annie Andrews flip the U.S. Senate seat previously held by the late Lindsey Graham and, before him, Strom Thurmond.
Nancy Lacore flipped the coastal 1st District back to blue with a 1-percentage-point win — the seat’s third flip in eight years and the first since the post-2020-census redrawing of voting lines made the seat safer for a Republican. And in the state House, Democrats ousted 10 Republicans to erase the chamber’s GOP supermajority.
But Republicans won all other statewide races, including Gov.-elect Alan Wilson, the state’s four-term attorney general and the congressman’s son.
Joe Wilson called the nationwide blue tsunami “an aberration.” He predicted a Republican will flip the 1st District back again in two years.
“The Republican future in South Carolina, I believe, is going to be very bright,” Wilson said.
Debbie Epling, chair of the Aiken County Republican Party, said she believes the small margin was due to Democratic momentum nationwide, rather than any reflection on Wilson.
“I really think he did about as much as he could this campaign cycle,” Epling said, adding that Wilson has appeared at several events in Aiken County.
The main takeaway, Epling said, is for voters to know to not take their vote for granted.
This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Judge weighs dismissing charges against journalists in anti-ICE church protest
description: Attorneys for five journalists facing felony charges over an anti-ICE protest inside a St. Paul church urged a federal magistrate judge during a Monday court hearing to reject the “vindictive” prosecution of the press by the Trump administration and dismiss the charges. Former CNN anchor Don Lemon, Center for Broadcast Journalism founder Georgia Fort and […]
text:
Journalists Don Lemon and Georgia Fort (off camera) interview Cities Church Pastor Jonathan Parnell during the protest inside the church on Jan. 18, 2026 (Screenshot from The Don Lemon Show)Attorneys for five journalists facing felony charges over an anti-ICE protest inside a St. Paul church urged a federal magistrate judge during a Monday court hearing to reject the “vindictive” prosecution of the press by the Trump administration and dismiss the charges.
Former CNN anchor Don Lemon, Center for Broadcast Journalism founder Georgia Fort and three other journalists — Michael Beute, Jerome Richardson and Shane Bollman — were charged after covering a January protest disrupting a Sunday service at Cities Church, where a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement field director serves as a pastor.
Attorneys for Lemon, Fort and the other journalists accused the federal government of criminalizing journalism and said that even if every allegation in the indictment were true, their clients’ actions would not constitute a crime.
“This is what a vindictive prosecution looks like,” Isabella Salomão Nascimento, an attorney representing Fort, told the judge Monday. (Salomão Nascimento of the firm Ballard Spahr has represented the Reformer on unrelated matters.)
The court’s decision could have implications for press freedom across the country. Allowing the case to proceed may have a chilling effect by forcing journalists to weigh the risk of a costly trial before covering protests or other newsworthy events the federal government views unfavorably.
Federal prosecutors said the journalist label can’t be used as a shield for illegal conduct, alleging all 39 defendants carried out a coordinated “invasion” of the church aimed at disrupting religious worship.
“They were not singled out because they were journalists. They were not singled out at all,” federal prosecutor Neville Hedley said.
Attorneys argued over the motions to dismiss before U.S. Magistrate Judge Douglas Micko in a packed downtown St. Paul courtroom. Micko will issue a recommendation on the motions to U.S. District Judge Laura Provinzino.
The Jan. 18 protest came at the height of Operation Metro Surge, when President Trump sent about 3,000 federal agents to Minnesota in what the Department of Homeland Security called its largest operation ever. Demonstrators, led by civil rights attorney Nekima Levy Armstrong and St. Paul School Board Member Chauntyll Allen, interrupted the service with chants of “Justice for Renee Good,” who was shot and killed by an ICE agent earlier that month.
Demonstrators targeted the church because one of its pastors, David Easterwood, is also an ICE field director. Easterwood was not present, but protesters confronted Lead Pastor Jonathan Parnell.
Fort, who was in court Monday, and Lemon, who hosts a show on YouTube and was not present, livestreamed the protest and asked Parnell questions. Beute was Lemon’s photographer and Richardson his assistant.
According to federal prosecutors, some congregants feared the demonstration was the start of a mass shooting, and a child asked whether their parents were going to die. They also acknowledged not every parishioner felt intimidated or scared.
All 39 defendants face the same two charges: conspiracy against the right of religious freedom at a place of worship and injuring, intimidating and interfering with the exercise of the right of religious freedom at a place of worship.
The felony charges were aggressive even for an administration known to tangle with the media, including suing over disagreeable coverage, mocking journalists based on their appearances and barring reporters from the White House.
The charges drew swift condemnation from news organizations, including from the Minnesota Reformer, which joined a consortium of news organizations in filing a “friend-of-the-court” brief calling for dismissal based on First Amendment grounds.
Right to gather news
Attorneys for the journalists argued that the First Amendment protects their right to observe and document newsworthy events, even if illegal activity occurs.
Abbe Lowell, an attorney for Lemon, said charging journalists for doing so “would make virtually all important journalism a crime.”
Lowell listed the verbs prosecutors used to describe Lemon’s conduct in the indictment: He “livestreamed,” “observed,” and “asked.” None amounts to threatening or intimidating worshippers, Lowell said.
Among the worst that Fort, Lemon, Richardson and Beute are accused of in the indictment is “largely” surrounding the pastor as Lemon “peppered him with questions,” which prosecutors allege “obstructed his freedom of movement.” Prosecutors also allege Lemon stood at the main entrance and confronted congregants.
Attorneys argued that even if their clients engaged in everything the government alleges, no crime was committed.
“The government has pleaded themselves out of court,” Matthew Ebert, an attorney for Fort, told the judge.
Prosecutors repeatedly referred to the group as a “mob” and urged Micko to consider the journalists’ conduct as part of a coordinated effort rather than in isolation.
Rob Keenan, a federal prosecutor, cited a Russian general whose name he couldn’t remember saying something along the lines of “quantity has a quality all of its own.” He also compared journalists to the getaway driver of a bank heist, alleging they were in on the crime even if they didn’t personally demand the teller fill up a bag with cash.
“It was joint mob action,” Keenan said.
FACE Act challenge
Defense attorneys also asked the court to strike down the portion of the Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances Act — the FACE Act — that protects religious worship, arguing that Congress exceeded its constitutional authority under the Commerce Clause when it adopted the law in 1994.
The law, signed by President Bill Clinton, came in response to attacks on abortion providers and patients. A Republican added protections to places of worship as a poison pill to doom its passage, but Democrats didn’t object.
Charges have rarely been brought under the FACE Act’s religious worship provision, and the constitutionality of it has not been decided by the courts.
The journalists’ attorneys argued that religious services are not inherently economic activity that involve interstate commerce and therefore fall outside Congress’ authority.
Federal prosecutor Katie Neff pushed back, noting that Cities Church receives many out-of-state donations, and it sends a portion of its revenue to the Southern Baptist Convention in Tennessee.
Micko, the judge, said it would seem problematic to conflate commercial activity with religious activity.
“That fundamentally misunderstands religion in America today,” Neff said.
Micko could recommend dismissing the charges without deciding the constitutionality of the law.
He did not rule Monday. His recommendation will go to Provinzino, who will determine whether the case can proceed toward trial.
Vindictive prosecution
The journalists’ attorneys also alleged the Trump administration brought the case in retaliation for coverage that angered the president, noting his extensive record of criticizing Lemon.
“This is a vindictive prosecution brought against one of the president’s perceived enemies,” said Joe Thompson, an attorney for Lemon and a former federal prosecutor who resigned during Operation Metro Surge.
Federal prosecutors denied that the journalists were targeted, but defense attorneys pointed to public statements from Trump and top administration officials condemning Lemon before charges were filed.
The day after the protest, Harmeet Dhillon, then the Justice Department’s assistant attorney general for civil rights, warned Lemon on social media that he was “on notice” and claimed the First Amendment did not protect his “pseudo journalism.”
President Donald Trump called Lemon a “loser” and “lightweight,” while Attorney General Pam Bondi characterized him as an “online agitator” during a Fox News appearance.
“That’s clear proof of actual vindictiveness,” Salomão Nascimento said.

title: Blue wave boosts Democratic hold on Nevada Legislature but falls short of Senate supermajority
description: Nevada Democrats won big this Election Day, flipping several state legislative seats and unseating an incumbent Republican governor. That’s because the party did not secure a two-thirds supermajority in the Nevada State Senate. That mean[...]
text:
(Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)Nevada Democrats won big this Election Day, flipping several state legislative seats and unseating an incumbent Republican governor. But they don’t have carte blanche to do everything unilaterally next year when they meet for the 2027 Legislative Session.
That’s because the party did not secure a two-thirds supermajority in the Nevada State Senate. That means Democrats will need the support of at least one Senate Republican to pass any bill that raises state revenue. And that threshold doesn’t just apply to attempted tax increases, which Governor-elect Aaron Ford has suggested he isn’t open to anyway. If a bill sets a new $5 fee for applicants of a new type of occupational license, that requires two-thirds support. So too does 1 of the 5 biennial budget bills that must be passed each legislative session.
So why didn’t an unprecedented national blue wave make it down to the Nevada State Senate?
In Nevada, state senators serve staggered 4-year terms, so only half of the chamber is up each election cycle. This year, 11 of 21 seats were up, and only 4 of those 11 seats were held by Republicans. All four districts are considered solidly red, meaning there was little opportunity left for Democrats.
Republican state Sen. Ira Hansen ran uncontested in his District 14 while Senate Minority Leader Robin Titus, state Sen. Lisa Krasner, and Assemblymember Danielle Gallant easily dispatched Democrats in their races for Districts 17, 16, and 20, respectively.
That leaves the makeup of the Senate exactly where it was before —  13 of 21, one seat short of a supermajority.
The Nevada State Assembly, where all 42 seats are up every two years, provided much more opportunity for Democratic gains.
Going into this year’s Election Day, Democrats controlled 27 seats, one shy of a supermajority. Results as of Monday night show they will now control at least 31. That’s their largest caucus for at least three decades.
As of Monday night, one race remained too close for the Associated Press to call. Republican Assemblymember Melissa Hardy trailed Democrat Shenea Booth, a world champion athlete and circus artist, by less than one quarter of 1 percentage point, or 77 votes.
If those results hold, Hardy will be unseated and Democrats will hold 32 of the 42 Assembly seats.
Republican Assemblymember Rebecca Edgeworth was ousted by Democrat Joe Spica, a Culinary union member in District 35. It was an outcome not wholly unexpected because the district is competitive.
More surprising to observers was District 13 where Republican Assemblymember Brian Hibbetts was taken out by Democrat Daniel Andrews, a retired Clark County School District teacher.
The blue wave also brought to victory two progressive Democrats that Republicans in campaign ads had decried as “too extreme” for Nevada because of their association with the Las Vegas branch of the Democratic Socialists of America. Vinny Spotleson and Alex Pereszlenyi both acknowledged joining the organization, though both have characterized it as not being a central tenet of their campaigns and neither was endorsed by the organization.
Also among the Democratic newcomers are Kamilah Bywaters and Eileen Eady — former public school teachers who two years ago ran for Clark County School Board but lost to conservative Moms for Liberty candidates. This year, Bywaters flipped Assembly District 2, an open seat vacated by Assemblymember Heidi Kasama, who unsuccessfully ran for Clark County Commission. Eady unseated Republican incumbent Lisa Cole in Assembly District 4.
Also joining the state Assembly as Democrats are recovery advocate Ryan Hampton, SEIU Local 1107 steward Alexis Esparza, and urban planner Miguel Davila.
Across the aisle, the Republican Assembly Caucus will welcome two newcomers: Denise Daniels Fanning, a former television commercial producer, and Julie Butler, who spent three decades working for the state’s budget division. Both newcomers ran in open seats.
The newly shaped Nevada State Legislature may revisit some of the dozens of bills vetoed by Lombardo over the past four years. They may also grapple with the continued fallout from President Trump’s Big Beautiful Bill, data center regulations, education, and affordability at large.
Ford and the Legislature will soon know how much money they’ll have at their disposal over the next biennium. The Nevada Economic Forum is scheduled to meet Monday, Nov. 16 to approve the state’s official revenue forecast, which is used as the base for the state budget. 
The 2027 Legislative Session is set to begin on Feb. 1.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Commentary: You have the floor. Now do the work.
description: For Democrats taking on new responsibilities after this election, the message should be straightforward: You have the floor. Now it is up to you to act. Not every voter who supported you endorsed your entire platform. Some wanted a change in direction. Some wanted a check on power. Others simply wanted leaders to pay attention […]
text:
Michigan Democratic Party members and supporters watch election night returns on Nov. 3, 2026, at a watch party in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)For Democrats taking on new responsibilities after this election, the message should be straightforward: You have the floor. Now it is up to you to act.
Not every voter who supported you endorsed your entire platform. Some wanted a change in direction. Some wanted a check on power. Others simply wanted leaders to pay attention to the pressures shaping their daily lives.
The work ahead should center on priorities such as:

Making everyday life more affordable, from groceries and utilities to housing and transportation.
Improving access to affordable health care, including prescription drugs and mental health services.
Strengthening economic opportunity so that work offers a realistic path to stability.
Restoring trust in government through transparency, ethical conduct and meaningful accountability.
Protecting democratic institutions and respecting the limits of public power.
Addressing immigration with workable policies that take both public concerns and human dignity seriously.

These are not problems that disappear when the campaign signs come down. Nor can they be solved by reminding voters how objectionable the other party is.
Explain what you intend to do. Make the case for your proposals. Listen when people identify shortcomings. Work across party lines where progress is possible, and explain the disagreement honestly where it is not.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
No party can promise immediate solutions to every problem. But voters should be able to expect clear priorities, sustained effort and an honest accounting of what has and has not been accomplished.
Republicans have responsibilities here, too. Losing an election does not excuse obstruction for its own sake, just as winning one does not excuse overreach. Both parties remain responsible for the people they represent.
The lesson of all-or-nothing politics should not be that Democrats now get their turn to dismiss the opposition. It should be that the public deserves something better than another round of the same behavior.
Michigan does not need its leaders to agree on everything. It needs them to take shared problems seriously enough to work through their differences.
You asked for the opportunity to lead. Now give people something more valuable than another opponent to blame.

name: California
title: How we classified nearly $900 million in contributions from individuals, companies and PACs
description: CalMatters analysis of campaign finance contributors helped uncover some of the major influences behind the propositions on Californians’ ballots this year.
text:
In summary
CalMatters analysis of campaign finance contributors helped uncover some of the major influences behind the propositions on Californians’ ballots this year.


Millions of campaign finance contributions poured in over the 2025-2026 election cycle to fund California candidates, proposition committees that support or oppose ballot measures, political action committees (PACs) and other political committees. Due to the scale of contributions and the fact that a large sum of this money is wrapped up in ambiguously named PACs, the raw data alone offers limited insight into what types of people and institutions are funding political campaigns. 
In order to uncover patterns behind who is bankrolling the candidates and propositions on the ballot this year, CalMatters classified and published financial contributions to the gubernatorial, insurance commissioner and statewide proposition official campaign committees (for example, Proposition 39, which would have required identification for voting). We did this by determining the industry affiliations of the largest contributors to each of those campaigns during the 2025-2026 election cycle. All results are published on our Voter Guide. 
Our team classified nearly $900 million in contributions raised by these campaigns and proposition committees and processed tens of thousands of contribution records. We analyzed raw data on state-level campaign contributions maintained by the California Secretary of State, accessed by using its Power Search tool. 
Methodology
Contributor Selection
CalMatters focused on the largest contributors to the gubernatorial, insurance commissioner and statewide proposition official campaign committees. We assigned one of 20 classifications to contributors that gave at least $5,000 to each candidate or proposition across the 2025-2026 election cycle. Contributors who gave less than $5,000 in the same period were not categorized. (See: Entity resolution)
Industry Categories
CalMatters designed a custom schema of industry categories to better serve our readers. The categories largely align with the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) codes, which is the standard used by federal agencies. We consolidated NAICS codes where appropriate and based some of our categories on more granular NAICS subsectors. 
In several cases, we grouped certain contributors into a custom category based on shared interests not reflected well with NAICS:
Major Donor category
This category was a fallback for individuals who didn’t clearly provide an employer we could categorize. Individuals who listed their employer as retired, student, homemaker, unemployed, self employed, or some variation of none automatically fell into this category. When an individual listed employers from different industries across multiple contribution records, they were also placed in the “Major Donor” category if we could not determine that they were primarily aligned with a single industry. (See: Multiple possible classifications)
Technology category
Given reader interest with technology companies in the state, and that NAICS does not provide a distinct code, we created a custom category to represent the technology industry.
We classified entities whose business centered around apps or websites to facilitate business as “Technology,” even though those entities could be categorized differently. This includes companies such as Uber, AirBnB, Amazon, Netflix, Meta and Google, as well as companies engaged in artificial intelligence, cryptocurrency and software.
Additional custom categories
Other custom categories not reflected in NAICS include “Self-Funding,” “Candidates/Political Parties” and “Small Donors.”
See: Appendix: CalMatters campaign finance categories
Classification Overview
CalMatters assigned contributors to a category through a multi-step process. We tried to match contributors to NAICS codes or our unique categories, by using five different techniques.
In order, we attempted to match contributors by:

Comparing existing NAICS codes and similar categories from multiple external data sources
Comparing contributors’ names, employers or occupation to a custom list of keywords that highly correlated with specific industry categories  
Using a CalMatters machine learning classifier to assign codes using the semantic meaning of a contributor’s name or employer (company) and occupation
Using two large language models (LLMs) to assign a classification to each unique contributor
Manually reviewing the data

Throughout these steps, CalMatters code flagged for manual review any instance of doubt. For example, if classifiers disagreed on a contributor’s category or if a contributor was only able to be classified by an LLM, it was flagged for manual review. CalMatters also performed manual spot checks on contributors who had been successfully classified without manual review. 
When we could not reliably identify the industry of a contributor, that contributor was left uncategorized. 
We categorized organizations and businesses directly and we classified individuals by the employer listed in their contribution record with a few exceptions. For example, we grouped individuals who listed their employer or occupation as retired, student, homemaker, self employed or some variation of none into the “Major Donor” category. We also manually evaluated how to classify contributors that reported more than one employer across multiple contributions, or if they could be classified in multiple ways. (See: Major Donor category)
Campaign finance tends to be a web of interconnected political committees that contribute to one another before using that money for independent expenditures or landing in the coffers of an official campaign committee. To account for this, we categorized contributions from a political committee based on the classifications of all contributors that gave it $5,000 or more and, in certain cases, smaller contributions when we could reasonably determine it came from employees of a single company, a union or an association’s membership. (See: Political Committees)
Data Sources
H1B Employer Hub
CalMatters collected data from the H1B Employer Data Hub, which provides a list of employers that have submitted petitions to hire foreign workers and the NAICS code associated with the employer. If the name of a contributing organization or a contributor’s employer was identical after basic data normalization (e.g. stripping out extra whitespace, converting names from uppercase) to an employer listed in this database, that contributor was assigned the corresponding NAICS code. 
EDD
California’s Employment Development Department (EDD) also maintains a search tool to find California businesses and their associated NAICS codes. CalMatters developed a program to search each contributing entity’s name. If company names matched exactly after basic data normalization, the contributor was assigned the corresponding NAICS code. If we found a likely partial match, such as comparing “KAISER” to “KAISER PERMANENTE,” we assigned the company’s corresponding NAICS code.
