In cases where we found multiple partial matches, we matched with the company with the highest number of employees. 
Open Secrets
OpenSecrets is a nonprofit organization that collects and analyses data on money in politics, including classifying campaign finance contributors according to its custom industry coding system. CalMatters looked for contributors in our data that also appeared in classified data we received from OpenSecrets. When a match was found, we translated the OpenSecrets category to the CalMatters schema. 
To match individuals to the OpenSecrets data, we built a record linkage algorithm to determine when individuals were the same across datasets based on their name, employer, occupation, city, state and zip code. Organizations were linked across the contribution data and OpenSecrets data using two methods: a fuzzy matching algorithm and name variant matching. For example, we created processed versions of organization names by stripping text in parentheses and removing corporate suffixes. If the processed names were shared across both datasets (e.g. Google vs. Google, Inc. and Affiliated Entities), they would be linked. 
Matching Using Custom Keywords
CalMatters developed a custom list of keywords, each one exclusively associated with one of our custom categories. Categories were assigned based on keyword matches to the contributor’s name, employer or occupation (all of which are fields listed in the contribution record).
For example, “law office” and “cattle rancher” are keywords. If a keyword is frequently associated with the contributor being always categorized into a specific category, we use the keyword to indicate they are likely in that category. 
Matching Using a Custom Machine Learning Classifier
For remaining contributors that were not assigned a code using the methods above, CalMatters developed a machine learning classifier to assign a custom code using the semantic meaning of a contributor’s name or employer (company) and occupation. 
The classifier begins after encoding each existing entity (e.g., a contributor’s employer/occupation in the case of individuals, name in the case of organizations) into an embedding vector using Microsoft’s all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence transformer (chosen for its plain English corpus). A logistic regression was then trained on each entity’s embedding vector and its associated category code. 
This model is then applied on the sentence-transformer embeddings for remaining unmatched entities, to generate a code and associated confidence score for each embedding of unmatched entities. These classifications were all cross-referenced against other classification methods.
For the machine learning classifier, individuals’ occupations were used as an additional signal for the model, providing context for cases when an employer’s name may not include words that help infer industry. For example, if a contributor listed their employer as “Altais,” a word with no semantic meaning associated with the company’s industry, and their occupation was “physician,” the model could still infer the contributor is likely associated with healthcare. 
We also tried to guard against cases in which an entity may contain words with semantic meaning unrelated to its industry, like State Farm, or in which an entity’s name contains many words in common with an entity from a different industry (e.g. Credit Union of Southern California vs. American Civil Liberties Union of Southern California) through the keyword matching step, described in the section above. Common employers (e.g. State Farm, Airbnb, Google, Meta, Comcast, and many more) and entities with strong single-token signals that were already assigned categorizations through keyword matches, were not processed by the machine learning model. Common business endings that are unrelated to a company’s industry, like “and affiliated entities”, “corporation”, “and its subsidiaries” were also removed to minimize unmeaningful token overlap between entities. 
Matching Using Large Language Models
CalMatters used large language models — Claude and Gemini — to assign a classification to each unique contributor. Gemini performed Google searches on the name of each organization that contributed, as well as on the name and employer of each individual that contributed, and provided a summary of each contributor and the industry they were associated with. As a second step, Gemini used these industry summaries to classify the contributor according to our custom schema. 
Claude classified well-known entities, such as labor unions, automatically, and similarly performed web searches on all other contributors. The LLMs assigned confidence levels of low, medium and high to each industry summary and categorization. LLMs were never the sole source of a final classification; discrepancies between the LLM and other classification sources were flagged for manual human review as well as cases where the LLM was the only method that provided a high-confidence classification.  
Matching Using Human Review
Finally, a human manually reviewed the generated classifications and corrected any discrepancies or addressed any flags produced by the system.  
We flagged in any instance where we had reason to doubt. For example: 

All instances where the LLM classification disagreed with other methods of classification were directed to manual review. 
Not all contributors had a match in the reference data from H1B Employer Data Hub, California EDD and OpenSecrets or were able to be classified via keyword. So any contributor for which a LLM was the only classification source was reviewed manually. 
Contributors for which we could not reliably determine an industry were left uncategorized and reviewed manually. 
We developed a system to flag disagreement between classification methods depending on the accuracy of the method and its confidence in the classification. For example, if the machine learning classifier and the LLM agreed on a category, but both cited low confidence, that classification would be flagged for review. If the category assigned by an EDD or H1B match aligned with the category assigned by an OpenSecrets match (both high-confidence methods), but disagreed with a low-confidence machine learning prediction, it would not be flagged.  
Contributors suspected of being the same entity, but received different categorizations, were flagged for manual review.

The reviewer would address each contribution flagged for manual review, verify the accuracy of the categorization and edit the results when required. Verification involved researching the individual, company or organization using business identity lookups, such as Cortera, company websites, ProPublica’s awesome nonprofit explorer and news articles.
Contributions not flagged for review were also spot checked by the reviewer, and any categorizations that created uncertainty were verified using the process above. Because our manual review happened throughout our classification process, over time, the automated process became better at accurately classifying contributions. 
Looping classifications
CalMatters conducted several rounds of classifications as new data came in. A regularly updated database of verified and categorized contributors helped avoid duplicating categorization efforts. If a new contribution record came in that matched an already-classified contributor or employer, that existing classification was assigned to the new contribution record. 
Handling classification disagreements
When multiple sources provided an industry code for a contributor, these codes were compared for consistency. If high-confidence sources (e.g. H1B, EDD, OpenSecrets) agreed on a code for a contributor, that contributor was assigned that code. Cases where some, but not all sources agreed were treated on a case-by-case basis depending on the priority of the classification source. LLM and machine learning classifications were treated as the lowest priority, while classifications for an entity that had been manually reviewed previously overrode any contradicting classifications. 
Political Committees
Most of the campaigns and propositions we tracked received a large amount of funding from political committees, including political action committees, political parties, candidate and ballot measures committees, and other recipient committees.As many political committees do not fit neatly into a single category due to receiving contributions from a wide variety of sources, CalMatters computed an industry breakdown for each committee. For example, if a committee received half of its funding from tech-affiliated contributors and the other half from insurance-affiliated contributors, 50% of the contributions made by this committee would be categorized under “Technology”, while the other 50% would be categorized under “Finance/Insurance.”
Similarly to how we classified candidate races and propositions, CalMatters determined which contributors gave $5,000 or more in total to each recipient committee over the course of the 2025-2026 election cycle and categorized each of these contributors individually. 
Political committees that could not be entirely classified by their large donors were reviewed manually to determine whether or not they fit into a single industry. If the committee was closely aligned with a particular industry, think employee, union and association PACs, the proportion of funding the committee received from entities that contributed less than $5,000 was allocated to the manually assigned industry. If the reviewer determined the committee did not fit into a single industry category, the proportion that committee received in contributions less than $5,000 was marked as uncategorized. 
In campaign finance data, political committee giving forms a complex web as committees  often give to one another. To classify one committee, we also needed to classify all of the other committees that contributed to that original committee, which required processing the contributors to the second layer of committees  as well. For each political committee that gave directly to one of the races or propositions we were classifying, CalMatters built a network of connected committees up to five layers deep. All connected committees  were classified using the same method. 
A single committee may use multiple IDs depending on the type of campaign finance filing; the ID used for reporting received contributions may be different from the ID associated with the same committee when they are a contributor. CalMatters used data on filer information from the California Civic Data Coalition to map the IDs used by a committee so that when a committee showed up as a contributor, we could pull contributions received by this committee based on the mapped ID. Filer IDs that were not included in the reference data were mapped manually. 
CalMatters did not process the contributions received by federal committees since they are not typically tracked by the California Secretary of State. For this reason, federal committees were not given an industry breakdown. They were reviewed manually and assigned a single industry category in cases where that committee was associated with a particular industry. Those that did not clearly align with a single industry were left uncategorized.
Similarly, the entire amount given by a candidate committee was allocated to the “Candidates/Political Parties” category, since the candidate was responsible for how it was spent. 
CalMatters found that some committees received very little, or no funding in the 2025-2026 election cycle. If the total contributions received by a political committee over this election cycle was less than 75% of what the committee gave during this election cycle, the committee was reviewed manually, and when possible, assigned a single industry category. 
Power Search does not identify which contributors are federal committees. CalMatters identified committees as federal if the contributor’s name contained its federal ID (very common for federal PACs) or language that indicated it was a federal PAC (e.g. “FEC”, “fed pac” or “federal political action”). Committees were flagged for review as likely federal PACs if the committee appeared to be based out of Washington, DC according to its contributions or if the committee’s received contributions indicated some of the contribution records would be found in Federal Election Commission data. CalMatters flagged candidate committees if the name of the contributor followed the pattern typical for these committees by listing a name, office and year. These committees were manually reviewed for confirmation.
Entity resolution 
In order to determine which contributors met the $5,000 threshold for classification, CalMatters linked multiple contributions made by a contributor to calculate how much they gave in total. 
Within each contest, we aggregated contributors according to the name listed on the contribution record. However, contributors often use a different name across records. For example, “Google” and “Google, LLC and Affiliated Entities” are clearly the same organization, but would not be grouped together based on a name match. CalMatters developed a custom record linkage algorithm to identify when multiple names were likely all referring to the same company. Results were manually reviewed and mapped to a standardized name.
When individuals have the same name, but are two different people, their contributions should not be aggregated. Our record linkage algorithm for individual names scored how similar two contributors were according to their name, employer, occupation, city and zip code. Then, it flagged the contributors for review. 
During manual review, a CalMatters journalist ran the names through people directories to determine whether there were records of multiple people with the same name living in the city listed on the contribution record. The reviewer used name, city, zip code, employer, occupation and contribution amount to determine which contributions should be linked. If a single contributor used very different names or identifying information across contribution records, all of their records may not have been successfully linked.
This process allowed CalMatters to distinguish different people who share the same name and gave to the same committee. It also allowed us to standardize the donor’s name when multiple names referred to the same person.
Data processing
The Secretary of State assigns IDs to contributors that are a recipient committee (political committees that receive $2,000 or more contributions from others in a year) and to major donors that contribute $10,000 or more in a calendar year. However, some contributors in the data had missing or incorrect IDs. 
To ensure we could classify these political committees correctly, we looked for patterns in the committee’s  name – such as when the ID was included in the name itself or a name that contained terms like “PAC,” “political action fund,” etc. We also used data from the California Civic Data Coalition, which tracks contributors’ names and IDs, to identify names in our data that are known to be connected to a filer ID. We manually reviewed each contribution record to assign the correct ID to the contributor. 
To our knowledge, there is not comprehensive data available on all existing names used by a committee. Since committees often use different names across contributions and not all committees contain language that indicates it is a political committee, we may not have been able to identify all cases where a committee was missing an ID. 
Limitations
Individuals who contributed
This analysis concentrated on the largest contributors to each campaign and proposition. The industry breakdown of large contributors may not reflect the breakdown of smaller contributors. 
We decided that if a company employee gave $5,000 or more, they likely aligned with the industry they worked for or there may have been coordination at the employer level to solicit contributions, which is not uncommon. That said, it is not possible to know what motivated each contributor to give.
Spotchecking successful classifications
Although we created a thorough system to flag classifications when there was doubt about the best industry code to use, if the sources were consistent with one another, there is a chance CalMatters would not have caught a classification error. To mitigate this, a CalMatters journalist manually reviewed a random sample of classifications that were not flagged for review. Those reviews helped identify any cases the models got wrong so we could work to update the classifiers accordingly.  
Mapping issues
The NAICS and OpenSecrets categories did not always map cleanly to our custom schema, and in these cases the category code translation could have been unreliable. To mitigate this, we also used LLMs to categorize every contributor, and when there was a discrepancy, the match was flagged for review.
Multiple employers
In some cases, individuals listed multiple employers across contribution records. During manual review, we found that some individuals were indeed associated with multiple industries. 
We typically classified these individuals in the “Major Donor” category, particularly if one of the disclosures by the contributor identified themselves as retired, or not employed, unless we were able to establish reasoning to apply to a specific category.  
For example, Reed Hastings identified his employer three different ways — “Netflix,” “NA” and “Not Employed.” Since Hastings is the CEO of a major company whose business is related to technology, CalMatters categorized his contributions as “Technology” rather than “Major Donors.” (Why not “Entertainment”? See: Technology category)
Similarly, businesses and organizations may span multiple industries, but were assigned a single classification according to their primary function.
Political committee looping
A small subset of committees had cyclical dependencies where a political committee received contributions from a committee it had also donated to. Since committees are classified by the industry of their contributors, this causes the classification process to break. For these cases, we determined which committee received less money from the other and classified that committee  first, leaving the money received from the dependent committee unclassified. The industry distribution of the other committee was then calculated as usual.
Entity resolution scope
Due to the scale of the data, name variant resolution was not done on entities that did not have the potential to cross the $5,000 threshold. It is possible that some contributors may have contributed more than $100 in aggregate if they made contributions under different spellings of their name, but it is unlikely that they would aggregate to more than $5,000. Similarly, small contributors to a committee who shared the same name were treated as the same person.
While we built several safeguards to resolve similar entities, there may have been misaggregation that meant some donors were not included in our analysis.
Federal committees
While we made great effort to identify federal committees  and identify committees with missing IDs, we may have missed some if they did not have language in their name that would identify them as a political committee or if the committee used a name variant not tracked in the California Civic Data Coalition ID maps.  
Conclusion
In total, our team categorized nearly 60,000 contribution records from individuals and organizations and processed close to 1,000 political committees, amounting to nearly $900 million in campaign finance contributions raised by gubernatorial, insurance commissioner and statewide proposition official campaign committees and over $1 billion in contributions received by committees that were indirectly linked to those candidate and proposition committees. 
Through our extensive manual review process, the CalMatters team reviewed more than 2,500 unique categorizations, more than 1,000 recipient committees and suspected PACs, and reviewed nearly 4,000 contributor names to determine how to link entities.
CalMatters analysis of campaign finance contributors helped uncover some of the major influences behind the propositions on Californians’ ballots this year. For example, the Building a Better California PAC spent nearly $400 million this cycle. More than $200 million of this went toward supporting Proposition 41 and 42, which would make it harder to pass new special taxes and ban new taxes on personal property. These propositions received virtually all of their funding from Building a Better California; in total, other sources contributed just over $200K to these two proposition committees. CalMatters classifications exposed that the Building a Better California PAC was principally funded by finance and tech donors, helping voters who use our Voter Guide understand what types of organizations and people may benefit if these props were to pass. 
The industry classifications also aided CalMatters journalists in reporting on Big Tech spending this election cycle. Reporters found that tech money substantially or in part funded half of the top 10 spenders among PACs that sought to influence  state legislative races. 
Acknowledgements
Thank you to Foaad Khosmood, a computer science professor at California Polytechnic State University and co-founder of Digital Democracy, for reviewing an earlier draft of this methodology.
We would also like to thank Jeremia Kimelman, CalMatters data reporter, and Thomas Gerrity, engineering manager for Digital Democracy, for sharing their expertise in campaign finance data and for helping develop the methodology.
Appendix: CalMatters campaign finance categories
You can download all the classifications we made and review the campaign finance categories we used on our public Github repo.

name: California
title: Race for LA’s new county executive post officially begins. It could be a historic battle
description: Los Angeles County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath announced Monday she will run for county executive in 2028. A large field of ambitious candidates will quickly emerge.
text:
It will be at least four years, and perhaps eight, until California voters elect another governor.
However, in just two years they will fill a brand new office that will rival the governorship in political importance. And it already has its first candidate.
Los Angeles County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath announced Monday she will run for county executive in 2028, and most likely will be one in a large field of candidates. Every ambitious politician in the county will at least consider running, including dozens of state legislators, members of Congress and L.A. City Council members.
The reason is simple: Whoever fills the office will not only be the top official in a county of 10 million residents — essentially its mayor — but automatically she or he will be the leading potential candidate for governor or U.S. senator.
Horvath, whose 3rd supervisorial district includes the county’s wealthiest neighborhoods, such as Santa Monica, Malibu and Beverly Hills, voted with three other supervisors to create the executive office and expand the Board of Supervisors from five members to nine.
County voters in 2024 endorsed the restructuring, the most far-reaching change in California’s local governments since the 19th century. It’s long overdue for a county that is more populous than many states, infinitely culturally and economically diverse and boasting a $54 billion budget.
Governance by a five-member board and an appointed executive often has been a recipe for confusion and sometimes gridlock. When problems arise, voters don’t know who should be held accountable. The system works well enough in smaller and less diverse counties but not so well in larger, more diverse counties.
That said, the only county that has something like the new Los Angeles structure, the city and county of San Francisco, has not been a paragon of effective governance. Its elected mayor and 11-member Board of Supervisors often spar over issues, and dozens of semi-autonomous commissions make matters more difficult than they should be.
However, San Francisco’s first-term mayor, Daniel Lurie, has assembled a working majority on the Board of Supervisors and has been chipping away at the confusing array of commissions. He won some city charter reforms in last week’s elections.
While the Los Angeles county executive will be elected in 2028, seats on the revamped Board of Supervisors will not be filled until 2032, when data from the 2030 census will be used to draw the nine districts.
“Los Angeles has never been a place that dreams small,” Horvath said in a statement. “But for too long, our county government has moved too slowly, failed to meet the moment, and allowed bureaucracy to stand in the way of progress. I fight every day to reform our government because I believe the people of Los Angeles deserve better — a  government that works for them, delivers real results, and is accountable to the people it serves. “
Ever since voters approved the reconfiguration of county government, there have been under-the-radar maneuvers over who might take a stab at the executive position. It’s not surprising that Horvath is running. Now that she’s broken the ice, we can expect others to quickly emerge, because in politics two years is just a moment in time.
And given what happened in the mayoral contest for the City of Los Angeles last week — Mayor Karen Bass’ defeat by Nithya Raman, a democratic socialist city council member — the 2028 election of county executive could be an historic ideological battle. The winner would be positioned for a top state office and for national prominence.

name: California
title: California Muslims gained a moment of hope and belonging after midterm election
description: For Muslims in California, the results of the midterms represent an opportunity to reclaim hope and reaffirm their place in the American story.
text:
Guest Commentary written by

Tahra Goraya
Tahra Goraya is the founder of Goraya Consulting and a member of the California Commission on Asian and Pacific Islander American Affairs. She is former president and CEO of the Monterey Bay Economic Partnership.


Some moments in our nation’s history make an election mean far more than who wins or loses. The 2026 midterm elections are one of them. 
For Muslims in California, this moment represents an opportunity to reclaim hope, reaffirm our place in the American story and recognize that fear, division and hatred do not have to define our country’s future.
For too long, Muslim Americans have lived in an environment in which our faith, patriotism and belonging have been questioned. We have watched our identity used as a political talking point and experienced the consequences of prejudice and bigotry. 
Yet we have continued to show up as neighbors, educators, entrepreneurs, public servants, parents and engaged citizens.
American Muslims are also essential contributors to our nation’s economic strength. We own and operate businesses, create jobs, invest in communities, serve in high-demand professions and contribute to industries ranging from healthcare and technology to education, manufacturing and hospitality. 
We are workers, innovators, consumers and employers. Our contributions help build local economies, strengthen neighborhoods and expand opportunity. 
Our belonging should never be measured by our economic contributions alone, but those contributions make clear what should already be understood: American Muslims are part of the fabric of this country, in every sense.
This election reminds us that democracy is strongest when people participate and when  representation reflects the nation’s diversity. 
Voters made clear that the issues shaping everyday life — including affordability, housing, healthcare, education and the economy — matter. Manufactured fear and attacks on entire communities are no substitute for leadership that addresses people’s real concerns.
The historic victories matter, too. Abdul El-Sayed’s election in Michigan makes him the first Muslim American elected to the United States Senate. Xavier Becerra’s election as California’s next governor adds another chapter to our state’s diverse political history.
These milestones matter not because elected officials should represent only one community, but because our institutions are stronger when people from every background have a seat at the table.
For Muslim children, representation is about belonging and possibility. As a mother of two preteen daughters, I want them to see that they can be unapologetically Muslim and proudly American. They can lead, serve, shape policy, build businesses and help define this country’s future. They do not have to wait for permission to belong. They belong right now.
Hate has not prevailed. 
That does not mean Islamophobia or discrimination has disappeared, or that the work of protecting civil rights is finished. It means that fear did not silence participation, community or hope. We must keep holding leaders accountable, defend religious freedom, challenge discrimination and build relationships across faiths and cultures.
I am excited about what this moment represents, not only for Muslims in California, but for America. I am hopeful about a generation willing to participate, lead and demand better. 
American Muslims are not standing outside the American story waiting to be included. We are helping build its economy, strengthen its communities and write its future. That is something worth celebrating.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: By undercutting gas pipeline expansion, Massachusetts risks making an energy affordability problem worse
description: Natural gas is not an obstacle to a clean energy future; it is the proven, affordable, lower-emission backbone that supports renewables with flexible, around-the-clock power.
text:
FOR MANY MASSACHUSETTS families, their energy bill is not an abstract policy issue. When energy costs rise, households may have to make painful tradeoffs between keeping the heat on, buying groceries, filling a prescription, or paying rent. As the leader of a trade association representing the natural gas industry, I am watching with growing concern as Massachusetts policymakers promise a clean, affordable energy future, while proposing policies that make both goals unattainable.  
Leaders in Boston say they share their constituents’ affordability concerns – yet the state Senate’s energy legislation, S. 3143, undermines the infrastructure investments needed to provide safe, reliable, and affordable energy at lower cost.  
Natural gas powers more than half of the electricity generation in New England. It is also the primary way Massachusetts residents choose to heat their homes. It is the reliable, dispatchable fuel that balances intermittent solar and wind, especially on the coldest days when renewables underdeliver and demand peaks.  
Yet for years, the Commonwealth has blocked or delayed critical pipeline expansions. These constraints have real consequences: diminished reliability for power plants, moratoria on new gas hookups in parts of the state, and higher energy prices. In fact, Massachusetts has some of the highest electricity prices in the country; our residential rates are approximately 56 percent higher than the national average.  Yet despite our region’s high energy prices, natural gas remains the most affordable option for home heating. 
Instead of addressing these constraints, pending Senate legislation doubles down on costly energy policies and seeks to phase out the Gas System Enhancement Program (GSEP), a crucial program enacted to address Massachusetts’ aging leak-prone natural gas infrastructure, which is among the oldest in the nation.   
The legislation frames such investments as “unnecessary and expensive,” but the need to replace aging infrastructure does not disappear because policymakers want to accelerate the energy transition. Pipes continue to age, safety obligations remain, and customers still depend on the system every day. Indeed, new research from the Blacksmith Group shows investments in pipeline infrastructure through programs like GSEP have been effective in ensuring the gas system operates safely.  Instead of investing in the existing, dependable, and affordable natural gas system, the legislation would hasten the transition away from Massachusetts’ most affordable fuel. 
Why This Matters for Massachusetts Consumers 
Massachusetts has invested heavily in wind, solar, transmission upgrades, and storage to meet its decarbonization goals.  Yet in 2025, renewable energy made up less than one-fifth of New England’s electric grid. Further, several major renewable projects have been delayed or cancelled. These developments underscore the need for a balanced approach to meeting future energy demand. 
The Senate’s proposal claims over $14 billion in savings by avoiding gas infrastructure investments. Yet analyses of similar policies project far higher overall costs for families and businesses. This isn’t an affordable, smooth transition away from fossil fuels. Rather, these policies will drive up energy bills, manufacturers will lose competitiveness, small businesses will suffer, and housing costs will rise. 
Past decisions to block natural gas infrastructure have left Massachusetts vulnerable to the price spikes experienced last winter, a reminder of what happens when energy demand outpaces infrastructure investments. The Senate’s proposal doubles down on this strategy, and risks repeating the same mistakes that got us here. 
A Better Approach for Massachusetts 
While the Senate claims savings primarily by phasing out natural gas infrastructure investments, the House’s energy legislation (H.5175) offers a more balanced approach. Rather than dismantling our reliable gas system, the House bill finds savings by trimming overhead and expanding energy procurement. Gov. Healey also supports an all-of-the-above approach to meet the state’s growing energy demand.  
This pragmatic path prioritizes affordability and reliability over rapid gas phase-outs. As policymakers consider the path forward, they should favor reforms that align with the real-world need for affordable, reliable energy. 
Natural gas is not an obstacle to a clean energy future; it is the proven, affordable, lower-emission backbone that supports renewables with flexible, around-the-clock power. Massachusetts should pursue a genuine all-of-the-above energy strategy: preserve safe, reliable natural gas infrastructure while advancing clean technologies where they make sense.  
By prioritizing affordability, reliability, and emissions reductions together, the Commonwealth can build an energy system that works for today’s families and tomorrow’s goals. Affordable energy, reliable energy, and lower emissions should advance together. Massachusetts needs policies that recognize the value of an all-of-the-above energy strategy and deliver all three. 
That’s the balanced approach that Massachusetts families, businesses, and communities deserve. 
José Costa is president and CEO of the Northeast Gas Association.

name: Nevada Current
title: A rare Nevada fish is on the rebound
description: The population of the endangered Devils Hole pupfish, one of the world’s rarest fish, more than doubled over the past year. Wildlife biologists counted 137 Devils Hole pupfish during a National Park Service survey on Oct. 10— nearly twice the 77 fish recorded during the spring 2026 survey and more than double the 69 observed […]
text:
Captive-raised Devils Hole pupfish at the Ash Meadows Fish Conservation Facility. Devils Hole pupfish are less than one-inch long and are the smallest of the desert pupfish species. (USFWS photo)
The population of the endangered Devils Hole pupfish, one of the world’s rarest fish, more than doubled over the past year.
Wildlife biologists counted 137 Devils Hole pupfish during a National Park Service survey on Oct. 10— nearly twice the 77 fish recorded during the spring 2026 survey and more than double the 69 observed in fall 2025.
The tiny blue fish, whose entire wild population lives on a shallow limestone shelf in a sinkhole within Nevada’s Ash Meadows National Wildlife Refuge, has struggled to keep its population over 100.
About a year ago, the population in Devils Hole abruptly plummeted to just 20 fish following two earthquakes – one in December 2024 and the other in February 2025 – that triggered waves in Devils Hole’s normally still waters and dislodged algae and fish eggs from the shallow limestone shelf.
“It’s exciting to see Devils Hole pupfish numbers increase so significantly over the past year,” said Death Valley National Park Superintendent Mike Reynolds in a statement. 
Wildlife biologists decided to release 72 captive-raised pupfish into Devils Hole to help rebuild numbers between March 2025 and February 2026, while providing supplemental feeding until the algae recovered.
It was the first time wildlife managers released captive-raised pupfish into Devils Hole from their backup population at Ash Meadows Fish Conservation Facility. The facility also helped biologists understand how to supplement the fish’s diet by studying their captive counterparts. 
The tiny fish live in fairly inhospitable conditions, where water temperatures reach between 90 and 93 degrees and oxygen and nutrients levels are low. 
Wildlife biologists believe most of the fish counted during the fall survey hatched and grew in Devils Hole, given that the average lifespan of the fish is just 10 to 14 months.
“These results reflect the dedication of our scientists and conservation partners working to protect this extraordinary species. While challenges remain, we’re encouraged by this progress and committed to its long-term survival,”  Reynolds in a statement. 
The Devils Hole pupfish was listed as endangered in 1967 under the Endangered Species Preservation Act, the predecessor to the current Endangered Species Act, which was enacted in 1973. Though iIts population began to decline in the 1990s, following growing groundwater pumping.
Biologists have been counting Devils Hole pupfish – which measure just 0.9 inches long on average — nearly every spring and fall since 1972.
During the spring surveys, over 200 fish were counted up until the mid 1990s. In the early 2000s, an average of 90 fish were counted each spring. The number suddenly declined to 35 fish in 2013.   
Population numbers climbed in recent years and reached a 25-year-high during the spring of 2024.  
Devils Hole pupfish populations naturally fluctuate, but biologists say the latest count is encouraging. They emphasized that “monitoring, research and habitat management remain essential to the species’ long-term survival.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Almost 20% of rape kits in Louisiana aren’t tested, audit finds
description: Nearly one in five rape kits collected over an 18 month period from 2024-25  in Louisiana was never submitted to a crime lab for testing, according to a report from the Louisiana Legislative Auditor.
text:
Photo by Chinnapong/iStock Getty Images)Nearly one in five rape kits collected over an 18 month period from 2024-25 in Louisiana was never submitted to a crime lab for testing, according to a report from the Louisiana Legislative Auditor.
The audit found 337 kits of the 1,879 collected  statewide, or 18%, from July 2024 through December 2025 had not been sent to a crime lab as of February. Law enforcement staff also aren’t testing all of the kits that end up at the lab, in part because no state law requires them to do so, according to the report.
“[O]ne crime lab stated that it tests all kits submitted by law enforcement, while the other five crime labs stated that they will not test a kit if law enforcement or the district attorney informs them that the case will not be pursued,” the report stated.
Several crime labs told auditors they use their own judgment to determine which kits to test based on “circumstantial or administrative factors,” according to the report.
The nearly 1,900 kits in question are “reported” kits, meaning a victim agreed to undergo a special medical exam in the hope that police would investigate their alleged sexual assault. Kits collected from victims who don’t want to work with law enforcement are referred to as “unreported” and aren’t supposed to be tested, according to the auditor.
In both cases, evidence is collected from victims during the exam, including DNA swabs. Even if police decline to pursue a case, advocates advise that all kits be tested, so DNA from an assault can be included in a database that might link the perpetrator to other crimes, according to the report.
In addition to concerns about testing, auditor found gaps in the online information available to the sexual assault victims about the location or status of their individual kits. In more than 25% of the cases surveyed, police failed to pick up the kit from the care provider who performed the exam or didn’t deliver it to a crime lab by the legally required deadlines, according to the report.
The state might struggle to force police agencies, care providers and crime labs to comply with deadlines and because Louisiana law includes no penalties for failing to obey them, the report concluded.
Legislative Auditor Michael Waguespack suggested that publicizing which agencies are not following the rules in an annual report on rape kits could help with compliance.
The Louisiana State Police Crime Lab, which oversees the rape kit tracking system, should also make some updates to its online database to make sure rape kit information can be used to its fullest potential to solve crimes, according to the report.
The Louisiana Legislature has passed a flurry of legislation dealing with the tracking and testing of rape kits since 2023. The changes have led to a surge in requests for rape kit testing. The number of kits submitted to crime labs went from 643 in fiscal year 2024 to 1,011 in 2025, according to the audit.
Crime lab staff told the auditor they haven’t been given enough resources to keep up with the demand.
“Several labs stated that testing kits involves greater complexity and resources than most other types of DNA testing, and that testing more kits limits how much DNA testing they can perform for other types of crimes, such as homicides,” the report stated.
The Louisiana State Police and other crime labs should also come up with a standardized way to report potential DNA matches in their system. There are currently gaps in communication between the crime labs and law enforcement agencies about these “hits” that could mean those potential leads aren’t being tracked down, according to the report.
State Police Superintendent Col. Frank Besson, who oversees the crime lab that performs about half the rape kit testing in the state, agreed to adopt the suggestions the auditor made to improve rape kit testing accountability.
“In support of that commitment, [State Police] has already initiated corrective actions and process improvements designed to strengthen oversight, enhance operational effectiveness and address the areas identified within the report,” Besson wrote in a letter to Waguespack.
The auditor said some fixes, such as clarification on whether all reported kits need to be tested, would require legislative action.
Morgan Lamandre, CEO of Sexual Trauma Awareness & Response, which provides assistance sexual assault survivors in several parts of the state, said “more digging needs to be done” to figure out what are the roadblocks to accountability.
In some communities, it might be a lack of staff and funding to properly process the kits. In other places, it could be complacency, she said.
In the 2027 legislative session, Lamandre said her priority will be a law change that requires hospitals and other medical providers to call in advocates, such as those from her organization, as soon as possible after a sexual assault victim arrives at a medical facility for treatment.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Is the honeymoon over for data centers in Washington?
description: Data center regulations are the event horizon that communities across the nation, including in Washington state, are calling on their elected officials to achieve.  The blue wave that flooded the nation after Tuesday’s election also made its landing in the Washington state House of Representatives, where, for the first time since 1929, Democrats hold a […]
text:
A data center along the Columbia River Gorge. (Photo by Jordan Gale/Oregon Capital Chronicle)Data center regulations are the event horizon that communities across the nation, including in Washington state, are calling on their elected officials to achieve. 
The blue wave that flooded the nation after Tuesday’s election also made its landing in the Washington state House of Representatives, where, for the first time since 1929, Democrats hold a supermajority. 
With an even stronger presence in the state Legislature, will Washington Democrats hone in on the issue next year?
Last week during a press conference, Gov. Bob Ferguson said he’s “confident” that the Legislature will pass “something” on data centers during the 2027 session. 
“There is … a political will to get to a resolution,” Ferguson said. “I do think it will lead to an outcome. I don’t think it’s going to leave some political stalemate.” 
Across the state, communities are demanding a moratorium on data centers. Their concerns are widespread: water consumption, noise pollution, location near communities, power consumption on a strained grid, groundwater contamination and a lack of transparency from elected officials. 
“I’m asking very simple questions and I can’t get a basic, simple number answer like, how much water are they going to use? How much electric are they going to use?” said Brittany Anderson, a Spokane-based activist who’s investigated hyperscale data centers in Eastern Washington. “This is unprecedented for our county. We do not have this particular type of development.”
Washington ranks 10th in the nation for the number of data centers in operation, though the number of facilities is disputed. More than 100 data centers are estimated to be operating in the state, according to Front and Centered, a coalition of more than 50 Washington community-based organizations. 
Some communities have taken action. Data center moratoria exist in Seattle, Spokane, Pasco, Federal Way, Burien and in the counties of Spokane, Snohomish, Pierce, Skagit, Skamania and Yakima. In October, communities across Washington protested in sync, demanding a statewide moratorium. Front and Centered has also called on the state to act. 
“Allowing the rapid build-out of hyperscale data centers without having more clarity about how existing facilities are harming Washingtonians sends a clear message that our decision-makers value profit over our own people,” reads a Front and Centered 76-page report released in July. 
The group describes a statewide moratorium “as a way to build upon Washington’s existing commitments to environmental justice and protecting overburdened communities.”
So far, lawmakers haven’t pursued that route. 
A moratorium is “a short-term solution,” said Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, who sponsored a sweeping data center regulation bill during the last session. “I’m far more interested in putting in place guardrails.”
What did pass this year was a bill that eliminated tax breaks for replacing or refurbishing older server equipment. A separate tax break is still in place for new facilities that purchase the equipment for the first time. The state also offers a tax break on labor to install that equipment.
Doglio’s bill fell short in the eleventh hour. She blames big tech.
“There was considerable pressure from the data center industry to kill the bill,” said Doglio, who chairs the House Environment and Energy Committee. “There are particular issues that continue to be challenging, and that includes curtailment.”
What is curtailment? During a major climate event, for example, when the grid is at peak capacity, Doglio wants data centers to temporarily shut off operations and rely on backup generators. This would ease grid pressure and could save folks from a power outage. 
“Just like any other large load that utilities serve, they should have some responsibility for curtailing their use in the very rare instances,” Doglio said. 
She’s bringing the bill back next year with a new provision: transparency. That includes banning non-disclosure agreements, she said.
Earlier this year, Walla Walla Port Commissioners announced that Amazon Web Services was behind the purchase of some 500 acres in a nearby industrial park. For three years, the commissioners kept the corporation’s name under wraps as part of a non-disclosure agreement signed in 2023, Patrick Reay, executive director, previously told the Standard. 
Doglio has also been working with the state’s Utilities and  Transportation Commission on another idea. In theory, utilities would charge data centers additional fees if they use a certain amount of energy. She wants to avoid passing massive power costs onto ratepayers. A similar provision was included in last session’s bill. 
Anderson, the Spokane-based activist says she’s “strongly dissatisfied” with Washington’s lack of regulations. She ran as a write-in candidate for Washington’s 5th Congressional District with a campaign focused on data center regulation.
“They’re not putting the people first,” she said.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Democrats hit a new milestone: 100 women in the House
description: This story was originally reported by The 19th.  Democrats are projected to win back the U.S. House — and hit a major milestone. For the first time ever, at least 100 Democratic women are expected to serve in the chamber simultaneously. “Women made history because we showed up to vote, and then voted in more […]
text:
WASHINGTON, DC - U.S. Rep. Betty McCollum (D-MN) will begin her 14th term next year, one of at least 100 Democratic women in the U.S. House, hitting the milestone for the first time ever. (Photo by Sarah Silbiger/Getty Images)
This story was originally reported by The 19th. 
Democrats are projected to win back the U.S. House — and hit a major milestone. For the first time ever, at least 100 Democratic women are expected to serve in the chamber simultaneously.
“Women made history because we showed up to vote, and then voted in more than 100 Democratic women to serve in the House,” Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez of New Mexico, the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, said in a Wednesday statement.
She added: “Women have borne the brunt of the Trump administration’s recklessness and Republicans’ extremist agenda, and on Tuesday they made it clear they have had enough.”
Elect Democratic Women (EDW), the campaign arm of the House Democratic Women’s Caucus, has had its sights set on achieving that goal since the beginning of the cycle, several House Democratic women told The 19th last year. 
“We think 100 is a great number. It’s sort of a showcase number,” Rep. Lois Frankel of Florida, a founding member of EDW, said in 2025. “Of course, we would want more, but I think there’s something about hitting 100, right?”
The milestone is the culmination of decades’ worth of work recruiting and fundraising for Democratic women by groups like EDW and EMILY’S List, founded in the 1980s.
“This is a powerful testament to what happens when we bet on women and help them build winning campaigns,” EMILY’s List president Jessica Mackler said in a statement.
“Time and again, women have proven to be Democrats’ strongest path to building power in Congress,” she added.
In 2026, the House battleground was at gender parity: of the 40 House seats Decision Desk HQ projected Democrats would flip as of noon  on Wednesday, 18 of those districts were flipped by women candidates.
“When you get women candidates, they just tend to be really high-quality candidates who are highly motivated, highly educated, in it for the right reasons and have a drive to support their communities, and I think that that affects the qualities of races that they run,” Rep. Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico said last year.
They won in a variety of races, picking up seats in districts across the country in contests fueled by voter anger over rising prices and perceptions of corruption.
In some races, women candidates challenged Democratic incumbents. Rep.-elect Jasmine Clark of Georgia launched a campaign against the late Rep. David Scott before he died in April at 80. Reps.-elect Melat Kiros of Colorado and Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, both democratic socialists, unseated sitting House Democrats in their safe-blue districts.
Clark will be the first Black woman Ph.D. scientist in Congress, Kiros will be the first Black woman to represent Colorado and the first Gen Z woman in Congress.
Jeannette Rankin became the first woman to serve in Congress in 1917, three years before the 19th Amendment granted women the right to vote — a right that was still restricted for many women of color. Women are half of the U.S. population, but hold just 28 percent of the seats in Congress. Just 445 women have served in Congress, making up only 3.5 percent of all those who have served in either the House or Senate.
The House had segregated gyms until 1985, when then-Rep. Barbara Boxer led a successful effort to integrate the far-superior men’s gym. There wasn’t a women’s restroom off the Senate floor until 1993, and it took another 18 years for House women to get a designated restroom off of the House floor, in 2011. A bipartisan but ultimately unsuccessful effort last year to allow new mothers in the House to vote by proxy showed how the Capitol is, in many ways, still not caught up to the realities of mothers in the workforce. 
Vice President Kamala Harris’ defeat in 2024 dashed, for the second time, the hopes of many to see the United States’ first woman in the Oval Office. But Stansbury believed 2026 would lay the groundwork to break that ultimate glass ceiling.
“I think this era that we’re living through, when we elect our first woman president, we’ll see that the work that we’re doing now is what made it possible for that to happen,” she said.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Josh Hawley blames GOP losses on abandoning working people, calls for fasting and prayer
description: U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley on Monday blamed Republican election losses on his party abandoning working Americans, criticizing cuts to Medicaid that he voted to approve last year. The Missouri Republican also called for what he described as a “historic response” to last week’s election: a one-hour gathering for fasting and prayer at the U.S. Capitol […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley speaks to reporters at the governor's ham breakfast at the Missouri State Fair in Sedalia on Aug. 15 , 2024 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley on Monday blamed Republican election losses on his party abandoning working Americans, criticizing cuts to Medicaid that he voted to approve last year.
The Missouri Republican also called for what he described as a “historic response” to last week’s election: a one-hour gathering for fasting and prayer at the U.S. Capitol next month.
Hawley’s comments came as Democrats prepared to take control of both chambers of Congress and Senate Republicans confronted growing pressure to reconsider their leadership and legislative priorities.
“When you abandon pro-lifers, when you abandon the needy, when you abandon the poor, when you abandon working people, the American people might have something to say about that,” Hawley told reporters at the Capitol, according to CNN.
Hawley pointed to a Congress that he said had neglected working families while pursuing other priorities.
“When you cut Medicaid but you fund data centers, when you cut rural hospital funding, then you fund Planned Parenthood, when you let the cost of healthcare for working people go through the roof but you can’t do anything for them on other issues of affordability from fertilizer to gas and everything else — yeah, you know what? The American public doesn’t like that very much,” he told reporters, according to Punchbowl News.
But Hawley was among the Republicans who voted in July 2025 for President Donald Trump’s sweeping tax and spending law, which the Congressional Budget Office estimated would reduce federal Medicaid spending by nearly $1 trillion over a decade.
GOP senators warn mega-bill’s new Medicaid cuts will hurt rural hospitals

The legislation passed the Senate on a 50-50 tie broken by Vice President JD Vance, with Hawley voting in favor.
Before the vote, Hawley had been one of the most vocal Republican critics of the proposed Medicaid reductions. In a May 2025 New York Times opinion column, he called cutting health coverage for working people “morally wrong and politically suicidal” and warned of the consequences for Missouri families and rural hospitals.
He ultimately supported the legislation after negotiators included a $50 billion rural health fund and delayed certain reductions in Medicaid funding mechanisms. Hawley argued those changes would help protect Missouri hospitals and pledged to fight the remaining cuts before they took effect.
Two weeks after his vote, Hawley introduced legislation to reverse some of the Medicaid reductions and expand the rural health fund to $100 billion. The measure was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has remained without further action.
The election results have renewed debate among Republicans about the party’s direction following a year in which they controlled the White House and both chambers of Congress.
Democrats captured the U.S. House and Senate in last Tuesday’s election. In Missouri, Democrats gained 16 seats in the state House and two in the Senate, ending Republican supermajorities in both chambers.
Democrat Fred Wellman also defeated Republican U.S. Rep. Ann Wagner in the 2nd Congressional District, while Missouri voters rejected a congressional redistricting plan championed by Trump. And Missouri voters rejected a proposed constitutional amendment reinstating a ban on abortion that voters repealed in 2024.
Roughly 55% of Missourians rejected the proposed ban last week, preserving abortion rights while also approving a separate constitutional amendment sharply limiting lawmakers’ ability to overturn voter-approved measures.
Hawley’s assessment of the election came amid a growing dispute over Senate Republican leadership elections scheduled for Tuesday.
Several senators, including Wisconsin’s Ron Johnson and Pennsylvania’s Dave McCormick, have called for postponing the vote to allow Republicans more time to examine the reasons behind their losses.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota has indicated that the election should proceed, although Republicans are expected to discuss the results before voting. No challenger to Thune has publicly emerged.
Asked Monday whether Republicans needed a change in leadership, Hawley declined to endorse the current leadership team.
“I’m not going to pledge my vote to leadership,” he told reporters. “I’ll tell you that.”
Hawley offered another response to the election Monday evening, announcing plans to bring Christians together at the Capitol on Dec. 15.
“What happened last Tuesday was shocking and historic,” he wrote on X. “It calls for a historic response. Christians need to gather and seek the Lord.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Commentary: Now the real work begins. Casting our votes was the easy part.
description: Voters sent resounding messages to elected officials about what they do not want to see continued in state legislatures across the country and in the halls of Congress. Accountability must become the driving force of the electorate moving forward. Did elected officials really hear us? Some messages became abundantly clear. Voters are not willing to: […]
text:
(iQoncept/iStock Images)Voters sent resounding messages to elected officials about what they do not want to see continued in state legislatures across the country and in the halls of Congress.
Accountability must become the driving force of the electorate moving forward.
Did elected officials really hear us?
Some messages became abundantly clear.
Voters are not willing to:
1) tolerate higher costs for families and industries caused by unpredictable tariffs and support entering into a questionable war with no end in sight;
2) be continually subjected to an atmosphere of toxicity and hopelessness fueled by brazen acts of disrespect for laws, traditions and institutions that have long defined America;
3) continue to support elected officials who fail to fulfill their duties by not addressing the conditions we face; and
4) be denied the very foundation of participatory democracy — the right to cast their votes.
There are other takeaways that can be gleaned from the midterm results.
Voters clearly conveyed, whether voting for state or congressional lawmakers, that they have had enough.
The real question is: Did all elected officials really hear voters and understand the significance of the turnout?
In particular, did many of the returning elected officials, and those not on the ballot, clearly understand what they need to do — and what they need to change — moving forward?
More importantly, are they willing to do it?
Though this was a historic rebuke of what is going on in our government on multiple levels, it is not the first time.
What is different about this time that will cause office holders to act in a different way, or will they simply resort to doing business as usual?
Missouri election results sent strong messages to lawmakers. Voters clearly sent the message that amendments and propositions passed by a majority of voters should stand and be implemented. Legislators are not to ignore, change or totally undo them as they have repeatedly done.
In recent years, Missouri lawmakers have gone to extreme measures to undo the will of voters when it comes to access to abortion and reproductive care, worker’s minimum wage and family leave, gerrymandering Congressional districts, and keeping and respecting the citizen petition initiative process.
Missouri voters also changed the make-up of the legislative chambers. There is no longer a Republican supermajority in either after decades of that being the case.
Will returning lawmakers believe what voters are telling them, or will they choose to believe that their actions and agenda are not the problem?
Worst of all, will they continue to pursue a personal agenda or one of their funders or special interests groups?
When the Missouri legislature convenes in January, a change in behavior remains to be seen.
Will newly-elected lawmakers be able to propose, negotiate, compromise and work with veteran lawmakers to achieve the policy changes that voters sent them to do?
How can we, as voting citizens, work to bring about the changes we voted for?
The overriding need now is accountability.
We must remain engaged and hold the people we voted for accountable to carry out the responsibilities of their offices and keep the promises they have made.
How can we do that?
First, we can pay close attention to what lawmakers in Jefferson City and Washington are saying and doing. We must be ever vigilant and ask are their words and actions consistent with the policy priorities, needs of their constituents, and the promises they made that earned your vote.
If not, make your voices and concerns heard and known before some undesirable legislation begins to move through the approval process and becomes law.
In Missouri there are many channels available to us to track proposed bills and pending legislation before and after the legislature convenes in January.
We can follow actions taking place in Congress as well. There are multiple sources available.
We can also stay in contact with our representatives in Washington online and through their local offices.
If city and county issues are most important to you, there are multiple convenient ways to convey your concerns to your elected representatives.
When the excitement or disappointment of the sea change — or tsunami as many have labeled it — subsides, the responsibility for realizing the needed changes will only intensify.
Making sure that those changes that are needed to fix our government will actually occur will be left up to us.
Leaving it to the elected officials alone is not a good option.
We must be ever watchful and hold them accountable.
If the past is prologue, and it often is, we can afford nothing less.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: ‘Somebody stepped in and helped’: Advocates press to keep Oklahoma’s mental healthcare ‘safety net’
description: Editor’s note: This story discusses suicide and mental health crises. If you or someone you know needs help, call or text 988, the U.S. suicide and crisis lifeline, or access online chat at 988lifeline.org.  MUSKOGEE, Okla. — Christopher Dean feels he has debt to repay by reducing the stigma surrounding mental health treatment. The Muskogee […]
text:
Christopher Dean, captain of the night shift for the Muskogee Police, is pictured July 23, 2026 at Green Country after speaking about his time receiving mental health-related services at the clinic. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)Editor’s note: This story discusses suicide and mental health crises. If you or someone you know needs help, call or text 988, the U.S. suicide and crisis lifeline, or access online chat at 988lifeline.org. 
MUSKOGEE, Okla. — Christopher Dean feels he has debt to repay by reducing the stigma surrounding mental health treatment.
The Muskogee Police night shift captain spent a week at a local inpatient facility being treated for suicidal thoughts about four years ago.
Then for a year and a half, he received therapy from Green Country Behavioral Health Services, a certified community behavioral health clinic, and one of its subsidiaries. At first, the services were just “checking a box,” but Dean said working on his mental health gave him a desire to figure out where the “wrong turn” happened in his life. 

This is the first of a three part series on Oklahoma’s certified community behavioral health clinics. 

“I survived something that many times people don’t survive due to those that were willing to reach out and provide that help,” Dean said. “Whether it be, you know, a mental health facility or an individual or a really good boss, somebody stepped in and helped.” 
For nearly a decade, certified community behavioral health clinics like Green Country have served as a lifeline for hundreds of thousands of Oklahomans who need access to mental health or substance use treatment, regardless of their ability to pay or insurance status. But now, the cash-strapped state Legislature and the clinics have both found themselves burdened with soaring costs, creating uncertainty over the long-term survival of these clinics. 
What is a certified community behavioral health clinic?
Since launching about 10 years ago, certified community behavioral health clinics have become an integral part of the Oklahoma mental health continuum. 
Initially approved by Congress in 2014, supporters hoped the Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic Medicaid Demonstration Program would help address unmet mental and behavioral health needs, and that in turn would lead to reductions in incarceration rates, hospitalizations and emergency room visits while improving school attendance and employment rates.
The federally designed model, which operates in 46 states, focuses on tailoring care to the specific needs of a community and the individual. All clinics are required to provide nine core services: crisis intervention, assessment and diagnosis, physical health screenings and monitoring, comprehensive care planning, mental health and substance use outpatient services, case management, psychiatric rehabilitation, peer support and veterans services.
Oklahoma was among the first eight states selected to pilot the program in 2017, with the federal government offering to pay about 90% of costs. The initial pilot was supposed to last two years, but was extended repeatedly by Congress. 
Over the years, Oklahoma’s participation grew to nine private providers serving various parts of the state.
A map of the certified community behavioral health clinics serving Oklahoma. This includes private providers who are set to take over service areas previously run by the state, though the transition is not yet complete. (Provided by the Oklahoma Department of Mental Health and Substance Abuse Services)
Supporters said the model seemed like an ideal fit for a state that has long struggled with high rates of mental illness, substance misuse and suicide, a shortage of providers, and high Medicaid enrollment and poverty rates.
“We’re the safety net for people who cannot go other places and get services,” said Joy Sloan, chief executive officer of Green Country in Muskogee and head of the Alliance of Mental Health Providers of Oklahoma, a group advocating for several certified community behavioral health clinics. 
Estimates provided by the group show that six of its providers reported serving about 150,000 Oklahomans combined across the state in each of the last two fiscal years. More than 96,000 Medicaid participants were served between July 2025 and June, according to the Oklahoma Health Care Authority. 
Despite Congress warning the state’s pilot period would not be extended again and the federal match would drop to about 67%, it’s not clear if Oklahoma lawmakers were prepared for the coming financial cliff, which would increase the state’s share by tens of millions of dollars each budget year. 
Amid a budget shortfall at the mental health department in 2025, lawmakers held a series of fiery budget hearings that ultimately culminated with them firing the state’s mental health director, who had struggled to explain the agency’s funding issues.
In the 2025 budget year, Oklahoma received more than $164 million in reimbursements from the federal government, leaving the state responsible to pay over $41 million, according to data provided by the Oklahoma Health Care Authority upon request by Oklahoma Voice.
Though the number does not yet reflect the full change in costs, the state saw a decrease of more than $74 million in federal funding.
An uncertain future
Despite the loss of some federal funding, the state Mental Health Department closed the funding gap with dollars appropriated by the Oklahoma Legislature in this year’s session outside of its annual budget, an agency spokesperson said. 
The agency received $98 million in supplemental funds from the Legislature to cover Medicaid costs for the past two budget years. Despite repeated requests made over months, an agency spokesperson could not detail how much of that was directed toward the certified community behavioral health clinics.
The agency also did not answer questions about how it planned to pay for the behavioral health clinic model in future budget years. Earlier this year, the agency announced it would no longer run its state clinics, and instead contracted with existing private providers to operate them. 
The Mental Health Department decided to privatize those operations as part of an ongoing focus on strengthening its financial position and aligning its budget with actual expenditures to establish a more accurate picture of agency spending, said Maria Chaverri, an agency spokesperson, in a statement. 
The cost and use of services from these community clinics will help inform the agency’s future funding decisions, she said. 
Sloan, who heads the Oklahoma group that advocates for community behavioral health providers, said the Mental Health Department has been behind on some payments or not provided some reimbursements that were historically made. 
“We do everything that we can, and we’re doing it in the hole,” she said. “It doesn’t take a CPA or an actuary or anyone — that is simple math.” 
A graph from a fact sheet created in 2025 by an Oklahoma behavioral health provider shows changes over time in reimbursements from the Oklahoma Department of Mental Health and Substance Abuse Services for uncompensated care provided by eight certified community behavioral health centers operated by members of the Alliance of Mental Health Providers of Oklahoma. (Provided and created by Family & Children’s Services)
Certified community behavioral health clinics are paid using a prospective payment system that estimates a monthly average, fixed and per-patient cost to provide services. The rate is unique to each provider based on its submitted cost reports. Other quarterly, supplemental payments are also provided based on a provider’s outcomes. 
Because these clinics are required to provide care regardless of a patient’s ability to pay, they rack up high bills for uncompensated care, which are services delivered but not paid for through Medicaid, private insurance or other payment methods. 
While these Oklahoma providers have never been reimbursed for 100% of this care and don’t expect to be, they were historically reimbursed for part of it, Sloan said. In recent years, the reimbursements for uncompensated care stopped without warning, she said, yet many providers’ funding models depend on these payments are made. 
“It’s not sustainable,” Sloan said.
Joy Sloan, the CEO of Green Country, is pictured Jan. 30, 2026, in Muskogee. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
In budget year 2025, for instance, certified community behavioral health clinics provided $87.6 million in uncompensated care yet, for the first time, received no reimbursement for it from the Legislature, providers in Sloan’s group, the Alliance, said.
House budget chair Rep. Trey Caldwell, R-Faxon, said he wasn’t sure if the end of the enhanced federal support contributed to the increased lack of payments for uncompensated care or the Mental Health Department’s budget problems. 
He said he doesn’t remember the agency’s leadership discussing the end of the health clinic’s pilot period during their budget requests, but said lawmakers were more concerned that budget requests at the time were “falsified” and inaccurate. 
“We needed a real number, and that was one of the biggest issues that we had over there where the Department of Mental Health was essentially trying to pay last year’s bills on next year’s money, and that caused all kinds of issues,” Caldwell said. 
Caldwell said it’s his understanding that the Mental Health Department believes it will be able to internalize the cost of losing enhanced federal funding through projected cost savings from privatizing the four state-run service areas. 
“If you look at the quality of care that they’re providing versus what the last four traditional state ones were doing, it’s night and day on the quality of care and how many more people they’re helping,” he said. 
Lawmakers value mental health and have increased resources and met needs when they’ve come up and would like to continue to see problems with care fixed, Caldwell said.
‘Oklahoma is unique’
Rebecca Farley David, a principal adviser overseeing behavioral health clinic-focused work for the National Council for Mental Wellbeing, said all eight original states that piloted the program, including Oklahoma, have either amended their state Medicaid plan to establish these clinics as a permanent provider option or are in the process of doing so.
Oklahoma is the only one of those states struggling to continue to cover the costs of uncompensated care, she said. Farley’s group represents and advocates for community-based providers of mental health and substance use treatment services.  
“Other states are making the payments for uncompensated care,” David said. “It’s not always enough to cover costs, but Oklahoma is unique, unfortunately, in the fact that the payments have just not been paid.”
The main entrance to Green Country, a certified community behavioral health clinic in Muskogee, is pictured Jan. 30, 2026. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)A sign at Green Country, a certified community behavioral health clinic in Muskogee, alerts clients that no one will be denied services due to an inability to pay. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)Pamphlets at the main entrance of Green Country, a certified community behavioral health clinic in Muskogee, direct clients to resources. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)A Green Country "Care-A-Van" is pictured Jan. 30, 2026 in Muskogee. The vehicle is used for mobile outpatient care. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
But she said savings aren’t always quantifiable on a Medicaid balance sheet. 
“It definitely is not a matter of waving a magic wand when that enhanced federal match goes away and making yourself whole,” she said. “States have had to kind of struggle to find how to put up that money, but they have chosen to prioritize finding those dollars.” 
Cost savings are found in areas such as incarceration, emergency room visits and hospitalizations, David said. Oklahoma’s clinics have become a national leader in improving employment opportunities both by helping their clients find jobs and by being major employers in their local communities, she said.
If the state were to stop prioritizing funding for the model, they would be less able to provide high-cost services such as psychiatric care or crisis intervention, David said, and more people would fall through the cracks and end up in hospitals, jails or homeless. 
“If the certification standards remain in place without the money to pay for the clinics to do all the things they’re supposed to do, I think, bluntly, you see clinics failing and having to close and not being able to serve their communities at all anymore,” she said. 
Dean, the Muskogee police captain, said it would be “devastating” if the services provided by Green Country were cut or if the clinic were ever forced to close. 
These providers are often the only place some people have as an option to turn to for help, he said. 
“It took an outside influence or an outside support to help me, and truthfully, literally save my life,” Dean said. “That’s not the same for everybody else. You know, I am unique in that I’m fortunate enough that I work for an agency that has these services. Not everybody else has that.”
Oklahoma Voice is part of the Mental Health Parity Collaborative, a group of newsrooms that are covering stories on mental health care access and inequities in the U.S. The partners on this project include The Carter Center and newsrooms in select states across the country.
