title: Did the Wyoming Boys’ School abuse young people? The first of six trials to answer that question is underway.
description:
Attorneys for a boy who was repeatedly put into isolation argue school staff mistreated a child who needed help. Lawyers for the state say staff members made decisions in the moment to keep residents and staff safe. 
The post Did the Wyoming Boys’ School abuse young people? The first of six trials to answer that question is underway. appeared first on WyoFil[...]
text:
After more than two years of litigation, the first trial concerning allegations of abuse at the Wyoming Boys’ School began Monday in Casper with two decidedly different views of the case.
Attorneys for the boy who says he suffered abuse at the state-run facility argue the case is about a child who needed help, but who was instead mistreated. Attorneys for the state contend the proceeding is “about difficult decisions made in difficult circumstances.”
The trial in U.S. District Court concerns the case of Blaise Chivers-King, one of six former boys’ school residents who lodged complaints against the facility in 2024. The school, which detains delinquent boys ages 12 to 21, is a 38-acre residential facility near Worland that’s overseen by the Wyoming Department of Family Services. 

Footprints in the snow lead to the Wyoming Boys’ School on Dec. 10, 2021 in Worland. The state-run facility houses delinquent boys ages 12 to 21. (Lauren Miller/Casper Star-Tribune) 

Chivers-King, who spent time at the boys’ school between 2020 and 2022, alleged school staff violated his 14th Amendment rights by placing him in isolation, using excessive force and infringing on due process. The defendants in this particular case are Wyoming Boys’ School staffers Thad Shaffer, Mike Nelson and Dale Weber, the school’s superintendent. The three sat in the courtroom Monday. 
Facing eight jurors, Ciara Boerman, one of the attorneys representing Chivers-King, described him as a child who struggled with anxiety, anger and other emotions that he didn’t always know how to handle. She acknowledged that he was “a difficult child, but still a child.” 
“Instead of helping him manage his emotions, they locked him away,” Boerman said of defendants Nelson and Weber. At some points, Chivers-King no longer wanted to live, she said.  
Meanwhile, Catherine Young, an attorney for the defense, asserted her clients “responded to safety concerns, and did their best to keep everyone, including Blaise, safe.” Those decisions weren’t always easy, Young said. But the defendants didn’t violate Chivers-King’s constitutional rights.
Staffers isolated Chivers-King eight times, with one of those stints lasting 15 days. Boerman referred to Chivers-King’s isolation as “solitary confinement,” though defendants contest that label. Throughout her opening statements, Boerman showed images of the room where Chivers-King, who is expected to testify Tuesday, was isolated. The room contained one window in the door, which staffers sometimes covered with a magnet, according to Boerman. When Chivers-King attempted to look under the door, a staff member covered the crack with a mattress, Boerman said. 
Staff members kept Chivers-King isolated even after he had calmed down, according to Boerman. At times, he hurt himself to get human interaction, Boerman said. She showed the jury photos of Chivers-King with an injury to his head after he had hit it against the wall in the room where he was isolated. Staff members’ reaction to this, according to Boerman, was to make Chivers-King clean his blood from the wall. 
Young asserted that staffers attended to Chivers-King when he was isolated. “It was far more work when Blaise was on detention status,” she said. That’s because he required more individual attention, according to Young. “You’ll see that it was not solitary confinement,” the attorney said. 
Boerman played a video for the jury of Shaffer, whom Chivers-King accused of using excessive force, holding a riot shield as he and several other staffers entered a room where Chivers-King was isolated. Chivers-King backed up as Shaffer pushed him against the wall and the group restrained him. 
Young said the altercation followed repeated problematic behavior from Chivers-King that staffers tried to stop. Shaffer had to enter Chivers-King’s detention room with a riot shield to keep them both safe, and it was safer for multiple staff members to be involved in the encounter, according to Young. Nursing also got involved to check Chivers-King afterward. “And he was OK,” Young said. She noted that Chivers-King was over 6 feet tall and weighed about 270 pounds. “You’ll hear that he was capable of hurting people, and sometimes did,” she said.  
Chivers-King continues to struggle with mental health issues related to his time at the boys’ school, Boerman concluded. “Blaise left the boys’ school, but the boys’ school has not left him.” Chivers-King is “more reclusive” and hardly leaves his room, according to Boerman. A doctor diagnosed Chivers-King with PTSD that, in the medical professional’s opinion, is directly related to his treatment at the boys’ school. 
But Chivers-King’s mental health struggles, including PTSD, preceded his placements at the Wyoming Boys’ School, according to Young, who described his early childhood as marked by repeated abuse and neglect. “In short, for much of Blaise’s childhood, chaos was his normal experience,” Young said.  
The school actually did good for Chivers-King, Young contended. He developed relationships with staffers, including the defendants, she said. Young showed a photo of Chivers-King outside walking a dog. Staff had arranged for him to visit an animal shelter off campus, she explained. Being with animals kept him calm and helped him deescalate. 
The trial, which began after attorneys spent the morning choosing jurors, is expected to take five to seven days.

title: The tricky art of saving suckers
description:
Wyoming Game and Fish rears native suckers to keep them off the endangered species list.
The post The tricky art of saving suckers appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
They don’t like the sun: not in the wild, and definitely not in holding tanks. The foot-or-so-long flannelmouth and bluehead suckers grouped together and then fled the moment Joe Gillis heaved the covers off their watery pens at the East Fork Hatchery southeast of Pinedale. In a prairie creek or river, the creatures might seek solace from the glare of the sun under the curve of an overhanging bank or the shade of a willow. Here they raced to a corner where a bit of shade still remained. 
Gillis spoke about the two sucker species with a mixture of irritation and admiration. He’s spent decades raising cold-water fish like rainbow and brown trout. He can help trout artificially reproduce by the literal millions before sending the offspring out across the state, region and even the country. But suckers, well, they proved not just challenging but downright difficult. 
“They don’t like change,” he said. “It was a big transition to go from the wild to captivity, and they didn’t relax for several years.”
About a decade ago, he accepted the challenge with little knowledge of how to raise a sucker and even less funding. But he knew that biologists worried about the suckers’ future. Climate change, long understood as a problem for cold-water trout, was and is becoming an increasingly large issue for native suckers. At the same time, the native suckers faced predation from introduced species like burbot and hybridization with longnose and white suckers, which can eventually wipe out a native species. 
Boulder Rearing Station and East Fork Hatchery Superintendent Joe Gillis uses a net to remove a bluehead sucker from a tank. The hatchery is the first one in Wyoming to successfully breed both species of native sucker. (Christine Peterson)
And so while fish hatcheries are generally known as the source of game fish and nurturer of species so endangered they risk blinking out, the Boulder Rearing Station created a space, called the East Fork Hatchery, dedicated to saving a species before it teetered on the edge of extinction. 
“If they are endangered it could even impact us putting out sportfish on the landscape,” said John Walrath, Wyoming Game and Fish’s Green River region fisheries supervisor. “So by working with them now we’re helping maintain their population and sportfish opportunity as well.” 
And after years of trial and error, their efforts appear to be paying off. 
More than a trash fish
The Boulder Rearing Station sits in a picturesque spot at the base of the western side of the Wind River Range, where water feeds long lines of open-air tanks full of rainbow and brown trout. Gillis oversees the rearing station and nearby East Fork Hatchery, calculating food quantities, helping squeeze spawning fish to release eggs and sperm, and answering questions from tourists who wander through. Most visitors want to see the rainbow trout spawners, the brood stock as they’re called, which swim lazily through one of the long breeding tanks. 
“The ones at the end of the facility provide the backbone of the catchable rainbow trout for the whole state,” he said on a hot July day pointing to one side of the facility.

Joe Gillis, Boulder Rearing Station and East Fork Hatchery Superintendent, grows artemia, a type of brine shrimp, to feed to baby flannelmouth and bluehead suckers. (Christine Peterson)

But drive up the hill a little, away from those prized breeders, and there sits the sucker tanks. 
For years he and his team tried everything they could think to coax the fish into reproducing. They changed water temperatures and flows, swapped foods, and encouraged spawning matches. When the fish finally decided to reproduce, he encountered eggs not the size of peas like trout, but the size of the tip of a pencil. Even hatched fry — the name for very young fish — were so small they slipped through the smallest mesh he could buy that covered in and outtake flows. 
Gillis consulted with experts at federal fish hatcheries and read anything he could find on the subject. Then slowly, painstakingly, he raised those tiny fish fry to 1-inch-long, then 2-inch-long suckers ready to reintroduce into the wild. 
Staving off a listing
Few people will likely ever encounter a bluehead or flannelmouth sucker. Both have long, dark bodies that function like camouflage on stream bottoms and in deep holes and long, sloped heads characteristic of so many sucker species. While flannelmouth suckers have fleshy downturned mouths used for suctioning insects, plant material or other choice bits from the river bottom, bluehead suckers have hard bottom lips. Those mouths are perfect for scraping algae off of rocks and other structures, but it also means they rarely, if ever, land on an angler’s hook.
But just like all of Wyoming’s suckers — often referred to as “trash fish” by some in the fishing community — the native species fill an important ecological niche. That’s why, more than a decade ago, Game and Fish biologists set out to give those suckers a hand, said Kevin Gelwick, one of Game and Fish’s assistant fish management coordinators. Biologists collected thousands of flannelmouth and bluehead suckers from the Muddy Creek and Big Sandy drainages over a series of years. They then filled portions of the creeks with Rotenone, a poison that targets animals with gills, to kill the longnose and white suckers hybridizing with bluehead and flannelmouth suckers.
Half-inch-long bluehead sucker fry swim in a tank at the East Fork Hatchery. (Christine Peterson)
Most of those fish went back into the rivers after the chemical cleared. Others stayed at the East Fork Hatchery. Since then, tens of thousands of both types of suckers have been stocked into Muddy Creek to augment the native populations, the first successful bluehead and flannelmouth captive breeding in the state.
“I don’t want to lose any of the species that are native to Wyoming, whether they’re listed or not,” Gelwick said. “This is our natural heritage, and it’s Game and Fish’s job to keep these species on the landscape.”

name: WyoFile
title: Hageman has no idea why so many American voters are angry at Trump
description:
Wyoming’s U.S. senator-elect’s reaction to GOP’s drubbing was to vow to fight leftists supposedly out to destroy America, columnist Kerry Drake writes.
The post Hageman has no idea why so many American voters are angry at Trump appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The person who Wyoming most needs to understand the shellacking Republicans earned in the midterm elections doesn’t get it. At all.
And based on what she said last week, U.S. Sen.-elect Harriet Hageman probably never will.

Opinion

That’s to the detriment of her home state and all of her constituents, including the voters who marked her name on 65% of the ballots cast and those who chose her Democratic opponent, former state legislator James Byrd of Cheyenne.
In a state that gave President Donald Trump huge majorities all three times he’s run for president, few expected that this year’s election would turn out any differently for Hageman as she sought the seat held by retiring U.S. Sen. Cynthia Lummis.
There was never going to be a blue tsunami here, unlike much of the country. Republicans easily won the two federal and five statewide races, and Democrats gained one seat to bring the party up to nine in the 93-member Legislature.
As Trump’s handpicked challenger four years ago to his nemesis, then-U.S. Rep. Liz Cheney, Hageman will be forever tied to Trump’s legacy. In Wyoming it means the nearly two-thirds of voters who chose her like her brand of politics.
Hageman will represent them, but she should also recognize that she will indeed hold a minority view in Congress. A large swath of the members who controlled both chambers will be gone, replaced by politicians with a far different view of the nation’s future.
What was Hageman’s reaction to her party’s historic losses from coast to coast, with a surprisingly strong repudiation from the heartland? It was her tiresome one-note: Anyone who does not agree with Trump is America’s enemy.
“We are about to engage in a battle for the future of this nation, and as we all recognize, the looming fight with the left is about much more than just policy differences,” she posted on Facebook. “It’s about the very survival of this country as it has been and as we know it.”
To Hageman, there are only two possibilities awaiting America. 
“Are we a capitalist nation, or will we slide precipitously into communism?” she asked. “The left hates our founding principles of freedom, just as they hate our strength and prosperity.”
That’s patently ridiculous. What a majority of Americans believe is that after six years of Trump in the White House, the prosperity we had is gone thanks to an unnecessary war, skyrocketing fuel prices, misguided tariffs and ever-rising grocery bills.
People are also sick of this grifter and his family getting rich conning the country, and want Trump and his henchmen punished for using the Constitution like a wet wipe.
Many on the left, center and right of the political spectrum want to go in a different direction, ASAP. 
Yet Hageman writes, “A strong United States of America embarrasses (the left), so they aim to tear it all down. And I aim to stand in their way.” 
State Senate President Bo Biteman, R-Ranchester, is as conservative a politician as I’ve ever seen. But his assessment was the opposite of Hageman’s, because he knows why the GOP got clobbered and isn’t afraid to say so.
“Turns out starting a war nobody wanted, sky-high inflation, trading America First for Israel First, covering up the Epstein scandal and breaking every single campaign promise doesn’t win you elections!” Biteman wrote on X.
“I saw this coming a mile away,” he added. “The GOP deserved every bit of this ass kicking.”
Biteman ran for Hageman’s U.S. House seat in the Republican primary and finished seventh out of nine candidates. Secretary of State Chuck Gray, who got Trump’s blessing, won 25% of that vote, sailed through the general election and is now headed to the U.S. Capitol, where he’ll be assigned a basement office by House leadership and hopefully not embarrass us as much as he has in his current gig.
“Wyoming is sending its best to help President Trump fight back against the liberals who are hell-bent on destroying this country,” was the Wyoming Republican Party’s post-election statement. Its leaders should join a comedy club circuit in red states, where they can whine to an audience that licks it up.
Gray will do or say anything to please Trump. The “not on my watch” tough-guy talk against data centers that marked his House campaign will flip once he’s given his marching orders from the pro-AI White House.
Some of Hageman’s Wyoming predecessors in the Senate were good examples of the way effective representatives act in a divided country. The late Sens. Alan Simpson and Mike Enzi often tried to find common ground with their adversaries to get things accomplished to benefit Wyomingites.
“Now it’s just sharp elbows, and instead of having a caucus where you sit down and say, ‘What are you doing for your country?’ you sit figuring out how to screw the other side,” Simpson once observed.
“It turns out that when we work together we can create a better bill than when we just try to do it alone or force others to accept our ideas,” Enzi said in his final speech on the Senate floor.
So, what did Rep. Hageman say after serving four years in the U.S. House as she prepares for her new job?
“Wyoming has a great deal at stake in the coming years as we know the forces of the left will stop at nothing to prevent us from safely accessing our own natural resources,” she wrote on Facebook election night. 
Hageman added that Wyoming must defend America’s energy independence because “not only does our economy depend on it, so does the very existence of the United States of America.”
Hageman introduced a bill in April that seeks to grant sweeping immunity to the fossil fuel industry against legal and financial accountability for climate change damages. If enacted, the bill would remove legal remedies for the public to hold corporations accountable.
It is unimaginable today that Hageman will do anything but carry the water for the fossil fuels industry during her six-year Senate term. She will no doubt continue to be rewarded with major campaign donations from individuals and energy industry-related PACs.
Don’t expect any statements about working across the aisle with senators who want to create a balanced energy blueprint that includes renewable resources that don’t pollute the planet. She’s demonstrated that protecting the wealth of Wyoming’s traditional energy industries is what matters to her.
It’s clear that Hageman and Wyoming’s senior U.S. Sen. John Barrasso are on the same page. On X, he wrote that “we should listen to what voters unmistakably said last night (because) their priorities must always come first.” 
Then he explained what he means about how Republican senators must show voters they are fighting for them.
“We will aggressively oppose terrible ideas that drive our country toward the socialism Democrats embraced,” Barrasso wrote. “Our commitment is to common sense.”
No, for decades Wyoming’s congressional delegation has shown that whenever they are not in power, they obstruct changes that millions of voters demanded Congress enact, and try to stay in office until the political winds shift their way again.
America would not have seen the seismic shift it had in Congress last week if people were happy about what Republicans are doing about the economy, inflation, immigration, and ending war and political corruption.
I’m sure Biteman isn’t the only one in his party who wants to see something different from Wyoming’s GOP lawmakers in Washington, D.C. If Hageman has a bipartisan bone in her body, it’s an optimum time for her to use it.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee senators talk state efficiency as Blackburn plans ‘Tennessee-style DOGE’ review
description: Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn said a review of state spending — a “Tennessee-style DOGE” operation modeled after the Trump administration’s Department of Government Efficiency led by Elon Musk — is among her first priorities. State legislators supported re-evaluation of state spending but urged thoughtfulness during The Sycamore Institute’s annual summit Frida[...]
text:
From left to right, Sycamore Institute Executive Vice President Mandy Spears hosts a panel on Tennessee's fiscal outlook featuring Sen. Raumesh Akbari, Sen. John Stevens, and Pew Charitable Trusts Senior Officer Peter Muller on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. (Photo: Cassandra Stephenson)Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn said a review of state spending — a “Tennessee-style DOGE” operation modeled after the Trump administration’s Department of Government Efficiency led by Elon Musk — is among her first priorities. State legislators supported re-evaluation of state spending but urged thoughtfulness during The Sycamore Institute’s annual summit Friday.
“Every dollar is a taxpayer dollar, and the legislators really want to work with me on this so that we’re eliminating positions that are not filled, programs that have outlived their usefulness, reviewing contracting, holding nonprofits accountable for the taxpayer money that they get,” Blackburn said following her gubernatorial victory.
The state’s budget season began Monday with economic forecast presentations to the State Funding Board. This year, Tennessee faces hundreds of millions of dollars in additional costs due to federal budget changes, in addition to a $58 billion highway project backlog and projected declines in the lottery proceeds that fund college scholarships.
Sen. John Stevens, a Huntingdon Republican and vice chair of the Senate Finance, Ways and Means Committee, said Friday that he is “always an advocate” for re-evaluating practices and looking for efficiencies. 
“Even if it isn’t a lot of money (saved) … we better be sure that what we’re taking your money and spending it on is efficient and it’s meeting your needs,” he said.
Stevens pointed to the TennCare Bureau’s document review function as an example for potential areas of technological advancement.
“Can AI read those documents and categorize them and submit a recommendation to a person that can then approve it or not approve it?” he said during a panel discussion. “Just, instead of a whole bunch of people doing it, fewer people doing it.”
Senate Minority Leader Raumesh Akbari, a Memphis Democrat, urged thoughtfulness in replacing human-run systems with technology.
“What does that do for a small town where the majority of the people work at that one government office?” Akbari said. “So it has to be smart, and it has to be balanced.”
Akbari said most state departments have been asked to submit downsized budgets each year since Gov. Bill Haslam’s administration.
“Gov.-elect Blackburn has a real opportunity here,” Akbari said. “I don’t think that you can any longer say … ‘We’re cleaning up what Democrats did when they were in charge.’ This is a continuation of a party that’s been in charge for 16 years. So how can we all work together to make the experience better for Tennesseans?”
Peter Muller, senior officer specializing in financial risk management at The Pew Charitable Trusts, said some states are exploring ways to use AI to increase efficiency, but noted that efficiency can also mean increasing accuracy rather than decreasing cost.
States will be required to pay a share of their Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefit costs for the first time this year as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. States that exceed the 6% goal error rate set by Congress will be financially penalized starting in October 2027. Depending on its error rate for the 2026 fiscal year, Tennessee may have to pay between $162 million to $171 million for the program, in addition to an increased share of program administrative costs. 
“The way the matching funds are set up, the more accurate your SNAP determinations or SNAP payments are, the lower your state’s matching rate is going to be,” Muller said. 
“We’ve seen a lot of states really heavily investing in the administration of their SNAP programs to try and really bring that error rate down because they see that as a way to save money over the long term,” he said.
Akbari’s efficiency goals center on constituent experience — how easy or difficult it is to apply for services such as unemployment benefits, for example.
“I read a book many years before I got elected … talking about understanding poverty and just how expensive it is to be poor,” she said. “If you engage in these services, you have to take time off from work. You might have to take two buses so that you can go sit in an office where they might not have the paperwork you need, and you have to repeat that process. That’s what I wanted to look at.”
A review of the federal DOGE’s efforts by libertarian-leaning policy research organization Cato Institute found that DOGE did not meaningfully reduce federal spending (most of which goes to programs controlled by Congress), but did cut federal employment by 9% in under a year. 
A report published by the Government Accountability Office in September showed that Trump’s administration spent about $6.7 billion on a deferred resignation program for federal employees as part of the staff reduction effort. The number of federal employees has decreased by more than 258,000 since January 2025, according to federal data. But by June 2026, federal agencies hired more than 20,500 employees to backfill positions vacated through the deferred resignation program, according to the Partnership for Public Service.

title: ‘Move quickly’: CoreCivic urges ICE to seal detention deals after Democrats win big
description: The CEO of Brentwood-based CoreCivic is urging Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials to act with speed in inking contracts for immigration detention centers after Democrats scored big wins in last week’s elections. “We would urge the ICE administration to move quickly,” President and CEO Lucibeth Mayberry said during a quarterly earnings call on Thur[...]
text:
Community members protest outside Mason ICE facility, CoreCivic, in Mason, Tennessee  September 2, 2026.  (© Karen Pulfer Focht)The CEO of Brentwood-based CoreCivic is urging Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials to act with speed in inking contracts for immigration detention centers after Democrats scored big wins in last week’s elections.
“We would urge the ICE administration to move quickly,” President and CEO Lucibeth Mayberry said during a quarterly earnings call on Thursday. “They have a need for capacity. We have the capacity. There’s no reason to wait.”
The private prison and immigration detention center operator netted $1.3 billion in its most recent quarter from the sales of four detention centers to the Department of Homeland Security as the second Trump administration ramped up immigrant detentions nationwide. The sales helped bolster publicly-traded company’s’ better-than-predicted profits in the third quarter of this year. 
Mayberry said the company is hoping to sell more. 
“We continue to have discussions with ICE about the potential acquisition of additional CoreCivic detention facilities,” she said, noting the discussions remain preliminary. “However, we do believe additional facility acquisitions continue to be a key element of ICE’s detention strategy.”
Historic Democratic victories on Nov. 3 could put a damper on future ICE deals after members of the newly-elected Democratic majority in the U.S. House and Senate are sworn into office in January. Democratic candidates across the country campaigned on reigning in controversial ICE enforcement tactics that have led to unprecedented numbers of immigrants being detained.
Democrats have pledged scrutiny, investigations and accountability for ICE’s enforcement tactics, which have resulted in tens of thousands of immigrants with no criminal backgrounds held in detention centers, the arrests of U.S. citizens and the deaths of two Americans.
CoreCivic has drawn scrutiny for its own role in the administration’s immigration crackdown, with reports about poor and unsafe conditions at its detention centers and new questions about its sales. 
A recent investigation by a Minneapolis television news station showed CoreCivic offered to sell a shuttered prison in Appleton, Minn. to the State of Minnesota for $75 million in 2025.  A year later, ICE paid $485.6 million for the facility, which is to be used as an immigration detention center. Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison has called for a Congressional investigation into the sale.
ICE, however, remains the highest-funded law enforcement agency in the nation, boosted over the past two years by more than $240 billion in appropriations to the agency and the U.S. Border Patrol by a GOP-controlled Congress. President Donald Trump, in the days since his party suffered big losses in the election, has offered mixed signals about plans for the agency going forward.
Trump on Sunday said his administration’s aggressive detention deportation policy may have been “too tough” and contributed to the GOP election losses during an interview with 60 Minutes on Sunday. However, the president also promoted the architect of his immigration policy, Stephen Miller, as his Chief of Staff. And key administration leaders have signalled the administration will stay the course on its immigration detention and deportation plans.
“Deportations will continue,” Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin wrote on X a day after the midterm elections.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Terri Sewell plans to refile legislation restoring Voting Rights Act
description: U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell, D-Birmingham, plans to refile a bill to restore major provisions of the Voting Rights Act gutted by the U.S. Supreme Court.  Sewell in a statement Monday that action on the new version of the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act, named after the icon of the Civil Rights Movement and […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell, D-Birmingham, addresses the Tabernacle Baptist Church In Selma, Alabama on May 16, 2026. Sewell said in a statement Monday she would reintroduce the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act, aimed at restoring parts of the Voting Rights Act gutted by the U.S. Supreme Court. (Andi Rice for Alabama Reflector)U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell, D-Birmingham, plans to refile a bill to restore major provisions of the Voting Rights Act gutted by the U.S. Supreme Court. 
Sewell in a statement Monday that action on the new version of the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act, named after the icon of the Civil Rights Movement and former Georgia congressman, was “more urgent than ever given the Supreme Court’s repeated decisions gutting the Voting Rights Act of 1965.”
The Supreme Court in Louisiana v. Callais, handed down in April, severely weakened Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, making it harder for plaintiffs to challenge congressional districts as racial gerrymanders. The decision, which led to widespread gerrymandering by Republican-controlled Legislatures in the South, helped spur Black turnout around the country, delivering control of Congress to the Democrats. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I am working closely with voting rights organizations and my colleagues in the House to ensure the next version of the bill responds directly to the Court’s recent rulings and provides stronger tools to combat modern-day voter discrimination,” Sewell’s statement said. “In particular, we are examining ways to address the harmful consequences of decisions like Callais, which paved the way for states like Alabama to adopt discriminatory maps in an effort to silence Black and minority voters.”
The John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act was first introduced by Sewell in 2021 as a response to the Shelby County v. Holder case, which gutted Section 5 of the 1965 Voting Rights Act, requiring states and areas with histories of racially discriminatory voting laws, such as Alabama, to have changes to election statutes pre-cleared by the U.S. Department of Justice. 
Challenges
The bill could pass Congress, but would likely face a veto threat from President Donald Trump, a Republican. Experts also said that the bill would have to confront the court’s holdings in Holder and Callais and its interpretation of a 1982 amendment to the Voting Rights Act, which itself was a response to the Supreme Court’s ruling in Mobile v. Bolden in 1980, which said a law had to have a racially discriminatory purpose to violate the Constitution, not discriminatory effects.
“Congress is empowered to talk about what we call the effects test, the effect of a rule that dilutes people’s votes, and so Congress has to be creative in how it does that, because the court said that the way that Congress did that through the original Voting Rights Act, or at least the 1982 amendment, was unconstitutional,” said Arthur Ago, director of strategic litigation and advocacy with the Southern Poverty Law Center, in an interview on Friday.
Because Democrats now control the U.S. House and Senate, Ago said passing the bill could be easier than last time.
“There is, I think, an appetite to pass this, and so now the work for them and alongside organizations such as ours, who does this advocacy work in this space, is really the beginning, and to signal to the country that it’s really important to pass this act,” he said.
David Hughes, a political science professor at University of Louisiana at Lafayette, said Monday addressing the Holder decision will be simple for Sewell, but addressing the court’s ruling in Callais will be more difficult. Callais, he said, told judges “how they have to interpret Section 2 and the relevant precedents around it when plaintiffs come asking for relief.”
“If I were putting on my political science hat, I would say don’t even bother trying to find the right magic words that are going to make the Supreme Court happy that accomplishes what you want to accomplish politically through updating the laws of the United States,” he said. “Your time would be better spent attacking the Supreme Court, trying to get some of the conservatives to retire or add new seats to the court that would eventually interpret your updated Section 2 the way you want them to interpret it.”
Redistricting looming
U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Montgomery, managed to win re-election in Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District last week despite a Republican gerrymander meant to draw him out.  He said in a statement Monday that the bill had to “guard against some of the tactics we’ve seen deployed this cycle, like mid-decade redistricting.”
“I’m ready to work with Congresswoman Sewell to introduce a strong bill in the new Congress that ensures free and fair elections,” the statement said.
Hughes said the legislation could be critical ahead of the U.S. Census in 2030, which will lead to redistricting.
“If pre-clearance is back, that means Texas would have to go to Washington D.C. and ask permission to re-gerrymander the state,” he said. “Whereas if the Voting Rights Act doesn’t get renewed, if the pre-clearance stays dead, then Republicans in Austin, should they retake the majority, can re-gerrymander the state and kick a bunch of Democrats out of office.”
But Hughes said if Sewell’s bill fails to pass, it could still be useful for Democrats in 2028. 
“The majority party can force votes on the Republicans they don’t want to take, and that gives you campaign fodder for the next election,” Hughes said. “Then you go back to your voters and say, ‘Why would you vote for this party? They’re denying you your voting rights.’”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee on pace for another surplus in 2026-27, as House Speaker proposes narrow grocery tax cut
description: Tennessee’s revenue officials predict the state is on pace for another billion-dollar surplus, giving state lawmakers and Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn more room to navigate budget negotiations.  The estimates were given as part of the department’s presentation to the State Funding Board, which will make an official recommendation on the bottom-line financial [...]
text:
Tennessee revenue officials are projecting another surplus in 2026-27. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee’s revenue officials predict the state is on pace for another billion-dollar surplus, giving state lawmakers and Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn more room to navigate budget negotiations. 
The estimates were given as part of the department’s presentation to the State Funding Board, which will make an official recommendation on the bottom-line financial numbers lawmakers and the governor can use to shape next year’s budget. 
Economists and state officials told the state funding board Monday that they expect state revenues to increase by 3.5% to 4.5%, essentially keeping pace with inflation. This growth follows last year’s $1.2 billion surplus, which lawmakers can spend later this year. 
For years, officials have conservatively estimated revenues, allowing the state to experience a “surplus” used for things like road funding, tax cuts and a reworking of the education funding formula.
Don Bruce, a professor at the University of Tennessee’s Boyd Center for Business and Economic Research, said the state continues to struggle to project its franchise and excise taxes on business. 
This year the state is projecting a $700 million surplus in franchise and excise taxes. Three years ago, volatility in franchise and excise taxes on business led the state to miss its revenue projections, leaving it to find a way to plug a nearly $600 million budget hole. 
“It could go anywhere from up to down double-digit percentage points,” said Bruce, referring to future business tax revenues.  
Tennessee does face at least some increasing costs. After the federal One Big Beautiful Bill legislation, the state is expected to have to cover around $170 million in its shared costs of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, SNAP.
Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton kicked off the legislative season Monday by introducing a bill to cut the sales tax on milk, eggs and bread. Lawmakers won’t convene until January, but can file legislation through the end of the year and into 2027.
Sexton’s narrowly tailored tax cut comes after Democrats have pushed for years to eliminate the food sales tax on all groceries. A bill introduced by two Democrats in 2025 would have eliminated the grocery sales tax. 
Eliminating all sales tax on groceries would cost about $1.2 billion in state and local tax revenue, according to legislative fiscal revenue officials at the time.
Tennessee is one of the lowest-taxed states in the nation, but a 2024 ThinkTennessee report found that lawmakers have steadily shifted more of the tax burden from corporations to people through a reliance on sales taxes, leaving low-income families with a “higher tax burden than wealthier families and businesses.” Tennessee also made multibillion-dollar corporate tax cuts in 2023 and 2024. 
No estimates yet show how much Sexton’s proposed tax cut would cost. Sexton’s bill is also a caption bill and will likely undergo significant changes before passage. 
The proposed legislation also follows Democrats flipping six state House seats in the 2026 election. Republicans now hold a 68-31 supermajority in the state House. 
The state funding board will issue its final prediction of state budget growth at a meeting on Nov. 23. 
State Treasurer David Lillard said he would caution the board in its revenue projections because so much of the predicted business tax revenue increase is based on estimated payments, and not actual collections. 
“We don’t want to be caught off guard,” Lillard said.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota land trusts to produce record distribution to schools, universities
description: The North Dakota agency responsible for managing state trusts announced Monday a record payout is expected during the next budget cycle.  The Department of Trust Lands, responsible for managing the Common Schools Trust Fund and 12 other permanent trusts, will distribute $762 million in earnings for the 2027-2029 biennium.  The payout will include more than [[...]
text:
Gov. Kelly Armstrong, right, Secretary of State Michael Howe, center, and Land Commissioner Joseph Heringer, left, listen to a presentation during a meeting of the Board of University and School Lands meeting on Dec. 11, 2025. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)The North Dakota agency responsible for managing state trusts announced Monday a record payout is expected during the next budget cycle. 
The Department of Trust Lands, responsible for managing the Common Schools Trust Fund and 12 other permanent trusts, will distribute $762 million in earnings for the 2027-2029 biennium. 
The payout will include more than $722 million from the Common Schools Trust Fund, which helps fund K-12 education. That’s about 24% higher than the contribution during the 2025-2027 budget cycle. 
Annual bonuses proposed for North Dakota teachers to improve recruitment, retention

“These record distributions will provide crucial support for educational institutions and students in classrooms across our great state, from kindergarten to college,” Gov. Kelly Armstrong said in a statement. Armstrong chairs the Board of University and School Lands.
The Common Schools Trust Fund collects revenue from several sources including oil and gas royalties, surface property rents and the income derived from investing these funds. It was valued at $9.3 billion as of June 30.
The state constitution requires 10% of the five-year average value of the trust’s assets to be distributed to K-12 schools each biennium. The trust fund contributed nearly $585 million, or 24% of the state’s per-pupil funding responsibility, during the 2025-2027 biennium. 
The agency also manages a dozen other trusts that distribute funding each biennium. The 2027-2029 biennium’s distributions include $10.6 million for North Dakota State University and $8.4 million for the University of North Dakota, as well as payouts to other education institutions. 
The distributions will also include $3.9 million for the Youth Correctional Center, $2.5 million for the State Hospital and $1.2 million to the North Dakota Veterans Home. 
“These historic distributions reflect the Land Board’s commitment to responsible stewardship and ensuring North Dakota’s trust assets deliver lasting value,” said Joseph Heringer, land commissioner. “By carefully managing these resources, we are strengthening educational opportunities across the state and investing in a brighter future for generations of North Dakotans.”
The Legacy Fund, another state investment portfolio that is managed by a different agency, is expected to have a record $894 million distribution for 2027-29. The Retirement and Investment Office’s preliminary estimate provided to lawmakers in August is 30% higher than the last payout from the Legacy Fund.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: NORC polling takeaways: Arkansans worried about economy, healthcare, data center impact
description: The midterm election last week handed Democrats historic wins across the country along with moderate gains in Arkansas’ statehouse. The results of the election also revealed many of the top issues that drove voters’ concerns. Findings released the day after the election by NORC’s Civic Health & Elections Project offered details on what voters in […]
text:
Voting tables with "I Voted" dividers at the Historic Arkansas Museum in Little Rock, Arkansas on Tuesday, Nov.3, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)The midterm election last week handed Democrats historic wins across the country along with moderate gains in Arkansas’ statehouse. The results of the election also revealed many of the top issues that drove voters’ concerns.
Findings released the day after the election by NORC’s Civic Health & Elections Project offered details on what voters in Arkansas and other states were most concerned about. The project surveyed more than 110,000 registered voters across all 50 states, including those who decided not to vote. NORC collected the data in the week before Election Day. In Arkansas, the project interviewed more than 1,500 people.
You can use the online dashboard to explore more of the project’s findings in Arkansas and other states. The polling methodology and information about the margin of error can be found here.
Here are some of the key findings the poll made about Arkansas:
The economy was the top issue
Economic issues were the top concern for a majority of Arkansas voters, according to the poll, with 58% of likely voters surveyed identifying the economy and jobs as one of the top issues facing the country. That mirrored the national numbers.
Forty-five percent of likely Arkansas voters identified healthcare as one of the top issues, and 32% identified immigration as a top issue.
 
(Courtesy NORC Civic Health & Elections Project)
 
Healthcare worries spurred action
Worries about healthcare prompted Arkansans to take action, the survey revealed, with 88% of likely voters saying protecting and improving the health of their families motivated them in some fashion to take civic action such as voting, contacting elected officials or attending a public meeting.
The polling showed that only a quarter of likely voters said they support replacing private insurance with a publicly run government health system, and 46% of respondents not supporting such an approach. But 47% of likely voters said they support a publicly run health insurance option that would be available alongside private health insurance, while 22% said they oppose.
And 66% of the state’s likely voters said they’d support regulating private insurance to make it more affordable.
 
(Courtesy NORC Civic Health & Elections Project)
Arkansans worried about AI, data centers’ impact
The polling showed heavy concerns among Arkansas voters about data centers, especially when it comes to utility costs. Nearly two-thirds of likely voters in Arkansas said they were extremely or very concerned about data centers impacting the price of utilities, including electricity and water, in the communities where they are built. Sixty percent data centers said they were extremely or very concerned about data centers impacting pollution of natural resources, including air and water, in the communities where they are built.
Fifty-seven percent of likely voters in the state said they somewhat or strongly oppose the construction of a data center in their area.
The responses come as communities around the state have enacted measures in recent months to temporarily prevent data centers from moving into their areas or to impose new regulations on them.
The surveys also showed widespread support for more guardrails on AI, with 65% of likely voters saying they support more regulation of artificial intelligence and 67% supporting policies to limit their use in public elementary and high schools.
 
(Courtesy NORC Civic Health & Elections Project)
 
Arkansans think they’re being divided for others’ gain
The NORC polling showed high levels of distrust in government and in elected officials.
Fifty-eight percent of likely voters in the state said they somewhat or strongly disagreed with the statement that most of the time we can trust people in government to do what is right. Sixty-eight percent said they somewhat or strongly agreed with the statement that most politicians are in politics only for what they can get out of it personally.
Nearly two-thirds of voters said they agreed with the statement that politicians benefit more from dividing people against each other than uniting them.
The surveys also revealed pessimism about the future with 52% of likely voters saying they believe America’s best days are behind us.
(Courtesy NORC Civic Health & Elections Project)
Arkansas voters show confidence in school districts, colleges
The polling showed that Arkansas voters have faith in their local school districts and their institutions of higher education.
Seventy-three percent of likely voters said they had a great deal or some confidence in the people running colleges or universities in their area, and 76% said the same about K-12 school districts in their area.
Forty-four percent said they strongly or somewhat favored taxpayer-funded school vouchers, with 35% somewhat or strongly opposed.
(Courtesy NORC Civic Health & Elections Project)

name: Colorado Newsline
title: 34% of Colorado households are cost-burdened, new state housing​ study finds
description: Over one-third of Colorado households spend more than 30% of their income on housing, with a heavier strain on the state’s renters, according to a statewide housing needs assessment released Monday. Nearly 34% of households were cost-burdened under that definition as of July 1 this year, including 49% of renters and 25% of homeowners. The […]
text:
A tower of downtown Denver residences is seen on Feb. 18, 2023. (Quentin Young/Colorado Newsline)Over one-third of Colorado households spend more than 30% of their income on housing, with a heavier strain on the state’s renters, according to a statewide housing needs assessment released Monday.
Nearly 34% of households were cost-burdened under that definition as of July 1 this year, including 49% of renters and 25% of homeowners. The lower the income level, the higher the share of cost-burdened households. Colorado tends to have a higher share of cost-burdened households than other states, according to separate research from Harvard.
The State Demography Office released its first statewide housing assessment as part of a requirement under 2024 legislation to analyze current housing stock and estimate statewide needs for the next 10 years.
“Behind every data point are families hoping for stability and an affordable place to put down roots. The data from the HNA will be critical for us to be able to successfully map out a plan for Colorado’s housing future,” Maria De Cambra, the state Department of Local Affairs executive director, said in a statement.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The assessment comes amid a surge of new statewide housing policies passed by a Democratic majority in the state Legislature and championed by outgoing Democratic Gov. Jared Polis. New laws from the past four years include efforts to increase density near public transit routes, make it easier to build accessory dwelling units and reform the state’s construction defect laws for condos. Voters also approved Proposition 123 in 2022 to fund various affordable housing projects.
A new Legislature and governor take power starting in January. Gov.-elect Phil Weiser, a Democrat, has a goal to add 40,000 more affordable units in the state by 2035 through policies like down payment assistance and development permitting reform.
“I think it might be a good time for some reflection, and an opportunity to take a look back and see, one, how far we’ve come and think through and maybe even measure the efficacy of some of these policies,” Brian Rossbert, the executive director of Housing Colorado, said.
But the upshot from the report is that affordability has declined over the past decade. State researchers estimate that a household needs to make $153,000 annually to afford a median-priced home at $547,900. Renters need to make $72,900 to afford the average apartment. The last time an average household could afford a median-priced home without being cost burdened was 2014. Put another way, the gap between income and how much a household needs to buy an average home is around $50,000 today, while it was just $2,600 in 2013.
“This gap has sidelined many households from becoming homeowners and has also been a driver in the increased supply of homes for sale,” the report says. Over the last three years however, home prices have remained relatively stable and incomes have risen slowly, shrinking the gap.
The area median income for a Colorado household of four people is $127,800.
“Affordability is one of the most dynamic elements of the housing conversation, the report says. “Developers can choose to build high-end housing in the single-family and multifamily space, but if households cannot afford to live there, the increase in supply will not solve the housing need for a community.”
There are 2.75 million housing units in the state, and 64.1% of those are occupied by owners. More houses are on the market than in any year since at least 2012, and the number of new multifamily units has exceeded demand over the past year. Mountain resort communities and the Front Range especially have a surplus of apartment units. Demographers found demand for market-rate renter housing on the Western Slope and Eastern Plains.
The report estimates an affordable housing shortfall of around 106,000 units. That would allow a 5% vacancy rate and reduce the number of residents — mostly young people — who are living with roommates or “doubling up” because they can’t afford not to. Last year, demographers estimated that the state needs 34,100 more housing units per year to prevent the shortfall from growing. They revised that this year to 34,950 per year to account for annual housing inventory losses.
Another figure in the report is an annual demand of 30,600 units over the next 10 years to support a projected population growth.
Additionally, as Colorado’s population ages, there will be more housing needs for older adults and people with disabilities. Demographers estimate there will be 238,000 more people with disabilities through 2036.
“This (assessment) gives us a little bit of a North Star in the housing community of a goal to work towards, which we haven’t had,” Rossbert said. “Since my time on the Affordable Housing Transformational Task Force back in 2021, we were always trying to put our finger on what the actual unit shortage is, and then how do we direct resources in the best way possible to meet that shortage. And this gives us a starting place.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Meet North Carolina’s US House members for the 120th Congress
description: North Carolina appears to be sending 10 Democrats and four Republicans to Washington in January.
text:
The U.S. Capitol on Oct. 1, 2025. (Photo by Shauneen Miranda/States Newsroom)After a blue tsunami swept the state during the 2026 midterm elections, North Carolina appears to be sending 10 Democrats and four Republicans to Washington in January. 
In unofficial results, since not all county elections boards have completed their count yet, Democrats appear to have flipped six seats in N.C. They’ve also gained a majority in both chambers of Congress. 
North Carolina’s U.S. House delegation during the 119th Congress consisted of 10 Republicans and four Democrats, after three Democratic incumbents opted not to seek reelection due to Republican redraws of their districts to favor Republicans. In the 118th, there was a 7-7 split for the 14-member delegation. 
District 1: Don Davis (D)
U.S. Rep. Don Davis (Photo: House.gov)
U.S. Rep. Don Davis held off a gerrymander to secure his third term in the U.S. House, where he’s represented the 1st Congressional District since 2023. The district covers the northeastern part of the state and some of the outer exurbs of the Triangle area. 
Aiming to secure another seat in Congress, state Republican lawmakers redrew the district in 2025 to include more GOP voters. It didn’t work — Davis still beat Republican Army veteran Laurie Buckhout in a rematch of their 2024 matchup.
The 2026 race broke records to become the most expensive U.S. House general election in history. 
This time, Davis won by 10,285 votes, according to unofficial results from the State Board of Elections. It’s a larger margin than 2024, where 6,307 votes separated the two.
A moderate Democrat, Davis has supported increased funding for crop insurance and pricing for local farmers, and opposed job cuts at Seymour Johnson Air Force Base in Goldsboro. 
He served in the Air Force and attended the U.S. Air Force Academy, Central Michigan University, and East Carolina University. 
District 2: Deborah Ross (D)
U.S. Rep. Deborah Ross (Photo: House.gov)
U.S. Rep. Deborah Ross easily won reelection to the 2nd Congressional District, which covers most of Wake County and some of its surrounding suburbs. She’s held the seat since 2021. 
Ross trounced Republican Eugene Douglass, winning more than three-quarters of the vote in the heavily Democratic district. 
The Democrat was a member of the North Carolina House of Representatives from 2003 to 2013. She’s a former civil rights attorney who strongly supports public education, affordable healthcare, and fighting climate change. 
She lives in the Boylan Heights neighborhood in Raleigh, and attended Brown University and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. 
District 3: Greg Murphy (R)
U.S. Rep. Greg Murphy (Photo: House.gov)
U.S. Rep. Greg Murphy appears to have narrowly won reelection to the 3rd Congressional District, a seat he’d held since 2019. The district covers most of North Carolina’s coast. 
Murphy leads Democratic challenger Raymond Smith by 233 votes or 0.09 points, according to unofficial results from the State Board of Elections. That’s after Republican lawmakers moved some Republican voters out of his district and into the 1st in an attempt to unseat Davis. 
The race could be subject to a recount.
A urologist, Murphy co-chairs the House GOP Doctors Caucus and is the only practicing surgeon in Congress. He’s a social conservative who introduced legislation to ban giving federal funds to graduate medical schools that offer diversity, equity, and inclusion training.
Murphy was in the North Carolina House of Representatives from 2015 to 2019.
He lives in Greenville and holds degrees from Davidson College and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. 
District 4: Valerie Foushee (D)
U.S. Rep. Valerie Foushee (Photo: House.gov)
U.S. Rep. Valerie Foushee coasted to victory in the 4th Congressional District, which she’s served since 2023. The heavily Democratic district covers all of Durham and Orange counties, as well as parts of Chatham and Wake counties. 
Foushee won nearly 80% of the vote, defeating Republican Max Ganorkar. 
She’s an original cosponsor of Medicare for All at the federal level, and fought to expand Medicare in North Carolina. 
Prior to Congress, Foushee was elected to the North Carolina House in 2012 and was subsequently appointed to serve in the Senate in 2013, which she did until 2023.
She graduated from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. 
District 5: Chuck Hubbard (D)
U.S. Rep.-elect Chuck Hubbard (Photo: Courtesy Hubbard campaign)
Chuck Hubbard appears to have unseated longtime incumbent Virginia Foxx in a surprise upset, although the race could be subject to a recount. He’ll represent the 5th district, which covers the central western portion of the state. 
Hubbard leads Foxx, who’s served since 2005, by only 99 votes in unofficial results. He’s attending freshman orientation in Washington this week. 
The Democrat is a former journalist and newspaper publisher who wants to expand access to affordable healthcare and support public education. He said he was inspired to run for Congress by his daughter Meredith, who is a member of the LGBTQ+ community.
Hubbard graduated from Wofford College and lives in Wilkesboro. 
District 6: Cyril Jefferson (D)
U.S. Rep.-elect Cyril Jefferson (Photo: Courtesy Jefferson campaign)
High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson defeated GOP freshman Addison McDowell in the 6th district, located in the north central part of the state. 
The district was drawn to be a safe Republican seat, but Jefferson beat McDowell by 6,264 votes, or 2.28 points, according to unofficial results. 
As mayor, Jefferson helped launch a business initiative called Thrive High Point, which has raised over $3 million to support local entrepreneurs. 
He was the youngest mayor elected in High Point’s history. He’s at freshman orientation in Washington this week. 
District 7: David Rouzer (R)
U.S. Rep. David Rouzer (Photo: House.gov)
U.S. Rep. David Rouzer has represented the deep-red 7th Congressional District since 2015, spanning the southern portion of the state. 
Rouzer beat Democrat Kimberly Hardy by 2,425 votes or 0.76 points, according to unofficial results from the State Board of Elections. The race could be subject to a recount.
He’s an arch-conservative who opposes abortion and same-sex marriage. He’s a founding member of the Congressional Coastal Communities Caucus, as well as the Primary Care Caucus.
Rouzer represented Johnston and Wayne counties in the North Carolina Senate from 2009 to 2013.
He attended North Carolina State University. 
District 8: Mark Harris (R)
U.S. Rep. Mark Harris (Photo: House.gov)
U.S. Rep. Mark Harris, a beneficiary of the state legislature’s new map for the 2024 cycle, appears to have held onto his seat in the 8th Congressional District. It covers the southern Piedmont area and is heavily Republican. 
Harris received 5,179 votes, or 1.77 points, more than Democrat Colby Watson, according to unofficial results. 
He supports efforts to cut spending and root out waste, fraud, and abuse. In his first term, he served on the Agriculture, Education, and Judiciary committees.
Harris is a pastor and previously ran unsuccessful bids for the U.S. Senate and U.S. House.
He holds degrees from Appalachian State University and Southeastern Baptist Theological Seminary.
District 9: Richard Ojeda (D)
U.S. Reps.-elect Chuck Hubbard, Jamie Ager, and Richard Ojeda at freshman orientation in Washington on Nov. 8, 2026. (Photo: Ojeda campaign on X)
Richard Ojeda unseated National Republican Congressional Committee chair Richard Hudson in North Carolina’s 9th Congressional District. 
The district was drawn to be a safe Republican seat, but Ojeda won 6,015 more votes than Hudson, who’s held the seat since 2013, according to unofficial results. 
The Democrat is a retired Army major who previously served in the West Virginia Senate. There, he played a prominent role in the 2018 statewide teacher strike. 
Ojeda, who pronounces his name with a hard “J”, will be the first Hispanic member of Congress from North Carolina. 
He graduated from West Virginia State University and Webster University. 
District 10: Pat Harrigan (R)
U.S. Rep. Pat Harrigan (Photo: House.gov)
Along with Harris, U.S. Rep. Pat Harrigan is the only other Republican freshman to survive the blue wave in the Tar Heel State. The 10th district, which is heavily Republican, is located in central and western North Carolina.
He beat Democrat Ashley Bell by 3,029 votes, or 1.03 points, according to unofficial results. 
Harrigan supports enforcing immigration laws, strengthening border security, and combating human trafficking and drug smuggling. 
He’s a firearms manufacturer and military veteran. 
Harrigan attended the U.S. Military Academy. 
District 11: Jamie Ager (D)
Jamie Ager at Hickory Nut Gap Farm in Fairview on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)
Democrat Jamie Ager is a fourth-generation farmer from a political family. He easily won North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District, which covers Western North Carolina.
Although the district was drawn to favor a Republican, Ager led Republican state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom by nearly 16 points. 
He owns Hickory Nut Gap Farm in Fairview and gained national prominence for an ad featuring his monthly barn dances. He’s a centrist who brands himself as a “Mountain Democrat.”
The district has been reliably red for most of the past 35 years. After disgraced incumbent U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards withdrew, the North Carolina Republican Party picked Balkcom as his replacement. 
A combination of candidate quality and the blue wave led to Ager’s dominant performance out west. Ager’s grandfather Jamie Clarke held the seat from 1983 to 1985 and 1987 to 1991. 
Ager graduated from Warren Wilson College. 
District 12: Alma Adams (D)
U.S. Rep. Alma Adams (Photo: House.gov)
U.S. Rep. Alma Adams won the greatest percentage of votes in North Carolina’s U.S. House races. She’s served the deep blue 12th Congressional District, covering northern and eastern portions of Charlotte and surrounding areas, since 2014. 
With Foxx’s defeat, Adams will become the longest-serving member of North Carolina’s congressional delegation. She received more than 80% of the vote. 
Adams supports reproductive freedom, strengthening the middle class, and has sponsored progressive policy proposals during her tenure in Congress. 
She was appointed to the North Carolina House in 1994 and served until 2014. 
Adams holds degrees from North Carolina A&T State University and Ohio State University. 
District 13: Paul Barringer (D)
Paul Barringer, the Democratic nominee running for North Carolina’s 13th Congressional District, poses with his dogs, Billy and Penny, at an early voting site in Clayton on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)
Paul Barringer eked out a win over GOP freshman Brad Knott in North Carolina’s 13th district, besting Knott by 7,652 votes, or 2.41 points. 
Known for its gerrymander, the district curves around Raleigh, spanning from Caswell County in the north to a thin piece east of Raleigh before going down to Lee County. The district was drawn in 2023 to be a safe Republican seat.
Last fall, Barringer rode his bike from his home in Lee County to Yanceyville, in the northwestern part of the district. A straight shot would be 66 miles, but through the district, Barringer said he rode for 183 miles.
It’s led to plenty of time on the road while campaigning. Barringer went over 350,000 miles on his 2006 Toyota Land Cruiser in October, he told NC Newsline. 
Barringer is a moderate who’s been a healthcare consultant and attorney. He grew up on his family’s tree farm in Lee County. 
He holds degrees from Davidson College, the University of North Carolina School of Law, and Princeton University. 
District 14: LaKesha Womack (D)
Lakesha Womack. right, and Shivawn Mitchell, left. pose with campaign sign. (Photo: Courtesy Womack campaign)
LaKesha Womack beat Republican freshman Tim Moore in a massive upset. She’ll represent the 14th district, which covers areas west of Charlotte.
Moore, the former Speaker of the North Carolina House, was one of the leaders of the Republicans’ 2023 redistricting efforts and carved out a district favorable for himself. Womack leads by 6,415 votes, or 2.22 points.
She founded Womack Consulting Group, helping small businesses and faith-based organizations with strategic plans.
After moving to North Carolina in 2016, Womack and her young son became unhoused when a medical emergency left her hospitalized in intensive care. She has an outstanding felony charge for allegedly failing to return a rental car on time in 2019. 
Womack ended the campaign with only $4,792.77 in cash on hand, according to her pre-election report filed with the Federal Election Commission. 
She graduated from Vanderbilt University.
