name: Nebraska Examiner
title: How Pete Ricketts ended the independent experiment in Nebraska’s US Senate race
description: From the beginning, Republican Nebraska U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts' reelection campaign focused voters' attention on whether Dan Osborn was a Democrat posing as an independent. The move put partisanship front and center in voters' minds.
text:
U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., greets thousands of Nebraskans gathered in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds for a midterms rally featuring President Donald Trump. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — One year ago in a Lincoln bar, Dan Osborn and his campaign manager said Republican U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts would be a better fit as the opponent for their prairie populism pitch than U.S. Sen. Deb Fischer because they would be able to paint Ricketts as “an elite” who doesn’t care about the common person. 
Roughly a year later, unofficial election results show Osborn is on track to lose to Ricketts by the same margin as his unsuccessful bid against Fischer in 2024. Ricketts’ win emerged last week as one of the bright spots for national Republicans as other reliably-red states saw their Republican U.S. Senate candidates swept away by a blue tsunami, including states Trump won by double digits just two years ago. 
Texas, Kansas, Iowa and South Carolina – states that seemed reliably Republican – went blue last week. Osborn, who had national attention in the months leading up to Election Day because his bid was seen as something that could be copied in red states, saw his race become more about him and less about the former governor.


Jessica Flanagain, a partner at Axiom Strategies and one of Nebraska’s most influential GOP political consultants, could see the 2006-style wipeout for Republicans coming in this year’s midterms. Her first-ever campaign was Ricketts’ 2006 bid. She saw him lose by roughly 26 points to Democrat Ben Nelson. 
Twenty years later, she vowed to make sure Ricketts wasn’t swept away and outran the terrible environment for Republicans. The GOP took Osborn’s bid more seriously than they did in 2024, spending every day of the campaign trying to paint Osborn as a Democrat.
“We also knew that wasn’t enough,” Flanagain told the Examiner. “We also had to undermine him on the authenticity front…our theory was that he’s not authentic. He’s no longer a mechanic.” 
She recalls often asking the Ricketts campaign, “How are we going to ruin Dan Osborn’s day today?”


Osborn faced multiple scandals amplified by Ricketts and Republicans, including questions about why he paid himself and his extended family for campaign work, an expenditure that is legal but often comes at a political price. There were also several Osborn audio leaks that Republicans promoted as “proof” he was a Democrat. The audio leaked to media outlets ranged from him saying Trump’s border wall is a “symbol of racism.” to profanity-laced jokes about a hypothetical Trump-supporting Red Cloud resident.  
In his victory speech on election night, Ricketts thanked his campaign for tracking Osborn, saying they were “able to expose” him as “the fraud that he is.”
University of Nebraska-Lincoln political professor Kevin Smith said partisanship was front and center for voters in the Senate race, with Osborn constantly playing defense and trying to prove he wasn’t a secret Democrat. 
“I think it ended up reminding voters, it’s like, ‘Yeah, we’re pretty mad at the Republican Party, but you know what? We don’t like the Democrats either,’” Smith said. “I think in other states, Democrats could speak with a more unified voice, tamp down the partisan issue, and try to pin an incumbent to an unpopular president and focus on the issues that everybody was worried about.”
One example of a unified front was in Texas, where U.S. Senator-elect James Talarcico and Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa often held events together, focusing on economic relief. 
Osborn and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Lynne Walz didn’t campaign together. Nebraska Democrats did choose to step aside and not run their own candidate against Ricketts, instead letting Osborn be the incumbent’s main opponent. 
“Billy Bob in f—— Red Cloud”
Of the campaign’s audio leaks, the one that seemed to do the most damage to the Osborn campaign included his comments about hypothetical Trump-supporting Red Cloud residents. Red Cloud, located in far southern Nebraska, lies within the state’s 3rd Congressional District, one of the most conservative congressional districts in the country.  
In the audio, Osborn said, “Billy Bob in f—— Red Cloud, Nebraska, who lives next to the f—— Trump store as you pull into town and is waving the flag, all he knows is that he’s on the winning team…(Trump has) been so effective at taking Billy Bob and his wife Mary Jane or Mary Jo and telling them … you’re on the winning team. And that’s all they care about, because their lives probably suck so f—— bad.”
Dan Osborn speaks at his town hall at Red Cloud Community Center on Oct. 1, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
The national news media covered the leak. Osborn apologized multiple times, and eventually went out to Red Cloud to speak with residents there. The reaction to his visit was mixed. 
President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance also lent the power of their voices to the Ricketts campaign, hosting rallies in two 3rd Congressional District cities – Grand Island and North Platte, respectively – in the weeks before Election Day.
The Ricketts campaign handed out signs at the rallies that said “I’m Billy Bob!” and “I’m Mary Jane!” – a sign of how impactful the comments were for the race.
In the end, election results show Ricketts got a greater share of votes in the 3rd Congressional District than Fischer did in 2024. While Osborn made gains in the 1st and 2nd Congressional Districts, it wasn’t enough because of his worse 3rd District performance.
 Is the independent experiment over?
During his concession speech on election night, Osborn blamed the newly-formed Nebraska Working People Party for his loss. But even the votes cast for that party’s U.S. Senate candidate, Robin Richards, wouldn’t have been enough for Osborn to win.
Osborn’s campaign manager Camilo Vilaseca told the Examiner the lesson of the campaign is “the same ones that I think we had last time… working-class people deserve a seat at the table in whatever body it is that’s representing them, and that’s what people are looking for.” 
“That the big takeaway…is that is what matters to voters…So, continuing to be a voice and advocate for hardworking Nebraskans and hardworking Americans across the country is who Dan is and what I think resonates,” Vilaseca said. “Just because we weren’t able to win this time does not mean that that work will end…  We’re not taking the possibility of getting independents elected in places that are looking for that sort of representation is over either.” 
Other independents running for U.S. Senate also lost last week. South Dakota’s Brian Bengs lost by 21 points. Montana’s Seth Bodnar lost by 11 points.


Smith, the professor, said the results show there is likely a ceiling for an independent bid because Osborn “could not move the needle” from 2024, even in an unfavorable environment for Republicans. 
“If you can’t beat a Republican incumbent in a statewide race in that electoral environment, it’s hard for me to imagine an electoral environment in which (Osborn) could win,” Smith said. 
Flanagain said it’s “really hard in this polarized environment to run as an independent because you have to answer the questions: Who are you going to vote for for president? Who are you going to caucus with?” 
Osborn had vowed repeatedly he wouldn’t caucus with either party.
“Osborn was more successful as an independent because he had the Democrat machine behind him, but having the Democrat machine behind him is kind of what exposes him,” Flanagain said. 
She added that this cycle showed that Republicans can’t take red states for granted and the GOP can never rest and always has to be organizing.
An independent bid – from Osborn or any other candidate – could struggle with the first step of Osborn’s 2024 and 2026 bids: convincing a party to step aside and not nominate its own candidate. Nebraska Democratic Party Chair Jane Kleeb told a Semafor reporter she doesn’t think she would “do it again in the future.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Dozens of NH school districts adopted tax caps. Now, a balancing act begins.
description: New Hampshire voters took out their affordability frustrations on more than just lawmakers last Tuesday.  As they elected Democrats into eye-popping legislative majorities in Concord Nov. 3, Granite Staters also voted in large numbers for a tax cap over their school districts, a policy many of those same Democrats opposed.  The numbers are decisive. A […]
text:
Lawn signs advocating for and against a tax cap on Election Day in Windham, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt, New Hampshire Bulletin)New Hampshire voters took out their affordability frustrations on more than just lawmakers last Tuesday. 
As they elected Democrats into eye-popping legislative majorities in Concord Nov. 3, Granite Staters also voted in large numbers for a tax cap over their school districts, a policy many of those same Democrats opposed. 
The numbers are decisive. A majority of school districts — 91 out of 168 — cleared the 60% requirement to impose a tax cap, according to a tally of Associated Press results by Chris Maidment, a Republican consultant. In total, 58.8% of voters statewide opted for a cap, the tally shows.
Now, school boards and superintendents in districts with the caps are grappling with a new mandate just in time for the winter budget-crafting season: Produce a budget that respects the will of their voters this November without upsetting them in March.  
For many, it’s a delicate task. Spiking prices for diesel, electricity and healthcare could require school board members to make cuts elsewhere to stay within their new tax caps, some say. Yet many of those board members say they recognize the financial pain that drove their constituents to seek out the tax cap — and want to respond. 
“I feel as though the tax cap is a way of our town saying, ‘OK, we’re feeling a lot of pressure in the wallet, and we’re nervous about food prices, gas prices, pick your poison,’” said Bob Loiacono, chairman of the Wakefield School Board, who was not speaking on behalf of the board. 
Tough calculations
Loiacono and other school board members say they are working to keep the budgets acceptable to voters, even if the cap does lead to cuts. 
“We would do everything possible to make sure it doesn’t affect the education of our students or have an impact on the parents,” he said.
But many school leaders in newly tax-capped districts say they are also confounded by a process that requires them to propose a budget next year without knowing the exact limits of the tax cap itself. 
Under guidance issued by the state Department of Revenue Administration Friday, the department will set the final tax rates — using the previous year’s “tax levy,” or total haul of property taxes, plus any increases in inflation and new taxable property growth — in November 2027. While that is standard practice for the department when setting local property tax rates, for tax cap districts, the timing could mean school boards will be passing a budget in March months before they know the final tax levy to pay for it. 
That will require estimating. 
“It would be as if you decided in March how much money you were going to spend next year, but you weren’t actually going to have your salary until November,” said Pelham School Board Chairman Greg Smith, speaking in his personal capacity.
Many boards say they are still confused, or have heard contradictory information.
“If you put 20 superintendents in the room, you’ll probably get five different answers because there are five different lawyers advising these 20 school districts,” said Fremont Superintendent Brian Stack. 
Smith, a former Republican state representative who retired in 2018, says the tax cap’s restriction to inflation — currently about 3.7% — does not on its own reflect specific expenses that have skyrocketed. 
In Pelham, healthcare costs from HealthTrust, the district’s insurer, climbed 14% this year, Smith said. Transportation costs are expected to spike 20% next year, he added.
“The only way to balance the books is to cut out other things that make the overall pie work out,” Smith said in an interview, speaking for himself and not the school board. 
To lay out what a district like Pelham might cut, it is easiest to begin with what it can’t cut, Smith says. 
The district can’t change staff salaries or benefits, which are mostly negotiated in collective bargaining agreements.
It can’t cut special education funding mandated by law, or transportation, which is required for all K-8 students, and optional for high school students, under state law. 
And it must absorb a number of fixed costs to keep its buildings heated, lit and safe. 
Because it can’t reduce benefits and salaries — and because 70 to 80% of a typical Pelham budget consists of benefits and salaries — if the district must make cuts, it has one clear avenue: cutting positions. 
“The only way to get there is through reducing headcount, ideally through attrition,” Smith said. It’s a situation he says he hopes to avoid this winter.
The timing is tight. School district employment contracts for teachers and other staff are typically issued in March, April and June. That means if a district deems it needs to reduce staff to adhere to its tax cap, it must make those decisions during its budget-writing process over the winter.
“You have to wrap those decisions up in January, because by January you’re having public hearings and deliberative sessions,” said Brian Stack, superintendent of Fremont School District. 
Democratic supporters hold signs outside a polling location at Warner Town Hall during the November 2026 midterm elections. The sign at right urges town voters to “Vote No” on the tax cap ballot question. Their effort was successful. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Concern, optimism
While some school boards are fretting, others say they are ready. 
The Middleton School District has absorbed some of the same spiking costs affecting its peers. In part, it has done so by cutting staff positions and hours in its last budget. But it has also stripped away what School Board Chairwoman Rebecca Eastman-Derrow called unnecessary spending.
“I think the tax cap has really been put in place to limit this frivolous spending that has been occurring within the school district,” Eastman-Derrow said. “With Middleton, we really haven’t had any frivolous spending.”
She noted that the district’s cost per pupil was among the lowest in the state: $19,699.60 for the 2024-2025 school year, below the state average that year of $22,700.
She credited that frugality to the board’s budgeting approach and its communication efforts with constituents.
Eastman-Derrow said she believes the board can pass a budget next year that will fall under the cap, without further staff reductions. But nothing is 100%.
“We’re hoping not,” she said. “But it’s something that is always a possibility. At the end of the day, we have to do what we have to do.”
For its part, Fremont is in a unique position that could spare it difficult decisions, at least for the first year of the cap, said Stack.
That’s because the district, which provides K-8 public education, is already set to save about $500,000 in its next budget due to a planned change in where it sends its high school students, Stack explained. 
Starting next year, the district will no longer send its students and pay tuition to Sanborn Regional High School, Stack said. Instead, it will offer its middle school graduates different choices with cheaper tuition rates. That transition, which will take at least four years to complete before the current cohort of students at Sanborn Regional graduate, will ease any immediate budget woes.
But that cushion may not last long, Stack warned.
“I can’t say my budget’s going to go down a year from now,” he said. “So I may be in this situation.” 
Stack disagrees with the notion that a tax cap will allow a district to maintain the status quo from the year before. Because of rising expenses like healthcare and diesel, it could result in cuts, particularly in smaller districts. 
Districts also face unpredictable costs, like incoming students with special education requirements or sudden building failures. 
For years, school boards have sought to thread a needle between paying for existing services and setting aside funds for emergencies while keeping taxes low. The tax cap will shrink that needle and require delicate balancing, school board members say. 
“Unfortunately, there are too many uncontrollable costs, and from the standpoint of a really small district, those uncontrollable costs get magnified so much more,” Stack said.
For a district, the consequences of overestimating the tax cap could be high. If the Department of Revenue Administration calculates a lower amount than the budget accounted for, the district might need to make emergency cuts, months into the 2027-2028 school year.
“Unless you have some other revenue stream, which most public schools do not,” Stack said. “So most superintendents are trying to use a best-guess estimate of what they think it will be, erring on the side of caution.”
Override chances murky
The tax cap law allows voters to override the cap for a specific budget, provided 60% of voters at a district meeting choose to do so.
But it is unclear how many New Hampshire school districts with new tax caps will pursue that route this spring, especially in the cap’s first year. Many superintendents and school board members say they want to respect the will of their voters and present budgets that adhere to the cap, even if it means tough decisions.
In Massachusetts, where statewide tax caps have applied to whole municipalities and their school budgets since Proposition 2.5 passed in 1980, state data indicates that a relatively small percentage of cities or towns successfully pass override measures each year. Of the state’s 351 municipalities, 57 put an override question on the ballot in fiscal year 2026 — about 16% of all cities and towns. Among the municipalities that attempted overrides that year, about 49% were successful.
Those numbers fluctuate; in 2006, for instance, more than 160 Massachusetts municipalities put override measures on the ballot, and again, about half of them passed.
Meanwhile, since 2000, 22 Massachusetts municipalities have voted to reduce their tax caps below the 2.5% allowable increase set out in the law, a process known as an “underride.” 
Stack stressed that the Fremont School District will likely not be requesting an override. But if it ever does down the line, he has an idea how to sell voters.
To pass an override, the district would present a budget that meets the tax cap but contains cuts, and add the most important of those cut programs into a separate warrant article, Stack said. Then, the board could make the case to voters to pass the article by 60% and override the cap if they want those items, he said.
In Wakefield, Loiacono plans to follow the cap, not resort to an override. 
Doing that won’t be easy, he admitted. It could require a number of uncomfortable questions for the K-8 school district, which sends its high schoolers to Spaulding High School in Rochester. 
“What’s the tuition to Spaulding?” Loiacono said. “What’s the transportation cost to Spaulding? Can we afford our pre-school? There’s so many items that are part of the budget that could end up having a spotlight on them.” 
Making taxes ‘a little bit harder’
The success of the tax cap initiatives on Election Day came after years of unsuccessful attempts to pass similar caps at annual school meetings, and after months of Democratic opposition to the law that put the question on the Nov. 3 ballot, House Bill 1300.
Democrats argued the question was confusing, and dealt with a matter that should be debated and passed at annual school district meetings in March, not in a ballot box. 
But Rep. Daniel Popovici-Muller said putting the measure on the November ballot was more democratic. The higher turnout in November would allow districts and school boards to take a better measure of what their constituents wanted, he said. 
Speaking outside the Windham High School on Election Day, Popovici-Muller brushed off any concerns over potential budgeting problems caused by tax caps. If school boards wanted to spend more, they could always present and advocate for a 60% override option, he noted. 
“All that the tax cap is about is making it a bit harder for the school boards to raise taxes,” he said. “I don’t think that making it a bit harder to increase property taxes is such a bad thing in New Hampshire today.”
Popovici-Muller, who formerly chaired the Windham School Board, recalled campaigning for a $39 million renovation of the Golden Brook School in that role, an expense that required a 60% vote because it involved a bond. While the measure passed in 2017, it only did so after multiple attempts, Popovici-Muller said, which he said required the board to thoroughly make its case.
One Londonderry voter brought personal experience to her vote on the cap. When Cathy Himmel was in high school in Massachusetts in 1980, voters passed Proposition 2.5, which applied the state’s default tax cap that stands today. Himmel saw immediate cuts to school districts. But those new restraints didn’t stop Himmel from later pursuing teaching herself, eventually capping off a 35-year career, retiring and moving to Londonderry.
On the one hand, she said, some Massachusetts schools initially cut music and art programs. On the other: “I think it has helped the schools stay in some kind of a line.” Throughout her career, Himmel declined to participate in teacher-union-led opposition campaigns to the caps.
“I wanted to have a positive effect on my students,” she said. “I wanted to be a good teacher, a good individual, contribute to society. That’s a much smaller personal contribution type picture compared to the administrative, political, money-based environment I had to live in.”
On Nov. 3, Himmel voted for a tax cap in Londonderry. The effort fell short, gaining just 51% of the vote there. But to Himmel, facing a mortgage, increasing home insurance and a recent $5,000 roof repair, her vote was necessary.
“The circumstance is not good for anybody,” she said. “Everybody’s taxes are high.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Luke Bronin comes to Washington for new member crash course
description: Luke Bronin, the newest member of CT's congressional delegation, joins one of the largest freshman classes after Democrats swept the midterms.
text:
Luke Bronin arrived in Washington, D.C., on Sunday, one of more than 100 newly elected members who will join Congress next year. They toured the House chamber, heard from leaders of both parties and attended receptions.
But Monday was all business — the start of a 10-day crash-course orientation in procedure, and unwritten rules, for new legislators.
Even with a long day ahead, Bronin flashed a smile as he descended the staircase to a windowless area of the U.S. Capitol to meet reporters and new colleagues in a legislative body that has been paralyzed much of the time by partisan gridlock.
The orientation is a lengthy exercise in getting up to speed with the inner workings of Congress, learning how to staff and run an office, and navigating a large complex resembling a labyrinth that trips up even the most veteran congresspeople and staffers.
But as they entered the building on Monday morning for a long day of programming and trainings, there was a first-day-of-school energy, particularly for Democrats who scored massive wins last week that will power them back into the House and Senate majority next year.
That excitement was palpable as Bronin and other members-elect spoke to throngs of cameras and reporters and shook hands with their new colleagues as they packed into a large auditorium for the day.
Bronin will be the only new member of Connecticut’s all-Democratic delegation, which will enter Congress next year as part of the majority and with sizable influence and seniority for a small contingent. He and others will get sworn into the 120th Congress on Jan. 3.
The former mayor of Hartford handily won Connecticut’s 1st Congressional District, which has been represented by U.S. Rep. John Larson since 1999. The harder feat was during the primary, when he was one of three Democratic challengers trying to unseat the incumbent. Bronin defeated Larson in the August primary in what he described as a “political earthquake.”
Now that he’s in Washington for the next week and a half, Bronin is most excited for meeting his cohorts, including many who share the same titles as him: mayor and military veteran.

U.S. Rep.-elect Luke Bronin attends new member orientation in Washington on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. The Connecticut Democrat will get sworn in as a member of Congress in January. Credit: Lisa Hagen / CT Mirror

“The most important thing so far has been meeting the members of this freshman class. It’s an extraordinary group of people — veterans, firefighters, mayors, small business owners, healthcare workers, and all people who feel a real sense of urgency and mission,” Bronin said as he stepped out from seminars and trainings at the Capitol. 
“It’s been fun talking to so many people who nobody expected to win. And in many cases, they didn’t expect to win,” he continued. “But they felt it was important to stand up and contest a seat, often in deep-red territory. And the number of people who are in that position is a reflection of just how strong a statement this election was.”
Bronin has never held federal office, but he’s not a total stranger to Washington. He served in the U.S. Department of the Treasury during President Barack Obama’s first term in a role that helped establish the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
He’ll be part of one of the largest freshman classes. Democrats are preparing to navigate an ideologically diverse majority with different factions trying to steer the agenda for the next two years. That’s on top of a delicate balance the party will need to strike between pushing back on the Trump administration and passing legislation that is likely to face a veto.
“To me, I just try to bring the same mindset that I did to the job of mayor, which is, you start with what the problem is and then you try to build a coalition of people who are interested in fixing it,” Bronin said. “And you don’t let the perfect be the enemy of the good, but you be bold about what you’re aiming to fix and do.”
Bronin will be meeting dozens of new people and colleagues over the course of the next 10 days. But some of them will be familiar faces — like Connecticut’s delegation.
While Hartford’s mayor, Bronin worked with every member of Congress who currently represents Connecticut. He said he plans to see his future colleagues while he’s in town through next week. That includes meetings to build relationships with fellow freshman members, including those who are mayors and veterans, on the sidelines of the orientation.
When asked if he’ll meet or speak with Larson while he’s in town, Bronin said he wasn’t sure, but, “I hope so.” Bronin said his office has reached out to the congressman’s and the two are working together on the transition.
Bronin is making some moves while giving himself the chance to figure things out in the coming months.
He still has time to sort out his committee assignments. The tax-writing House Ways and Means Committee may be on his radar in the long term, Bronin said, but he’s also previously expressed interest in committees with jurisdiction over issues like healthcare, housing and electricity and more general oversight authority.
Members representing Connecticut’s 1st Congressional District have had a seat on the House Ways and Means Committee since the early 1980s, including Larson and his predecessor, Democrat Barbara Kennelly. Larson currently serves as the Democratic ranking member on the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security.

U.S. Rep.-elect Luke Bronin speaks during a post-Election Day news briefing at the state Capitol in Hartford on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / ct mirror

Bronin won’t get seated on committees until next year, when the new session begins. In the meantime, he’s joining the New Democrats Coalition, which has a membership of about half of the House Democratic caucus. Three members of Connecticut’s House delegation — U.S. Reps. Joe Courtney, Jim Himes and Jahana Hayes — are already part of the group.
The group describes itself as a center-left coalition of Democrats who want to “work across the aisle and across the Capitol to advance innovative, inclusive, and forward-looking policies.” Its membership could swell to more than 140 members next year, according to Politico.
The New Democrat Coalition falls somewhere in the middle of the moderate Blue Dog Coalition and the Congressional Progressive Caucus on the left. Bronin left the door open to other possible memberships but said he doesn’t feel confined to a specific group or policy platform.
“I am, at heart, a policy wonk, and I enjoy the policy conversations in the New Dems Coalition,” Bronin said. “But I don’t feel bound to any particular platform or ideology other than what I expressed in my own campaign, which is I think we have to be serious about stopping corruption and making some fundamental reforms to make this kind of corruption impossible in the future.”
As they prepare for the majority, Connecticut Democrats have argued they can’t squander the opportunity afforded by their midterm wins.
“If we want last night’s election to be remembered as more than a historic backlash to a corrupt president, then we need to get to work, solving problems that the American people desperately want us to see us solve,” Bronin said in press conference in Hartford last Wednesday.
For Bronin, that means accountability as it relates to corruption and self-enrichment related to the administration while pursuing legislation to ban members of Congress from trading stocks, along with “serious” efforts on campaign finance reform.
Even with big majorities next year, Democrats will still need to contend with a president who can wield a veto pen. And they’ll need to negotiate with Republicans who will still have some leverage on must-pass legislation like government funding.
But Bronin argues that will show where Republicans are as Democrats look to build momentum into 2028.
“If the man in the White House vetoes those things,” Bronin said last week, “then it will be more evidence that he doesn’t give a damn about what the American people want.”
As Rep. Hakeem Jeffries — who hopes to become the first Black speaker of the House next year — starts to outline House Democrats’ agenda, Bronin said the party will need to focus on both oversight of the Trump administration and the pursuit of legislative efforts to address cost-of-living issues that were paramount for voters this year.
Bronin said he’ll support Jeffries for speaker, though the New York Democrat faces some pushback within the incoming caucus. During the primary campaign, Jeffries came to the Hartford-based district to support Larson when he faced three opponents, including Bronin.
“I think we need to do both,” Bronin said on Monday. “I think the oversight work is critical to the anti-corruption work, and that is substantive policy effort.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Commentary: New Hampshire employers have spoken. Here is what they said.
description: Workers cannot find homes they can afford. Parents are turning down jobs because they cannot find childcare. Recent graduates are choosing cities like Chicago over Manchester because the rent is lower. We heard employers trying everything they can to grow and make the state a better place for business and residents. But they cannot do […]
text:
"To the legislators taking their seats in January: The employers in your districts are not asking you to solve everything at once. They are asking you to keep moving." (Photo by Dana Wormald/New Hampshire Bulletin)Workers cannot find homes they can afford. Parents are turning down jobs because they cannot find childcare. Recent graduates are choosing cities like Chicago over Manchester because the rent is lower. We heard employers trying everything they can to grow and make the state a better place for business and residents. But they cannot do it alone.
Earlier this year, New Hampshire Businesses for Social Responsibility sat down with 44 businesses across the state. We heard from manufacturers and restaurateurs, from small family businesses and large regional employers. We asked them what was getting in the way of growing their businesses and keeping their workers. They told us the same things, in their own words, regardless of where they were located or what industry they were in.
With the election behind us and a new legislative session ahead, here are their main takeaways.
What the numbers are not telling you
New Hampshire ranks sixth in the country for business friendliness. We are proud of that, and we should be. Our low taxes and steady regulatory environment are genuine strengths, and the employers we work with value them.
But the same national ranking that puts us sixth for business friendliness puts us 43rd for infrastructure and 43rd for the economy. That gap tells the real story. Low taxes get a business to look at New Hampshire. Homes that workers can afford, childcare that lets parents show up, schools that build the next generation of workers, and energy costs that do not eat into the bottom line are what get a business to stay.
These are not worker issues. They are business issues, and they need to be given the attention they are due if New Hampshire wants to remain economically competitive. That is what we are asking the new Legislature to take seriously.
The issues that cannot wait
The advocates that have been working on housing, childcare, public education and energy in this state for years have built a strong foundation. What employers are telling us is that these issues are not separate problems with separate solutions. They are connected, and progress on any one of them depends on progress on all of them.
On housing, the state has taken meaningful steps, and implementation is underway. But the gap between what workers earn and what it costs to rent or buy in New Hampshire has not closed. Median two-bedroom rent has risen nearly 60% since 2015. New developments marketed as affordable routinely rent for $2,000 or more against wages of $18 to $19 an hour. The math does not work, and employers are feeling it every time they make an offer that gets turned down. Restoring funding to the housing programs that were cut in recent sessions and establishing dedicated revenue streams for housing investment are the practical next steps.
On childcare, the new business tax credit was a meaningful step forward, and there is more work to do. The largest gap in the childcare system right now is not the number of available slots. It is the shortage of childcare workers to fill them. Without enough people to do the work, new capacity simply shifts children from one center to another without solving the underlying problem. Raising the childcare scholarship threshold so that more working families can access the system that already exists is an achievable step this session, and keeping childcare workers in the profession through better wages and benefits is the conversation that needs to follow.
On public education, the foundation matters more than most people realize. Employers are connecting the dots between what happens in middle school STEM classrooms and what shows up in their hiring pipeline a decade later. If students disengage before they reach high school, the skilled workforce that life sciences, manufacturing and technology depend on never materializes. Getting that foundation right, starting with making sure students have the stability they need to learn, is the long-term investment the state’s economy cannot afford to shortchange.
On energy, New Hampshire businesses pay among the highest electricity rates in the country. At the same time, state and federal actions have weakened or blocked the incentives and policies that would allow businesses to invest in renewable energy and gain greater control over their own costs. Net metering reform is a concrete, near-term opportunity to change that. Giving businesses the ability to generate and use their own energy allows them to be competitive regionally, and the Legislature can act on it this session.
What the new Legislature needs to prioritize
New Hampshire has made real progress on these issues, and the employers we represent recognize that. The transportation plan that passed with overwhelming support, the childcare tax credit, the housing reforms now taking effect: These are signs that the state can act when it decides to. The question for this session is whether that momentum continues.
There is reason for optimism. Gov. Kelly Ayotte has named housing, childcare and energy as her own priorities for the session ahead. Democratic legislative leaders have made affordability the centerpiece of their agenda. For once, the conditions exist across party lines to make real progress on the things employers have been asking for. That alignment is rare, and it should not be wasted.
To the legislators taking their seats in January: The employers in your districts are not asking you to solve everything at once. They are asking you to keep moving. Solutions built with all the voices at the table from the start tend to hold. They do not get reversed when the political winds shift, because they were never purely political to begin with. They were practical. Design them that way from the beginning, with business at the table, and they will last.
New Hampshire Businesses for Social Responsibility will be at the table, with the stories, the data and the voices of employers to make the case. Because when New Hampshire’s businesses succeed, everyone in the state benefits.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: 89-year-old ‘last Jewish gangster’ charms Kansas City-area audience with tales and takes
description: Myron Sugerman, the 89-year-old self-proclaimed “last Jewish mobster,” displayed an easy way with most everyone, whether chatting over warm cinnamon rolls at Best Regards Bakery, or speaking to an engaged audience of roughly 100 people at a local synagogue. He flirted with abandon, had people scurrying in search of a restaurant serving pasta e fagioli, […]
text:
Myron Sugerman, author of "The Chronicles of The Last Jewish Gangster: From Meyer to Myron," speaks at Overland Park's Kehilath Israel Synagogue. (Photo by Mark McCormick for Kansas Reflector)Myron Sugerman, the 89-year-old self-proclaimed “last Jewish mobster,” displayed an easy way with most everyone, whether chatting over warm cinnamon rolls at Best Regards Bakery, or speaking to an engaged audience of roughly 100 people at a local synagogue.
He flirted with abandon, had people scurrying in search of a restaurant serving pasta e fagioli, and seemed pleasantly surprised by the warmth of the Kansas Citians who received him.
“Back in New Jersey,” he said, “if nobody insults you, it means they don’t like you.” 
For Sugerman, his years in the mob were part La Cosa Nostra and part Kosher Nostra.
A bit profane but definitely endearing, Sugerman visited Overland Park’s Kehilath Israel Synagogue with stories of intrigue and to sell his book, “The Chronicles of The Last Jewish Gangster: From Meyer to Myron.” He spun vivid stories from a chair on stage, then signed books and chatted for hours.
Sugerman, like many of us, balances two sides. His duality, however, took him from Newark, New Jersey, to South America, to Africa, to Europe, through two assassination attempts, and to a startling perspective about the future of Jewish life in America. 
Amid the intrigue and double-crosses — dealing with people such as John Gotti, Tony “Bananas” Caponigro and Carlo Gambino — Sugerman’s escapades sometimes blurred the line between gangster and patriot. 
Fighting Nazis and antisemites after World War II, Sugerman said the the mob would pack weapons and ammunition in crates marked as farm equipment or sewing machines and send them off in support of the then-fledgling Jewish state of Israel.
He said he once helped Nazi hunter Simon Wiesenthal, who tried to track down the ghoulish Nazi Josef Mengele, known as the “Angel of Death.” Wiesenthal pursued Mengele but never found him. 
In the fight against Nazis, “whether you were a pimp, a gangster, a cigarette girl or a prostitute, if you heard anything, you told,” Sugerman said.
Myron Sugerman signs copies of his book after an event in Overland Park. (Photo by Mark McCormick for Kansas Reflector)
Born in 1938 in Newark, by age 21 he followed his father into the family business — coin-operated amusements. Like his father, Barney “Sugie” Sugerman, Myron sold and operated slot machines, jukeboxes and anything else that entertained people in bars, nightclubs and hangouts.
He entertained the weekend synagogue audience for hours.
Someone asked how early he’d joined the mob.
“As I came out my mother’s womb,” Sugerman replied.
He told a boxing story in which a Jewish referee told a knocked-down fighter (who the referee thought was Jewish) that he was getting a “Jewish 10-count” so he could get up and continue the fight.
“You say one — then you wait a half-hour.”
When the fighter protested that he wasn’t Jewish, the ref said quickly, “Oh s***! Seven, eight, nine, 10, you’re out!” 
It was the fight for the Jewish state that animated a good part of Sugerman’s question-and-answer session following his speech. 
“We have about 25 years left in this country,” Sugerman told the audience, adding that antisemitism is as bad now as it has ever been, and getting worse. “I’m not trying to be negative, but I am realistic. The future of the Jew is in Israel.”
He said every Jewish home should have a weapon and know how to use it. An audience member named some Jewish gun clubs, including, “Bagels and Bullets” and “Lox and Loaded.”
After signing books and chatting up every person who’d waited in line for a book at the synagogue, he and a circle of friends hit Johnny Cascone’s Italian restaurant, where the search for pasta e fagioli continued.
In the dim restaurant, conversation turned to politics. Sugerman said he knew members of the Kushner family (Jared is the president’s son-unlaw), that his father knew most of the police officers from Newark, and that he remembered Rudy Giuliani as a gang-busting district attorney and good mayor. 
Politicians and gangsters often align. They know everyone in the neighborhood. They live by their wits and think fast on their feet. They’ve mastered observation. And since both politics and crime are blood sports, fear and violence serve as tireless aides.
During the day’s conversations, there were things Sugerman couldn’t “give two s***s about,” but his charisma balanced the occasional bawdy impulses. 
He was funny. 
He asked someone at the table to phone a wealthy relative so he could joke about running up a $1,000 bill and desperately needing money not only for the food, but also for a 20% gratuity.
He showed social dexterity.
When a waiter approached, Sugerman asked him where he was from. When he learned the young man hailed from Mexico, he began speaking to him in fluent Spanish at each interaction.
As he headed for the airport, he handed out his business card. It bore a simple elegance. His name, Myron Sugerman, is printed in cursive on the thin, white card with a wax paper feel.
Under his name and next to his phone number, his email address began with “charming@…”
Mark McCormick is a journalist and a nonprofit executive. He’s also the author of four books including “Barry Sanders: Now You See Him” (a New York Times bestseller), “Some Were Paupers. Some Were Kings: Dispatches from Kansas,” and his latest, “Kansas Matters: America’s Social Faultlines.” Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Incoming Ohio AG says he’ll put pocketbook, paycheck issues front and center
description: As part of Tuesday’s blue tsunami, Democrat John Kulewicz was elected to be Ohio’s next attorney general. He says he plans to make a priority of issues that affect the livelihood of Ohioans, many of whom are struggling. As the state’s lawyer and its top law enforcement officer, the Ohio attorney general has sweeping powers. […]
text:
Ohio Attorney General-elect John J. Kulewicz. (Photo from campaign.)As part of Tuesday’s blue tsunami, Democrat John Kulewicz was elected to be Ohio’s next attorney general. He says he plans to make a priority of issues that affect the livelihood of Ohioans, many of whom are struggling.
As the state’s lawyer and its top law enforcement officer, the Ohio attorney general has sweeping powers. The office has 1,400 employees working in 30 distinct sections, from antitrust to workers compensation.
Kulewicz, a 72-year-old graduate of Yale Law School, comes to the office after winning by less than a percentage point over Republican Keith Faber. But he said he was elected by voters seeking a change.
It’s no secret that under solidly Republican rule, Ohio state government has been plagued by several high-profile corruption scandals over the past 15 years. And anger over corruption was a big factor in Democrats’ resounding success on Tuesday night.
“There was a general sense among the people that we need to correct things through these elections and that it involved bringing in new people,” Kulewicz said in a phone interview.
He added that he visited all 88 counties and tried to explain to voters that the attorney general could help them by making things fairer. 
“I focused on the economic responsibilities of the attorney general and what that could mean to people in Ohio,” he said.
Across the country, voters appeared to see a nexus between their own economic struggles and public corruption that enriched connected special interests. Between 2018 and 2020 Ohio was a case study.
Akron-based FirstEnergy paid $61 million in bribes to elect a Republican majority that made Larry Householder of Glenford speaker. From that perch he shepherded a $1.3 billion ratepayer-funded bailout for the utility.
After the FBI broke open the conspiracy, Householder got a 20-year prison sentence on two others who were implicated died by suicide.
As attorney general, Kulewicz would have to oversee a second state trial of FirstEnergy’s top executives after the first ended in a hung jury. So he’s limited in what he can say about the case before taking office.
But he said as a general matter, corruption is the consumer issue that voters take it to be.
“No. 1, it’s bad for the economy,” Kulewicz said. “We all pay a price for it, and I think that finally people got fed up enough with it and believed that it’s time for somebody who’s going to clean up the state government.” 
He added that he also wanted to fight for consumers on other fronts, such as “consumer fraud, wage theft, monopoly pricing, utility rate discrimination; the things that hurt our paychecks or our pocketbooks.”
Ohio has a strong, state-level antitrust law, and the attorney general has a division tasked with enforcing it. 
In 2023, former AG Dave Yost used the law to sue a giant health conglomerate, accusing it of unlawfully driving up the cost of prescription drugs purchased by the state. It remains pending.
Kulewicz said he also will use the Antitrust Division on behalf of Ohio consumers.
“The attorney general has broad investigative and subpoena power when it comes to the enforcement of the antitrust laws, and I intend to use that to the fullest extent,” he said. “I want to focus on sectors of the economy that deal with the necessities of our lives. Our food. Our fuel. Those kinds of things.”
After President Donald Trump signed a Republican bill slashing Medicaid spending in July 2025, his administration and Republican state-level officials started hyping allegations of Medicaid fraud, often in blue states. Critics called it an attempt to refocus voters’ anger over Trump’s healthcare cuts and rising healthcare costs.
When U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche came to Ohio in July to tout the Trump anti-fraud effort, no mention was made of health conglomerates that Yost has accused of overbilling Ohio by tens of millions of dollars.
Kulewicz said he wants to determine what is fact and what is fiction in the Trump administration claims.
“The compelling thing to me is that there are allegations of billions of dollars of Medicaid provider fraud, but the prosecutions only amount to millions of dollars,” he said. “So there’s a big discrepancy. I want to find out why.”
As part of the FirstEnergy scandal, Gov.-elect Mike DeWine and Lt. Gov.-elect Jon Husted met with the company’s top executives on Dec. 18, 2018 to discuss whether Sam Randazzo would be acceptable to be chairman of the industry regulator, the Public Utility Commission of Ohio. The executives drove straight from that meeting to Randazzo’s German Village condo and negotiated a $4.3 million bribe, the company later conceded.
From his perch as chairman, Randazzo helped write the corrupt bailout legislation. After he was charged, he died by suicide.
But even before that episode, the PUCO had a long history of granting utilities billions of dollars worth of upcharges that the Ohio Supreme Court later deemed illegal. Even so, the regulator didn’t force the utilities to give the money back to ratepayers.
Kulewicz said he would use the powers of the AGs office to ensure that the PUCO protects Ohio ratepayers.
“There are two things the attorney general can do,” he said. “No. 1, make sure that we appoint a Consumers’ Counsel board that’s going to name an effective Ohio Consumers’ Counsel to protect the interests of residential ratepayers.
“Secondly, the attorney general represents the state of Ohio, which is a consumer of utilities and has standing to challenge the fairness of the rates.”
As a candidate, Kulewicz filed a complaint with the Ohio Inspector General about possible conflicts of interest at JobsOhio, the state’s quasi-private economic development authority. The chairman of the JobsOhio board is a lobbyist with clients that have received millions from JobsOhio and even more from the state.
But prior to taking office, Kulewicz was circumspect about how he might deal with the controversial agency.
“The complaint that I filed with the inspector general speaks for itself,” he said. “But to the extent that there are other alleged conflicts in the state government, I want to explore those and point them out where necessary and do something about them.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: High court considers sovereign immunity claim for some sex abuse lawsuits
description: Maryland's highest court was asked Monday to consider whether the state still enjoys immunity against about 1,300 institutional sex abuse claims that occurred before 1982, despite a 2023 law that eliminated time barriers for someone to file an abuse claim.
text:
The Maryland Supreme Court building. (File Photo by Bennett Leckrone/Maryland Matters)Maryland’s highest court heard arguments on an appeal Monday that will affect 1,300 lawsuits filed under the Child Victims Act.
The 2023 law effectively eliminated time barriers for someone to file a court claim of institutional sex abuse. At issue are the roughly 1,300 cases in which the alleged sexual assaults took place before 1982, a time when the state had absolute immunity from lawsuits. The Supreme Court of Maryland is being asked to decide if the General Assembly, when it passed the landmark 2023 law, clearly and knowingly waived that immunity.
Jonathan Massey, attorney for a plaintiff known only as J.C., said the waiver of damage caps in the 2023 law are proof of the legislature’s intent.
The change “is the waiver of state sovereign immunity, and make changes that assume there will be a damages cap, assuming there will be liability to the state, right? That’s why you need a damages cap because there’s going to be liability to the state. I don’t think the legislature was silent in 2023 on the issue of sovereign immunity,” Massey said during oral arguments.
Monday’s appeal involves a claim of sexual abuse from 1977, when J.C. was a patient at the old Prince George’s Hospital Center, where she claimed a doctor molested her during a stay there.
State claims immunity from some sexual abuse lawsuits filed under the Child Victims Act

Lawyers for the state argued that the state at the time was protected by sovereign immunity. Prior to 1982, the state could not face civil lawsuits, and the state’s lawyers asked a Prince George’s County judge to dismiss the case on those grounds.
Attorneys representing the state filed roughly 200 motions to dismiss cases involving claims before July 1, 1982. The state has argued that the legislature must expressly waive the 40-year old immunity provision, something they said the 2023 law did not do.
Judges at the Circuit Court level granted four motions at the time the appeal was filed with the state’s highest court.
The Prince George’s County court denied the state’s motion without a hearing or explanation. But judges in Frederick County and Baltimore City have agreed with the state. Each dismissed cases under the sovereign immunity argument.
The Supreme Court’s ruling on the issue comes with a dollar sign attached.
Cases involving allegations occurring before 1982 comprise about 11% of the 12,000 cases that have been filed under the Child Victims Act. The 2023 law capped damages against the state at $890,000 per occurrence, but the definition of an “occurrence” is still being debated.
The full extent of the state’s potential liability has never been publicly stated. A rough estimate shows potentially budget-busting consequences.
If each plaintiff alleged just one occurrence and received the maximum award, the potential liability to the state could be about $11 billion. That estimate is nearly four times the structural budget gap projected for the fiscal 2028 budget to be introduced in January.
The potential payout could go up if a court or jury defines “occurrence” as each instance of abuse, rather than bundling instances based on any number of related circumstances. Settlements could reduce the potential liability.
If lawyers for the state are successful in getting the pre-1982 cases blocked, it would reduce the state’s potential liability by “more than a billion dollars,” the Office of the Attorney General argued in a filing earlier this year.
Budget officials ask agencies to tighten belts, including a 10% cut scenario

During the nearly hour-long oral arguments Monday, justices seemed focused on whether the Child Victims Act waived sovereign immunity in an “unambiguous manner.” And if that was not the case, could legislative intent be used to rule that the General Assembly had in fact waived the immunity.
“If their intent was to undo sovereign immunity, isn’t it a little odd that they didn’t mention it?” Chief Justice Matthew Fader asked Massey during the hearing.
Massey argued that the General Assembly made it clear through setting caps and through its debates that it understood what it was doing and the potential costs.
But Fader wondered aloud if anyone in the legislature was aware of the immunity which ended in the 1980s and the passage of the Maryland Tort Claims Act.
“What it doesn’t necessarily indicate to me is an intent to undo a sovereign immunity protection that they seemingly were just unaware of,” Fader said. “And if that’s the case, if they thought that liability would go back before 1982 because they just weren’t aware that there was a sovereign immunity protection in place, that doesn’t seem to me to be an an intent to undo that sovereign immunity protection. It’s just an unawareness of it.”
Ryan Dietrich, an assistant attorney general, told the justices that nothing in the law could be interpreted as a waiver. Legislative intent would not be enough.
“I think what we heard from a friend on the other side about the legislative history is they say we think, we assume, and when we think and when we assume, that’s hallmarks of ambiguity,” Dietrich said.
“To the extent that the legislature did not speak clearly, unambiguously, and expressly, this court must err on the side of saying that sovereign immunity has not been waived, and send it back to the legislature to say, ‘What did you really mean?'” he said.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ukrainian TPS holders in Ohio left in limbo after federal non-decision decision
description: While most Ohio lawmakers were out campaigning for reelection last month, Ohio state Rep. Sean Brennan, D-Parma, was driving across Poland’s border with Ukraine to deliver a couple dozen ambulances and medical supplies. The trip was part of Ukraine Focus’s 19th mission to Ukraine. The Virginia-based nonprofit sources and delivers ambulances, among other prog[...]
text:
Ohio state Rep. Sean Brennan, D-Parma, with an ambulance to be delivered to Ukraine. (Photo courtesy of Sean Brennan)While most Ohio lawmakers were out campaigning for reelection last month, Ohio state Rep. Sean Brennan, D-Parma, was driving across Poland’s border with Ukraine to deliver a couple dozen ambulances and medical supplies.
The trip was part of Ukraine Focus’s 19th mission to Ukraine. The Virginia-based nonprofit sources and delivers ambulances, among other programs to support to the war-torn country. The United Ukrainian Organizations of Ohio helped organize participants from Ohio.
“We delivered around 50 ambulances, as I recall,” Brennan explained. “Along with other vehicles, along with humanitarian and medical supplies for the Ukrainian military to use in the in their war efforts to maintain their sovereignty, which they’re entitled to and deserve.
Brennan’s Parma-area district has the largest Ukrainian-American population in the state, and many Ukrainians sheltering in the U.S. while the war continues have settled in the area. Those families face an uncertain future.
Roughly 100,000 Ukrainians are living in the U.S. under Temporary Protected Status — the same protections recently terminated for nearly 350,000 Haitians living in the U.S.
Ukrainians’ TPS status lapsed on Oct. 19. But rather than formally extending or ending protections, the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services did nothing. In a terse statement, the agency said an announcement “will be made at the appropriate time,” and until then, TPS holders can maintain their work authorization.
“They’ve put the people in limbo,” United Ukrainian Organizations of Ohio President George Jaskiw said.
“Is this just a reprieve before the election and then after election the hammer will come down? That’s what somebody asked me,” he said. “I have no answer. I don’t know what’s in the mind of (Department of Homeland Security) administration.”
Volunteers, including George Jaskiw (second from left) and Ohio state Rep. Sean Brennan, D-Parma, (second from right) delivering ambulances in Ukraine. (Photo courtesy of Sean Brennan)
The trip
Brennan’s European sojourn started in Prague. He and several other volunteers (including Jaskiw) picked up ambulances and drove through Krakow in Poland, and then on to Lviv in Western Ukraine. Brennan was struck by the extent to which Ukrainians were carrying on with their lives despite four years of armed conflict.
“Now that being said, there were signs of war,” Brennan said, “There were a couple of mornings where the air raid sirens went off, and we had to go down into the bunker of our hotel for our safety.”
Security was tight at the border, he said, and they passed check points for several miles on their way to Lviv. After they arrived, the volunteers handed over the vehicles to members of the Ukrainian armed forces and toured a handful of the civilian efforts to support the war.
“We got to sit down with them and tie some of the ties onto the nets that are used on the front to camouflage vehicles and other equipment from the drones,” Brennan described. “We also visited a place where they dry food. They dry fruits, vegetables, and meat to create (meals ready to eat) for soldiers on the front. That was pretty amazing.”
But most surprising, he said, was a dilapidated Soviet-era building.
“They took us into the building onto one of the floors,” Brennan described. “They opened up the door, and there were about I would say 100 3-D printers making items for drones.”
“It was something out of a spy novel.”
While the volunteers were delivering ambulances, news broke that President Trump was going to rescind sanctions on Russian diesel and purchase millions of barrels from the country. The administration’s stated justification for the deal was to lower fuel costs.
“Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority,” President Trump said in a Truth Social post.
Experts doubt those purchases will materially affect the cost of fuel in the U.S., but they does offer a financial lifeline to the Russian government.
“People were dumbfounded,” Brennan said. “As was I, and I think I’m speaking on behalf of everybody that was on our trip.”
“Russia Supports Iran,” he added. “So, you know any American dollars that go to Russia for diesel, is going to be shot right back at us, and I don’t think anybody wants that.”
The TPS legal process
In Ohio, Ukrainian families are waiting anxiously to see what happens with their immigration status. USCIS’s non-decision grants them a reprieve, but not much of one.
Aleksandar Cuic is a law professor at Case Western Reserve University who works with the school’s immigration law clinic.
“I’ve never seen them not do anything,” he said. “Historically they’ve either terminated it, took away the designation, or they’ve extended it. That’s always historically what’s been done.”
Federal law requires the Secretary of Homeland Security to consult with “appropriate agencies” about the conditions in a country before terminating its TPS designation.
“TPS for Ukraine is due to a war,” Cuic said. “Unless they’re going to determine that the war is over or it’s safe to go back. That’s something that they have to do. They have to kind of show that hey, the conditions, why we created TPS, are now gone.”
At least on paper, it’s a thoughtful process, but in practice, it doesn’t always work out that way. In June, the U.S. Supreme Court allowed the Department of Homeland Security to end protections for more than 400,000 Haitians and Syrians living in the United States.
In Haiti, gangs control 90% of the country and five million people can’t get enough to eat.  Attorneys challenging the revocation of TPS noted the U.S. State Department warns travelers that “no part of Syria is safe from violence.”
Then just days before the court issued its ruling, attorneys representing TPS holders uncovered documents indicating then-Secretary Kristi Noem never actually consulted the U.S. State Department about conditions in Haiti. The attorneys petitioned the court to set the case aside. Instead a 6-3 conservative majority sided with the Trump administration.
“I think it’s fair to say it’s kind of a political maneuver right now,” Cuic said. “You know, you’re looking at the countries that they’re pulling TPS from, (they) are countries that the Trump administration has, for lack of a better term, targeted.”
If federal officials decide to terminate Ukraine’s TPS designation, recipients will have 60 days to leave the country.
Ukrainian TPS recipient Ivan Prodanyk. (Photo by Graham Stokes for Ohio Capital Journal)
TPS holders’ uncertainty
Ivan Prodanyk left Ukraine with his wife and two daughters the day the war began. His family has Temporary Protected Status and they’ve settled in Cleveland. The government’s lack of a decision has rattled him.
“At first, it’s uncertainty,” he said. “You do not know what to do because you already started to do something here. You need to (be) working. You need to pay bills.”
In some ways, Prodanyk said, the situation in Ukraine today is even worse today than it was when he left, and he isn’t eager to uproot his family once again.
“You need to leave and start the life one more time?” he asked, “Where? In another country? Or come back to Ukraine and be under the missiles and bombs?”
Prodanyk said he and his wife both work and pay taxes. He was a lawyer in Ukraine and has been able to make his way through law school again here in the U.S. He’s frustrated at the “unfairness” of the government potentially forcing out people who are contributing to their communities.
“I don’t know why government not appreciate Ukrainians,” he said, “and they don’t want Ukrainians to stay here, even right now when the situation in Ukraine is terrible.”
If push comes to shove, and federal officials do terminate their status, Prodanyk and his family will leave. But he said he won’t put his children in danger, and won’t separate himself from his family, so they’ll be forced to find some other country that would welcome them.
While Prodanyk’s family braces for USCIS’s eventual decision, the agency’s delay is already having real world, negative impacts on other Ukrainian immigrants.
Alex is a mechanical engineer from Ukraine, living in Ohio under TPS. Ohio Capital Journal isn’t using his last name over fears of retribution.
“Due to all this issue, I lost my work,” Alex explained. “My company, who I worked for, they decided to terminate contract with me because there is no dates on my documents.”
“They didn’t want me to work illegal,” he added, “and just they decided I had to quit because I have no information about when my documents will be expired, if they will be extended, or no.”
Right before our interview, Alex visited the Bureau of Motor Vehicles to renew his driver’s license. He got turned away. Alex worries that for him, and other TPS holders, USCIS simply allowing work authorization to continue might not be enough for Ukrainian job seekers to land a gig.
“So, if their HR or whoever is gonna check the ability to work (they) will verify through the eVerify,” Alex said. “Most likely it will say that that person is liable for work, but that person cannot get to work without driving a car, which is the problem.”
Alex’s family comes from Bucha, the site of massacre in 2022 which still sees regular bombardment from drones or airstrikes. Alex has two children; a son who was born in the U.S. and a daughter in grade school. He explained she had a difficult time with classes at first because she couldn’t speak English, but now she’s doing much better.
“She’s comfortable. She likes to be here. She likes to live here. She has some American friends,” Alex said. “They are all happy together, and all that I want (is to) just stay here, build my future life.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Commentary: A group of Ohioans went to Ukraine for a humanitarian and fact-finding mission. It was wrenching
description: “I felt so empty,” said Dr. George Jaskiw, head of the United Ukrainian Organizations of Ohio, on leaving Ukraine. He had seen a brave and battered ally, horribly betrayed by the world’s leading democracy, remain bonded — still — with most Americans who, like besieged Ukrainians, share a profound affinity to live free. Jaskiw traveled […]
text:
Volunteers, including George Jaskiw (second from left) and Ohio state Rep. Sean Brennan, D-Parma, (second from right) delivering ambulances in Ukraine. (Photo courtesy of Sean Brennan)“I felt so empty,” said Dr. George Jaskiw, head of the United Ukrainian Organizations of Ohio, on leaving Ukraine. 
He had seen a brave and battered ally, horribly betrayed by the world’s leading democracy, remain bonded — still — with most Americans who, like besieged Ukrainians, share a profound affinity to live free.
Jaskiw traveled to the Eastern European country recently with a group of Ohioans on a humanitarian/fact-finding mission. It was wrenching to depart for home as things were getting worse. 
Russia is bombing the hell out of its sovereign neighbor. People who are glued 24x/7 to their air siren app (to survive incoming missiles and drones) are exhausted but “grimly determined” to keep going, he said. 
Ukrainians “are resilient but they are facing a brutal winter. Vladimir Putin will do everything he can to make their country uninhabitable. He’ll bomb bridges, schools, hospitals, power stations, sewer stations.” 
Ukraine is pushing back “but Putin’s response is to be a terrorist — which he always was.” 
Jaskiw, a psychiatry professor at Case Western Reserve University School of Medicine with deep ties to Ukrainian culture, history and advocacy, joined a 12-member team from northeast Ohio bound for Ukraine. 
The coalition gathered a broad mix of ethnic and political participants that included state Rep. Sean Brennan, D-Parma, who represents the state’s largest Ukrainian population, and Chris Ronayne, Cuyahoga County Executive. 
Money was raised beforehand to buy several used ambulances for delivery to the Ukrainian front lines through an organization (Focus Ukraine) that purchases them in Europe. 
Jaskiw explained that ambulances have “a very short half life” in the war because Russia targets them all the time. 
“If you get an ambulance, you get a three-person hit. You kill the driver, you kill the medic, and you kill the soldier, at the very least.” 
Ohioans drove the vehicles from Prague to Ukraine in a convoy and, in a moving ceremony, handed them over to soldiers in Lviv, more than 300 miles from the combat zone. The original destination (Kiev) was scratched as the capital city suffered heavy, indiscriminate bombing.
Jaskiw and his companions spent days in western Ukraine talking with local officials, meeting with volunteer organizations, visiting logistic centers, drone factories, net-weaving places, soup kitchens. 
“We spoke with many ordinary people on the streets, taxi drivers, restaurant workers” who were weary to the bone from a war that has dragged on for five long years. But they soldier through the horror because “they have no choice,” said Jaskiw. 
“They all know what happens in the areas occupied by Russia. It’s genocidal terror, you know, summary arrest, disappearances, executions, torture. So the only option they have is to fight on or to die, basically.” 
Cemeteries are running out of space. Jaskiw, who has made several trips to Ukraine, returned to a prominent military burial ground called Field of Mars in Lviv where the price of war, of Ukraine’s resistance, is evident everywhere. 
“The saddest part was seeing mothers coming to the cemetery with their young kids, infants, two and three-year-olds” to see where their father is buried. “It breaks your heart to see the human cost of what’s going on.”
Something else broke Jaskiw’s heart. The son of Ukrainian refugees was in the country when the Trump regime did a 180 on supporting Ukraine’s existential battle for survival against sadistic Russian annihilation. 
The president abruptly announced a deal to buy diesel from Putin when diesel prices averaged $6.18 a gallon in the U.S. going into the midterm election. 
Not only did the convicted felon reward Putin with billions in new revenue while Ukraine burned, but he pressured Ukraine to suspend its attacks on Russia’s energy infrastructure even as Russia continued to assault its cities and power grids. 
Days later, Trump waived and paused major sanctions and tariffs against Russia. 
Then vital Starlink connections were mysteriously throttled in Ukraine leaving the country defenseless against incoming Russian drones. 
Ukraine also said it received no expected warning from U.S. intelligence sharing about scores of ballistic missiles launched by Russia against Ukraine throughout October. 
Were the interruptions in vital communications or internet connectivity intentional?
Adding insult to injury was an American “envoy” gushing over Putin as a “humanitarian” for releasing an American (that should never have been taken hostage) on the same day a Russian jet-powered drone slammed into a crowded train station in Ukraine killing at least 14 people. 
“As someone in Ukraine said, ‘we feel like we’ve been stabbed in the back.’ I was speechless,” recalled Jaskiw. “I mean, we are basically giving succor and money” to a “genocidal power” resolved to subjugate, if not destroy an ally, that also “seeks to undermine us, psychologically, militarily, financially. The question I got asked is, ‘You know that Russia helps Iran develop its rockets and gives it coordinates that can kill Americans in the Middle East and you know North Korea’s dictator is getting ballistic technology from Moscow, right?? So how can you support Moscow? I had no answer.” 
But the Ukrainian advocate is also resilient. 
“I hope when this midterm election passes, we return to some semblance of balanced government and that there’s a bipartisan effort to right” what has gone so wrong with the United States aligning itself with a ruthless authoritarian adversary over a fledgling democracy allied with America. 
Jaskiw is confident there is a bipartisan majority in both the House and the Senate that is not supportive of Russia and that, like a majority of Americans, backs Ukraine. 
“We will liaise with our political representatives and with our ethnic allies,” said Jaskiw. 
He left Ukraine relieved to be in a place “where I could rest my head knowing there’d be power and water but gripped by emptiness. For betrayed and terrorized Ukrainians who still brook a fierce American kinship to live free.

 Catching Our Eye

• Gas tax holiday for whom? Signal Ohio’s Jake Zuckerman reports, “Gas stations aren’t passing on gas-tax holiday savings, some Ohio drivers say.”
About 30 days before Republicans suffered their biggest midterm election in decades this week, party leaders in the Statehouse made a big promise to drivers to temporarily cut Ohio’s gas tax, starting just as early voting began.
As planned, gas prices listed on retailers’ signs would fall the whole 38.5 cents per gallon (47 cents per gallon of diesel) for the 90-day “gas tax holiday.”
But the savings haven’t made it to customers, at least according to about 200 Ohioans who filed complaints with the Ohio Attorney General’s Office.
• State budget. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Sarah Donaldson reports, “Blue governor, red legislature: How will Ohio budget unfold next year?”
When she takes the reins in January, Democratic Governor-elect Amy Acton has to begin work on her 2028-2029 executive budget proposal almost immediately.
After the inauguration, Acton has just two months to get her ideas on how Ohio will or won’t fund various agencies and services to members of the Ohio General Assembly. The executive budget proposal is due to lawmakers by March 15.
She, through Democrats in both legislative chambers, will then need to find common ground with Republicans. They still hold majorities in the Ohio House and the Ohio Senate, even after losing ground Tuesday night.
• Fighting for consumers. The Ohio Newsroom’s Kendall Crawford reports, “For half a century, one Ohio agency has been fighting utility price battles.”
An Ohio agency is celebrating a half a century of championing fair utility prices.
The Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel is the only government agency whose sole mission is to advocate for consumers. In 1976, the state legislature created the counsel office to represent Ohioans in legal battles against utility companies.
Agency director and counsel Maureen Willis said the office was founded at a time when utilities were frequently asking for rate increases and expenses were rising.
