name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Haitians are more than a headline
description: Back in 2024, Donald Trump said that Haitian immigrants were eating people's pets. This claim wasn't true. But it kept spreading anyway.
text:
I couldn’t believe what I was hearing when Donald Trump started saying that Haitian immigrants in Ohio were eating people’s dogs.
I’m Haitian. Growing up, I had storytellers at holiday celebrations, Creole spoken during meals, and really loud family debates mixed with even louder love and hugs. Because of all this, I don’t want to get involved in this topic, but it’s about my family, and that makes it personal.
I’m 21. Not many people my age know anything about deportation to Haiti. Every day, our feeds are filled with memes, music videos, and trends, but stories about Haitian families being deported rarely get the same attention. But this is happening right now, and more young people should understand what is at stake.
Here is what happened: after the disaster of the 2010 earthquake in Haiti that killed more than 220,000 people, the United States granted Haitians Temporary Protected Status, or TPS. The idea was simple. Haitians could legally live and work in the United States while conditions in Haiti improved, since the country was not stable enough for people to be safely sent back.
The Trump administration decided to stop TPS for over 500,000 Haitians this summer, the Supreme Court agreed, and the protection ended in late July.
Because gangs control roughly 70% or more of Port-au-Prince and surrounding regions, the first deportation flight from the United States following the end of TPS carried over 160 people and touched down in Cap-Haïtien instead of the capital city. Everyone agrees that truly dangerous people shouldn’t get special treatment, yet only some passengers on that flight had past criminal records. That same flight also transported former TPS holders. 
Meanwhile, the U.S. State Department continues warning American citizens to avoid traveling to Haiti. If the government itself says Haiti is too risky for Americans to visit, why would it be acceptable to send Haitian families there?
When questioned about it, the Department of Homeland Security stated that it was “closing time,” which meant that Haitians were not required to return home but were not permitted to remain. These are families we are talking about. Whether you agree with strict immigration laws or disagree with them, this is the important part. 
Haiti is not a safe country right now. This information comes from the United Nations, not just from what my family says. About 12 million people live in Haiti, but gang violence has made roughly 1.5 million of them leave their homes. That’s over 10% of the whole population. According to the UN, more than 3,100 people were killed between January and June of this year, 2026. In August, an attack by gangs near the capital killed 47 people, and five of them were children.
Following the TPS decision, about 75 Haitians have been held in detention in Ohio, and five Springfield, Ohio, residents were sent back to Haiti by early October. Springfield has somewhere between 12,000 and 20,000 Haitians living there, and close to 1,000 American-born children have Haitian parents. I want you to picture yourself as a kid born in America. The big U.S. shouldn’t have to worry about anything —”Land of the Free”—and being scared that your parents might not be waiting for you when you walk out of school.
My uncle lives in Canada right now. Different countries have different laws, so I didn’t think it affected us. But then my dad started having really quiet, serious phone calls with him. This was happening when news started coming out about people from Haiti being deported from the United States. Most people would think that Canada would be a safe backup plan. But it’s way more complicated than that. My family and others like us feel thankful that Canada isn’t sending people back to Haiti right now because of all the serious problems happening there currently. The problem is that rules that exist today could totally change next week, in the same way that TPS did.
Back in 2024, Donald Trump said that Haitian immigrants were eating people’s pets. This claim wasn’t true. But it kept spreading anyway. When false stories like this spread through the world, they turn real people into something to laugh at. When a country starts calling people “aliens” instead of “neighbors,” or “humans,” it makes it easier to kick them out of the U.S. This shows how words can actually become real policies, especially in the world we live in today.
Haiti gets treated the same way. People only talk about it when something really bad happens. Nobody ever mentions that Haiti was the first Black republic in the world or talks about how proud, funny, hardworking, and loyal Haitian people are. We are more than just our worst moments. This isn’t just about Haiti. People from 17 different countries have TPS protections. If one group can lose their protections really fast, then another group could lose theirs too. When we don’t speak up for the first group, it becomes easier for people to ignore other communities as well.
I’m not saying nations can’t keep their laws in place. I’m saying that sending people to a place the UN says is facing a major humanitarian problem is totally different from just enforcing the laws. UN Secretary-General António Guterres went to Haiti and said it perfectly himself: “The saddest thing is when nobody cares, when the world looks away and ignores things for way too long.”
What can you really do to help solve this problem? Sure, most of us aren’t the ones making immigration rules and policies. Still, you have the power to educate yourself before jumping to conclusions because of the media. Instead of just reading about Haitian people, try reading stories that Haitian writers have actually written themselves. Try meeting your Haitian neighbors. Even if it makes you uncomfortable, have conversations about this with the people you care about. Look into organizations in your area that support immigrant families, like Springfield’s Haitian Community Help and Support Center. 
Also, if you’re able to vote or know someone who can, keep in mind that these issues come up during elections.
My uncle, the Springfield families, and the children who might return home to an empty house are not helped by silence. You are aware now. Don’t turn away, please.
Jamar Medor is a junior at Mitchell College, majoring in criminal justice.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT Republicans cannot afford more of the same
description: Ben Proto should step aside and allow the GOP State Central to select a new chairman with the vision, urgency, and organizational ability to rebuild the party.
text:
Connecticut Republicans have no shortage of issues on which to challenge the Democratic majority. Rising costs, excessive state spending, housing mandates, public safety, and the erosion of local control should give the party ample reason to compete. Yet Democrats continue to dominate state government, while Republicans struggle to turn public frustration into electoral success.

Karen Fassuliotis

It is time to ask why. Is the Republican State Central Committee, under Chairman Ben Proto, providing the leadership Connecticut Republicans need? An honest assessment suggests it is time for a change. Proto should step aside and allow State Central to select a new chairman with the vision, urgency, and organizational ability to rebuild the party.
This is not about personalities. It is about performance and accountability.
Having the right issues is not enough. Winning requires strong town committees, qualified candidates, sustained fundraising, effective voter outreach, and a clear message that reaches beyond election season. These are basic responsibilities of a statewide party organization.
State Central has pointed to improvements in technology, voter data, communications, and relationships with local party leaders. Those efforts matter. But the question is not how many initiatives exist. It is whether they produce results.
How many competitive districts have strong Republican candidates? Where are town committees too weak to recruit and support candidates? Are candidates identified early, trained, funded, and equipped to compete? Is there a coordinated communications strategy that gives Republicans a recognizable statewide voice? And where is the regular accounting of what works, what fails, and what must change?
The party’s decision to leave certain heavily Democratic districts uncontested illustrates the need for a broader strategy. Proto has described this as a way to limit public campaign funds available to Democratic opponents, estimating that the decisions would prevent Democrats from receiving approximately $1.7 million. Under the Connecticut’s Citizens’ Election Program, an unopposed major-party candidate generally receives 30 percent of the applicable grant rather than the full grant available with qualifying major-party opposition.
That is a legitimate financial calculation. But reducing an opponent’s grant is not the same as building a political party. Every district without a Republican candidate is also a district where Republicans surrender the opportunity to engage voters, develop future candidates, strengthen local organizations, and give residents a choice. A short-term financial tactic cannot substitute for competing throughout Connecticut.
Republicans also need a serious plan to engage cities such as Hartford, Bridgeport, and Danbury. These communities should not be written off as permanently Democratic territory. Residents deserve an honest examination of the results of policies pursued by their elected officials, along with practical alternatives on education, employment, economic opportunity, housing, public safety, taxes, and municipal services.
The challenges are substantial. U.S. Census Bureau estimates for 2020–2024 put poverty at 26.3 percent in Hartford, 21 percent in Bridgeport, and 11.7 percent in Danbury. These cities have different circumstances, and poverty cannot be attributed to one party or policy. But persistent economic hardship and unequal opportunity deserve scrutiny. Republicans should examine state policies and municipal decisions, identify where approaches have fallen short, and offer credible solutions.
That means listening to residents, engaging community leaders, recruiting candidates who understand their cities, and remaining present between elections. A statewide party must compete statewide —not just in communities where it already has an established base.
Connecticut needs a Republican governing agenda that speaks to the entire state, from its cities and smaller communities to its suburbs and rural towns. It must address residents’ practical concerns and explain how proposed policies would improve their lives. Criticism of Democratic leadership is not enough. Republicans must show voters what they would do differently and why it matters.
State Central’s success should be measured by stronger local committees, qualified candidates, better-supported campaigns, and the ability to compete across Connecticut. The next chairman must present measurable goals for recruitment, grassroots development, fundraising, communications, and statewide outreach.
A leadership transition will not solve every problem, but continuing with the same approach without a convincing accounting of results is not a strategy. The transition should be orderly, transparent, and based on leadership and ability —not factional loyalties.
It is time for Ben Proto to step aside. Connecticut Republicans cannot afford another election cycle spent explaining why they were unprepared, why districts went uncontested, or why their message failed to reach voters. The work of rebuilding must begin now.
The time for business as usual is over.
Karen Fassuliotis lives in Greenwich.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Political notes: Moore and ‘the question,’ Donofrio heads to LCV, and eyeing AI
authors: Bryan P. Sears, Christine Condon, William J. Ford
description: Gov. Wes Moore appears on another network show and is asked another question about his political future, the League of Conservation Voters taps Jason Donofrio as its next director, and Progressive Maryland wants to talk artificial intelligence, in political notes.
text:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) during an August 2026 meeting with reporters in the Maryland State House. (Photo Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Fresh off his reelection, Gov. Wes Moore (D) appeared Monday on MS NOW’s “State of Play with Peter Alexander,” fielding questions on a number of national political issues. including midcycle redistricting and the potential for a government shutdown in December.
And, inevitably, the discussion turned to speculation of Moore’s political future and whether he is planning to run for president in two years.
Moore, who’s had plenty of practice at responding to — if not actually answering — the question, adroitly sidestepped questions about whether he was committing to “serving a full term through 2031.”
The governor said he told voters he was not “running for re-election because we were thinking about anything else. You know, I think that Maryland deserves to be part of this conversation. Maryland will be a part of this conversation, but I do think it’s important for us to be able to, you know, spend time and and really focus on what the voters told us on Tuesday. ”
But Moore did say that if he were to seek higher office — he is repeatedly mentioned as a potential candidate for president in 2028 — that his platform from his first run for governor would be the foundation for any run for higher office.
“I can tell you why I ran for governor, and it’s to end child poverty. That’s the reason why I ran for governor,” Moore said. “I do not understand how any society can condone children growing up in poverty and … having their life determined before they even have a say.”
Moore also avoided questions about a timeline for making a decision to run for president.
“To be very honest, my timeline on continuing to serve the people of Maryland has already started,” Moore said. “I’m excited about the work that we’re doing in the state of Maryland, and we’ll continue going through our process.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Donofrio to take over at League of Conservation Voters
The Maryland League of Conservation Voters has named its next executive director.
Jason Donofrio, who was most recently the vice president of development at the National Marine Sanctuary Foundation in Silver Spring, will lead the 47-year-old political advocacy organization following the retirement of Kim Coble, who had served as LCV’s executive director for seven years. He arrives with Maryland’s climate promises in a difficult position due to state budget shortages, rising energy costs and federal government backtracking.
“I am deeply honored to be joining such an incredible organization during such a vital time,” Donofrio said in a news release issued Monday. “I am excited to work alongside so many talented and dedicated staff, Board members, and community partners as we work towards ensuring a healthy environment for everyone in Maryland.”
Donofrio will also be taking the helm of the Maryland LCV Education Fund, founded in 2000, which focuses on climate education.
Donofrio currently serves on the steering committee for the Climate Strong Islands Network and on the board of governors for the school of architecture founded by Frank Lloyd Wright in Arizona.
Previously, Donofrio was chief development and external relations officer at The Ocean Foundation in Washington, D.C. He is also a previous statewide director of the Arizona Public Interest Research Group.
“Jason is a proven environmental leader with a strong record of building coalition support and deep experience engaging policymakers. We’re excited for the next chapter under his leadership,” said Patrick Miller, chairman of the Maryland LCV board.
Donofrio will host a virtual meet and greet this Thursday at noon.
AI talk
Progressive Maryland is co-hosting two community sessions this weekend to talk artificial intelligence.
The first is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Saturday at the Exploration Commons at 50 East in Westminster and the second is set for 3:30 p.m. at the Central Branch – Howard County Library in Columbia.
Larry Stafford, executive director of Progressive Maryland. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
Progressive Maryland is partnering with Humans in Control, a nonprofit organization based in Covina, California, that’s focused on assessing AI regulations, on the sessions labeled “Reality Check.” The goal is to work on AI proposals and present them to the Maryland General Assembly when it convenes Jan. 13. Those who want to participate and attend one of the sessions can register here.
Progressive Maryland Executive Director Larry Stafford Jr. said more events will be held leading into the new year.
“The rapid development of artificial intelligence is the most consequential issue facing humanity today. AI is already impacting many aspects of our lives including jobs and the economy, mental health, and our environment,” Stafford said in a text message Monday. “The technology is even said to potentially pose an existential risk to human civilization. Maryland must help led the way when it comes to regulation the risks of AI and ensuring that this technology that the combined sum of human knowledge helped to create ultimately benefits all of us not just the billionaire tech elites.”
The legislature approved several policies dealing with artificial intelligence during this year’s session, such as the Artificial Intelligence Ready Schools Act sponsored by Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard and Montgomery).
Part of that bill required the Maryland State Department of Education to issue its own AI recommendations and gave school districts 120 days from the date of that guidance to issue their own guidelines. Several districts, including Frederick, Montgomery and Prince George’s counties. issued their own AI guidelines prior to the legislation being signed into law.

name: California
title: It’s official: California voters reject Prop. 40 billionaire tax
description: Billionaires spent $378 million to defeat Prop. 40, exposing a rift among California Democrats on taxing the rich.
text:
In summary
Billionaires spent $378 million to defeat Prop. 40, exposing a rift among California Democrats on taxing the rich. 


California will not become the first state to levy a wealth tax on its richest residents — at least not this election. 
Voters rejected Proposition 40, a proposal to tax billionaires based on their net worth and financial holdings, by 52.8% to 47.2%, according to The Associated Press Monday. The measure had trailed behind for days before The Associated Press confirmed results. 
Leaders for Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, seemed to concede the race minutes before the polls closed but vowed to try again in 2028 if California’s Legislature “fails to deliver a real solution” to fund healthcare hammered by recent federal law. 
“That’s not a hypothetical. That’s our plan,” said Dave Regan, president of SEIU-UHW. 
Election Day was projected to be an all-around defeat for the union, known for aggressively pursuing ballot measures. Voters defeated union-backed Proposition 44, an effort to control how clinics spend money. Proposition 42, a billionaire tax countermeasure prohibiting future wealth taxes, was leading Monday evening by 51.6% to 48.4%. That measure could get in the way of SEIU-UHW’s future plans to try taxing wealth again.
The billionaire tax would have generated $100 billion for healthcare and education through a one-time, 5% tax on billionaires, according to SEIU-UHW. Opponents of the measure celebrated its defeat. 
“Proposition 40 was a reckless experiment conducted on our state’s economy with little regard for the harms it would cause,” according to a statement from Evan Westrop, a campaign strategist for No on Prop. 40.
The opposition campaign, which was backed by wealthy tech investors and healthcare organizations, argued the measure had already driven billionaires from the state and permanently harmed income tax revenue. On Monday they said the state still faces “enormous pressure” to find other ways to fund healthcare hit by federal cuts.
Billionaire tax divided Democrats
From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions among the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it.
Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents, attempting through backroom negotiations to keep it off of the ballot altogether. He endorsed the billionaire-backed counter measure, Prop. 42, designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and  California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. 
The California Democratic Party and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needed more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off of health insurance.
Lorena Gonzalez, former Assemblymember and president of the California Federation of Labor Unions, said Prop. 40’s failure puts even more pressure on state and federal lawmakers to backfill federal Medicaid cuts.
Supporters of Prop. 40 blamed its loss on billionaires vastly outspending the Yes campaign, which raised $33.5 million.
Billionaires poured hundreds of millions of dollars into the campaign to stop Prop. 40. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the charge, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40, including by funding the counterpropositions 41 and 42. Collectively, ultra-wealthy opponents donated $378.4 million to oppose the billionaire tax.
Building a Better California did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“That is incredibly corrosive and corrupting to our democracy and our political system, and that’s been dominating the discussion here in California,” Regan said.
Ultimately, opponents’ efforts succeeded.
Polling just ahead of the election indicated falling support for Prop. 40 despite growing sentiment for taxing billionaires more in general. According to a UC Berkeley Citrin-POLITICO poll, 45% of voters believed in taxing billionaires more to fund public services compared to 35% who believed the state should prioritize keeping billionaires in state because of the tax revenue and jobs they generate — but just 46% favored Prop. 40. 
Infighting among Democrats could have also contributed to Prop. 40’s demise, said John Matsusaka, an economist and direct democracy expert at USC, ahead of the election. Research shows money doesn’t buy people’s votes or values on core issues like abortion, Matsusaka said, but it can exploit uncertainty.
“People these days are very tribal. When your tribe is arguing, people start to listen to the counterarguments,” Matsusaka said.
This story has been updated.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Peltola extends lead over Sullivan in Alaska’s U.S. Senate race as ballot-counting continues
description: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola extended her lead over incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan in an updated vote total published Monday by the Alaska Division of Elections. While Peltola has had more first-choice votes since Election Day, preliminary calculations by the Alaska Beacon have shown Sullivan leading when the results of the stat[...]
text:
Mary Peltola greets supporters on election night, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at a Mary Peltola watch party in downtown Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola extended her lead over incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan in an updated vote total published Monday by the Alaska Division of Elections.
While Peltola has had more first-choice votes since Election Day, preliminary calculations by the Alaska Beacon have shown Sullivan leading when the results of the state’s ranked choice runoff are considered.
But on Monday, Peltola gained enough first-choice votes to outweigh Sullivan’s runoff advantage. As of 4 p.m., she led Sullivan by 2,517 votes out of 219,342 cast. Republican candidate Gerald Heikes and independent Dan J. Sullivan were a distant third and fourth, respectively.
Under Alaska’s election system, if one candidate in a race has more than 50% of the first-choice votes, they win. If no candidate does, a ranked choice runoff is used to decide the winner.
The candidate with the fewest first-choice votes is eliminated, and voters who picked them have their votes go to their second choices.
The elimination process continues until two candidates are left, and the person with the most votes wins.
Preliminary calculations from Election Day showed Sen. Sullivan would gain more than enough votes from that redistribution to overcome Peltola’s lead.
But with Monday’s update, Peltola has a big enough advantage in first-choice votes to overcome the Sullivan redistribution.
With 48.5% of the first choice votes, she is also coming closer to the threshold needed to win the race without the runoff. 
That could change on Tuesday.
Altogether, the division added 4,947 counted ballots to the statewide tally on Monday, but tens of thousands of ballots are expected to be added to the tally on Tuesday as the division includes absentee and early votes received in the days immediately before Election Day.
Those ballots were withheld while elections officials cross-checked Election Day poll registers to prevent Alaskans from casting two votes.
The scheduled update on Tuesday could be decisive for more than just the U.S. Senate race. In the governor’s race, Democratic candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins had 49.4% of first-choice votes on Monday.
Republican governor candidate Dave Bronson, running in third place, said last week that Kreiss-Tomkins’ victory appears inevitable. Republican candidate Bernadette Wilson, in second with 28.8% of first-choice votes, has not yet conceded the race.
In the race for U.S. House, incumbent Republican Rep. Nick Begich III has 49.1% of the first-choice votes, well ahead of independent challenger Bill Hill, with 40.7%. Democratic candidate Eric Hafner, a federal inmate in New York state, has 7.3%. 
Ballot Measure 2, seeking to repeal the state’s open-primary and ranked-choice election system, continues to trail, with 52.3% of participating voters choosing “no.”

In an Oct. 29 memo, DOA Commissioner Paula Vrana wrote, “The procurement process has now concluded and the State has cancelled the RFP. Instead of pursuing a contract […]
text:
The State Office Building in Juneau is seen on Thursday, Feb. 20, 2025. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)The Alaska Department of Administration has canceled a request for proposals that could have led to the privatization of the state’s payroll system for 14,000 public employees.
In an Oct. 29 memo, DOA Commissioner Paula Vrana wrote, “The procurement process has now concluded and the State has cancelled the RFP. Instead of pursuing a contract for these services, we will continue to move forward with the payroll structure as it is and will focus our efforts on process improvements and system enhancements within the existing structure.”
Vrana’s memo came weeks after the Department of Administration said it was considering whether to outsource the state’s payroll system to a private contractor.
DOA has struggled for years to pay state employees accurately. In fiscal year 2025 alone, according to a state study, employees filed more than 1,500 “notice of pay problem” reports with DOA. A state feasibility analysis suggested that privatization could cost $4 million per year. The state currently spends $10 million per year on its payroll program.
In a letter to the state’s public employee unions, labor relations manager Matthew Jendrusina cited three reasons for canceling a request for proposals from companies interested in working as a payroll contractor — “ambiguous or otherwise inadequate specifications were part of the solicitation; the solicitation did not provide for consideration of all factors of significance to the state; and the award is not in the best interest of the state.”
Public employee unions had opposed the privatization effort and filed grievances seeking to stop it. Members of the Alaska Legislature expressed concerns about the proposal and wrote letters asking the state to pause it.
Danelle Beck is president of Confidential Employees Association Local 6133, which represents 75 payroll employees and others across the state. She praised the move in a statement published Oct. 29.
“What we saw today is the power of working people standing together. CEA members stood up and fought back against a rushed and opaque move by the Dunleavy Administration on its way out the door” she said.
“Our members were not going to sit quietly while decisions were made that threaten our livelihoods, and the public services Alaskans depend on.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah Gov. Cox: Republicans ‘suffered a historic defeat.’ Now, he says they have to ‘listen’
description: Utah Gov. Spencer Cox on Monday addressed the stunning blue wave from last week’s election that put Democrats on track to claim more than a dozen seats from Republicans in the GOP-controlled Utah Legislature.  “Republicans suffered an historic defeat across the country,” Cox said during a news conference broadcast by PBS Utah. “While many of […]
text:
Gov. Spencer J. Cox speaks during the governor's news conference broadcast by PBS Utah at the Eccles Broadcast Center in Salt Lake City on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. (Pool photo by Scott G Winterton/Deseret News)Utah Gov. Spencer Cox on Monday addressed the stunning blue wave from last week’s election that put Democrats on track to claim more than a dozen seats from Republicans in the GOP-controlled Utah Legislature. 
“Republicans suffered an historic defeat across the country,” Cox said during a news conference broadcast by PBS Utah. “While many of us expected a difficult election nationally, I don’t think anyone — myself included — anticipated the extent to which that wave would reach and impact Utah, particularly in our state legislative races.” 
‘Blue tsunami’ hits Utah: House Republicans on pace to lose 17 seats, breaking supermajority

The massive blue wave that swept the country on Election Day last week installed not just a majority of Democrats in Congress, but also flipped many gubernatorial offices and state legislatures blue across the country. 
In Utah, the House’s Republican supermajority has been broken for the first time in more than 30 years, with about 16 Republican seats on track to be lost to 14 Democrats and two unaffiliated candidates as of Monday morning. While the Senate will still be controlled by a GOP supermajority, the House will have a simple Republican majority. 
That means the Utah Legislature no longer has one party with two-thirds control — or the power of one party to override the governor’s veto. 
Will Cox wield his veto pen more often now?
Cox acknowledged to reporters that he now has more power behind his pen, but he stopped short of saying he’ll wield it more often. He said he plans to continue having a collaborative relationship with lawmakers.  
“It depends on the issues,” Cox said when asked if he’ll veto more bills now. “Look, in the conversations I’ve had with legislative leadership, I think this is going to be a different kind of session than we’ve seen in the past. I suspect that some bills that I maybe would have vetoed before but knew that they would get overridden, probably don’t get run in the first place this time around because of the significant changes. But time will tell.” 



Cox said there’s an “aphorism that goes around” at the National Governor’s Association that “the only thing worse than having the Legislature be a majority of the opposing party is to have a supermajority of your own party because your veto is completely meaningless.” 
“Now that’s not true for me because I have such a great working relationship with the Legislature,” he said. “We’ve always worked closely on issues.” 
He said having a “non-veto-proof majority doesn’t allow you to get more stuff done.” Rather, he said it acts as “more of a brake than a gas pedal.” 
“It means I can stop some things from happening that maybe I couldn’t before,” he said. “But I have such a great working relationship with the Legislature that they’ve always been willing to engage, regardless of whether they could override my veto or not. But certainly, it means that we’ll be having more collaboration going forward than maybe we have.” 
Gov. Spencer J. Cox speaks to reporters during the governor’s news conference broadcast by PBS Utah at the Eccles Broadcast Center in Salt Lake City on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. (Pool photo by Scott G Winterton/Deseret News)
Cox analyzes the blue wave 
The governor called it a “repudiation election” with “crazy” margins that reflected a swing in Utah that he’s never seen in his lifetime. 
He said it’s a moment that Republicans — both nationally and in Utah — need to seriously reflect on. 
“First,” he said, “I think this election is a powerful reminder of something we must never forget. Article I of the Utah Constitution is ‘all power is inherent in the people.’ Not in the governor. Not in the Legislature. Not in the Republican Party or the Democratic Party. In the people.” 
He said elected officials only hold power “because the people have entrusted us with a portion of their power.” 
“It does not belong to us, and the people have every right to take it back,” he said. 
When voters send a message “that those in power may not want to hear,” Cox said, “that’s not a flaw in our system. That’s the beauty, the perfection, in our system.”
Utah House Democrats’ wins come with mixed feelings over loss of some moderate Republicans

Cox also said Utah’s leaders “have to be willing to listen to what the voters are telling us.” 
“Now it would be very easy for me and everyone else to look at these results in Utah and conclude that this was all about what was happening in Washington, D.C.,” he said. “And definitely, the national political environment played an enormous role in the outcomes here in Utah. But I think it would be a mistake to stop there.” 
Cox said the frustrations he’s hearing from Utahns the most are concerns about housing, growth and development, including data centers. He said he’s also hearing frustrations about transparency, “trusting government” and “whether people making decisions are really listening to the people that are affected by them.” 
“These are valid concerns, and they deserve real answers,” he said. “We can be the best state in the nation and still have a lot of work to do. Those things aren’t mutually exclusive. And that includes me. I don’t have all the answers today, but I am committed to working to find them. I want to spend more time listening to Utahns, including people who disagree with me. Maybe especially the people who disagree with me.” 
Most broadly, Cox said the biggest problem is too many Utahns simply feel unheard. 
Unions celebrate Utah Legislature’s planned vote to repeal anti-collective bargaining bill

“Not listening to people is not a conservative or, you know, liberal issue,” he said. “I think that’s just what happens when a party has been in power for a long time. Sometimes we get a little lazy when it comes to what we should be doing and what we should be listening to.” 
Cox said according to national exit polls, the top issues for Republicans’ loss were “very clear,” with the top two being cost of living and corruption. Next came the war in Iran and immigration. 
While Utah leaders can’t do much about the war in Iran, the price of housing is a sharp issue for Utahns, Cox said, and “the corruption piece is something that I think we all have to be incredibly wary of.” 
“Whether real or perceived, it doesn’t matter, that’s what voters think (is) happening, and so we have to be very cautious of that and work to build trust,” he said. “So we’re going to be working with legislative leadership, whatever that looks like, to make sure that we’re not falling into those same traps that are happening nationally.” 
On data centers, Cox pointed to his executive order setting a framework for considering data center projects — but also said “we’re working on a bill right now” that would enshrine “many of those restrictions in place in legislation.” 
He also said an anti-public unions bill was also “deeply unpopular and completely unnecessary,” he said, adding that “I got more calls on that bill than any other.” 
Trump ‘shares the blame’ 
President Donald Trump “certainly shares some blame” for Utah’s blue wave, Cox said. 
While Cox added “we have a good relationship (and) we’re working on many important issues,” he also said he hopes “that the same reflection that’s happening here with leadership in Utah is happening at the national level, including with his administration.” 
Nationally, Cox said he doesn’t think Americans have “suddenly embraced every idea on the political left,” but rather “the lesson is something much more fundamental.” 
He pointed out that this year’s blue wave was an “extraordinary” reversal from just two years ago, when voters chose Republicans to control both the White House and Congress. 
Trump open to immigration deal, calls crackdown ‘too tough,’ despite Miller promotion

“We seem to be caught in a cycle where one side wins, the other side gets angry, and two years later the roles reverse,” he said. “Each election becomes a repudiation of the last one. Each victory becomes an excuse to push harder, and the contempt, the outrage, and the division just keep getting worse.”
He argued “people are tired of the way we’re doing politics in our country today. They’re tired of the fighting. They’re tired of the extremes … and they’re tired of being told that if they don’t agree with everything their party says or does, they somehow don’t belong.” 
That sentiment aligns with Cox’s depolarization calls in his recently published book, “Off Ramp: How to be a Peacemaker in an Age of Contempt.” 
“My hope is that this election becomes something more than just another swing of the political pendulum,” he said. “Instead of simply trading places, trading blame, and trading insults, we actually learn something. That we have the humility to recognize where we’ve fallen short, the courage to change where change is needed, and the character to work together even when it’s hard. That’s what I want for our country. That’s what I want for Utah, and that’s what I’m going to be working toward in the years ahead.”
Cox says he had warned lawmakers about changing ballot initiatives
Cox said in recent years he’d issued warnings to the Legislature to “do things differently, when we needed to slow down, listen more carefully, or be more responsive.” 
“I think the message from this election makes the need for that kind of reflection even clearer,” he said. “I don’t believe voters are asking their elected officials to be perfect, but I do believe they’re asking us to do better, and we should take that seriously.”
Asked what will change, Cox told reporters “we’ll be doing a lot more listening.” He pointed out newly-elected Senate President Sen. Evan Vickers and House Speaker Mike Schultz had a similar message on Friday. 
In a closed-door vote, Republicans pick Sen. Evan Vickers to be next Senate president

When it comes to voters feeling unheard, Cox said redistricting is “maybe where it starts” — and that issue was compounded by the Legislature making changes to voter-approved laws, like Proposition 4 in 2018 that banned partisan gerrymandering and created an independent redistricting commission. 
“That was a big one,” he said. “I’ve warned the Legislature about this many times over the years.” 
He pointed to an amicus brief in Utah’s redistricting lawsuit, in which he warned the Legislature “that they change initiatives at their own peril.” 
“Now, I was making the case that they have the authority to do that, and if you don’t like it, you should vote them out,” he said. 
Asked about how he thinks the Legislature should handle redistricting or ballot initiatives moving forward, Cox said lawmakers need to be “incredibly cautious” in making changes to ballot initiatives that pass at the ballot box. 
“This is what I’ve been warning about for years is if you do this too many times, people will take that authority away from you, and it will cost you,” Cox said. 
In 2021, when the Legislature ignored an independent redistricting commission’s recommendations and instead adopted congressional boundaries that they drew themselves — which the courts have since ruled unlawful as the result of an unconstitutional process — Cox acknowledged that some people called on him to veto the maps, but he didn’t because he firmly believes the Legislature itself has the authority to draw political boundaries. 
“I take some of the blame for this,” Cox said. “People said I should have vetoed the maps or I should have pushed back more. … I’ve always said the way to push back is at the ballot box … and I think part of that is why we’re here.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Groups ask DEQ to reject application for public water supply to serve data center project
description: A state agency’s plan to exempt a water supply well from a full environmental review would “hide the true scope” of a data center project that could be the largest in Montana history.
text:
A server room in a data center. (Photo by Getty Images)Approving a water supply well to serve the Quantica Big Sky Campus would “hide the true scope” of a data center project that could be the largest in Montana history, a group of watchdog and conservation organizations allege in a letter to a state agency.
But a Department of Environmental Quality spokesperson said the agency is still reviewing public comment about the well application — such as the one from the groups — and additional environmental review could be warranted.
Quantica Big Sky Campus is a 5,100-acre data center development located 30 miles north of Billings, according to a May news release from Quantica Infrastructure.
Quantica said the site, near Broadview, is designed to support “multiple data center buildings,” with the first expected to be operational in 2029.
Big Sky Digital Infrastructure, of Quantica, and consultant Tetra Tech submitted an application to the Department of Environmental Quality for testing a public water supply well.
The DEQ describes the project as a proposed well that would provide water during construction and, later, drinking water for the campus.
In a news release and application, Quantica said the campus is expected to use as much as 150,000 gallons of water per day to support workforce needs and construction activities during the construction phase, and water use would “decline significantly” to 20,000 gallons a day during operations.
The DEQ describes the site construction footprint for the well as roughly 100 feet by 100 feet and said the maximum footprint needed to house “the necessary water treatment” would be “similar to a small shed.”
The DEQ also said the well may be used to “provide cooling water” to the data center’s cooling system.
In an initial decision, the DEQ found the project qualified for a “categorical exclusion,” or an exemption from closer environmental scrutiny in the Montana Environmental Policy Act. The groups ask the DEQ to withdraw that decision.
In an extensive letter, the 13 organizations represented by Earthjustice and Western Environmental Law Center said the application is asking the DEQ to review the project in “piecemeal fashion,” and in doing so, disregarding the effects of the “massive” undertaking.
The groups also allege the DEQ’s ambiguous permitting process interferes with the constitutionally protected right to know and right to participate.
“DEQ and Quantica must release additional information about the proposed data center and any associated electricity generation assets — including a reported 1,785-megawatt gas plant — to ensure that the public can meaningfully participate in a public comment process,” the groups said.
They call on the DEQ to reject the application as flawed and incomplete, deny Quantica’s request to expedite the application, and conduct a full environmental impact statement, or complete review, including greenhouse gas emissions.
“Documents submitted to DEQ prove that the well exists solely to facilitate a much larger undertaking, including a hyperscale data center,” said a letter from the groups. “Quantica asks DEQ to hide the true scope of this project from the public by seeking review of the application in isolation.”
They said DEQ records show Quantica is pursuing permits for 585 megawatts of gas-fired engines and 1,200 megawatts of gas-fired turbines, which “exceeds the combined capacity of every gas plant now operating in Montana.”
They also said much more details are needed from Quantica or the DEQ about the proposed cooling system, such as how much water needs to be added periodically, any chemicals added, and what happens when the system is flushed.
The organizations submitting the letter are the following: Butte Watchdogs for Social and Environmental Justice, Citizens for Clean Energy, Families for a Livable Climate, Honor the Earth, Montana Conservation Voters, Montana Environmental Information Center, Montana Health and Climate, Montana Public Interest Research Group, Northern Plains Resource Council, Park County Environmental Council, Sierra Club Montana Chapter, Upper Missouri Waterkeeper and 350 Montana.
On Oct. 21, DEQ announced it had extended the public comment period for the water supply well through Nov. 6. Monday, a spokesperson for the DEQ said the agency will begin reviewing comments, and an environmental impact statement is possible.
“DEQ will consider the public comments and supporting information and determine whether additional environmental review is warranted,” said DEQ spokesperson Madison McGeffers.
A spokesperson for Quantica did not comment Monday on the letter from the groups, but the company earlier said it is focused on responsible development that “pays its own way for power, creates good jobs and invests in local communities.”
In a statement in August, Big Sky Digital Infrastructure general counsel Damon Obie said he grew up on a ranch in Montana and doesn’t take water for granted.
“We designed the Big Sky Campus to use minimal water and to source it deep underground, away from the wells our neighbors rely on,” Obie said. “Protecting Montana’s water is a responsibility we take seriously.”
In the letter, the groups present a lengthy review of the project and call for more information about it.
They allege the DEQ is providing contradictory information about the project — for example, describing just “one public water supply well” in one document that would exempt the project from a full environmental review while not acknowledging a second well referenced in the application.
“Granting Quantica’s application would authorize the first water-supply infrastructure for what may become one of the largest industrial developments in Montana’s history,” the groups said.
McGeffers said the DEQ has asked Quantica’s consultant to clarify “the use of the second well location,” and DEQ will need to reconcile the information in the application with other materials.
“Based on Quantica’s response DEQ will evaluate if an additional public comment period is appropriate,” McGeffers said in an email.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ officials hear pleas for more funding for mental health, housing, childcare
description: Advocates urged New Jersey officials on Monday to increase state funding for critical social services amid federal cutbacks.
text:
Advocates urged New Jersey officials on Monday to increase state funding for critical social services amid federal cutbacks. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Advocates urged the state to invest more in programs for mental health and substance abuse, housing homeless people, supporting seniors and people with disabilities, providing childcare, and more during a budget listening session with state officials Monday.
The annual meeting was a preliminary step for Department of Human Services officials as they prepare the department’s next budget – this year’s topped $37 billion, 56% from federal dollars — and it came as New Jersey braces for the growing impact of massive federal funding cuts that could reduce revenue for health and social services by billions annually in the years to come.
Some witnesses during Monday’s hourslong meeting expressed fear about the coming impact of the federal changes, which are expected to strip Medicaid benefits from up to 300,000 and leave another 50,000 without their current food aid benefits, according to the department. Several organizations that provide mental health services warned they would need additional state funding to meet the increased demand they anticipate as people lose Medicaid coverage.
Cathy Rowe, executive director of New Jersey Advocates for Aging Well, encouraged state officials to protect funding for existing elder programs, including money to support caregivers, hearing aid purchases, and prescription drugs. Programs like this “must remain strong and accessible, even in a challenging economic climate,” she said.
Many organizations said the pending federal shortfalls will amplify their existing funding needs, and their leaders called on the state to fill the gaps.
“Providers are already struggling,” said Libby Vinson, head of the New Jersey Association of Community Providers, which represents groups that serve people with disabilities. “They’ve been doing more with less for years. There’s only so much they can absorb.”
Melissa Acree, CEO of NJ 211, a nonprofit hotline to connect residents with social services, urged the department to include stable funding for the program, which serves hundreds of thousands of people annually, linking them to heat assistance, housing, food help, and more.
“We anticipate even greater demand in January,” she said.
Nursing home residents urged the department to increase funding for their personal needs and tighten scrutiny around nursing home operations. Deaf advocates recommended greater investment in sensitivity training for state and local agencies, and expanding accessible communications. People who have been homeless begged the state not to forget them too.
Several childcare advocates said more money is needed to help low-income families connect with daycare options that enable parents to work and provide kids with a strong foundation for learning. Providers are struggling to stay in business, they said.
“Childcare must be treated as a public good,” said Yarrow Willman-Cole, a leader in the Time to Care Coalition, an advocacy group seeking to expand publicly financed care options.
Before calling for more money for child welfare services, Julie Dees of the Children’s Home Society of New Jersey told state officials, “I don’t know how you make the decisions you do. All these programs should be funded.”
Gov. Mikie Sherrill will compile a statewide budget proposal to be introduced in February. Lawmakers must finalize a plan she can sign into law by July 1.

title: Democratic wins create abortion rights opportunities in states with strict laws
description: Sweeping Democratic election wins could advance abortion access in states with tight restrictions, especially in Georgia, Iowa and Texas, where Democrats seized the governor’s office for the first time in decades. All three states will have Democratic attorneys general, and in Georgia and Texas, Democrats will control the state House while Republicans retain[...]
text:
Georgia Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms spoke last week at the state Capitol about her transition into office. In Georgia, Iowa and Texas, sweeping Democratic election wins could advance abortion access. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)Sweeping Democratic election wins could advance abortion access in states with tight restrictions, especially in Georgia, Iowa and Texas, where Democrats seized the governor’s office for the first time in decades.
All three states will have Democratic attorneys general, and in Georgia and Texas, Democrats will control the state House while Republicans retain the state Senate. Texas has a strict abortion ban, while Iowa and Georgia only allow it up to about six weeks of pregnancy.
Meanwhile, in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, Democrats have won new “trifectas” — control of the governor’s office and both legislative chambers — creating new opportunities to expand abortion rights. Both Pennsylvania Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and Wisconsin Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley have already pledged to codify abortion rights through state law or constitutional amendment.
Abortion rights supporters also won victories in three of the four states — Missouri, Nevada and Virginia — where abortion-related measures were on the ballot. The lone exception was Idaho, where voters preserved their state’s strict abortion ban.
State consequences are already on display in Texas, where Democratic Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson has promised to stop suing telehealth abortion providers in other states. Johnson’s proclamation is a stark reversal of the policy of his Republican predecessor, Ken Paxton, who failed in his bid to become a U.S. senator.
“My hope in humanity has been restored a little bit, and I don’t think I even realized how much that was wearing on me behind the scenes for the last two years,” said Kaitlyn Kash, who left Texas in 2021 to obtain an abortion in Kansas after fatal fetal complications threatened her pregnancy and potentially her own health.
Kash was among several plaintiffs who joined the 2023 Zurawski v. Texas lawsuit seeking to clarify the state’s medical emergency exceptions to its abortion ban. In 2024, the Texas Supreme Court ruled 9-0 in favor of the state.
But future abortion cases could see different outcomes: Last week, Democrats won all four Texas Supreme Court seats that were up for election. That leaves the GOP with a narrow 5-4 advantage on the state Supreme Court.
“To not have a vindictive attorney general anymore is going to save lives,” Kash said, referring to actions Paxton has taken, including bringing legal actions against abortion providers inside and outside the state and petitioning the state Supreme Court to halt a court ruling allowing the termination of a nonviable pregnancy.
Less impact in Washington
Despite huge Democratic gains in Congress, the change at the federal level is likely to be less significant, at least in the short term. President Donald Trump won’t leave office until January 2029, and Democrats did not win a filibuster-proof 60 seats in the Senate, let alone the two-thirds majority in the House and Senate they would need to override a presidential veto.
“As long as Trump holds executive and veto powers, we have more work than celebrating to do,” said Brittany Fonteno, president and CEO of the National Abortion Federation in a written statement. “The next two years will be a critical time to prepare for the kind of governing power that will deliver real and lasting reproductive freedom.”
Nevertheless, national abortion rights leaders have signaled high expectations for candidates they helped send to Congress, and they want Democrats to fight to preserve telehealth abortion. If Dr. Heidi Overton, Trump’s controversial pick to oversee the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, is not confirmed during the upcoming lame duck session, abortion-rights advocates will look to the new Democratic-dominated Senate to block her nomination.
“The Senate just became the backstop,” said Gowri Buddiga, campaign director of Free & Just, an abortion rights advocacy group, in a written statement. “An FDA nominee who’s spent years calling medication abortion dangerous now has to get past a chamber that’s heard from the women these bans have hurt.”
Unlike the 2022 midterms, which were held just months after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the federal right to an abortion, there is debate over just how important abortion was in this election. According to an exit poll conducted for The Associated Press, 39% of voters cited the economy as their top issue, 33% said it was the state of American democracy and 14% pointed to immigration. No other issue broke single digits and abortion was not among the top six.
But abortion law expert Mary Ziegler said that while abortion appears to have been less of a top-of-mind issue this year, that’s not because voters care less about it.
“It’s that there was nothing happening with abortion right now, and that isn’t just a fun coincidence,” said Ziegler, a professor at UC Davis School of Law. “That’s because the Trump administration has been trying really hard to kick down the road any litigation or federal restrictions that would have made it front of mind for voters again.”
Ziegler said there are certain avenues that congressional Democrats could explore to expand access to abortion federally. Even if those efforts fail, she said, they might benefit Democrats politically leading up to the next presidential election in 2028.
“While Republicans have successfully drawn attention away from abortion, they haven’t really actually made abortion a good issue for Republicans,” she said. “So I don’t see what the harm would be in passing a bill that would be popular and having Trump veto it and have J.D. Vance and Marco Rubio have to defend it, because it’s been very good for Republicans not to have to talk about this issue at all.”
For their part, anti-abortion organizations have blamed Republicans and Trump for not campaigning on the issue and ignoring an important voting base, pointing to the highly funded and victorious anti-abortion win in Idaho as evidence.
“Let’s be clear: the GOP didn’t run on abortion in 2026. It ran an ostrich campaign: a big elephant with its head buried in the sand,” wrote Students for Life of America President Kristan Hawkins in a subscriber email the day after Election Day.
Hawkins also noted that several prominent Republican congressional candidates who said they supported abortion rights, including U.S. Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, U.S. Rep. Mike Lawler of New York and U.S. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, lost their seats.
Storytelling strategy
Abortion rights advocates argue that many voters were moved by the personal stories they heard from candidates and their surrogates.
On the campaign trail in Texas, Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa talked about her own nonviable pregnancy and argued that women and families should be able to make their own reproductive health decisions. She has publicly supported ending Texas’ abortion ban and restoring abortion access, a steep challenge given that Republicans still control the state Senate.
In Georgia, Turiya Tomlin-Randall campaigned for Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms and Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff, who was reelected.
Tomlin-Randall lives in Kansas City, Missouri, but her sister Candi Miller was living in Georgia in 2022 when she became pregnant. Miller and her husband had three kids and Miller had lupus, diabetes and hypertension, which made pregnancy dangerous. But she was terrified of getting into legal trouble after Georgia passed its new law. She ordered abortion pills online, but when she started experiencing a life-threatening infection, she was too scared to go to the hospital and died at home in November 2022.
Tomlin-Randall said she only learned two years later that her sister’s death was connected to the state’s abortion law, because of ProPublica’s reporting on deaths related to abortion bans in Georgia and Texas.
“This journey has taught me so much more about the effects of the ban,” said Tomlin-Randall, who is now raising two of the three children Miller left behind. “I’ve learned that most women who have abortions aren’t having abortions because they just don’t want to have a child. A lot of the women that I’ve encountered had to have abortions for their own safety.”
Tomlin-Randall said she’s hopeful Bottoms will be a vocal advocate for abortion rights. Georgia Democratic Attorney General-elect Tanya Miller also has opposed the state’s six-week abortion ban and promised to defend access to legal reproductive health care. Miller defeated a prominent anti-abortion lawmaker in her race.
Lauren Peterson, co-founder and CEO of Abortion in America, which organizes storytellers and advocates for abortion rights, called abortion the “unsung hero” of this election. She said abortion storytelling is an effective political strategy.
“Our work is not over,” Peterson said. “Even in states where we won, we are going to have to now do the important work of holding people accountable to the promises they made.”
